5.F-1#1.title: Read it on a place-value chart
5.F-1#1.text: Put 47,283 in a chart with columns for ten-thousands, thousands, hundreds, tens and ones. The chart reads 4, 7, 2, 8, 3. Now read each column as its own number: 40,000 and 7,000 and 200 and 80 and 3. Add them and you get 47,283 back. Move the 7 one column left and its part becomes 70,000, ten times as much. Move it one column right and it shrinks to 700.

5.F-1#2.title: See it as a rectangle
5.F-1#2.text: Draw a rectangle 38 units wide and 27 units tall. Its area is 38 × 27. Now draw a line across it so the top part is 20 tall and the bottom part is 7 tall. The top part has area 38 × 20 = 760 and the bottom part has area 38 × 7 = 266. The line did not add or remove any space, so the whole rectangle is 760 + 266 = 1,026.

5.F-1#3.title: Check chunks by multiplying back
5.F-1#3.text: Division and multiplication undo each other, so every chunk you peel off can be checked. For 432 ÷ 6, the answer 72 splits into 70 and 2. Multiply back: 70 × 6 = 420 and 2 × 6 = 12, and 420 + 12 = 432. The pieces rebuild the starting number exactly, with nothing missing and nothing left over. That is why the chunk sizes can be any friendly numbers you like.

5.F-1#4.title: Use expanded form
5.F-1#4.text: Write 4,562 as a sum with one part for each digit: 4,000 + 500 + 60 + 2. Each part shows what one digit is really worth. The part that came from the digit 5 is 500. Check by adding the four parts: they make 4,562 again, so the 5 is worth 500.

5.F-1#5.title: Zero out the other digits
5.F-1#5.text: Keep the 8 where it is in 28,514 and change every other digit to 0. The 2, the 5, the 1 and the 4 all become zeros, and what is left is 8,000. Those zeros hold the 8 in its seat, so 8,000 is what the 8 is worth. Check with a sum: 20,000 + 8,000 + 500 + 10 + 4 = 28,514.

5.F-1#6.title: Count in tens
5.F-1#6.text: Think of 40 as 4 tens. Then 60 × 40 means 60 groups of 4 tens, which is 240 tens, because 60 × 4 = 240. And 240 tens is 2,400. Another check: 60 × 40 is double 60 × 20. Since 60 × 20 = 1,200, doubling gives 2,400 again. Both ways agree on the same product.

5.F-1#7.title: Use an easy nearby fact
5.F-1#7.text: Start from 24 × 10 = 240, which only needs a zero. Thirteen groups is ten groups plus three more groups. Three more groups of 24 is 72. Add them: 240 + 72 = 312. You can also check with 25 × 13 = 325, then take away one group of 13, because 24 is one less than 25: 325 − 13 = 312.

5.F-1#8.title: Split 432 into friendly parts
5.F-1#8.text: Break 432 into two numbers that 6 divides easily: 360 and 72. Then 360 ÷ 6 = 60, because 36 ÷ 6 = 6. And 72 ÷ 6 = 12. Add the two answers: 60 + 12 = 72. The chunks are different from 420 and 12, but the total number of sixes is the same.

5.F-1#9.title: Halve one, double the other
5.F-1#9.text: A product stays the same if you halve one number and double the other. So 24 × 13 = 12 × 26. Do it again: 12 × 26 = 6 × 52. Now it is a small problem: 6 × 50 = 300 and 6 × 2 = 12, which makes 312. Three different ways of cutting up the numbers all give 312.

5.F-2#1.title: Think of coins
5.F-2#1.text: Suppose you have 1 quarter and 1 dime. You have 2 coins, but you do not have 2 quarters or 2 dimes, and the value is not 2 of anything. You must first turn both into cents: 25 cents and 10 cents make 35 cents. Fractions are the same. One half plus one third is not two of anything until both are renamed as the same kind of piece.

5.F-2#2.title: Find the match with a list
5.F-2#2.text: Count by each bottom number until the lists meet. Counting by 2 gives 2, 4, 6, 8. Counting by 3 gives 3, 6, 9. The first number in both lists is 6, so sixths work for both fractions. A clock shows the same idea: half an hour is 30 minutes and a third of an hour is 20 minutes. Minutes are a piece that fits both.

5.F-2#3.title: Watch it on a ruler
5.F-2#3.text: Look at a ruler marked in eighths of an inch. Put your finger on 3/8 and slide 2 more marks to the right. You land on 5/8. The marks did not change size while you slid. Only your count of marks changed, from 3 to 5. If the bottom number changed to 16, that would mean the marks got smaller, and they did not.

5.F-2#4.title: Use quarters of a dollar
5.F-2#4.text: One fourth of a dollar is a quarter, worth 25 cents. Two quarters are worth 25 + 25 = 50 cents. Fifty cents is half of a dollar. So 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2, and you can see why 2/4 and 1/2 are the same amount.

5.F-2#5.title: Count back on a number line
5.F-2#5.text: Draw a line from 0 to 1 and mark it in eighths. Start at 5/8 and hop back one mark. You land on 4/8. Now look where 4/8 sits: there are 4 marks before it and 4 marks after it, so it is exactly the middle of the line. The middle of 0 to 1 is 1/2.

5.F-2#6.title: Use an hour of time
5.F-2#6.text: Think of one hour, which has 60 minutes. Half an hour is 30 minutes and a third of an hour is 20 minutes. Together that is 50 minutes. Fifty minutes out of 60 is 50/60. Divide top and bottom by 10 and you get 5/6 of an hour.

5.F-2#7.title: Use money
5.F-2#7.text: Three fourths of a dollar is 75 cents. One half of a dollar is 50 cents. Take 50 cents away from 75 cents and 25 cents are left. Twenty-five cents is one quarter of a dollar, so 3/4 − 1/2 = 1/4.

5.F-2#8.title: Add minutes on a clock
5.F-2#8.text: Use one hour as the whole. Two thirds of an hour is 40 minutes and three fourths of an hour is 45 minutes. Together that is 85 minutes, which is one full hour and 25 minutes more. Twenty-five minutes out of 60 is 25/60, which simplifies to 5/12. The sum is 1 5/12.

5.F-2#9.title: Check with a clock
5.F-2#9.text: One fourth of an hour is 15 minutes. One sixth of an hour is 10 minutes. Add them to get 25 minutes. Now write 25 minutes as a fraction of the 60 minutes in an hour: 25/60. Divide top and bottom by 5 to get 5/12. That matches the answer from listing multiples.

5.F-3#1.title: Take a part of a part
5.F-3#1.text: Start with numbers instead of a drawing. A day and a night are 24 hours. A quarter of that is 6 hours. Half of those 6 hours is 3 hours. Now ask what fraction 3 hours is of the full 24: it is 3/24, which is 1/8. So half of a quarter is an eighth, exactly what 1/2 × 1/4 gives when you multiply tops and bottoms.

5.F-3#2.title: Read the times sign as groups
5.F-3#2.text: The times sign already means groups of. 3 × 40 is 3 groups of 40, which is 120. 1 × 40 is 1 group of 40, which is 40. Keep shrinking the first number: 1/2 × 40 is half a group of 40, which is 20. So 3/5 × 40 is three fifths of a group of 40. One fifth of 40 is 8, and three of those is 24.

5.F-3#3.title: Check by multiplying back
5.F-3#3.text: Division can always be checked with multiplication. If 4 ÷ 1/3 = 12, then 12 pieces of size 1/3 must make 4. They do: 12 thirds is 12/3, which is 4. Try a smaller guess like 2: 2 thirds is less than one whole, nowhere near 4. You need many small pieces to build 4 wholes, so the answer has to be bigger than 4.

5.F-3#4.title: Use an hour of minutes
5.F-3#4.text: A quarter of an hour is 15 minutes. Half of that is 7 and a half minutes. How many of those fit in a full hour? Two fit in each quarter hour, and there are 4 quarter hours, so 8 fit. One piece is 1/8 of the hour.

5.F-3#5.title: Try it with eggs
5.F-3#5.text: A carton holds 12 eggs. Half of the carton is 6 eggs. A third of those 6 eggs is 2 eggs. Two eggs out of the full 12 is 2/12, which simplifies to 1/6. So a third of a half is a sixth.

5.F-3#6.title: Take away the missing third
5.F-3#6.text: Two thirds is the whole thing with one third removed. One third of 12 is 4. Take that away from 12 and you get 12 − 4 = 8. Check with groups: 12 counters in 3 equal rows gives rows of 4, and two rows hold 8 counters.

5.F-3#7.title: Count up by halves
5.F-3#7.text: Count by halves until you reach 6: 1/2, 1, 1 1/2, 2, 2 1/2, 3, 3 1/2, 4, 4 1/2, 5, 5 1/2, 6. That list has 12 numbers, so it takes 12 halves to make 6. It is the same as asking how many half-dollar coins make 6 dollars.

5.F-3#8.title: Add quarters until you reach 3
5.F-3#8.text: Count how many quarter steps it takes to walk from 0 to 3. Four steps get you to 1. Four more get you to 2, which is 8 steps so far. Four more get you to 3, which is 12 steps. A ruler shows it too: 3 inches has 12 quarter-inch marks.

5.F-3#9.title: Add two thirds twelve times
5.F-3#9.text: Two thirds of 12 is the same as 12 groups of 2/3. Every 3 groups make 2 wholes, because 2/3 + 2/3 + 2/3 = 6/3 = 2. Twelve groups is 4 sets of 3 groups. Each set makes 2 wholes, so the total is 4 × 2 = 8. Same answer, with no fraction work at the end.

5.F-4#1.title: See what goes wrong otherwise
5.F-4#1.text: Try adding 2.5 + 1.75 by pushing both numbers to the right edge, the way you do with whole numbers. The 5 tenths would sit over the 5 hundredths and you would get 2.00, which is silly because 2.5 alone is already bigger. Think of money instead: 2 dollars 50 cents plus 1 dollar 75 cents is 4 dollars 25 cents, or 4.25. Lining up the points gives that answer.

5.F-4#2.title: Find them on a meter stick
5.F-4#2.text: A meter stick has 100 centimeters. The decimal 0.5 of a meter is the mark halfway along, at 50 centimeters. The decimal 0.45 of a meter is the mark at 45 centimeters, which comes 5 centimeters earlier. So 0.5 is farther along the stick and is the bigger number. The longer decimal is not always the bigger one.

5.F-4#3.title: Estimate where the point goes
5.F-4#3.text: You can place the point by asking what size the answer should be. For 0.5 × 0.8, the digits give 40. The answer is half of 0.8, so it must be near 0.4. It cannot be 40 or 4, so it is 0.40. For 1.5 × 4, the digits give 60. One and a half fours is about 6, so the answer is 6.0 and not 60 or 0.6.

5.F-4#4.title: Think in cents
5.F-4#4.text: Read the numbers as money. 0.2 of a dollar is 2 dimes, which is 20 cents. 0.35 of a dollar is 35 cents. Together they make 20 + 35 = 55 cents. Fifty-five cents written in dollars is 0.55.

5.F-4#5.title: Add tenths first
5.F-4#5.text: Break 0.45 into 0.4 and 0.05. Add the tenths: 0.3 + 0.4 = 0.7. Then put the 0.05 back on: 0.7 + 0.05 = 0.75. It is like having 3 dimes, then getting 4 more dimes and a nickel. That is 75 cents.

5.F-4#6.title: Count up to make change
5.F-4#6.text: Count up from 0.85 to 2, the way a cashier gives change. From 0.85 to 1.00 is 0.15. From 1.00 to 2.00 is 1.00 more. Add the two jumps: 0.15 + 1.00 = 1.15. No borrowing is needed. The change from two dollars is 1 dollar and 15 cents.

5.F-4#7.title: Take half of 0.8
5.F-4#7.text: The decimal 0.5 is one half, so 0.5 × 0.8 means half of 0.8. Half of 8 tenths is 4 tenths, which is 0.4. In money, half of 80 cents is 40 cents. Fractions agree: 5/10 × 8/10 = 40/100, and that is 0.40.

5.F-4#8.title: Add four times
5.F-4#8.text: Multiplying by 4 means adding four copies: 1.5 + 1.5 + 1.5 + 1.5. The first two make 3 and the last two make 3, so the total is 6. Or double twice: 1.5 doubled is 3, and 3 doubled is 6.

5.F-4#9.title: Shade a hundred grid
5.F-4#9.text: Draw a square cut into 10 columns and 10 rows, which makes 100 small squares. Shade 3 columns to show 0.3. Now look only at 7 of the rows. The squares that are in the 3 shaded columns and also in those 7 rows number 3 × 7 = 21. Twenty-one squares out of 100 is 0.21.

5.F-5#1.title: Count hours and minutes
5.F-5#1.text: Try it with time. An hour is a big unit and a minute is a small one, and 1 hour holds 60 minutes. A 2-hour movie lasts 2 × 60 = 120 minutes. The movie did not get any longer. The number grew from 2 to 120 only because each minute is so much shorter than an hour.

5.F-5#2.title: Bundle minutes into hours
5.F-5#2.text: Suppose a trip takes 180 minutes. Every 60 minutes can be swapped for 1 hour. The first 60 make 1 hour, the next 60 make 2 hours, and the last 60 make 3 hours. That is 180 ÷ 60 = 3. The trip is just as long as before. The number shrank from 180 to 3 because hours are bigger than minutes.

5.F-5#3.title: One fact works both ways
5.F-5#3.text: Take the single fact 12 inches = 1 foot and see how much it gives you. Going to the small unit, 5 feet is 5 × 12 = 60 inches. Going to the big unit, 36 inches is 36 ÷ 12 = 3 feet. Half a foot is 6 inches. One anchor answers every feet and inches question, and the other four anchors do the same for their units.

5.F-5#4.title: Build one with blocks
5.F-5#4.text: Take 24 small blocks and build a box. Make a row of 3 blocks, then put a second row beside it. That floor has 6 blocks. Build three more floors on top, each with 6 blocks, so there are 4 floors: 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24 blocks. Counting them all gives the same number as 3 × 2 × 4.

5.F-5#5.title: Add one meter at a time
5.F-5#5.text: One meter is 100 centimeters. Two meters is one meter and then another meter, so add 100 + 100 = 200 centimeters. Picture two meter sticks laid end to end: the second stick starts where the first one stops at 100 and ends at 200.

5.F-5#6.title: Make a feet and inches table
5.F-5#6.text: Build a table, adding 12 inches for each new foot. 1 foot is 12 inches, 2 feet is 24, 3 feet is 36, 4 feet is 48 and 5 feet is 60. The last row gives the answer, 60 inches. You can also split it: 5 × 10 = 50 and 5 × 2 = 10, and 50 + 10 = 60.

5.F-5#7.title: Count up by hundreds
5.F-5#7.text: Count meters as you count centimeters by hundreds. 100 centimeters is 1 meter, 200 is 2 meters, 300 is 3 meters and 400 is 4 meters. Four counts reach 400, so the length is 4 meters. Check the other way: 4 × 100 = 400.

5.F-5#8.title: Turn the box on its side
5.F-5#8.text: Rest the box on a different face. Now the floor is 2 wide and 4 long, so one layer holds 2 × 4 = 8 cubes. The box is 3 layers high this way, and 8 × 3 = 24. Turning a box does not change how many cubes fit inside, so the volume is still 24 cubic units.

5.F-5#9.title: Count the cubes in slices
5.F-5#9.text: Think of a puzzle cube that is 3 small cubes along every edge. Slice it like bread into 3 flat squares. Each slice is 3 by 3, so it has 9 small cubes. Three slices hold 9 + 9 + 9 = 27 small cubes. The volume is 27 cubic units.

5.F-5#10.title: Split the box in half
5.F-5#10.text: Cut the box into two smaller boxes by splitting the width of 4 into 2 and 2. Each small box is 5 long, 2 wide and 3 tall, so it holds 5 × 2 × 3 = 30 cubes. Put the two halves back together: 30 + 30 = 60 cubic units.

5.F-6#1.title: Like a seat in a theater
5.F-6#1.text: A theater ticket says something like seat 3 in row 2. You walk along to seat 3 first, then find row 2. Everyone reads the ticket the same way, so no two people fight over one seat. Try both orders on a grid: (3, 2) is 3 across and 2 up, but (2, 3) is 2 across and 3 up. They are different dots, so the order must never be swapped.

5.F-6#2.title: Make a table of jumps
5.F-6#2.text: Write the term number above each term of 0, 4, 8, 12, 16. Term 1 is 0, term 2 is 4, term 3 is 8, term 4 is 12 and term 5 is 16. Now divide each term by the jump of 4: you get 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Each result is one less than the term number. So term 100 is 99 jumps of 4, which is 396.

5.F-6#3.title: Turn the plot into a list
5.F-6#3.text: A line plot is a short way to write a list. Suppose the pencils on a desk measure 1/2, 1/2, 3/4, 1/4 and 3/4 of a foot. Put one X above the right number for each pencil. You get one X above 1/4, two above 1/2 and two above 3/4. Five pencils, five Xs. Reading the plot backwards gives you the list again.

5.F-6#4.title: Check by walking back
5.F-6#4.text: Test the dot by undoing the directions. From the dot, go down 2 steps. You should land on the bottom line at 3. Then go left 3 steps and you should arrive at the corner, (0, 0). If you end anywhere else, the dot was in the wrong place. The dot at (3, 2) passes this test.

5.F-6#5.title: Drop lines to the axes
5.F-6#5.text: Draw a straight line from the dot down to the bottom axis. It hits the axis at 4, so x is 4. Draw another line from the dot across to the side axis. It hits at 2, so y is 2. Write the bottom number first: (4, 2).

5.F-6#6.title: Spot the five times table
5.F-6#6.text: The terms 5, 10, 15 are 5 × 1, 5 × 2 and 5 × 3. So the next ones are 5 × 4 = 20, 5 × 5 = 25 and 5 × 6 = 30. It is the same as counting nickels: 5 cents, 10 cents, 15 cents, then 20, 25 and 30 cents. Both ways show the pattern jumps by 5 each time.

5.F-6#7.title: Jump along a number line
5.F-6#7.text: Draw a number line and put a dot on 0 for the 1st term. Jump 4 to land on 4, the 2nd term. Jump to 8 for the 3rd, to 12 for the 4th and to 16 for the 5th. You drew 5 dots but only 4 jumps, and the last dot is on 16.

5.F-6#8.title: Make a tally table
5.F-6#8.text: Copy the plot into a table with one row per amount. The stacks have 2, 3, 4 and 1 Xs. Add the rows: 2 + 3 is 5, then 5 + 4 is 9, then 9 + 1 is 10 bottles. The biggest row is the 4, and it belongs to 3/4 cup. A quick check: 3 + 1 is 4, 2 + 4 is 6, and 4 + 6 is 10.

5.F-6#9.title: Use the four times table
5.F-6#9.text: The pattern 0, 4, 8 is the four times table starting from 4 × 0. The 1st term is 4 × 0, the 2nd is 4 × 1, the 3rd is 4 × 2. Each time the multiplier is one less than the term number. So the 5th term is 4 × 4 = 16.

5.F-7#1.title: Two piles of ten
5.F-7#1.text: Here is a second way to split 20: think of it as 10 + 10. Ten copies of 142 is 1,420, because every digit moves up one place. Twenty copies is two of those piles, and 1,420 + 1,420 = 2,840. Multiplying by 2 and then by 10 gives 284 and then 2,840. Both splits use only easy steps and both land on the same number.

5.F-7#2.title: Watch the pattern
5.F-7#2.text: Look at a family of easy divisions. 8 ÷ 2 = 4. Make both numbers ten times bigger: 80 ÷ 20 = 4. Do it again: 800 ÷ 200 = 4. The answer never changes, because the amount and the group size grow together. Going the other way works too, so 960 ÷ 40 has the same answer as 96 ÷ 4. Check: 24 × 4 = 96 and 24 × 40 = 960.

5.F-7#3.title: Trap the answer
5.F-7#3.text: Another way to estimate is to trap the answer between two easy products. For 5,812 ÷ 29, try 29 × 100 = 2,900, which is too small. Try 29 × 1,000 = 29,000, which is far too big. So the answer is in the hundreds. Then 29 × 200 = 5,800 is almost exact. If your long division said 2,004 or 20, you would know right away that a digit slipped.

5.F-7#4.title: Split 142 by its places
5.F-7#4.text: Leave the 20 alone and break 142 into 100 + 40 + 2. Then 100 × 20 = 2,000, and 40 × 20 = 800, and 2 × 20 = 40. Add the three parts: 2,000 + 800 + 40 = 2,840. This is the same answer as doubling and then multiplying by 10. Splitting either number works, so pick the one that feels easier.

5.F-7#5.title: Double one, halve the other
5.F-7#5.text: Doubling one number and halving the other keeps a product the same. So 203 × 12 becomes 406 × 6. Now split 406 into 400 and 6: 400 × 6 = 2,400 and 6 × 6 = 36. Add them to get 2,436. This matches the area model, where the two parts were 2,030 and 406.

5.F-7#6.title: Multiply by 3, then by 4
5.F-7#6.text: Since 12 = 3 × 4, multiply 203 in two small steps. First 203 × 3 = 609. Then 609 × 4: 600 × 4 = 2,400 and 9 × 4 = 36, which makes 2,436. Three different ways of splitting the numbers all agree. So the product of 203 and 12 is 2,436 whichever way you cut it.

5.F-7#7.title: Peel off groups of 40
5.F-7#7.text: Take out groups of 40 in friendly chunks. Twenty groups use 40 × 20 = 800, and 960 − 800 leaves 160. Four more groups use 40 × 4 = 160, and nothing is left. That is 20 + 4 = 24 groups. Check by multiplying back: 24 groups of 40 is 960.

5.F-7#8.title: Test round guesses
5.F-7#8.text: Try a few round answers and multiply each by 30. A guess of 100 gives 3,000, which is much less than 5,812. A guess of 300 gives 9,000, which is much more. A guess of 200 gives 6,000, which is close. So the quotient is about 200.

5.F-7#9.title: Use 25 rows instead
5.F-7#9.text: Twenty-five rows of 36 is easy, because 25 is a quarter of 100. A hundred rows would hold 3,600 crayons, and a quarter of that is 900. The store has only 24 boxes, so take one box of 36 away: 900 − 36 = 864 crayons.

5.F-8#1.title: A table of powers
5.F-8#1.text: Make a small table. 10 to the power 1 is 10, which is ten. Power 2 is 100, one hundred. Power 3 is 1,000, one thousand. Power 6 is 1,000,000, one million. In every row, the exponent matches the number of zeros. Think of trading money: ten 1-dollar bills make a ten, ten tens make a hundred, ten hundreds make a thousand. Each trade is one more power of 10.

5.F-8#2.title: Try it with money
5.F-8#2.text: Suppose a ticket costs 3.60 dollars and you buy 10 of them. Ten lots of 3 dollars is 30 dollars. Ten lots of 60 cents is 600 cents, which is 6 dollars. The total is 36 dollars. The digits 3 and 6 are still there, side by side, but each one is now worth ten times more. Buy 100 tickets and the total is 360 dollars.

5.F-8#3.title: A sharing story
5.F-8#3.text: Ten friends share 450 dollars equally. Each one gets 45 dollars. The digits 4 and 5 are the same, but each sits one place lower than before. If ten people then share the 45 dollars, each gets 4.50 dollars, and the digits have dropped one more place. Sharing among 10 never changes the digits. It only makes each digit worth a tenth of what it was.

5.F-8#4.title: Hundred times a thousand
5.F-8#4.text: Split the five tens into a group of two and a group of three. Two tens multiplied make 100, and three tens multiplied make 1,000. Then 100 × 1,000 is a hundred thousands, which is 100,000. Count the zeros to check: 2 zeros and 3 zeros make 5 zeros.

5.F-8#5.title: Split into wholes and tenths
5.F-8#5.text: Break 3.6 into 3 and 0.6. One hundred groups of 3 is 300. One hundred groups of 0.6 is 60, because 100 lots of 6 tenths is 600 tenths, and 600 tenths make 60 wholes. Add the two parts: 300 + 60 = 360.

5.F-8#6.title: Count the thousands
5.F-8#6.text: Ask how many thousands are in 4,500. The 4,000 is 4 whole thousands. The 500 that is left is half of a thousand, and half is 0.5. So 4,500 is 4 and a half thousands, which is 4.5.

5.F-8#7.title: Split 62 into 60 and 2
5.F-8#7.text: The power 10⁴ is 10,000. Break 62 into 60 and 2. Sixty ten-thousands is 600,000. Two ten-thousands is 20,000. Add them: 600,000 + 20,000 = 620,000. Each part only needed zeros written after it, and the two parts fill different places, so adding them is easy.

5.F-8#8.title: Use tenths as a fraction
5.F-8#8.text: The decimal 0.7 is 7 tenths. One hundred groups of 7 tenths is 700 tenths. Every 10 tenths make 1 whole, so 700 tenths make 700 ÷ 10 = 70 wholes. In money, 100 lots of 70 cents is 7,000 cents, and that is 70 dollars.

5.F-8#9.title: Count by thousands of pennies
5.F-8#9.text: One thousand pennies is 10 dollars, because 10 groups of 100 pennies make 10 dollars. So 2,000 pennies is 20 dollars. The 500 pennies left over are 5 dollars. Add them: 20 + 5 = 25 dollars. This matches sliding the digits of 2,500 two places to the right.

5.F-9#1.title: Switch to centimeters
5.F-9#1.text: Measure two ribbons: 1.2 meters and 0.35 meters. In centimeters they are 120 and 35, and 120 + 35 = 155 centimeters, which is 1.55 meters. Now look at the decimal sum 1.20 + 0.35. With the points lined up, the 2 tenths sit over the 3 tenths and the columns give 1.55 as well. Lining up the points does the same job as changing everything to one small unit.

5.F-9#2.title: Look at a ruler
5.F-9#2.text: On a centimeter ruler, the mark for 7 can also be read as 7.0, because it is 7 centimeters and 0 extra millimeters. To find 7 − 0.4, start at that mark and step back 4 millimeter lines. You pass 6.9, 6.8, 6.7 and stop at 6.6. Writing 7 as 7.0 just names the same mark in tenths, so there are tenths to take away from.

5.F-9#3.title: Hop past the whole number
5.F-9#3.text: Put 0.4 + 0.7 on a number line marked in tenths. Start at 0.4. It takes 6 hops of a tenth to reach 1.0. You had 7 hops to make, so 1 hop is still left, and it lands on 1.1. The line does not stop at 0.9 and start over. It rolls on into the next whole number, and that roll is the carry.

5.F-9#4.title: Make a whole number first
5.F-9#4.text: The number 2.7 is only 0.3 away from 3. Borrow that 0.3 from 3.4, which turns 3.4 into 3.1 and turns 2.7 into 3. The total has not changed, and now the sum is easy: 3.1 + 3 = 6.1.

5.F-9#5.title: Count up from 3.2
5.F-9#5.text: Find the gap by counting up from 3.2 to 8.6. Add 5 whole ones to go from 3.2 to 8.2. Then add 0.4 more to go from 8.2 to 8.6. The two jumps together are 5 + 0.4 = 5.4.

5.F-9#6.title: Round one price up
5.F-9#6.text: The pretzel price of 2.75 is 25 cents short of 3 dollars. Move 25 cents over from the juice: the juice becomes 1.15 and the pretzel becomes 3.00. The total is the same, and 3.00 + 1.15 = 4.15 dollars.

5.F-9#7.title: Subtract in tenths
5.F-9#7.text: Write 7 as 7.0 and think in tenths. Seven wholes are 70 tenths, and 0.4 is 4 tenths. Subtract: 70 − 4 = 66 tenths. Sixty-six tenths is 6 wholes and 6 tenths, written 6.6. Counting up and subtracting in tenths give the same answer.

5.F-9#8.title: Read them as money
5.F-9#8.text: Think of 1.25 as 1 dollar and 25 cents, and 0.5 as 50 cents. Add the cents: 25 + 50 = 75 cents. With the 1 dollar, that is 1 dollar and 75 cents, written 1.75. Fifty cents is written 0.50, which is why the 5 lines up under the 2.

5.F-9#9.title: Work in cents
5.F-9#9.text: Change both amounts to cents so there are no decimal points. Five dollars is 500 cents and the snack is 365 cents. Subtract: 500 − 300 = 200, then 200 − 65 = 135 cents. As dollars, 135 cents is 1.35.

5.F-10#1.title: Follow the shrinking pattern
5.F-10#1.text: Start with 3 × 4 = 12. Make one factor ten times smaller: 0.3 × 4 is 0.3 + 0.3 + 0.3 + 0.3 = 1.2, so the answer is ten times smaller too. Make the other factor ten times smaller as well: 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.12. Each time a factor loses a place value, the answer moves one more place. Two decimal places in the problem means two in the answer.

5.F-10#2.title: Try it with cents
5.F-10#2.text: Think of one dollar. The decimal 0.4 of a dollar is 40 cents. Now take 0.3 of that 40 cents. One tenth of 40 cents is 4 cents, so three tenths is 12 cents. Twelve cents is 0.12 of a dollar. That is less than 40 cents and less than 30 cents, because you took only a part of an amount that was already a part.

5.F-10#3.title: Cut a ribbon
5.F-10#3.text: A ribbon is 4.8 meters long and must be cut into 6 equal pieces. In centimeters the ribbon is 480, and 480 ÷ 6 = 80 centimeters for each piece. Eighty centimeters is 0.8 of a meter. Check by laying the pieces end to end: 6 × 0.8 = 4.8 meters. The digits 48 ÷ 6 = 8 did the work, and the unit told you where the point goes.

5.F-10#4.title: Count 60 cents seven times
5.F-10#4.text: Read 0.6 as 60 cents. Seven lots of 60 cents is 420 cents, because 7 × 6 = 42 and there is a zero on the end. Four hundred twenty cents is 4 dollars and 20 cents, which is 4.20, or 4.2.

5.F-10#5.title: Take three tenths of 0.4
5.F-10#5.text: Multiplying by 0.3 means taking three tenths. One tenth of 0.4 is 0.04, because dividing by 10 moves each digit one place to the right. Three of those is 0.04 + 0.04 + 0.04 = 0.12.

5.F-10#6.title: Halve it, then split in three
5.F-10#6.text: Sharing among 6 can be done in two easy steps, because 6 = 2 × 3. First cut 4.8 in half to get 2.4. Then share 2.4 among 3: 24 tenths ÷ 3 = 8 tenths. Each share is 0.8. Check by multiplying back: 6 shares of 0.8 make 4.8.

5.F-10#7.title: Split 1.5 into 1 and a half
5.F-10#7.text: Think of 1.5 as one and a half. One group of 2.3 is 2.3. Half a group of 2.3 is 1.15. Add them: 2.3 + 1.15 = 3.45. This agrees with moving the point two places in 345.

5.F-10#8.title: Trap it between two products
5.F-10#8.text: Since 2.3 is between 2 and 3, the answer must be between 2 × 1.5 = 3 and 3 × 1.5 = 4.5. The number 3.45 fits in that gap. A misplaced point would give 34.5 or 0.345, and neither one is between 3 and 4.5. So 3.45 is sensible.

5.F-10#9.title: Measure in centimeters
5.F-10#9.text: A ribbon of 0.6 meters is 60 centimeters long. Five ribbons need 5 × 60 = 300 centimeters. One meter is 100 centimeters, so 300 centimeters is 3 meters. No decimal point is needed until the very end.

5.F-11#1.title: Test it with easy numbers
5.F-11#1.text: Check the idea with fractions you can work out in your head. 6/3 means 6 things in 3 shares, and 6 ÷ 3 = 2. 8/4 is 8 ÷ 4 = 2. 10/5 is 10 ÷ 5 = 2. Now try one that does not come out whole: 1/2 is 1 ÷ 2, and one cookie shared by two people is half a cookie each. The bar in a fraction works just like a division sign.

5.F-11#2.title: Count quarters of a dollar
5.F-11#2.text: Four quarters make one dollar, so a quarter is 1/4 of a dollar. If you have 9 quarters, you have 9/4 dollars. Four of them make the first dollar, four more make the second dollar, and 1 quarter is left. That is 2 dollars and 25 cents, clearly more than one dollar. Any time you hold more coins than it takes to make a dollar, you have more than one whole.

5.F-11#3.title: Build it back up
5.F-11#3.text: Check the mixed number by going the other way. Start with 3 2/5. Each whole is 5 fifths, so 3 wholes are 3 × 5 = 15 fifths. Add the 2 extra fifths to get 17 fifths, which is 17/5. Multiplying and adding took you from the mixed number to the improper fraction. Dividing and keeping the remainder is the same trip in reverse.

5.F-11#4.title: Share three dollars
5.F-11#4.text: Share 3 dollars equally among 4 people. Three dollars is 300 cents, and 300 ÷ 4 = 75 cents each. Seventy-five cents is three quarters of a dollar. So 3 ÷ 4 = 3/4, with the amount being shared on top.

5.F-11#5.title: Check by giving it back
5.F-11#5.text: If each kid gets 2/5 of a pizza, then 5 kids together should have the 2 pizzas. Add 2/5 five times: that is 10 fifths. Five fifths make one pizza, so 10 fifths make 2 pizzas. The shares rebuild both pizzas, so 2/5 each is right.

5.F-11#6.title: Take away one whole at a time
5.F-11#6.text: One whole is 5/5. Take it away from 17/5 and 12/5 is left. Take away another whole and 7/5 is left. Take away a third whole and 2/5 is left, which is too small to make another whole. You removed 3 wholes and have 2/5 left over: 3 2/5.

5.F-11#7.title: Use a decimal
5.F-11#7.text: Work out 17 ÷ 5 as a decimal. Five goes into 15 three times, and the 2 left over is 20 tenths, which gives 4 tenths more. So 17 ÷ 5 = 3.4. The 0.4 is 4/10, which simplifies to 2/5. That gives 3 2/5 again.

5.F-11#8.title: Share seven pizzas
5.F-11#8.text: Picture 7 pizzas shared by 8 people. There are fewer pizzas than people, so nobody can have a whole one. Each person gets 7/8 of a pizza, which is one slice short of a whole pizza cut in eighths. So 7 ÷ 8 is less than 1.

5.F-11#9.title: Give out halves first
5.F-11#9.text: Cut two of the sandwiches in half. That makes 4 halves, one for each friend. Cut the last sandwich into 4 quarters and give one to each friend. Everyone now has a half and a quarter. A half is 2 quarters, so each friend has 3 quarters: 3/4.

5.F-12#1.title: Check both parts
5.F-12#1.text: Split 15 into fifths and look at everything. One fifth is 3, so the fifths are 3, 3, 3, 3 and 3. Two of them make 6 and the other three make 9. Together 6 + 9 = 15, so nothing was lost. You can also multiply first: 2 × 15 = 30, and 30 ÷ 5 = 6. Dividing then multiplying, or multiplying then dividing, gives the same 6.

5.F-12#2.title: Hop along a number line
5.F-12#2.text: Draw a number line marked in thirds. Start at 0 and make a hop of 2/3 for each batch. The first hop lands on 2/3. The second lands on 4/3, which is 1 1/3. The third lands on 6/3, which is exactly 2. Three equal hops of 2/3 is what 3 × 2/3 means, and the line shows the total without any rule.

5.F-12#3.title: Try another pair
5.F-12#3.text: Estimate 7/8 + 1/10. Seven eighths is nearly a whole pizza, so call it 1. One tenth is a thin sliver, so call it 0. The estimate is 1 + 0 = 1. The exact sum is 0.875 + 0.1 = 0.975, so the estimate was very close. Benchmarks will not give the exact answer, but they tell you fast that an answer like 8/18 or 2 must be wrong.

5.F-12#4.title: Start from full cups
5.F-12#4.text: Two thirds of a cup is a full cup with 1/3 missing. Three full cups would be 3 cups. Each batch is 1/3 short, so three batches are 3 thirds short, and 3 thirds is 1 whole cup. Take it away: 3 − 1 = 2 cups.

5.F-12#5.title: Use tenths
5.F-12#5.text: Two fifths is the same as four tenths. One tenth of 15 dollars is 1.50 dollars, because dividing by 10 moves each digit one place. Four tenths is 4 × 1.50 = 6.00. Jordan saves 6 dollars.

5.F-12#6.title: Half plus a quarter
5.F-12#6.text: Three fourths is a half and a quarter put together. Half of 6 quarts is 3 quarts. A quarter of 6 quarts is half of that, which is 1.5 quarts. Add them: 3 + 1.5 = 4.5 quarts.

5.F-12#7.title: Take off one fourth
5.F-12#7.text: Three fourths of something is all of it with one fourth removed. One fourth of 6 is 1.5. Take that away from 6: 6 − 1.5 = 4.5. Multiplying first, dividing first and subtracting a fourth all give 4.5.

5.F-12#8.title: Use decimals
5.F-12#8.text: Turn each fraction into a decimal. 5/8 is 0.625 and 1/3 is about 0.333. Add them: about 0.958. That is just a little less than 1, so Ella ate about 1 whole bar. The exact sum, 23/24, agrees with that estimate.

5.F-12#9.title: Four laps make a mile
5.F-12#9.text: Each lap is a quarter of a mile, so 4 laps make 1 whole mile. Six laps is 4 laps and then 2 more. The 2 extra laps are 2 quarters, which is half a mile. Total: 1 mile and a half.

5.F-13#1.title: A lunch bill
5.F-13#1.text: You buy one sandwich for 5 dollars and 2 drinks at 3 dollars each. The bill is 5 + 2 × 3. The drinks cost 6 dollars, so you owe 5 + 6 = 11 dollars. Adding first would give 7 × 3 = 21 dollars, as if you had bought 7 drinks. Multiplying first matches what really happened. Parentheses are for the times when you truly do mean to add first.

5.F-13#2.title: Try another sentence
5.F-13#2.text: Take the words double the sum of 4 and 6. Say it with numbers: the sum is 10, and double 10 is 20. Now test two ways of writing it. 2 × (4 + 6) = 2 × 10 = 20, which matches. 2 × 4 + 6 = 8 + 6 = 14, which does not. Only the version with parentheses says what the words say.

5.F-13#3.title: Check it with the numbers
5.F-13#3.text: This one time, do the arithmetic to see that the shortcut is true. 245 + 17 = 262. Three times that is 3 × 262 = 786. Now divide: 786 ÷ 262 = 3. The big number really is 3 times the small one. Change 245 + 17 to any other sum and the same thing happens, so next time you can skip the arithmetic.

5.F-13#4.title: Multiply each number by 5
5.F-13#4.text: Five groups of 7 + 3 hold five 7s and five 3s. Five 7s are 35 and five 3s are 15. Add them: 35 + 15 = 50. This matches adding first and then multiplying 5 × 10. Spreading the 5 over both numbers never changes the value.

5.F-13#5.title: Divide each number by 4
5.F-13#5.text: Sharing 36 − 12 into 4 groups can be done one number at a time. 36 ÷ 4 = 9 and 12 ÷ 4 = 3. Then subtract: 9 − 3 = 6. This works here because both 36 and 12 divide evenly by 4. It is the same answer as subtracting first and then dividing 24 by 4.

5.F-13#6.title: Test both orders
5.F-13#6.text: Try both orders and see which makes sense. Subtracting first gives 17 × 4 = 68. That is bigger than 20, even though the expression takes something away from 20. Multiplying first gives 20 − 12 = 8. Check by adding back: 8 + 12 = 20.

5.F-13#7.title: Add first, then triple
5.F-13#7.text: Do the parentheses first: 8 + 5 = 13. Three times 13 is 13 + 13 + 13. Two of them make 26, and one more makes 39. The answer matches 24 + 15. Sharing out the 3 and adding first are two routes to the same value.

5.F-13#8.title: Test it with the value
5.F-13#8.text: Work out what the words mean: the sum of 8 and 5 is 13, and three times 13 is 39. Now test the expression 3 × (8 + 5). It gives 3 × 13 = 39, which matches. Without parentheses, 3 × 8 + 5 gives 29, so that one is wrong.

5.F-13#9.title: Count each kind
5.F-13#9.text: Count the stickers and pencils separately. Four bags with 6 stickers each is 24 stickers. Four bags with 2 pencils each is 8 pencils. Together that is 24 + 8 = 32 things. This is the same total as 4 bags of 8 things.

5.F-14#1.title: Look at a calendar
5.F-14#1.text: Pick the first day of a month and suppose it is a Monday. The next Monday is day 8, then day 15, then 22, then 29. The rule is add 7, because a week has 7 days. Start on a different day, say day 3, and the same rule gives 3, 10, 17, 24, 31. One rule can make many patterns. The starting number and the rule together decide every number.

5.F-14#2.title: Fence posts and gaps
5.F-14#2.text: Put 6 fence posts in a row and count the gaps between them. There are only 5 gaps, because the first post has no gap before it. If each gap is 3 feet wide, the last post is 5 × 3 = 15 feet from the first. The numbers in a pattern are the posts and the jumps are the gaps, so there is always one fewer jump than numbers.

5.F-14#3.title: Check the pairs with a rule
5.F-14#3.text: Look at the pairs (0, 0), (2, 4) and (4, 8) as numbers. In each one, the second number is double the first: 0 is double 0, 4 is double 2, and 8 is double 4. The next A number is 6 and the next B number is 12, and 12 is double 6 again. Every pair obeys the same doubling rule, and that shared rule is what lines the dots up.

5.F-14#4.title: Use the three times table
5.F-14#4.text: The pattern is the three times table starting from 3 × 0. The 1st number is 3 × 0, the 2nd is 3 × 1, and the 3rd is 3 × 2. The multiplier is always one less than the position. So the 6th number is 3 × 5 = 15.

5.F-14#5.title: Read a clock face
5.F-14#5.text: Look at the minute marks on a clock. The hand at the 12 means 0 minutes. At the 1 it means 5 minutes, at the 2 it means 10, at the 3 it means 15 and at the 4 it means 20. Those are five numbers made by adding 5 each time: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20.

5.F-14#6.title: Subtract the matching numbers
5.F-14#6.text: Take each A number away from its B number. 0 − 0 = 0, 4 − 2 = 2, 8 − 4 = 4 and 12 − 6 = 6. The differences 0, 2, 4, 6 are the A numbers again. So each B number is its A number plus the same amount once more, which makes B twice A.

5.F-14#7.title: List some and check
5.F-14#7.text: Write a few numbers to test the claim. A gives 0, 2, 4, 6, 8. B gives 0, 4, 8, 12, 16. Compare them in order: 4 is double 2, 8 is double 4, 12 is double 6 and 16 is double 8. The lists agree that B is 2 times A.

5.F-14#8.title: Follow the steps on a graph
5.F-14#8.text: Plot the pairs. From (0, 0) to (2, 6) you move 2 across and 6 up. From (2, 6) to (4, 12) you again move 2 across and 6 up. Every step climbs 6 for each 2 across, which is 3 up for each 1 across. So the B number is always 3 times the A number.

5.F-14#9.title: Make a savings table
5.F-14#9.text: Write both savings week by week. Maya has 3, 6, 9 and 12 dollars. Leo has 6, 12, 18 and 24 dollars. In every week Leo's number is double Maya's. It makes sense, because each week Leo puts in two 3-dollar amounts for every one of Maya's.

5.F-15#1.title: Slice it three ways
5.F-15#1.text: Take a box that is 6 long, 3 wide and 2 tall and count its cubes in three ways. Flat layers: 6 × 3 = 18 cubes in each, and 2 layers make 36. Slices from the front: 6 × 2 = 12 in each, and 3 slices make 36. Slices from the side: 3 × 2 = 6 in each, and 6 slices make 36. The cubes are the same however you slice, so the three lengths can be multiplied in any order.

5.F-15#2.title: Build a table
5.F-15#2.text: Write out feet and inches side by side. 1 foot is 12 inches, 2 feet is 24, 3 feet is 36, and so on up to 7 feet, which is 84. Read the table left to right and you are multiplying by 12. Read it right to left and you are dividing by 12, for example 36 inches back to 3 feet. The length never changes, only the count.

5.F-15#3.title: Use the plot to find a total
5.F-15#3.text: Suppose a plot of juice glasses has 2 Xs above 1/4 cup and 1 X above 1/2 cup. That is 3 glasses, because there are 3 Xs. The Xs can tell you more than a count. Two glasses of 1/4 cup hold 1/2 cup together, and the last glass holds another 1/2 cup. All the juice adds up to 1 whole cup.

5.F-15#4.title: Start with the end face
5.F-15#4.text: Look at the small end of the box, which is 3 inches wide and 2 inches tall. One slice there holds 3 × 2 = 6 cubes. The box is 6 inches long, so there are 6 slices. Six slices of 6 cubes make 36 cubic inches.

5.F-15#5.title: Fill half-liter bottles
5.F-15#5.text: A half-liter bottle holds 500 milliliters, because that is half of 1,000. To hold 2.5 liters you need 5 of those bottles, since two bottles make each liter and one more makes the half. Five bottles hold 5 × 500 = 2,500 milliliters.

5.F-15#6.title: Skip-count by twelves
5.F-15#6.text: Count one foot at a time, adding 12 inches for each. The count goes 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 72, 84. That is seven numbers, one for each foot, and the last one is 84. The shelf is 84 inches tall.

5.F-15#7.title: Slice from the end
5.F-15#7.text: Cut the box into slices starting from one end. Each slice is 4 wide and 3 tall, so it holds 4 × 3 = 12 cubes. The box is 5 long, so there are 5 slices. Five slices of 12 cubes make 60 cubic units.

5.F-15#8.title: Compare with a full cup
5.F-15#8.text: Four bottles of 1/4 cup would fill exactly 1 cup. There are only 3 bottles, so the total is one quarter cup short of a full cup. One cup minus 1/4 cup is 3/4 cup.

5.F-15#9.title: Count ten slices
5.F-15#9.text: Look at the end of the tank, which is 5 cm wide and 4 cm tall. A slice 1 cm thick holds 5 × 4 = 20 cubes. The tank is 10 cm long, so it has 10 slices. Ten slices of 20 make 200 cubic centimeters.

5.F-16#1.title: Hallway, then elevator
5.F-16#1.text: Think of a building with a row of elevators. To reach a room you walk along the ground floor to the right elevator, then ride up to the right floor. You cannot ride up before you have walked across. For the point (5, 2), walk across to 5, then ride up 2. The point (2, 5) uses the same two numbers but takes a different elevator to a different floor.

5.F-16#2.title: Find them around you
5.F-16#2.text: Look for triangles in real things. A slice of pizza has two equal long sides and all small angles, so it is isosceles and acute. The corner of a book folded flat makes a right triangle. A yield sign has three equal sides, so it is equilateral. A coat hanger has one wide angle at the hook, so it is obtuse. Every triangle gets two names, one for angles and one for sides.

5.F-16#3.title: Puppies and dogs
5.F-16#3.text: Every puppy is a dog, but not every dog is a puppy. A puppy is a dog with one extra rule: it must be young. Shapes work the same way. A square is a rectangle with one extra rule: all four sides must be equal. So every square is a rectangle, but a rectangle that is 6 long and 2 wide is not a square.

5.F-16#4.title: It sits on the x-axis
5.F-16#4.text: With 0 steps up, the point never leaves the bottom line of the grid. It sits right on the x-axis at the mark for 6, so it is (6, 0). Compare it with (0, 6), which is 0 across and 6 up and sits on the y-axis instead.

5.F-16#5.title: Put it in a table
5.F-16#5.text: Suppose the walker goes 4 miles every hour. A table would read: 1 hour, 4 miles. 2 hours, 8 miles. 3 hours, 12 miles. The point (3, 12) is the third row of that table drawn as a dot. It says that after 3 hours, 12 miles have been covered.

5.F-16#6.title: Fold a square corner to corner
5.F-16#6.text: Fold a square piece of paper along its diagonal. Each half is a triangle. It keeps one corner of the square, which is 90°. The other two corners of the square were each cut in half, so they are 45° each. Two sides of the triangle are sides of the square, so they are equal. It is a right isosceles triangle.

5.F-16#7.title: Sort them into hoops
5.F-16#7.text: Lay a big hoop on the floor for rectangles and put a small hoop inside it for squares. Every shape in the small hoop is also inside the big hoop, so every square is a rectangle. A long door shape goes in the big hoop but outside the small one. So not every rectangle is a square.

5.F-16#8.title: Tell each story
5.F-16#8.text: Use hours across and miles up. The point (3, 12) says 12 miles after 3 hours, a steady walk. The point (12, 3) says only 3 miles after 12 hours, which is hardly moving. Two very different trips cannot be the same dot, so these are different points.

5.F-16#9.title: Go north first
5.F-16#9.text: Try the steps in the other order. Walk 3 steps north from the tree to reach (0, 3). Then walk 4 steps east and you arrive at (4, 3). It is the same spot as going east first. The walk can be done in either order, but the pair is still written with the east number first: (4, 3).

6.EE-1#1.title: Fold a sheet of paper
6.EE-1#1.text:
Fold a sheet of paper in half and it is 2 layers thick. Fold it again and each layer doubles, so there are 4. A third fold makes 8.
Every fold is one more "times 2", so three folds give 2 × 2 × 2 = 2³ = 8 layers. The exponent is the number of folds, and the base is what each fold multiplies by.

6.EE-1#2.title: Rows of dots for 3²
6.EE-1#2.text:
Draw 3 rows with 3 dots in each row. That square of dots is 3², and it holds 3 × 3 = 9 dots.
Now draw only 2 rows of 3 dots. That is 3 × 2, and it holds 6 dots.
The two pictures are different sizes, so a power is not the base times the exponent. The exponent says how many times the base is used as a factor.

6.EE-1#3.title: Walk the powers downward
6.EE-1#3.text:
List the powers of 4 from big to small: 4³ = 64, then 4² = 16. Each step down removes one copy of 4, which divides the value by 4.
Take one more step down: 16 ÷ 4 = 4, so 4¹ must be 4. A first power always lands on the base itself, because only one copy is left and there is nothing to multiply it by.

6.EE-1#4.title: Skip count five fives
6.EE-1#4.text:
Five squared means 5 groups of 5. Picture 5 rows of dots with 5 dots in each row.
Count the rows by skip counting: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25.
Five rows were counted and the last number said was 25, so 5² = 25. This is the same as 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5.

6.EE-1#5.title: Build a cube from layers
6.EE-1#5.text:
Three cubed is the number of small blocks in a cube that is 3 blocks long, 3 wide and 3 tall.
One flat layer is a 3 by 3 square, which holds 9 blocks.
The cube is 3 layers tall, so it holds 9 + 9 + 9 = 27 blocks. That matches 3 × 3 × 3 = 27.

6.EE-1#6.title: Count back through a family tree
6.EE-1#6.text:
You have 2 parents. Each of them has 2 parents, so you have 4 grandparents. Go back again and there are 8 great-grandparents, and once more gives 16 great-great-grandparents.
Each step back multiplies by 2, and there were four steps, so the count is 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 2⁴ = 16.

6.EE-1#7.title: A big cube of small cubes
6.EE-1#7.text:
Picture a large cube made of tiny cubes, 10 along each edge.
A single row has 10 tiny cubes. A flat layer has 10 rows, so it holds 100. The whole cube has 10 layers, so it holds 10 hundreds, which is 1,000.
Row, layer, cube: ten, hundred, thousand. So 10³ = 1,000.

6.EE-1#8.title: Times 4 is doubling twice
6.EE-1#8.text:
Multiplying by 4 is the same as doubling two times, so 4³ can be found with doubling alone.
Start with one 4. Multiply by 4 by doubling twice: 8, then 16. That is 4².
Multiply by 4 again by doubling twice more: 32, then 64.
So 4³ = 64, with no long multiplication.

6.EE-1#9.title: See it as a square
6.EE-1#9.text:
The two pairs make 4 × 4, and 4 × 4 is the number of small squares in a grid with 4 rows and 4 columns.
Count the grid one row at a time: 4, 8, 12, 16.
The grid holds 16 squares, so 2⁴ = 16. This also shows that 2⁴ is the same number as 4².

6.EE-2#1.title: An older sister story
6.EE-2#1.text:
Suppose your sister is 6 years older than you. When you are 1 she is 7. When you are 10 she is 16. When you are 40 she will be 46.
One short phrase covers every year of your lives: if your age is n, her age is n + 6. The letter n is your age, whatever it happens to be right now.

6.EE-2#2.title: Test phrases with real numbers
6.EE-2#2.text:
Not sure how to translate a phrase? Swap the letter for 10 and see what answer makes sense.
"6 more than 10" is 16, which is 10 + 6. "The product of 6 and 10" is 60, which is 6 × 10. "6 less than 10" is 4, and only 10 − 6 gives 4, since 6 − 10 does not.
Now put n back where the 10 was: n + 6, 6n and n − 6.

6.EE-2#3.title: Like saying 2 dozen
6.EE-2#3.text:
People already talk this way with units. "2 dozen eggs" means 2 × 12 = 24 eggs, and nobody says "2 times a dozen". "3 feet" means 3 × 12 inches.
A variable works like the word dozen. If x stands for 12, then 2x is 24. If x stands for 4, then 2x is 8. The number in front says how many of that thing you have.

6.EE-2#4.title: Packs first, then loose ones
6.EE-2#4.text:
Think of 2x + 3 as 2 packs of gum with x pieces in each pack, plus 3 loose pieces.
If each pack holds 5 pieces, you would count the packs first: 5 + 5 = 10 pieces. Then you add the 3 loose pieces to get 13.
Nobody would add the loose pieces to the number of packs first. The story puts the multiplying before the adding, just as the order of operations does.

6.EE-2#5.title: Hop on a number line
6.EE-2#5.text:
Mark any spot on a number line and call it n. "Six more" means the number that is 6 hops to the right of that spot, and hopping right is adding, so it is n + 6.
Check with a real number: if n is 10, six more than 10 is 16, and 10 + 6 is 16 too.

6.EE-2#6.title: Four groups of x
6.EE-2#6.text:
The product of 4 and x means 4 groups that each hold x. Written as addition, that is x + x + x + x.
Four copies of the same letter are written 4x for short.
Check with a number: if x is 3, the four groups hold 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12, and 4 × 3 is also 12.

6.EE-2#7.title: Make a ten
6.EE-2#7.text:
After substituting, the sum is 6 + 9. The 9 is only 1 away from 10, so borrow 1 from the 6.
That turns 6 + 9 into 5 + 10, which is easy to see as 15.
The value of x + 9 when x is 6 is 15, the same as adding straight across.

6.EE-2#8.title: Write 2x as x + x
6.EE-2#8.text:
Two copies of x can be written as x + x, so the expression 2x + 5 is the same as x + x + 5.
Now put 4 in for each x: 4 + 4 + 5.
There is only addition left, so no order rule is needed. 4 + 4 is 8, and 8 + 5 is 13.

6.EE-2#9.title: Add three copies
6.EE-2#9.text:
Multiplying by 3 means adding three copies of the bracket: (a − 2) + (a − 2) + (a − 2).
With a = 5, each copy is 5 − 2, which is 3.
So the expression is 3 + 3 + 3 = 9. Three equal copies of 3 give the same answer as 3 × 3.

6.EE-2#10.title: Jumps on a number line
6.EE-2#10.text:
With y = 2, the term 5y means 5 jumps of 2 along a number line starting from zero: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.
The "− 3" means walk back 3 steps from where you landed: 9, 8, 7.
You finish on 7, so 5y − 3 is 7 when y is 2. The jumps come before the walk back, which is multiplying before subtracting.

6.EE-2#11.title: Three friends at a shop
6.EE-2#11.text:
Three friends each bring a = 5 dollars and each spend 2 dollars.
Count by money: together they brought 3 × 5 = 15 dollars and together they spent 3 × 2 = 6 dollars, so 15 − 6 = 9 dollars are left. That is 3a − 6.
Count by person instead: each has 3 dollars left, and 3 × 3 = 9. Both counts describe the same three friends, so both give 9.

6.EE-3#1.title: Three lunch orders
6.EE-3#1.text:
Three friends each order a burger that costs b dollars and a drink that costs c dollars.
One way to find the bill: each friend owes b + c, and there are 3 friends, so the bill is 3(b + c).
Another way: the kitchen made 3 burgers and 3 drinks, so the bill is 3b + 3c.
It is the same bill either way. Notice that the drinks are tripled too, not only the burgers.

6.EE-3#2.title: Check it with numbers
6.EE-3#2.text:
Let x be 10. Then 3x + 2x is 30 + 20 = 50, and 5x is also 50. Let x be 7 instead: 21 + 14 = 35, and 5 × 7 is 35 again.
Now try to combine unlike terms. With x = 10, the expression 3x + 2 is 32, but 5x would be 50. They do not match, so a term with x and a plain number must stay separate.

6.EE-3#3.title: Two names for one amount
6.EE-3#3.text:
One dollar can be 4 quarters or 10 dimes. The coins look different, but the amount is identical every time. Equivalent expressions are like that: 3(x + 2) and 3x + 6 are two looks for one amount.
Expressions that only look similar fail the test. At x = 1, 3(x + 2) is 9, but 3x + 2 is only 5, so those two are not equivalent.

6.EE-3#4.title: Try two different values
6.EE-3#4.text:
Pick x = 2. Then 4x + 5x is 8 + 10 = 18, and 9 × 2 is also 18.
Pick x = 10. Then 4x + 5x is 40 + 50 = 90, and 9 × 10 is also 90.
Both tests agree with 9x. They do not agree with a wrong answer such as 9x², which would give 36 and 900.

6.EE-3#5.title: Write them out, cross two off
6.EE-3#5.text:
Write 7a the long way: a + a + a + a + a + a + a.
Subtracting 2a means crossing off two of those letters.
Count what is left and you find five letters, a + a + a + a + a, which is written 5a. Nothing happened to the letter itself, only to how many there are.

6.EE-3#6.title: Draw the area model
6.EE-3#6.text:
Draw a rectangle 3 units tall. Make its width in two pieces, one of length x and one of length 2, so the full width is x + 2.
The left piece has area 3 times x, which is 3x. The right piece has area 3 times 2, which is 6.
The whole rectangle is 3(x + 2), and it is also the two pieces together, 3x + 6.

6.EE-3#7.title: Test the expansion with numbers
6.EE-3#7.text:
Check 5y + 15 against the original by choosing values for y.
If y = 1, then 5(y + 3) is 5 × 4 = 20, and 5y + 15 is 5 + 15 = 20.
If y = 10, then 5(y + 3) is 5 × 13 = 65, and 5y + 15 is 50 + 15 = 65.
The common slip 5y + 3 would give 8 and 53, which do not match.

6.EE-3#8.title: Bags and loose marbles
6.EE-3#8.text:
Let x be a bag of marbles, with the same unknown number in every bag.
The expression says: 2 bags, then 3 loose marbles, then 1 more bag.
Push the bags together and you have 3 bags. The 3 loose marbles stay loose, because you cannot call them a bag.
Three bags and 3 loose marbles is 3x + 3.

6.EE-3#9.title: Write out every copy
6.EE-3#9.text:
Two groups of (x + 4) can be written as (x + 4) + (x + 4), and 3x can be written as x + x + x.
Now count what is on the page. There are five letters x in all, two from the groups and three from the end. There are two 4s, which add up to 8.
Five x and 8 is 5x + 8.

6.EE-3#10.title: Mental math with x = 10
6.EE-3#10.text:
Let x be 10, so 3(x + 2) becomes 3 × 12. Most people find 3 × 12 in their heads by splitting it: 3 tens are 30, 3 twos are 6, and 30 + 6 = 36.
That mental trick is the same move with a number in place of x. The 30 is 3 times x and the 6 is 3 times 2, so with the letter back the result is 3x + 6.

6.EE-4#1.title: Try it on a true sentence
6.EE-4#1.text:
Start with a number fact that is clearly true: 5 + 7 = 12.
Subtract 7 from both sides and you get 5 = 5, which is still true.
Subtract 7 from the left side only and you get 5 = 12, which is false.
The same thing happens when a letter is in the equation. Changing both sides the same way keeps a true statement true.

6.EE-4#2.title: There and back again
6.EE-4#2.text:
Stand on 5 on a number line. Walk 7 steps right and you reach 12. Walk 7 steps left and you are back on 5.
Multiplying works the same way. Triple 5 to get 15, then split 15 into 3 equal parts and you have 5 again.
In x + 7 = 12 someone has already walked the 7 steps for you. Walking back from 12 shows where they started.

6.EE-4#3.title: A riddle and its answer
6.EE-4#3.text:
The equation x + 3 = 8 is a riddle: "I am thinking of a number. When I add 3 to it, I get 8."
The line x = 5 is the riddle answered: "My number is 5."
Both say the same thing about x, but only the second one tells you outright. You can test the answer against the riddle: 5 + 3 is 8, so it fits.

6.EE-4#4.title: Guess, check and adjust
6.EE-4#4.text:
Try values for x and watch what x + 7 gives.
If x = 3, the left side is 10, which is too small.
If x = 4, the left side is 11, which is still 1 short.
If x = 5, the left side is 12, which matches the right side.
So x = 5. Each guess that was too low pointed toward a bigger number.

6.EE-4#5.title: Give the stickers back
6.EE-4#5.text:
Read x − 4 = 10 as a story. You had x stickers, gave 4 to a friend, and now you have 10.
To find what you started with, imagine your friend handing the 4 stickers back. Your pile of 10 grows to 14.
So you started with 14 stickers, and x = 14. Giving 4 away from 14 does leave 10.

6.EE-4#6.title: Skip count by threes
6.EE-4#6.text:
The equation 3x = 15 says that x jumps of 3 land on 15.
Count the jumps on your fingers: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15.
You raised 5 fingers before reaching 15, so it takes 5 jumps and x = 5. Skip counting until you hit the target is division in slow motion.

6.EE-4#7.title: Two halves make the whole
6.EE-4#7.text:
Dividing by 2 is cutting something in half, so x ÷ 2 = 8 says that half of x is 8.
The other half must be 8 as well, because the two halves are equal.
Put the halves back together: 8 + 8 = 16. So x = 16, and half of 16 is 8.

6.EE-4#8.title: Count up through 10
6.EE-4#8.text:
Ask how far it is from 9 up to 20, and travel through a friendly number on the way.
From 9 to 10 is 1 step. From 10 to 20 is 10 more steps.
That is 1 + 10 = 11 steps in all, so 9 + 11 = 20 and x = 11.

6.EE-4#9.title: Halve both sides twice
6.EE-4#9.text:
Dividing by 4 can be done as two easy halvings.
Four of x make 28, so two of x make half as much: 2x = 14.
Halve again: one x is half of 14, so x = 7.
Each halving was done to both sides, so the equation stayed balanced the whole way.

6.EE-4#10.title: Shade a bar model
6.EE-4#10.text:
Draw a bar made of 12 squares to stand for the right side of the equation.
Shade 7 of the squares to show the 7 that is added to x.
The squares left unshaded are x, because x and 7 together fill the whole bar. Count them and you find 5.
So x = 5.

6.EE-5#1.title: Four signs you might see
6.EE-5#1.text:
Each symbol matches a rule from daily life.
A bridge sign says trucks must weigh less than 5 tons: w < 5. A free shipping offer needs more than 20 dollars: m > 20.
A lift holds at most 8 people, and 8 is allowed: p ≤ 8. A film is for ages 13 and up, and 13 is allowed: a ≥ 13.
Ask whether the limit itself is allowed. If it is, use the symbol with the line under it.

6.EE-5#2.title: Compare with an equation
6.EE-5#2.text:
The equation x + 2 = 5 is like a lock with one key. Only 3 opens it.
The inequality x > 3 is like a height rule at a fair: "taller than 3 feet". A child of 3.5 feet passes, and so does an adult of 6 feet. Nobody can list every height that passes.
A child of exactly 3 feet does not pass, because that is not taller than 3 feet.

6.EE-5#3.title: Two age rules
6.EE-5#3.text:
A club says "older than 12". A 12 year old cannot join, so 12 is the edge but is left out. On a number line that is an open circle at 12, with shading to the right.
Another club says "12 or older". Now a 12 year old can join, so the circle at 12 is filled in.
The shading is the same for both clubs. Only the edge is different.

6.EE-5#4.title: Count the tips
6.EE-5#4.text:
Look at the shape of the symbol >. On its open side there are two tips. On its closed side there is one point.
Two is more than one, so the side with two tips goes next to the bigger number. In 9 > 4 the two tips are beside the 9.
In 4 < 9 the symbol is flipped, but the two tips are still beside the 9.

6.EE-5#5.title: Place n on a number line
6.EE-5#5.text:
Mark 7 on a number line. Numbers get bigger as you move right, so a number greater than 7 sits somewhere to the right of 7.
Put n there. Reading left to right you see 7 and then n, which says 7 < n. Read from the n side and it says n > 7.
Both are the same fact, and n > 7 follows the order of the words.

6.EE-5#6.title: List what is allowed
6.EE-5#6.text:
Think of a lift with a sign: at most 10 people.
Try some numbers of people. 8 is fine. 9 is fine. 10 is fine, because the lift is full but not over. 11 is not allowed.
The symbol has to accept 10 and reject 11. A plain < would reject 10, so the right one is ≤, and the inequality is n ≤ 10.

6.EE-5#7.title: Test a row of numbers
6.EE-5#7.text:
Test each whole number from 0 to 4 in x ≥ 2 and write yes or no.
0 is no. 1 is no. 2 is yes, because 2 equals 2. 3 is yes. 4 is yes.
The yes answers begin exactly at 2 and carry on to the right. So the graph has a closed circle at 2 and is shaded to the right.

6.EE-5#8.title: The express lane rule
6.EE-5#8.text:
Imagine a shop lane with the rule "fewer than 5 items". That rule is x < 5.
A shopper with 4 items may use the lane. A shopper with 5 items may not, because 5 items is not fewer than 5.
So 5 is not a solution. It is the first number that fails, which is why the graph has an open circle there.

6.EE-5#9.title: Split ≤ into two questions
6.EE-5#9.text:
The symbol ≤ asks two questions and only needs one yes.
First question: is 4 less than 4? No.
Second question: is 4 equal to 4? Yes.
One yes is enough, so 4 is a solution of x ≤ 4. With the symbol < only the first question would be asked, and 4 would fail.

6.EE-5#10.title: A two dollar snack
6.EE-5#10.text:
Turn x ≥ 2 into a story. A snack costs 2 dollars, so you need at least 2 dollars to buy it.
If you have exactly 2 dollars, you can buy the snack. Exactly 2 counts as "at least 2".
A number that counts is drawn as a filled dot, so the circle at 2 is closed.

6.EE-6#1.title: Pencils at a school shop
6.EE-6#1.text:
Pencils cost 2 dollars each. You walk in and decide how many to buy: 1, 3 or 10. Nobody tells you the cost first and makes you work out the pencils.
The number of pencils is your free choice, so it is the independent variable. A good test is to ask, "Which number do I get to pick?"

6.EE-6#2.title: Say it with "depends on"
6.EE-6#2.text:
Put the two quantities into the sentence "___ depends on ___" and see which order sounds right.
"The water in the bath depends on how long the tap runs" makes sense. "How long the tap runs depends on the water in the bath" sounds backwards.
The quantity in the first blank is the dependent variable. It is the one you measure after the other has been set.

6.EE-6#3.title: Rows the table left out
6.EE-6#3.text:
A table for d = 50t might show only t = 1, 2 and 3. What about 7 hours, or 2.5 hours? The table has no row for those.
The equation still answers at once: 50 × 7 = 350 and 50 × 2.5 = 125.
A table is a few snapshots. The equation is the recipe that makes every snapshot, including the ones nobody wrote down.

6.EE-6#4.title: Three copies of 5
6.EE-6#4.text:
The rule y = 3x says y is three copies of x, so y = x + x + x.
With x = 5 that is 5 + 5 + 5.
Skip count the fives: 5, 10, 15. So y = 15, the same as 3 × 5. Multiplying by 3 is only a faster way to add three equal numbers.

6.EE-6#5.title: Slide along the number line
6.EE-6#5.text:
The rule y = x + 4 says to start at x on a number line and slide 4 places to the right.
Start at 10 and count the slides: 11, 12, 13, 14.
You stop on 14, so y = 14. Any other starting number would also end up exactly 4 places to its right.

6.EE-6#6.title: One mile every minute
6.EE-6#6.text:
A speed of 60 miles in one hour is 60 miles in 60 minutes, which is 1 mile each minute.
Two hours last 120 minutes.
At 1 mile per minute, 120 minutes covers 120 miles. That agrees with 60 × 2 = 120 miles.

6.EE-6#7.title: Double, then double again
6.EE-6#7.text:
One ticket costs 5 dollars.
Two tickets cost double that, which is 10 dollars.
Four tickets are two lots of two tickets, so double again to get 20 dollars.
The cost of 4 tickets is 20 dollars, the same as 5 × 4.

6.EE-6#8.title: Add each x to itself
6.EE-6#8.text:
Doubling a number is the same as adding it to itself, so y = 2x can be read as y = x + x.
For x = 1, 1 + 1 = 2. For x = 2, 2 + 2 = 4. For x = 3, 3 + 3 = 6. For x = 4, 4 + 4 = 8.
The y column is 2, 4, 6, 8, which are the even numbers in order.

6.EE-6#9.title: Think in tens
6.EE-6#9.text:
Sixty is 6 tens, so 60 × 2 is 6 tens taken twice.
Two lots of 6 tens make 12 tens, because 6 × 2 = 12.
Twelve tens is 120, so the car travels 120 miles in 2 hours. A small fact, 6 × 2, did the work for the bigger one.

6.EE-7#1.title: Cars on a train
6.EE-7#1.text:
Picture an expression as a train. Each term is a car, and the + and − signs are the couplings between cars.
In 3x + 7y − 5 there are two couplings, so there are three cars: 3x, 7y and 5.
The 3 and the x ride in the same car, because nothing separates them. To count terms, count the cars.

6.EE-7#2.title: Cups in a recipe
6.EE-7#2.text:
A recipe says "4 cups of flour". The 4 tells you how many cups, just as the 4 in 4x tells you how many x.
Another line says "a cup of milk". No number is written, yet everyone knows it means 1 cup. A lone x works the same way and means 1x.
The coefficient is the "how many" that sits in front of the letter.

6.EE-7#3.title: Shoe rental at the bowling alley
6.EE-7#3.text:
Bowling costs 7 dollars to rent shoes and 3 dollars for each game, so x games cost 7 + 3x dollars.
Play 1 game or 5 games and the game charge changes, but you rent the shoes once and pay 7 dollars either way.
That fixed fee is the constant. It is the part of the bill that does not care how many games you play.

6.EE-7#4.title: Sort your coins first
6.EE-7#4.text:
You have 3 dimes in one pocket, 2 dimes in another and 4 pennies in your hand. How many kinds of coin is that?
It might look like three piles, but two of the piles are both dimes. Put them together and you have 5 dimes and 4 pennies, which is two kinds.
In the same way 3x + 2x + 4 becomes 5x + 4, with two terms.

6.EE-7#5.title: Watch how the value grows
6.EE-7#5.text:
Work out 4y for a few values of y. When y = 1 the value is 4. When y = 2 it is 8. When y = 3 it is 12.
Each time y goes up by 1, the value goes up by 4.
That steady jump is the coefficient at work. It is 4, the number that multiplies y.

6.EE-7#6.title: Set x to zero
6.EE-7#6.text:
Choose x = 0, which wipes out every term that has an x in it.
The expression 7 + 3x becomes 7 + 0, which is 7.
What is left when the variable part is gone is the constant. So the constant is 7. With x = 2 the value is 13, but the 7 inside it has not changed.

6.EE-7#7.title: Tickets and a parking fee
6.EE-7#7.text:
Let 5x + 8 be the cost of a trip: 5 tickets at x dollars each, plus 8 dollars for parking.
The bill has two separate charges, tickets and parking, so there are two terms.
The 5 is how many tickets you buy, so it is the coefficient. The 8 is paid once and stays the same whatever a ticket costs, so it is the constant.

6.EE-7#8.title: Read the parts from a table
6.EE-7#8.text:
Work out x + 9 for x = 0, 1, 2 and 3. The values are 9, 10, 11 and 12.
The value at x = 0 is 9. Nothing with a letter is left there, so 9 is the constant.
Each time x goes up by 1 the value goes up by 1. That jump is the coefficient, so the coefficient of x is 1.

6.EE-7#9.title: Check with x = 10
6.EE-7#9.text:
Put x = 10 into 5x − 2 + 3. That gives 50 − 2 + 3, which is 51.
Fifty-one is 50 + 1, or five tens and one more. With x back in place of 10, that is 5x + 1.
So the three written chunks are worth the same as the two chunks 5x and 1, and the expression has 2 terms.

6.EE-7#10.title: Follow the pattern down
6.EE-7#10.text:
Look at a family of expressions: 3x + 9, then 2x + 9, then x + 9.
The coefficients are 3, then 2, and the pattern is going down by 1 each time. The next coefficient has to be 1.
So x + 9 is 1x + 9 with the 1 left unwritten. It cannot be 0, because 0x + 9 would have no x in it at all.

6.EE-8#1.title: Count one picture two ways
6.EE-8#1.text:
Draw 2 rows. In each row put x stars and then 3 circles.
Count by rows: each row holds x + 3 shapes and there are 2 rows, so 2(x + 3).
Count by shape: there are 2x stars and 6 circles, so 2x + 6.
Nobody added or removed a shape between the two counts. That is why the totals agree for every number of stars.

6.EE-8#2.title: One test fails, one test fools
6.EE-8#2.text:
Compare 2(x + 3) with 2x + 3 at x = 2. The first is 10 and the second is 7. They differ, so they are not equivalent, and no more work is needed.
Now compare x + x with x × x at x = 2. Both are 4. But at x = 3 they are 6 and 9.
A mismatch settles the question. A match only means "keep checking".

6.EE-8#3.title: The key that fits
6.EE-8#3.text:
Think of x + 5 = 9 as a lock and each number as a key you can try.
Try 3: the left side is 8, not 9, so the lock stays shut. Try 5: the left side is 10, so that fails too.
Try 4: the left side is 9, which matches. The key that fits is called the solution.

6.EE-8#4.title: Solve it, then compare
6.EE-8#4.text:
Find the solution yourself and see whether it is 4.
The equation asks what number plus 5 makes 9. Take the 5 away from 9 and 4 is left.
The solution is 4, which is the value being tested. So yes, x = 4 is a solution.

6.EE-8#5.title: Find the real solution
6.EE-8#5.text:
Work out what x has to be, then compare it with 3.
The equation 2x = 8 says two equal groups make 8. Sharing 8 into two equal groups gives 4 in each group, so the true solution is 4.
The value being tested is 3, not 4. So no, x = 3 is not a solution.

6.EE-8#6.title: Walk it on a number line
6.EE-8#6.text:
Put your finger on 5 on a number line, because that is the value being tested for x.
The equation says to subtract 3, so hop left three times: 4, 3, 2.
You land on 2, which is the number on the right side of the equation. So yes, x = 5 is a solution of x − 3 = 2.

6.EE-8#7.title: Pull out the common factor
6.EE-8#7.text:
Work on the other expression this time. In 2x + 6, both terms are multiples of 2: 2x is 2 times x, and 6 is 2 times 3.
Take the shared 2 out to the front and write what is left in a bracket: 2(x + 3).
That is the second expression exactly, so yes, the two are equivalent.

6.EE-8#8.title: Three teams on a field
6.EE-8#8.text:
Three teams arrive at a field. Each team has x players and 2 coaches.
Count by team: each team brings x + 2 people, so there are 3(x + 2) people.
Count by job: there are 3x players and 6 coaches, so there are 3x + 6 people.
The same crowd was counted both times, so yes, the expressions are equivalent whatever the team size.

6.EE-8#9.title: Line the two expressions up
6.EE-8#9.text:
Write 2x as x + x. Now the two expressions are x + x and x + 2.
They both start with an x. After that, one adds another x and the other adds 2.
Those are the same only when x happens to be 2. For any other value they differ, so no, the expressions are not equivalent.

6.EE-8#10.title: Same start, same step
6.EE-8#10.text:
Look at how each expression grows.
At x = 0, 3(x + 2) is 3 × 2 = 6, and 3x + 6 is also 6. They start together.
Raise x by 1 and the bracket grows by 1, so 3(x + 2) grows by 3. The term 3x also grows by 3.
Same start and same step each time means they stay together for every whole number, so they are equivalent.

6.EE-9#1.title: Like the key on a map
6.EE-9#1.text:
A map uses small symbols, and the key in the corner says what each one means. Without the key, a blue dot could be a lake or a car park.
A "let" statement is the key for your equation. Say Mia read some pages on Monday and 6 on Tuesday, 14 in all. Write "let x = pages read on Monday" and then x = 8 clearly means 8 pages on Monday.

6.EE-9#2.title: A worked sentence
6.EE-9#2.text:
Take the sentence "The product of 4 and a number is 20."
The first phrase, "the product of 4 and a number", becomes 4x.
The word "is" becomes the equals sign.
The last part, "20", stays as 20.
Put the pieces in order and you have 4x = 20. A quick check: 5 works, because the product of 4 and 5 is 20.

6.EE-9#3.title: Stand on the starting number
6.EE-9#3.text:
Use a number line. For "n less than 12", stand on 12 and walk n steps to the left. You began at 12, so 12 is written first: 12 − n.
A thermometer works the same way. "Today is 5 degrees less than yesterday" means start at the temperature from yesterday and go down 5.
The number you start from is written first, wherever it appears in the sentence.

6.EE-9#4.title: Rewind the story
6.EE-9#4.text:
Say the story was: Ana had some stickers, got 6 more, and now has 14. That is x + 6 = 14.
Play the story backwards. Start with the 14 she has now and take away the 6 she was given. She is back to 8.
Play it forwards to check: 8 stickers, 6 more, 14 in all. The answer fits the story, so x = 8.

6.EE-9#5.title: Spot the pattern in a table
6.EE-9#5.text:
Write what Marcos has after each week.
After 1 week he has 25 dollars. After 2 weeks he has 50. After 3 weeks he has 75.
Each total is 25 times the week number: 25 × 1, 25 × 2, 25 × 3.
For week number w the same pattern gives 25 × w, which is written 25w.

6.EE-9#6.title: Cookies on a plate
6.EE-9#6.text:
A plate holds 12 cookies and n of them get eaten. The number left is "n less than 12".
You always begin with the 12 on the plate and take the eaten ones away, so the expression is 12 − n.
If 5 are eaten, 12 − 5 = 7 are left. Writing n − 12 would mean taking 12 cookies away from the 5, which makes no sense here.

6.EE-9#7.title: Draw a tape diagram
6.EE-9#7.text:
Draw a long bar and label its full length 14.
Cut the bar into two pieces. Label one piece x for the unknown number and label the other piece 6.
The two pieces laid end to end are exactly as long as the whole bar. Written in symbols, that picture says x + 6 = 14.

6.EE-9#8.title: Count up from 6
6.EE-9#8.text:
Ask how far it is from 6 up to 14, and stop at 10 on the way.
From 6 to 10 is 4. From 10 to 14 is another 4.
That is 4 + 4 = 8 in all, so 6 + 8 = 14 and x = 8.

6.EE-9#9.title: Deal the cards out
6.EE-9#9.text:
Take the 21 cards and deal them into 3 piles, one card to each pile in turn.
Each round of dealing uses 3 cards. The cards run out after 7 rounds, because 3 × 7 = 21.
Every pile got one card per round, so each pile has 7 cards. That gives p = 7 cards per pack.

6.EE-9#10.title: Skip count to 21
6.EE-9#10.text:
The equation 3x = 21 says x jumps of 3 land on 21.
Count the jumps: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21.
That is seven numbers, so it takes 7 jumps and x = 7. This works even if you have forgotten the multiplication fact.

6.EE-10#1.title: A price list never changes its mind
6.EE-10#1.text:
Tickets cost 4 dollars each, so the cost is y = 4x for x tickets.
Buy 3 tickets today and you pay 12 dollars. Buy 3 tickets tomorrow and you pay 12 dollars again. It would be strange if 3 tickets sometimes cost 12 and sometimes 15.
Each number of tickets has one cost, and that is what one y for each x means.

6.EE-10#2.title: Compare two tables
6.EE-10#2.text:
Make a table for y = 4x with x = 1, 2, 3. The y values are 4, 8, 12, and they climb by 4.
Make a table for y = x + 4 with the same inputs. The y values are 5, 6, 7, and they climb by 1.
A step of 4 points to "times 4". A step of only 1 means x is not being multiplied, so look for a number being added.

6.EE-10#3.title: Watch a wrong guess fail
6.EE-10#3.text:
Take the pairs (1, 5), (2, 10) and (3, 15).
Guess "add 4". It works on the first pair, since 1 + 4 = 5. On the second pair it gives 2 + 4 = 6, but y is 10. The guess is wrong.
Guess "times 5". It gives 5, 10 and 15, right on all three pairs.
One pair can fit many rules. Only the rule that fits them all is kept.

6.EE-10#4.title: Double it twice
6.EE-10#4.text:
Multiplying by 4 is the same as doubling two times.
Double the input 6 to get 12.
Double 12 to get 24.
So y = 24 when x = 6, the same as 4 × 6. Two doublings make four copies of the input, which is what the rule asks for.

6.EE-10#5.title: Find one, then count on
6.EE-10#5.text:
Use the rule for the first row only: 1 + 3 = 4.
In this rule nothing is multiplied, so when x goes up by 1, y goes up by 1 as well.
Count on from 4 for the next two rows: 5, then 6.
The y values are 4, 5 and 6.

6.EE-10#6.title: Spot the 3 times table
6.EE-10#6.text:
Read the y values in order: 3, 6, 9. Those are the first three numbers you say when you skip count by 3.
The x values 1, 2, 3 tell you the position in the count. The first number is 3, the second is 6 and the third is 9.
So y is the number in position x of the 3 times table, which is y = 3x.

6.EE-10#7.title: Count it in nickels
6.EE-10#7.text:
A nickel is worth 5 cents.
One nickel is 5 cents, two nickels are 10 cents and three nickels are 15 cents. Those are exactly the pairs (1, 5), (2, 10) and (3, 15).
The value in cents is always 5 times the number of nickels. With x for the nickels and y for the cents, the rule is y = 5x.

6.EE-10#8.title: Climb the table from zero
6.EE-10#8.text:
Start at x = 0. The 2x part is zero there, so y is just the 1.
Each time x goes up by 1, the 2x part adds 2 to y.
Climb four steps and write each value: 1, then 3, 5, 7, 9.
The fourth step up is x = 4, and the value there is y = 9.

6.EE-10#9.title: Use the step size
6.EE-10#9.text:
The y column reads 6, 12, 18. It climbs by 6 each time x goes up by 1.
Step back one row to x = 0 and y would be 6 − 6 = 0, so nothing extra is added to the rule.
A table that starts at 0 and climbs by 6 follows y = 6x. Check the row asked for: 6 × 3 = 18, so y = 18 when x = 3.

6.EE-10#10.title: Step back to zero
6.EE-10#10.text:
The table climbs by 3, so going back one row takes 3 away.
The row before x = 1 would be x = 0, and its y would be 3 − 3 = 0.
A table that begins at 0 and adds 3 for each step of x is the 3 times table. So the rule is y = 3x, with no extra number added.

6.G-1#1.title: Tile a bathroom floor
6.G-1#1.text: Think of a floor that is 7 feet by 3 feet, covered with tiles that are 1 foot on each side. You could count the tiles by columns: there are 7 columns with 3 tiles in each, and 3 counted seven times is 21. Counting by rows gives 21 as well. The number of tiles is the area, and it is the same whichever way you count.

6.G-1#2.title: Cut a sheet of paper
6.G-1#2.text: Take a sheet of paper 6 units wide and 4 units tall. Its area is 6 × 4 = 24. Cut it from one corner to the opposite corner. You get two triangles that match exactly when you stack them, so each one has area 12. That is the same as ½ × 6 × 4. A triangle that leans can be split into two of these corner-cut triangles, so the half rule still holds.

6.G-1#3.title: The leaning ladder
6.G-1#3.text: A ladder 10 feet long leans against a wall and touches it 8 feet above the ground. How high does it reach? Only 8 feet, not 10. The 10 is the slanted side, and the 8 is the height. Your own height is measured the same way: standing straight against the wall, not leaning. Use the straight-up number in the area formula.

6.G-1#4.title: Split 7 into 5 + 2
6.G-1#4.text:
Cut the rectangle into two smaller ones with a line: a 5-by-3 piece and a 2-by-3 piece.
The first holds 5 × 3 = 15 squares and the second holds 2 × 3 = 6 squares.
Together that is 15 + 6 = 21 square units, the same as 7 × 3.

6.G-1#5.title: Box it, then halve
6.G-1#5.text: Draw a rectangle around the triangle that is 8 wide and 5 tall. It covers 8 × 5 = 40 square units. The triangle fills exactly half of that rectangle, so its area is 40 ÷ 2 = 20 square units. This multiplies first and halves last, and it lands on the same 20.

6.G-1#6.title: Halve the height instead
6.G-1#6.text: The half can go on either number. Half of the height 4 is 2. Picture the top of the triangle cut off and tucked in beside the bottom part, making a rectangle 10 wide and 2 tall. Its area is 10 × 2 = 20 square units. Halving the base works too: 5 × 4 = 20.

6.G-1#7.title: Use 6 × 10, then trim
