6.G-1#7.text: Nine is one less than ten, so start with an easier rectangle. A 6-by-10 rectangle has area 60. The 6-by-9 rectangle is one strip of 6 squares narrower, so take that strip away: 60 − 6 = 54 square units. No half is needed because a rectangle is the whole box.

6.G-1#8.title: Two copies make a parallelogram
6.G-1#8.text: Make a second copy of the triangle, flip it, and fit it against the first. The pair forms a parallelogram with base 12 and height 5, so its area is 12 × 5 = 60. One triangle is half of the pair: 60 ÷ 2 = 30 square units.

6.G-1#9.title: Multiply first, halve last
6.G-1#9.text: When you are not sure which number to halve, leave the half until the end. Multiply the base and height: 7 × 6 = 42. That is the rectangle around the triangle. Now take half of it: 42 ÷ 2 = 21 square units. An even product is easy to halve, so this order always works when one number is even.

6.G-1#10.title: Split into two right triangles
6.G-1#10.text: Draw the height. Suppose it lands 2 units from one end of the base, so the base splits into 2 and 4. The left piece is half of a 2-by-4 box: 8 ÷ 2 = 4. The right piece is half of a 4-by-4 box: 16 ÷ 2 = 8. Together 4 + 8 = 12 square units. Wherever the height lands, the two pieces add to 12.

6.G-2#1.title: Like a dot-to-dot puzzle
6.G-2#1.text: In a dot-to-dot puzzle you join dot 1 to dot 2 to dot 3, and the picture appears. Vertices work the same way. Joining (1, 1), (5, 1), (5, 4), (1, 4) in that order and back to the start draws a rectangle. Join them as (1, 1), (5, 4), (5, 1), (1, 4) and the lines cross like a bow tie. Same dots, wrong order, wrong shape.

6.G-2#2.title: Ride the elevator
6.G-2#2.text: Think of x as the street a building stands on and y as the floor. Going from (2, 1) to (2, 6) means staying in the building on street 2 and riding from floor 1 to floor 6. The elevator passes floors 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, so it climbs 5 floors. The street number never changes, so it plays no part in the distance.

6.G-2#3.title: Houses on one street
6.G-2#3.text: Two houses stand on the same street, at number 1 and number 7. The street is the shared y-value, 3. Walking from house 1 you pass 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and arrive at 7, which is 6 steps. You never cross to another street, so only the house numbers matter. That is the points (1, 3) and (7, 3): 6 units apart.

6.G-2#4.title: Move the shape, same answer
6.G-2#4.text: A rectangle has corners (2, 3), (7, 3), (7, 6) and (2, 6). Its sides are 7 − 2 = 5 and 6 − 3 = 3, so the area is 15 and the perimeter is 16. Now slide it so one corner sits at (0, 0). The corners become (0, 0), (5, 0), (5, 3), (0, 3). The sides are still 5 and 3, so nothing changes. Only the lengths matter.

6.G-2#5.title: Count the jumps up
6.G-2#5.text: Put a finger on (2, 1) and hop up one grid line at a time. The hops land on y = 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. That is 5 hops, so the side is 5 units long. You can check with addition: starting at 1 and adding 5 gives 6, the y-value of the top point.

6.G-2#6.title: Add on to check
6.G-2#6.text: Ask what must be added to the smaller x-value to reach the larger one. Starting at x = 1, add 6 and you arrive at x = 7. So the two corners are 6 units apart. Counting grid lines agrees: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 is six steps to the right along the line y = 3.

6.G-2#7.title: Count the unit squares
6.G-2#7.text: Draw the rectangle on grid paper. Between y = 0 and y = 3 there are 3 rows of squares. Each row runs from x = 0 to x = 4, so it holds 4 squares. Counting by rows gives 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 square units. No subtraction is needed when the grid is in front of you.

6.G-2#8.title: Slide both points up 2
6.G-2#8.text: Sliding a segment does not change its length. Move both points up 2 units so the lower one sits on the x-axis. The point (3, −2) becomes (3, 0) and the point (3, 5) becomes (3, 7). Now the distance is easy to read: from 0 up to 7 is 7 units.

6.G-2#9.title: Build the square and count
6.G-2#9.text: A side of 5 means the other two corners are (5, 5) and (0, 5). Draw the square on the grid. It has 5 rows, and every row has 5 unit squares. Count by fives: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25. The area is 25 square units, the same as 5 × 5.

6.G-2#10.title: Walk around the corners
6.G-2#10.text: Start at (0, 0) and walk the border. To (6, 0) is 6 units. Up to (6, 3) is 3 units. Back to (0, 3) is 6 units. Down to (0, 0) is 3 units. Keep a running total as you go: 6, then 9, then 15, then 18. The trip around is 18 units.

6.G-2#11.title: Straighten out the border
6.G-2#11.text: Imagine the border is a piece of string. Cut it at one corner and pull it straight. It is made of four pieces: 6, 3, 6 and 3. Slide the equal pieces next to each other: 6 + 6 = 12 and 3 + 3 = 6. The whole string is 12 + 6 = 18 units long, which is the perimeter.

6.G-3#1.title: Slice the box a different way
6.G-3#1.text: Take the same 2 × 3 × 5 box and look at it from the side. One side wall is 3 by 5, so a slice against it holds 15 cubes. The box is 2 slices thick, so it holds 15 + 15 = 30 cubes. Starting from the floor gave 6 × 5 = 30. Whichever face you start from, you count the same cubes, so the three numbers can be multiplied in any order.

6.G-3#2.title: The fish tank test
6.G-3#2.text: A fish tank has a bottom that is 4 by 3. Multiply those two numbers and you get 12 square units. That tells you how much glass covers the bottom, but not how much water goes in. For water you also need the depth. If the tank is 2 deep, the water takes 12 × 2 = 24 cubic units. Two numbers describe the glass. Three numbers describe the water.

6.G-3#3.title: Stack two half boxes
6.G-3#3.text: A box is 4 by 6 and only ½ unit tall. Put a second box just like it on top. Together they make a box 4 by 6 by 1, which holds 24 unit cubes. The two boxes are equal, so each holds 24 ÷ 2 = 12 cubic units. The formula agrees: 4 × 6 × ½ = 12. A fraction edge just means part of a full layer.

6.G-3#4.title: Start from a side wall
6.G-3#4.text: Look at the 3-by-5 face instead of the floor. A slice one cube thick against that face holds 3 × 5 = 15 cubes. The box is 2 cubes thick in the other direction, so there are 2 slices. That gives 15 × 2 = 30 cubic units, the same total as floor times layers.

6.G-3#5.title: Add three layers of nine
6.G-3#5.text: The bottom layer of the cube is a 3-by-3 square, which is 9 unit cubes. The cube is 3 tall, so there are three layers exactly alike. Add them one at a time: 9 + 9 = 18, and 18 + 9 = 27. The cube holds 27 cubic units.

6.G-3#6.title: Slices from the end
6.G-3#6.text: Look at the box from its end, where the face is 2 by 3. That face shows 6 cubes. The box is 4 long, so it is like a loaf cut into 4 slices of 6 cubes each. Count by sixes: 6, 12, 18, 24. The volume is 24 cubic units.

6.G-3#7.title: Pair the half with the 4
6.G-3#7.text: Multiplying can be done in any order, so let the fraction meet an even number first. Half of 4 is 2. Now the box is like one with edges 2 and 3, and 2 × 3 = 6 cubic units. Pairing ½ with an even edge removes the fraction in one step.

6.G-3#8.title: Halve the 6 first
6.G-3#8.text: Let the half act on one edge before any other multiplying. Half of 6 is 3. What is left is 3 × 4 = 12 cubic units. You could also halve the 4 to get 2, and then 2 × 6 = 12. Every order gives 12, so pick the one that feels easiest.

6.G-3#9.title: Stack layers until 40
6.G-3#9.text: The floor is 4 by 2, so each layer one unit tall holds 8 cubes. Keep adding layers and count by eights: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40. The count reaches the volume of 40 on the fifth layer. So the box is 5 units tall, with no division needed.

6.G-3#10.title: Slices instead of layers
6.G-3#10.text: Turn the box and cut it the other way. The end face is 4 by 3, which shows 12 cubes. The box is 5 long, so there are 5 slices of 12. Counting by twelves gives 12, 24, 36, 48, 60. The volume is 60 cubic units, the same as three layers of 20.

6.G-4#1.title: Unfold a small gift box
6.G-4#1.text: Picture a gift box that is 3 long, 2 wide and 1 tall. Unfold it and you find six flat pieces: two that are 3 by 2 (the lid and the base), two that are 3 by 1 (the long sides) and two that are 2 by 1 (the short ends). Nothing new was made and nothing was lost. The net is just the same six faces lying side by side.

6.G-4#2.title: Stickers on a block
6.G-4#2.text: Cover a 2 × 2 × 2 block with square stickers that are 1 unit on each side, with no gaps and no overlaps. Each face needs 4 stickers. There are 6 faces, so you use 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 24 stickers. That count is the surface area: 24 square units. Stickers are flat squares, which is why the unit is square, not cubic.

6.G-4#3.title: Look around a room
6.G-4#3.text: A room is a box you can stand in. The floor and the ceiling are the same size. The two long walls match each other, and so do the two short walls. For a room 5 long, 4 wide and 3 tall, the floor is 20, a long wall is 15 and a short wall is 12. One of each adds to 47, and doubling gives 94 square units for all six.

6.G-4#4.title: Trace the footprint
6.G-4#4.text: Set the box down on its 2-by-3 face on grid paper and trace around it. The outline covers 2 rows of 3 squares. Counting them gives 3 + 3 = 6 squares. So that face has an area of 6 square units. The height of 1 does not matter for this face.

6.G-4#5.title: A band plus two ends
6.G-4#5.text: The four side faces join into one strip that wraps around the cube. The strip is 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8 long and 2 tall, so its area is 16. The top and the bottom are 4 each, which adds 8. Altogether the surface is 16 + 8 = 24 square units.

6.G-4#6.title: Three pairs of faces
6.G-4#6.text: Group the six faces in opposite pairs. The top and bottom are 9 each, so that pair is 18. The front and back also make 18, and so do the left and right. Add the pairs: 18 + 18 + 18 = 54 square units.

6.G-4#7.title: Count it like quarters
6.G-4#7.text: Each face has area 25, the same as the cents in a quarter. Four quarters make 100 cents, and two more make 50 cents. Six quarters are worth 150 cents. In the same way, six faces of 25 cover 150 square units.

6.G-4#8.title: Wrap a label around
6.G-4#8.text: Sit the box on its 2-by-3 face. A label around the four sides is as long as the trip around that face: 2 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 10. The box is 1 tall, so the label covers 10 × 1 = 10. The top and bottom are 6 each, adding 12. The total is 10 + 12 = 22 square units.

6.G-4#9.title: Fold the net in your head
6.G-4#9.text: Many box nets look like a cross: a row of 4 rectangles with 1 flap above and 1 flap below. Fold it in your mind. The row of 4 wraps around to become the front, right, back and left. The two flaps close the top and the bottom. That is 4 + 1 + 1 = 6 faces, so a net with fewer than 6 pieces is missing one.

6.G-4#10.title: Band around, plus two ends
6.G-4#10.text: Stand the box on its 3-by-4 face, so it is 5 tall. A band around the four sides is 3 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 14 long and 5 tall, which covers 14 × 5 = 70. The top and the bottom are 12 each, adding 24. The surface area is 70 + 24 = 94 square units.

6.G-5#1.title: One L-shape, two cuts
6.G-5#1.text: An L-shape is 6 wide along the bottom and 5 tall on the left. Its tall part is 2 wide and its low part is 2 tall. Cut it with an up-and-down line: a 2-by-5 tower and a 4-by-2 block, 10 + 8 = 18. Cut it with a side-to-side line instead: a 6-by-2 strip and a 2-by-3 block, 12 + 6 = 18. Both cuts give 18.

6.G-5#2.title: Tiles for two rooms
6.G-5#2.text: A kitchen floor takes 12 tiles and the hallway next to it takes 6 tiles. The doorway between them is only a line, so no tile belongs to both rooms and no part of the floor is left bare. To tile both you buy 12 + 6 = 18 tiles. Adding the areas of the pieces of a shape works for the same reason.

6.G-5#3.title: A picture frame
6.G-5#3.text: A wooden frame measures 10 by 8 on the outside, and the opening for the photo is 8 by 6. How much wood shows? The full outline covers 10 × 8 = 80 square units, but the opening has no wood in it. The opening is 8 × 6 = 48. The wood covers 80 − 48 = 32 square units. Subtracting is quicker than adding four separate strips.

6.G-5#4.title: Subtract from the surrounding box
6.G-5#4.text: Draw one big rectangle around the whole L. It is 9 wide and 2 + 2 = 4 tall, so it covers 36. The top strip is only 4 wide, so a gap 9 − 4 = 5 wide and 2 tall is empty. The gap is 5 × 2 = 10. The L covers 36 − 10 = 26 square units.

6.G-5#5.title: Skip-count the columns
6.G-5#5.text: Stand the joined shape so its columns are 4 squares tall. The first rectangle has 3 columns: count 4, 8, 12. The second rectangle adds 2 more columns, so keep counting: 16, 20. Every square has been counted once, and the combined area is 20 square units.

6.G-5#6.title: Split what is left
6.G-5#6.text: Picture the hole at a corner. A full strip 5 wide and 5 − 2 = 3 tall sits beside it, with area 15. Next to the hole there is a piece 5 − 2 = 3 wide and 2 tall, with area 6. The part that remains is 15 + 6 = 21 square units. Moving the hole somewhere else would not change the amount left.

6.G-5#7.title: Flatten the roof
6.G-5#7.text: A triangle with base 6 and height 2 covers the same area as a rectangle 6 wide and 1 tall, because half of the height is 1. Trade the roof for that flat strip. Now the house is one rectangle 6 wide and 3 + 1 = 4 tall. Its area is 6 × 4 = 24 square units.

6.G-5#8.title: Think in quarters
6.G-5#8.text: Fold the 10-by-10 square in half both ways. It splits into four 5-by-5 squares, and each one covers 25. The corner bite removes exactly one of the four. Three are left, so the area is 3 × 25 = 75 square units.

6.G-5#9.title: Whole box minus the notch
6.G-5#9.text: Skip the hunt for missing sides and use the outside measurements. A full rectangle 8 wide and 5 tall covers 40. The notch is 3 wide and 2 tall, so it takes away 6. The L covers 40 − 6 = 34 square units, which matches the answer from splitting.

6.G-5#10.title: Split the L instead
6.G-5#10.text: Take the bite to be 2 wide and 4 tall. Draw a line level with the bottom of the bite. Below it is a full strip 8 wide and 6 − 4 = 2 tall, with area 16. Above it is a piece 8 − 2 = 6 wide and 4 tall, with area 24. Together they cover 16 + 24 = 40 square units.

6.G-6#1.title: Cover the pool or fill it
6.G-6#1.text: Think about a swimming pool. In winter you pull a flat cover over the top. The size of the cover depends on the length and the width of the pool: that is area. In summer you fill the pool with water. How much water depends on the depth too: that is volume. One pool, two different questions, and two different kinds of unit.

6.G-6#2.title: One pair of numbers, three shapes
6.G-6#2.text: Use the numbers 6 and 4 three ways. A rectangle 6 by 4 has area 24. A triangle with base 6 and height 4 is half of that rectangle, so its area is 12. A prism with a 6-by-4 floor and a height of 2 stacks two layers of 24 cubes, so its volume is 48. Halve for a triangle. Multiply by a third number for a solid.

6.G-6#3.title: One room, three questions
6.G-6#3.text: A room is 5 long, 4 wide and 3 tall. "How much carpet covers the floor?" asks for area: 5 × 4 = 20 square units. "How much air is in the room?" asks for volume: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60 cubic units. "How much trim goes around the floor?" asks for perimeter: 5 + 4 + 5 + 4 = 18 units. The numbers are the same each time. Only the question tells you what to do with them.

6.G-6#4.title: Two squares side by side
6.G-6#4.text: An 8-by-4 rectangle is flat, so the question is about area. Cut it down the middle into two 4-by-4 squares. Each square covers 4 × 4 = 16. The two together cover 16 + 16 = 32 square units.

6.G-6#5.title: Whole box, then half
6.G-6#5.text: A triangle is flat, so this is area. Draw the rectangle around it, 6 wide and 9 tall. That rectangle covers 6 × 9 = 54. The triangle is half of it, and half of 54 is 27 square units. The half in the formula is this last step.

6.G-6#6.title: Make a ten first
6.G-6#6.text: Three edges mean volume, and the three numbers can be multiplied in any order. Pair 2 with 5 because they make 10. Then 10 × 3 = 30 cubic units. Looking for a pair that makes ten keeps the arithmetic short.

6.G-6#7.title: Double, then double again
6.G-6#7.text: A cube is a solid, so count cubes. The bottom layer is 4 by 4, which is 16 cubes. Two layers are 16 + 16 = 32. Four layers are double that: 32 + 32 = 64. The volume is 64 cubic units.

6.G-6#8.title: A parallelogram from two triangles
6.G-6#8.text: Flip a copy of the triangle and fit it against the first one. The pair makes a parallelogram with base 10 and height 3, covering 10 × 3 = 30. The triangle is one of the two equal parts, so its area is 30 ÷ 2 = 15 square units.

6.G-6#9.title: Count towers of cubes
6.G-6#9.text: "Inside" means filling the box, so count cubes. Look down on the 3-by-4 floor: it has 12 spots. On each spot a tower 2 cubes tall fits under the lid. Twelve towers of 2 make 24 cubes, so the space inside is 24 cubic units.

6.G-6#10.title: Cut and turn the tip
6.G-6#10.text: Use the leg of 5 as the base and the leg of 8 as the height. Cut the triangle straight across at half the height, 4 units up. Turn the small top triangle around and fit it beside the bottom piece. The result is a rectangle 5 wide and 4 tall, and 5 × 4 = 20 square units.

6.G-7#1.title: A plus sign
6.G-7#1.text: Take a plus sign in which every arm is 2 wide and 2 long. One way to slice it: five 2-by-2 squares, one in the middle and four arms, so 5 × 4 = 20. Another way: one long bar 6 by 2 across the middle, plus a 2-by-2 square above and one below, so 12 + 4 + 4 = 20. Different cuts, same simple pieces, same total.

6.G-7#2.title: Painting a wall
6.G-7#2.text: You paint the end wall of a house. The main part is 10 wide and 8 tall: 80. Above it is a triangular peak with base 10 and height 2. It is part of the wall, so add ½ × 10 × 2 = 10 to get 90. A window 3 by 2 is not painted, so take away 6. The paint covers 90 − 6 = 84 square units.

6.G-7#3.title: Two ways up the same wall
6.G-7#3.text: An L-shape is 7 tall on its left side. On the right side the same climb is made in two parts: a lower edge and an upper edge. If the lower edge is 3, the upper edge must be 7 − 3 = 4, because both routes go from the bottom to the top. The same works across: a bottom of 10 and a top piece of 4 leave a step of 6.

6.G-7#4.title: Count the columns by twos
6.G-7#4.text: Both rectangles are 2 tall, so every column of the joined shape holds 2 squares. The first rectangle has 3 columns and the second has 2, which makes 5 columns. Count by twos: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. The total area is 10 square units.

6.G-7#5.title: Start from two equal pieces
6.G-7#5.text: Pretend both rectangles are 5 by 4. Two of them would cover 20 + 20 = 40. The second rectangle is really 5 by 3, which is one row of 5 squares smaller. Take that row away: 40 − 5 = 35 square units.

6.G-7#6.title: Two rectangles are left
6.G-7#6.text: With the square gone from a corner, cut the rest along a line level with the edge of the cutout. One piece is a full strip 6 wide and 5 − 2 = 3 tall, with area 18. The other is 6 − 2 = 4 wide and 2 tall, with area 8. The area left is 18 + 8 = 26 square units.

6.G-7#7.title: Level the roof
6.G-7#7.text: A triangle with base 8 and height 4 covers as much as a rectangle 8 wide and 2 tall. Swap the pointed roof for that flat block. The house becomes one rectangle 8 wide and 5 + 2 = 7 tall. Its area is 8 × 7 = 56 square units.

6.G-7#8.title: Split the leftover shape
6.G-7#8.text: Picture the 3-by-2 piece cut from a corner. Under the cut lies a full strip 10 wide and 6 − 2 = 4 tall, which covers 40. Beside the cut is a piece 10 − 3 = 7 wide and 2 tall, which covers 14. The area left is 40 + 14 = 54 square units.

6.G-7#9.title: Box the T, remove the corners
6.G-7#9.text: Draw a rectangle around the whole T: 9 wide and 6 tall, covering 54. The stem is only 3 wide, so beside it there are empty corners that are 9 − 3 = 6 wide in total and 4 tall. They cover 6 × 4 = 24. The T covers 54 − 24 = 30 square units.

6.G-7#10.title: Split into bar and stem
6.G-7#10.text: Take each corner to be 3 wide and 4 tall. The top bar is the full 10 wide and 8 − 4 = 4 tall, so it covers 40. The stem between the corners is 10 − 3 − 3 = 4 wide and 4 tall, so it covers 16. The T covers 40 + 16 = 56 square units.

6.G-8#1.title: Loading a moving truck
6.G-8#1.text: A truck is being packed with boxes that are all the same cube shape. Four boxes fit along the length of the floor and two fit across, so the floor holds 8 boxes. The boxes can be stacked 3 high. The truck holds 8 + 8 + 8 = 24 boxes, which is 4 × 2 × 3. If each box is 1 cubic foot, the truck space is 24 cubic feet.

6.G-8#2.title: Half of a half dollar
6.G-8#2.text: Think of money. Half of a dollar is 50 cents. Half of that half is 25 cents, a quarter of a dollar. So ½ × ½ = 1/4, and in decimals 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25. The same thing happens with space: a cube that is ½ unit on each edge is so small that 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 of them fill one unit cube, so its volume is 1/8.

6.G-8#3.title: A table of cubes
6.G-8#3.text: Build cubes from small blocks and count. Edge 1: just 1 block. Edge 2: two layers of 4, so 8 blocks. Edge 3: three layers of 9, so 27 blocks, like a puzzle cube. Edge 4: four layers of 16, so 64 blocks. The list 1, 8, 27, 64 is what s³ gives for s = 1, 2, 3, 4.

6.G-8#4.title: It is a single layer
6.G-8#4.text: An edge of 1 means the box is only one cube thick. Lay it flat and it looks like a 3-by-5 rectangle of cubes. Count the rows: 5 + 5 + 5 = 15 cubes. With just one layer, the volume is the same number as the area of the floor: 15 cubic units.

6.G-8#5.title: Find the ten
6.G-8#5.text: The edges can be multiplied in any order. Pair 2 with 5 first, since 2 × 5 = 10. Then multiply by the edge that is left: 10 × 4 = 40 cubic units. This is like standing the box on its 2-by-5 face and stacking 4 layers of 10.

6.G-8#6.title: Row, square, cube
6.G-8#6.text: Build the cube in three stages. Put 3 blocks in a row. Lay 3 of those rows side by side to make a flat square of 9 blocks. Stack 3 of those squares to make the cube: 9, 18, 27 blocks. Each stage is 3 times the one before, which is what 3 × 3 × 3 means.

6.G-8#7.title: Two half cubes
6.G-8#7.text: The 1-by-2 floor is made of two unit squares. The box is only ½ tall, so above each square sits half of a unit cube. Two halves make one whole. The box holds exactly 1 cubic unit, even though one edge is 2 long.

6.G-8#8.title: Chop the stick and bundle it
6.G-8#8.text: This box is a long thin stick, ½ by ½ and 4 long. Chop it into four pieces that are each 1 long. Stand the four pieces together in a 2-by-2 bundle. The bundle is ½ + ½ = 1 wide, 1 deep and 1 tall. It is a unit cube, so the stick holds 1 cubic unit.

6.G-8#9.title: Halve the 8 first
6.G-8#9.text: Let the fraction meet the biggest even edge. Half of 8 is 4. Then multiply by the last edge: 4 × 3 = 12 cubic units. Halving 8 at the start keeps every number small, and the answer is the same 12.

6.G-8#10.title: Trap it between two boxes
6.G-8#10.text: The edge 3½ is halfway between 3 and 4. A box 3 × 2 × 4 holds 24 cubic units. A box 4 × 2 × 4 holds 32 cubic units. The real box must be halfway between them. Halfway between 24 and 32 is 28, so the volume is 28 cubic units.

6.G-9#1.title: Read it like a ruler
6.G-9#1.text: Lay a ruler along a horizontal segment. If one end sits at the 3 mark and the other end at the 11 mark, the segment is 11 − 3 = 8 long. You do not care where on the page the ruler lies. The points (3, 2) and (11, 2) work the same way: the shared 2 says where the ruler lies, and the x-values are the marks. The length is 8.

6.G-9#2.title: Read it like a thermometer
6.G-9#2.text: A thermometer is a vertical number line. If the reading climbs from 2 degrees to 9 degrees, it has risen 9 − 2 = 7 degrees. The points (4, 2) and (4, 9) are just like that. The shared x-value, 4, says which vertical line the thermometer stands on. The y-values are the two readings, and the segment is 7 units long.

6.G-9#3.title: From owing to having
6.G-9#3.text: Say you owe a friend 3 dollars, which is like standing at −3. Later you have 2 dollars of your own. How much money came in? You needed 3 dollars to pay off the debt and 2 more to keep, so 5 dollars. The amount is positive even though you started below zero. That is why the distance from −3 to 2 is 5.

6.G-9#4.title: Check by counting squares
6.G-9#4.text: A rectangle has corners (1, 2), (6, 2), (6, 5) and (1, 5). Across the bottom, x goes from 1 to 6, which is 5 units. Up the side, y goes from 2 to 5, which is 3 units. The area is 5 × 3 = 15. Draw it on a grid and count: 5 columns with 3 squares in each is 15 squares.

6.G-9#5.title: Hop along the line
6.G-9#5.text: Both points sit on the line y = 1. Start at x = 2 and hop one unit to the right each time. The hops land on 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7. That took 5 hops, so the segment is 5 units long.

6.G-9#6.title: Slide it down to the axis
6.G-9#6.text: Both points have x = 1, so the segment is vertical. Slide it down 2 units so the bottom end rests on the x-axis. The ends are now (1, 0) and (1, 4), and the length reads straight off: 4 units. Sliding moves a segment but does not stretch it.

6.G-9#7.title: Slide it to start at zero
6.G-9#7.text: Move the whole segment 3 units to the right. The point (−3, 4) lands on (0, 4) and the point (2, 4) lands on (5, 4). The length has not changed, and now it is easy to see: from 0 to 5 is 5 units. The negative sign is gone before any subtracting starts.

6.G-9#8.title: Two triangles from a diagonal
6.G-9#8.text: Draw the diagonal from (0, 0) to (4, 3). It cuts the rectangle into two right triangles, each with legs 4 and 3. Each triangle has area ½ × 4 × 3 = 6. The two together give 6 + 6 = 12 square units, the same as width times height.

6.G-9#9.title: Two rows of five
6.G-9#9.text: Sketch the rectangle on the grid. It is only 2 units tall, so it has 2 rows of squares. Each row runs from x = 0 to x = 5 and holds 5 squares. The area is 5 + 5 = 10 square units.

6.G-9#10.title: Split along the axes
6.G-9#10.text: The axes cut this rectangle into four pieces. Left of the y-axis the width is 2, and right of it the width is 3. Below the x-axis the height is 1, and above it the height is 2. The pieces are 2 × 1 = 2, 3 × 1 = 3, 2 × 2 = 4 and 3 × 2 = 6. Their sum is 2 + 3 + 4 + 6 = 15 square units.

6.G-9#11.title: Shift it off the negatives
6.G-9#11.text: Slide the rectangle 3 units to the right. Its left edge moves from x = −3 to x = 0, and its right edge moves from x = 4 to x = 7. A slide does not change the width. Now the width reads directly: from 0 to 7 is 7 units.

6.G-10#1.title: The hidden sides of a die
6.G-10#1.text: Hold a die and look at it from one corner. You can see at most three of its numbers. The other three are on the back and underneath. Now imagine the die unfolded into a flat cross of six squares. All the numbers from 1 to 6 show at once. A net does that for any box, which makes it easy to check that all six faces are counted.

6.G-10#2.title: Cardboard for a tissue box
6.G-10#2.text: A tissue box is 4 long, 2 wide and 3 tall. To make it you cut six pieces of cardboard. The top and bottom are 4 × 2 = 8 each. The front and back are 4 × 3 = 12 each. The two ends are 2 × 3 = 6 each. The cardboard needed is 8 + 8 + 12 + 12 + 6 + 6 = 52 square units, counting every face once.

6.G-10#3.title: A table of cube surfaces
6.G-10#3.text: Try a few edges and watch the pattern. Edge 1: each face is 1, so the surface is 6. Edge 2: each face is 4, so the surface is 24. Edge 4: each face is 16, so the surface is 96. Edge 10: each face is 100, so the surface is 600. Every time, you square the edge and then take 6 of them.

6.G-10#4.title: Label plus two lids
6.G-10#4.text: Think of a box as a label wrapped around four sides, with a lid on top and a lid on the bottom. For a box 4 by 3 on the floor and 2 tall, the label is 4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 14 long and 2 tall, so it covers 28. Each lid is 4 × 3 = 12. The total is 28 + 12 + 12 = 52. The pairs formula gives 2 × (12 + 8 + 6) = 52 too.

6.G-10#5.title: Count the room you are in
6.G-10#5.text: A room is shaped like a rectangular prism. Look down: there is 1 floor. Look up: there is 1 ceiling. Turn all the way around and count the walls: 4. That is 1 + 1 + 4 = 6 flat surfaces. Every face has been looked at once, so the prism has 6 faces.

6.G-10#6.title: Strip around the sides
6.G-10#6.text: Unroll the four side faces into one strip. It is 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12 long and 3 tall, so it covers 36. The top and the bottom are squares of 9 each. The total is 36 + 9 + 9 = 54 square units.

6.G-10#7.title: Sides first, then the ends
6.G-10#7.text: The four side faces make a strip 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20 long and 5 tall. That strip covers 20 × 5 = 100. The top and bottom squares are 25 each, which adds 50. The surface area is 100 + 50 = 150 square units.

6.G-10#8.title: Wrap the 3-by-4 base
6.G-10#8.text: Stand the prism on its 3-by-4 face, so it is 2 tall. The distance around the base is 3 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 14. A strip that long and 2 tall covers the four sides: 14 × 2 = 28. The top and bottom are 12 each, adding 24. The surface area is 28 + 24 = 52 square units.

6.G-10#9.title: Write out all six
6.G-10#9.text: List every face instead of doubling at the end. Top and bottom: 2 and 2. Front and back: 3 and 3. Left and right: 6 and 6. Add them in order: 2 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 6 + 6 = 22 square units. Seeing six numbers in the sum is a quick check that no face was skipped.

6.G-10#10.title: Read the net as a strip
6.G-10#10.text: In the net, four rectangles sit in a row and fold around the 2-by-3 ends. That row is 2 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 10 long and 4 tall, so it covers 40. The two end flaps are 2 × 3 = 6 each. The whole net covers 40 + 6 + 6 = 52 square units.

6.G-10#11.title: A band and two big faces
6.G-10#11.text: Lay the prism on its 5-by-6 face, so it is 2 tall. A band around the four thin sides is 5 + 6 + 5 + 6 = 22 long and 2 tall, covering 44. The top and the bottom are 5 × 6 = 30 each, adding 60. The surface area is 44 + 60 = 104 square units.

6.NS-1#1.title: See what goes wrong
6.NS-1#1.text:
Try 3.4 + 1.25 the wrong way, with the last digits lined up. The 4 lands under the 5 and the 3 under the 2, so you really add 0.34 + 1.25 and get 1.59.
A quick estimate catches it: 3 and a bit plus 1 and a bit must be more than 4.
With the points lined up, the sum is 4.65, which fits the estimate.

6.NS-1#2.title: Tenths traded for hundredths
6.NS-1#2.text:
Picture a square cut into 10 strips. Shading 4 strips shows 0.4.
Now cut every strip into 10 small squares. The same shaded part is 40 small squares out of 100, which is 0.40.
Nothing was added or removed, so 0.4 = 0.40. The zero only says the pieces were cut smaller.

6.NS-1#3.title: An estimate agrees
6.NS-1#3.text:
Take 2.6 + 3.45. Added as plain digits, 260 + 345 gives 605. Where does the point go?
Round the numbers: 3 + 3 = 6, so the answer has to be near 6. Only 6.05 fits. 60.5 and 0.605 are far too big or too small.
The estimate puts the point in the same column as the points above it, every time.

6.NS-1#4.title: Jump along a number line
6.NS-1#4.text:
Draw a number line from 0 to 1 with a mark at every tenth.
Start at 0.3, which is the third mark. Adding 0.4 means jumping 4 marks to the right: 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7.
You land on the seventh mark, so 0.3 + 0.4 = 0.7.

6.NS-1#5.title: Wholes first, then parts
6.NS-1#5.text:
Split each number into its whole part and its decimal part: 3.4 is 3 and 0.4, and 1.25 is 1 and 0.25.
Add the wholes: 3 + 1 = 4.
Add the parts as money: 40 cents plus 25 cents is 65 cents, or 0.65.
Put them back together: 4 + 0.65 = 4.65.

6.NS-1#6.title: Count it in quarters
6.NS-1#6.text:
Think of the numbers as money. 0.75 is three quarters of a dollar, and 0.5 is half a dollar, which is two quarters.
Three quarters plus two quarters makes five quarters.
Four of them make one whole dollar, with one quarter left over. One dollar and one quarter is 1.25.

6.NS-1#7.title: Count up from 2.3
6.NS-1#7.text:
A subtraction is the gap between two numbers, so count up from 2.3 to 5.
From 2.3 to 3 is a jump of 0.7.
From 3 to 5 is a jump of 2.
The gap is 2 + 0.7 = 2.7, with no borrowing needed.

6.NS-1#8.title: Make a whole number first
6.NS-1#8.text:
2.6 is only 0.4 short of 3, so move 0.4 over from the other number.
2.6 + 0.4 = 3, and 3.45 − 0.4 = 3.05.
The total has not changed, because what one number gained the other lost.
Now the sum is easy: 3 + 3.05 = 6.05.

6.NS-1#9.title: Count up, no borrowing
6.NS-1#9.text:
Find the gap by counting up from 1.75 to 4.2.
From 1.75 to 2 is a jump of 0.25, like one more quarter making 2 dollars.
From 2 to 4.2 is a jump of 2.2.
Add the jumps: 0.25 + 2.2 = 2.45. That is the same answer the borrowing gave.

6.NS-1#10.title: Subtract dollars, then dimes
6.NS-1#10.text:
Take the 2.30 away in two easy bites.
First remove the 2 whole dollars: 5.00 − 2.00 = 3.00.
Then remove the 30 cents. Thirty cents off 3 dollars leaves 2 dollars and 70 cents.
So the answer is 2.70, the same as 270 cents.

6.NS-2#1.title: Watch the pattern shrink
6.NS-2#1.text:
Start with whole numbers: 4 × 3 = 12.
Make one factor ten times smaller: 0.4 × 3 = 1.2. The answer is ten times smaller too.
Make the other factor ten times smaller as well: 0.4 × 0.3 = 0.12. The answer shrinks by ten again.
Two decimal places in the factors meant two shrinks by ten, so two decimal places in the answer.

6.NS-2#2.title: A dime of a dime
6.NS-2#2.text:
One tenth of a dollar is a dime. One tenth of a dime is a penny, and a penny is one hundredth of a dollar. So 0.1 × 0.1 = 0.01.
Now 0.6 × 0.4 is 6 tenths of 4 dimes. That makes 6 × 4 = 24 of those pennies, which is 0.24.
Tenths of tenths are always hundredths.

6.NS-2#3.title: Change the unit, not the count
6.NS-2#3.text:
Cut 4.8 meters of ribbon into pieces 0.6 meters long. How many pieces?
Measure in tenths of a meter instead. The ribbon is 48 tenths long and each piece is 6 tenths long, so there are 48 ÷ 6 = 8 pieces.
Changing the unit did not change the ribbon or the pieces. That is all sliding both points does.

6.NS-2#4.title: Trap the answer between two products
6.NS-2#4.text:
Take 4.8 × 2.5. The digits come from 48 × 25 = 1200.
Now trap the answer. It must be more than 4 × 2 = 8 and less than 5 × 3 = 15.
Of 1.2, 12 and 120, only 12 lies between 8 and 15.
So 4.8 × 2.5 = 12, and the point was placed without counting any places.

6.NS-2#5.title: Multiply them as fractions
6.NS-2#5.text:
Write each decimal as tenths: 0.3 is 3/10 and 0.7 is 7/10.
Multiply tops and bottoms: 3 × 7 = 21 and 10 × 10 = 100, so the product is 21/100.
Twenty-one hundredths is written 0.21. The 100 on the bottom is where the two decimal places come from.

6.NS-2#6.title: Shade a hundred grid
6.NS-2#6.text:
Draw a square with 10 columns and 10 rows, so each small square is one hundredth.
Shade 6 columns for 0.6. Inside those columns, keep only 4 rows for 0.4.
The part shaded both ways is 6 squares wide and 4 squares tall, so it has 24 small squares.
24 hundredths is 0.24.

6.NS-2#7.title: Add it three times
6.NS-2#7.text:
Multiplying by 3 means adding the number three times: 1.2 + 1.2 + 1.2.
The wholes give 1 + 1 + 1 = 3.
The tenths give 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 tenths, which is 0.6.
Together that is 3 + 0.6 = 3.6, the same answer as counting places.

6.NS-2#8.title: Count half-dollar coins
6.NS-2#8.text:
Think of 2.5 as 2 dollars and 50 cents, and 0.5 as one half-dollar coin.
How many half-dollar coins make that amount? Each dollar is 2 coins, so 2 dollars is 4 coins.
The extra 50 cents is 1 more coin.
That makes 4 + 1 = 5 coins, so 2.5 ÷ 0.5 = 5.

6.NS-2#9.title: Skip-count by 0.6
6.NS-2#9.text:
The division asks how many jumps of 0.6 it takes to reach 4.8.
Count them: 0.6, 1.2, 1.8, 2.4, 3.0, 3.6, 4.2, 4.8.
The eighth jump lands exactly on 4.8, with nothing left over.
Eight jumps were needed, so 4.8 ÷ 0.6 = 8.

6.NS-2#10.title: Take half of 0.8
6.NS-2#10.text:
The decimal 0.5 is one half, so 0.5 × 0.8 means half of 0.8.
0.8 is 8 tenths, and half of 8 tenths is 4 tenths.
So the product is 0.4. No zero ever shows up this way, which confirms that 0.40 and 0.4 are the same number.

6.NS-2#11.title: Use cents
6.NS-2#11.text:
Read 0.4 as 40 cents. Then 0.6 × 0.4 asks for 0.6 of 40 cents.
One tenth of 40 cents is 4 cents, so six tenths is 6 × 4 = 24 cents.
24 cents written as part of a dollar is 0.24, which matches the fraction method.

6.NS-3#1.title: Making identical kits
6.NS-3#1.text:
You have 12 pencils and 18 erasers and want to pack identical kits with nothing left over.
The number of kits must divide 12 and also divide 18. You could make 1, 2, 3 or 6 kits.
The most kits you can make is 6, each with 2 pencils and 3 erasers. That largest number of kits is the GCF.

6.NS-3#2.title: Packs that come out even
6.NS-3#2.text:
Sausages come in packs of 4 and buns in packs of 6. You want the same number of each, with none left over.
Sausage totals can be 4, 8, 12, 16. Bun totals can be 6, 12, 18.
The smallest total you can make both ways is 12: three packs of sausages and two packs of buns. That is the LCM of 4 and 6.

6.NS-3#3.title: Test it on 8 and 12
6.NS-3#3.text:
The GCF of 8 and 12 is 4, and 4 is smaller than both numbers. The LCM is 24, and 24 is bigger than both.
In order, the four numbers are 4, 8, 12, 24: GCF first, LCM last.
A quick test for any answer: a GCF must divide both numbers, and both numbers must divide an LCM.

6.NS-3#4.title: Bags of beads
6.NS-3#4.text:
You have 18 red beads and 24 blue beads, and you fill 6 identical bags.
Each bag gets 18 ÷ 6 = 3 red beads and 24 ÷ 6 = 4 blue beads.
So all the beads together are 6 bags of (3 + 4) beads.
That is the same as writing 18 + 24 = 6(3 + 4). Both ways count 42 beads.

6.NS-3#5.title: Use prime factors
6.NS-3#5.text:
Break each number into primes: 8 = 2 × 2 × 2 and 12 = 2 × 2 × 3.
Match up what they share. Both have two 2s. The third 2 belongs only to 8, and the 3 belongs only to 12.
Multiply the shared primes: 2 × 2 = 4. So the GCF is 4, the same as the lists gave.

6.NS-3#6.title: Test the factors of 12
6.NS-3#6.text:
The GCF cannot be bigger than 12, so try the factors of 12 from the top: 12, 6, 4, 3, 2, 1.
Does 12 divide 18? No, there is 6 left over.
Does 6 divide 18? Yes, 18 ÷ 6 = 3.
The first one that works is the greatest, so the GCF is 6.

6.NS-3#7.title: Check multiples of 6 only
6.NS-3#7.text:
The LCM has to be a multiple of 6, so there is no need to list the multiples of 4. Just test each multiple of 6.
6 ÷ 4 leaves 2 over, so 6 fails.
12 ÷ 4 = 3 exactly, so 12 works.
The first multiple of 6 that 4 divides is 12, so the LCM is 12.

6.NS-3#8.title: Test the multiples of 5
6.NS-3#8.text:
Go through the multiples of 5 and ask each time whether 3 divides it.
5 ÷ 3 leaves 2 over. 10 ÷ 3 leaves 1 over. 15 ÷ 3 = 5 exactly.
So 15 is the first number that both 3 and 5 divide, and the LCM is 15.
It took three tries because 3 and 5 share no factor.

6.NS-3#9.title: List the factors
6.NS-3#9.text:
Write every factor of each number.
16: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.
24: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24.
The numbers on both lists are 1, 2, 4 and 8. The largest is 8, so the GCF is 8, the same as the prime method gave.

6.NS-3#10.title: Rows of dots
6.NS-3#10.text:
Draw 18 dots as 6 rows of 3. Next to them draw 24 dots as 6 rows of 4.
Push the two blocks together. Now there are 6 rows, and each row has 3 + 4 dots.
The picture shows 18 + 24 = 6(3 + 4). Counting it as 6 rows of 7 gives 42 dots either way.

6.NS-3#11.title: Multiply, then divide by the GCF
6.NS-3#11.text:
Multiply the two numbers: 4 × 6 = 24. This is a common multiple, but it may be too big.
It is too big because 4 and 6 share a factor of 2, which got counted twice.
Divide it out once: 24 ÷ 2 = 12.
So the LCM is 12, matching the prime factor method.

6.NS-4#1.title: Floors in a building
6.NS-4#1.text:
Think of a tall building with a parking garage under it. The ground floor is 0.
Floors above ground are 1, 2, 3 and so on. The basement levels go the other way: one level down is −1, two levels down is −2.
An elevator at −3 is three levels under the ground floor. The minus sign tells you which side of the ground floor you are on.

6.NS-4#2.title: Who has to catch up?
6.NS-4#2.text:
Two players have scores of −7 and −2. Who is ahead?
The player at −7 needs 5 more points to reach −2, because −7 + 5 = −2.
The one who has to add points to catch up has the smaller score. So −7 is less than −2, even though 7 looks bigger than 2.

6.NS-4#3.title: The trip meter
6.NS-4#3.text:
A car's trip meter counts miles driven. Drive 7 miles east of home and it reads 7. Drive 7 miles west of home and it also reads 7.
The meter never shows a negative number, because it does not care which way you went.
Absolute value is that meter: |7| = 7 and |−7| = 7.

6.NS-4#4.title: Use the sign rule
6.NS-4#4.text:
There is a rule that works without a picture. If the number inside the bars is positive or zero, leave it alone. If it is negative, take its opposite.
Here the number inside is −7, which is negative. Its opposite is 7.
So |−7| = 7, the same as the seven steps counted on the number line.

6.NS-4#5.title: What must be added?
6.NS-4#5.text:
Ask how to get from one number to the other.
Start at −5. Adding 3 takes you to −2, because −5 + 3 = −2.
Adding a positive amount always makes a number greater. So the number you arrive at, −2, is greater than the number you left, −5.

6.NS-4#6.title: Read it as a debt
6.NS-4#6.text:
Think of −15 as a bank balance. The account is 15 dollars below zero.
How big is the debt? You would need to pay in 15 dollars to get back to a balance of 0.
The size of the debt is 15, with no minus sign. That size is the absolute value: |−15| = 15.

6.NS-4#7.title: Sort by sign, then by debt
6.NS-4#7.text:
First split the numbers by sign. 2 is the only positive number, so it is the greatest and goes last.
The other two are negative. Read them as debts: −8 means owing 8 and −3 means owing 3. The bigger debt is the worse one, so −8 is the least.
The order is −8, −3, 2.

6.NS-4#8.title: Flip the diver above the water
6.NS-4#8.text:
Imagine the diver's position mirrored above the surface. A depth of 30 ft becomes a height of 30 ft.
Now both are on the same side and easy to compare: 30 ft up against the kite's 12 ft up.
30 is more than 12, by 18 ft. So the diver is the one farther from sea level.

6.NS-4#9.title: Read a thermometer
6.NS-4#9.text:
Turn the two numbers into temperatures: −5 degrees and −2 degrees.
On a thermometer, −5 is five marks below zero and −2 is only two marks below zero, so −2 is higher up the tube.
Higher on the thermometer means warmer, and warmer means the greater number. So −2 > −5.

6.NS-5#1.title: Like a claw machine
6.NS-5#1.text:
A claw machine has two controls. One slides the claw sideways and the other moves it forward or back. A point works the same way, with x as the sideways control.
For (−4, 1): slide 4 to the left, then go 1 up.
For (4, −1): slide 4 to the right, then go 1 down. Same digits, different signs, and a completely different spot.

6.NS-5#2.title: One point in each quadrant
6.NS-5#2.text:
Take the numbers 2 and 5 and try every pair of signs.
(2, 5) is right and up: Quadrant I.
(−2, 5) is left and up: Quadrant II.
(−2, −5) is left and down: Quadrant III.
(2, −5) is right and down: Quadrant IV.
Going through them in this order traces a circle counterclockwise around the origin.

6.NS-5#3.title: Floors in one elevator shaft
6.NS-5#3.text:
Two points with the same x are like two floors served by the same elevator. The ride is straight up or down.
From floor 1 to floor 7 the elevator passes 6 floors.
From basement level −2 to floor 3 it goes 2 up to the ground floor and 3 more, so 5 floors.
The number of floors travelled is the distance, and it is never negative.

6.NS-5#4.title: Flip a whole triangle
6.NS-5#4.text:
Take a triangle with corners (1, 1), (4, 1) and (4, 3) and reflect it across the y-axis.
The corners become (−1, 1), (−4, 1) and (−4, 3).
Every height is unchanged: 1, 1 and 3. Every x has the same size but the other sign.
The triangle has the same shape and now sits on the left side instead of the right.

6.NS-5#5.title: Read the signs first
6.NS-5#5.text:
You can name the region before plotting anything.
The x-coordinate, −2, is negative, so the point must be on the left half of the plane.
The y-coordinate, 3, is positive, so it must be on the top half.
The only region that is both left and top is Quadrant II, and plotting the point agrees.

6.NS-5#6.title: Start from a point you know
6.NS-5#6.text:
The point (3, 5) has two positive coordinates, so it is in Quadrant I, the top right.
The point (−3, 5) is at the same height, 5, but on the other side of the y-axis. It is the mirror image of (3, 5).
Moving straight across from the top right puts you in the top left, which is Quadrant II.

6.NS-5#7.title: Rule out quadrants
6.NS-5#7.text:
Use one coordinate at a time to cross out quadrants.
x = 6 is positive, so the point is on the right side. That leaves Quadrants I and IV.
y = −2 is negative, so the point is on the bottom half. That leaves Quadrants III and IV.
The only quadrant on both lists is IV.

6.NS-5#8.title: Slide both points down
6.NS-5#8.text:
Moving both points by the same amount does not change how far apart they are.
Slide each point down 1 unit. (2, 1) becomes (2, 0) and (2, 6) becomes (2, 5).
Now one point sits on the x-axis and the other is at height 5, so the distance is clearly 5 units.

6.NS-5#9.title: List the x-values
6.NS-5#9.text:
Both points are at height 4, so walk along that line and write down each x-value you pass.
Starting at −3, the next ones are −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
That is 8 moves of one unit each to get from −3 to 5, so the points are 8 units apart.

6.NS-5#10.title: Use the sign rule
6.NS-5#10.text:
Reflections across the y-axis follow one short rule: change the sign of x and keep y.
For (4, 3), the x-coordinate 4 becomes −4. The y-coordinate 3 stays as it is.
The image is (−4, 3). The rule gives the same point as measuring 4 steps to the mirror and 4 steps beyond it.

6.NS-5#11.title: Fold the paper
6.NS-5#11.text:
Plot (3, 2) on grid paper and fold the paper along the y-axis.
The right half lands on top of the left half. The dot at (3, 2) presses onto the square that is 3 to the left of the fold and still 2 up.
Unfold the paper. The mark is at (−3, 2), which is the reflection.

6.NS-6#1.title: Scoops of sugar
6.NS-6#1.text:
A recipe needs 1/2 cup of sugar, but you only have a 1/4 cup scoop. You need 2 scoops, so 1/2 ÷ 1/4 = 2.
With an even smaller 1/8 cup scoop you would need 4 scoops.
The amount of sugar stayed the same. The smaller the scoop, the more scoops it takes, so dividing by a small fraction gives a large count.

6.NS-6#2.title: Test it by multiplying back
6.NS-6#2.text:
Division can always be checked with multiplication, because 12 ÷ 3 = 4 means 4 × 3 = 12.
Keep-Change-Flip says 3/4 ÷ 1/2 = 3/4 × 2/1 = 6/4, which is 3/2.
Check it: 3/2 × 1/2 = 3/4. The answer times the divisor gives back the starting fraction, so the rule has found the right number.

6.NS-6#3.title: Follow the pattern down
6.NS-6#3.text:
Look at what happens as the divisor gets smaller.
8 ÷ 4 = 2. 8 ÷ 2 = 4. 8 ÷ 1 = 8.
Each time the divisor is cut in half, the answer doubles. Keep going: 8 ÷ 1/2 must be 16, and 8 ÷ 1/4 must be 32.
Those are 8 × 2 and 8 × 4. Dividing by 1/2 or 1/4 is multiplying by the flipped number.

6.NS-6#4.title: Count squares in a grid
6.NS-6#4.text:
Find 2/3 × 4/5 with a rectangle. Cut it into 3 rows and 5 columns, which makes 3 × 5 = 15 equal squares.
Shade 2 of the rows and keep 4 of the columns. The part that counts is 2 × 4 = 8 squares.
So the product is 8/15. The tops gave the squares you keep, and the bottoms gave the squares in all.

6.NS-6#5.title: Rename the half as quarters
6.NS-6#5.text:
Give both fractions the same bottom. One half is the same as 2/4.
Now the problem is 2/4 ÷ 1/4: how many single quarters fit into two quarters?
Two of them fit, so the answer is 2. No flipping was needed, and it matches Keep-Change-Flip.

6.NS-6#6.title: Jump along a ruler
6.NS-6#6.text:
Draw a line from 0 to 1 and mark it in sixths: 1/6, 2/6, 3/6 and so on.
One third is at the mark 2/6.
Start at 0 and take jumps of 1/6. The first jump lands on 1/6 and the second lands on 2/6, which is 1/3.
It took 2 jumps, so 1/3 ÷ 1/6 = 2.

6.NS-6#7.title: Fit the halves in
6.NS-6#7.text:
Picture a bar that is 3/4 long, made of three quarter pieces.
One half is two quarters, so one full half fits and uses two of the pieces.
One quarter piece is left. A quarter is half of a half, so it counts as 1/2 of another piece.
In all, 1 and 1/2 halves fit, and 1 and 1/2 is 3/2.

6.NS-6#8.title: Cut the thirds into sixths
6.NS-6#8.text:
Two pieces are hard to share among 4 people, so cut each third in half.
Now 2/3 is 4 pieces, and each piece is 1/6 of the whole.
Four pieces shared among 4 people is one piece each.
Each person gets 1/6, the same answer as Keep-Change-Flip.

6.NS-6#9.title: Use sixths for both
6.NS-6#9.text:
Rename 1/2 so both fractions are counted in sixths: 1/2 = 3/6.
Now the problem is 5/6 ÷ 3/6, which asks how many groups of 3 sixths fit into 5 sixths.
That is just 5 ÷ 3, or 5/3.
One full group fits with 2 sixths left over, which is 2/3 of a group, so 1 and 2/3 agrees.

6.NS-6#10.title: Switch to decimals
6.NS-6#10.text:
Both fractions are easy to write as decimals: 3/4 = 0.75 and 1/2 = 0.5.
Divide 0.75 ÷ 0.5. Slide both points one place to get 7.5 ÷ 5, which is 1.5.
The decimal 1.5 is one and a half, and that is 3/2. A third method gives the same answer.

6.NS-7#1.title: What a crooked stack does
6.NS-7#1.text:
Try 482 + 37 with the 37 pushed one column too far left, so the 3 sits under the 4 and the 7 under the 8.
The columns now add 482 + 370, which gives 852.
An estimate shows the mistake: 480 + 40 is about 520.
Stacked correctly, with the 7 under the 2, the sum is 519.

6.NS-7#2.title: Split into tens and ones
6.NS-7#2.text:
Add 48 + 27 by breaking each number apart.
The tens are 40 + 20 = 60. The ones are 8 + 7 = 15.
But 15 is really 10 + 5, so it holds one more ten. Move that ten over: 60 + 10 = 70, and 5 ones are left.
The sum is 75. Carrying the 1 is this same move, written in a shorter way.

6.NS-7#3.title: Rename the top number
6.NS-7#3.text:
Take 52 − 27. As 50 + 2 the top number does not have enough ones, so write it as 40 + 12. It is still 52.
Now subtract each part: 40 − 20 = 20 and 12 − 7 = 5.
The answer is 20 + 5 = 25.
Borrowing is exactly this renaming: one ten is moved over and counted as ten ones.

6.NS-7#4.title: Add the tens, then the ones
6.NS-7#4.text:
Start at 34 and add 25 in two jumps.
First add the 2 tens: 34 + 20 = 54.
Then add the 5 ones: 54 + 5 = 59.
Working from the big part to the small part is easy to do in your head, and it gives the same 59.

6.NS-7#5.title: Add from the left
6.NS-7#5.text:
Add each place value on its own, starting with the biggest.
Hundreds: 600 + 200 = 800.
Tens: 10 + 70 = 80.
Ones: 8 + 4 = 12.
Now add the three results: 800 + 80 + 12 = 892. The 12 ones are what caused the carry in the column method.

6.NS-7#6.title: Use the friendly neighbor 375
6.NS-7#6.text:
375 would be a friendlier number than 376, because 425 + 375 is exactly 800: the 25 and the 75 make another hundred.
But 376 is 1 more than 375, so the real sum is 1 more than 800.
425 + 376 = 801, with no carrying to keep track of.

6.NS-7#7.title: Subtract in three bites
6.NS-7#7.text:
Take 387 away one place value at a time: 300, then 80, then 7.
952 − 300 = 652.
652 − 80 = 572.
572 − 7 = 565.
Each bite is easy enough to do in your head, and the result matches the column method.

6.NS-7#8.title: Subtract from 499 first
6.NS-7#8.text:
All the borrowing comes from the zeros in 500. So use 499 instead, which is 1 less.
499 − 173 needs no borrowing at all: 9 − 3 = 6, 9 − 7 = 2, 4 − 1 = 3, giving 326.
The real top number was 1 bigger, so the answer is 1 bigger too: 326 + 1 = 327.

6.NS-7#9.title: Count up from 247
6.NS-7#9.text:
Find the gap between 247 and 1003 by counting up.
From 247 to 250 is 3.
From 250 to 1000 is 750.
From 1000 to 1003 is 3 more.
Add the jumps: 3 + 750 + 3 = 756. No borrowing across zeros is needed.

6.NS-7#10.title: Take away 200, then give back
6.NS-7#10.text:
187 is close to 200, and 200 is easy to subtract: 1250 − 200 = 1050.
That took away too much. 200 is 13 more than 187, so put 13 back.
1050 + 13 = 1063.
This agrees with the total of the jumps from counting up.

6.NS-8#1.title: Think of heights
6.NS-8#1.text:
Use height above or below sea level in place of a number line. A hilltop is at 40 meters, the beach is at 0, a reef is at −6 and a shipwreck is at −30.
The higher place always has the greater number: 40 > 0 > −6 > −30.
This holds above the water, below the water, and across the surface.

6.NS-8#2.title: Zero stands in between
6.NS-8#2.text:
To compare −100 and 1, go through zero.
−100 is less than 0, because it is negative. 0 is less than 1, because 1 is positive.
Chain them: −100 < 0 < 1. So −100 < 1.
The same two steps work for any negative and any positive, which is why you never need to look at the digits.

6.NS-8#3.title: A mirror reverses the order
6.NS-8#3.text:
On the positive side, 4 comes before 9, so 4 < 9.
The negative side is a mirror image of the positive side, and a mirror swaps left and right. The order of the reflections is reversed: −9 comes before −4.
So −9 < −4, which is the same as −4 > −9. Flip both signs and the inequality sign flips too.

6.NS-8#4.title: Count the steps to the right
6.NS-8#4.text:
Start at −3 on the number line and walk toward 1.
The steps go −2, −1, 0, 1. That is 4 steps, all of them to the right.
You had to move right to get from −3 to 1, so 1 is the greater number. In symbols, −3 + 4 = 1.

6.NS-8#5.title: Add to get across
6.NS-8#5.text:
Start at −9 and ask what must be added to reach −4.
You need to add 5, because −9 + 5 = −4.
Adding a positive number makes a number greater. So the number you reach, −4, is greater than the number you started from, −9.

6.NS-8#6.title: Basement levels
6.NS-8#6.text:
Picture a building with levels under the ground. Level −1 is one floor below the ground floor, and level −7 is seven floors below it.
Level −1 is higher up in the building than level −7.
Higher means greater, so −1 > −7.

6.NS-8#7.title: Think of three wallets
6.NS-8#7.text:
Read each number as money. −5 means owing 5 dollars, −2 means owing 2 dollars, and 0 means having nothing and owing nothing.
The person owing 5 is worst off, then the person owing 2. The person with 0 is best off.
From least to greatest: −5, −2, 0.

6.NS-8#8.title: Sort by sign first
6.NS-8#8.text:
Split the numbers into groups before comparing digits.
2 is the only positive number, so it is the greatest.
−3 and −5 are both negative. Five below zero is lower than three below zero, so −5 is the least.
Put the groups together: −5, −3, 2.

6.NS-8#9.title: Warm every city by 10 degrees
6.NS-8#9.text:
Adding the same amount to every temperature does not change which city is coldest.
Add 10 degrees to each: Oslo becomes 2, Denver becomes 13 and Chicago becomes 8.
Now all three are positive and easy to compare. The smallest is 2, which belongs to Oslo, so Oslo is the coldest.

6.NS-8#10.title: Place them on a line
6.NS-8#10.text:
Draw a number line and put a dot at −8, at −5 and at −2.
The dot at −8 is the furthest to the left. Next comes −5, and −2 is the closest to zero on the right.
Reading the dots from left to right gives least to greatest: −8, −5, −2.

6.NS-9#1.title: The pair that adds to zero
6.NS-9#1.text:
Opposites are two numbers that cancel each other. Earn 5 dollars and then spend 5 dollars, and you are back where you started: 5 + (−5) = 0.
To find the opposite of any number, ask what must be added to get 0.
For −5 the answer is 5. For 0 the answer is 0, so zero is its own opposite.

6.NS-9#2.title: Count the minus signs
6.NS-9#2.text:
Try it with three signs: −(−(−4)).
Work from the inside. The opposite of 4 is −4. The opposite of that is 4. The opposite of that is −4.
Three flips ended on the negative side. An even number of flips always brings the number home, and an odd number leaves it on the other side.

6.NS-9#3.title: A bird and a fish
6.NS-9#3.text:
A bird flies 6 meters above a lake, at +6. A fish swims 6 meters under the surface, at −6.
Both are 6 meters from the surface, so |6| = 6 and |−6| = 6.
A leaf floating on the water is at 0, and its distance from the surface is 0. No distance can be less than that.

6.NS-9#4.title: What adds to zero?
6.NS-9#4.text:
A number and its opposite always add to zero.
So ask: 7 plus what number equals 0?
Going up 7 and then down 7 gets you back to 0, so the missing number is −7.
Check: 7 + (−7) = 0. The opposite of 7 is −7.

6.NS-9#5.title: Opposite of a debt
6.NS-9#5.text:
Read −15 as owing 15 dollars.
The opposite situation is having 15 dollars, which is +15.
The two cancel exactly: if you owe 15 and then get 15, you have nothing left and owe nothing, so −15 + 15 = 0.
The opposite of −15 is 15.

6.NS-9#6.title: Ride the elevator up
6.NS-9#6.text:
Imagine a deep garage where level −12 is twelve floors under the ground floor.
To get back to the ground floor, level 0, the elevator has to go up 12 floors.
The length of that ride is the absolute value. It is 12 floors, so |−12| = 12.

6.NS-9#7.title: Compare with
6.NS-9#7.text:
The bars give the distance from zero, and two numbers are 9 steps from zero: 9 and −9.
For −9 the bars change what you see, because |−9| = 9.
For 9 nothing changes, because 9 is already the distance: |9| = 9.
So the bars only ever change a negative number. A positive number passes through as it is.

6.NS-9#8.title: Find what cancels −3
6.NS-9#8.text:
The expression −(−3) means the opposite of −3, and opposites always add to zero.
So ask what number added to −3 gives 0.
If you owe 3 dollars, getting 3 dollars clears the debt: −3 + 3 = 0.
The number that cancels −3 is 3, so −(−3) = 3.

6.NS-9#9.title: Mark both on one number line
6.NS-9#9.text:
Put both results on the same number line.
The absolute value of −8 is a distance of 8, so mark it at 8, on the right of zero.
The opposite of 8 is the mirror image of 8, so mark it at −8, on the left of zero.
The two marks are 16 units apart, so the two results are certainly not the same.

6.NS-9#10.title: A seal under the ice
6.NS-9#10.text:
A seal is 6 meters under the ice, at −6. The surface is at 0.
To come up for air, the seal has to swim 6 meters.
The swim is a length, so it is written without a minus sign. That length is the absolute value: |−6| = 6.

6.NS-10#1.title: Try it both ways round
6.NS-10#1.text:
Take the points (4, 2) and (4, 9). They share x = 4, so one is straight above the other.
Subtract the y-values one way: 9 − 2 = 7.
Subtract them the other way: 2 − 9 = −7, and the absolute value turns that into 7.
Either order gives 7 units, which is why the rule uses absolute value.

6.NS-10#2.title: Houses on one street
6.NS-10#2.text:
Two points with the same y are like two houses on the same street.
Take (3, 5) and (11, 5). Both are on street number 5, at house 3 and at house 11.
Walking from house 3 to house 11 passes 11 − 3 = 8 house lengths.
The street number never entered the sum. Only the house numbers did.

6.NS-10#3.title: Slide the pair along
6.NS-10#3.text:
Sliding two points by the same amount does not change the gap between them.
Take −2 and 5 and slide both 2 steps to the right. They land on 0 and 7.
The gap from 0 to 7 is plainly 7.
The slide added 2 to the 5, which is exactly what 5 − (−2) = 5 + 2 does.

6.NS-10#4.title: Read it off the corners
6.NS-10#4.text:
Try the corners (2, 1), (8, 1), (8, 5) and (2, 5).
Only two x-values appear, 2 and 8. They are 6 apart, so the width is 6.
Only two y-values appear, 1 and 5. They are 4 apart, so the height is 4.
That gives a perimeter of 6 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 20 units and an area of 6 × 4 = 24 square units.

6.NS-10#5.title: Read the coordinate
6.NS-10#5.text:
The first point is the origin, where every count starts.
The second point, (0, 6), has directions "0 across, 6 up". Those directions describe the trip from the origin.
There is no sideways part, so the whole trip is 6 units straight up. The y-coordinate itself is the distance.

6.NS-10#6.title: Slide both down to the axis
6.NS-10#6.text:
Move both points down by 2 units. The gap between them stays the same.
(3, 2) lands on (3, 0), which is on the x-axis. (3, 7) lands on (3, 5).
A point at height 5 is 5 units above the axis, so the distance is 5 units.

6.NS-10#7.title: Measure both from the y-axis
6.NS-10#7.text:
Both points are at height 4, on the right side of the y-axis.
The point (1, 4) is 1 unit from the y-axis. The point (6, 4) is 6 units from it.
The second point is 6 − 1 = 5 units further out along the same line, so the two points are 5 units apart.

6.NS-10#8.title: Shift everything right by 2
6.NS-10#8.text:
Move both points 2 units to the right, which keeps them the same distance apart.
(−2, 4) lands on (0, 4), right on the y-axis. (5, 4) lands on (7, 4).
Now the trip starts at x = 0 and ends at x = 7, so it is 7 units long.

6.NS-10#9.title: Subtract in the other order
6.NS-10#9.text:
Start from the other point this time and subtract the x-values the other way round.
−3 − 4 = −7. Going down 4 more from −3 lands on −7.
A distance cannot be negative, so take the absolute value: |−7| = 7.
The order of the points does not matter. The distance is 7 units either way.

6.NS-10#10.title: Walk the border, count the squares
6.NS-10#10.text:
For the perimeter, walk around the corners in order: 4 units right, 3 units up, 4 units left and 3 units down. That is 4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 14 units.
For the area, count unit squares. Between x = 1 and x = 5 there are 4 columns, and between y = 1 and y = 4 there are 3 rows. Four columns of 3 squares make 12 square units.

6.NS-10#11.title: Use the subtraction rule
6.NS-10#11.text:
The points share x = 1, so the distance is the absolute value of the difference of the y-values.
|7 − 2| = |5| = 5.
Naming the points in the other order gives |2 − 7| = |−5|, which is also 5.
Both agree with the five steps counted on the grid.

6.RP-1#1.title: A recipe is a ratio
6.RP-1#1.text: A lemonade recipe uses 3 cups of water for every 2 scoops of mix. That is a ratio of 3 to 2. It does not say how much lemonade you make. It only says how the two amounts go together: whenever you pour 3 of one, you add 2 of the other. Written as 3:2, as 3 to 2 or as 3/2, it is still the same recipe.

6.RP-1#2.title: Swap the numbers, change the drink
6.RP-1#2.text: Mix 3 cups of juice with 1 cup of water and the drink is strong. Mix 1 cup of juice with 3 cups of water and it is weak. Both drinks use the numbers 3 and 1, but they are not the same drink. Juice to water is 3:1 for the first and 1:3 for the second. The order of the numbers tells you which drink you get.

6.RP-1#3.title: See it in a table
6.RP-1#3.text: Write 2:3 as a row, then keep adding the same row: 2 and 3, 4 and 6, 6 and 9, 8 and 12. In every row the second number is one and a half times the first. That never changes, because each row is only the first row counted again. Moving back up the table is dividing, which is what simplifying does.

6.RP-1#4.title: Circle matching groups
6.RP-1#4.text: Draw 4 gray squares and 6 white squares. Circle them into 2 matching groups, each with 2 gray and 3 white. Now try to split one group into smaller matching groups. You cannot do it without cutting a square in pieces. That is the signal to stop. The simplest form, 2:3, is the smallest group that still uses whole things.

6.RP-1#5.title: Draw it and count
6.RP-1#5.text:
Draw 3 circles for the cats and 4 squares for the dogs. The question says cats to dogs, so count the circles first, 3, and then the squares, 4. The ratio is 3:4.
Now try to share the drawing into equal smaller groups. Three cats cannot be split into 2 or 4 equal groups of whole cats, so the picture cannot shrink. The answer stays 3:4.

6.RP-1#6.title: Share into two bowls
6.RP-1#6.text: Deal the fruit into 2 bowls so that both bowls get the same. Each bowl ends up with 2 apples and 3 oranges, and nothing is left over. One bowl has the same mix as the big bowl, only smaller, so 4:6 is the same comparison as 2:3. A bowl with 2 apples and 3 oranges cannot be shared evenly again, so the simplest form is 2:3.

6.RP-1#7.title: Ask how many times bigger
6.RP-1#7.text:
Compare the two counts directly. 10 is exactly twice 5, so there are 2 dogs for every 1 cat. Cats are named first in the question, so the ratio is 1:2.
Check by building back up: 5 groups, each with 1 cat and 2 dogs, make 5 cats and 10 dogs. That is the shelter, so 1:2 is right.

6.RP-1#8.title: Label first, then fill blanks
6.RP-1#8.text:
Write a label for each amount: flour 2, milk 3. Then copy the question's words as blanks: milk ___ to flour ___. Fill each blank from its label to get milk 3 to flour 2, which is 3:2.
A quick check: the recipe has more milk than flour, and milk comes first, so the first number should be the bigger one. It is.

6.RP-1#9.title: Treat it as a fraction
6.RP-1#9.text:
Write blue to red as the fraction 6/9. Simplifying a ratio is the same job as simplifying a fraction. Both 6 and 9 are in the 3 times table, so 6/9 becomes 2/3. Turn it back into a ratio: 2:3.
Check: 3 handfuls, each with 2 blue and 3 red marbles, make 6 blue and 9 red.

6.RP-1#10.title: Halve, then halve again
6.RP-1#10.text:
You do not need the biggest factor right away. Both 8 and 12 are even, so halve them: 4:6. Both are still even, so halve again: 2:3. Now 3 is odd, so halving stops, and nothing else divides both 2 and 3.
Two halvings are the same as dividing by 4, so this reaches the same answer, 2:3.

6.RP-1#11.title: Count up from the answer
6.RP-1#11.text:
Check 2:3 by building it back up. List its equivalent ratios by adding 2 and 3 each time: 2:3, 4:6, 6:9, 8:12, 10:15, 12:18.
The sixth ratio in the list is 12:18. So 12:18 is six copies of 2:3, which is why dividing both parts by 6 gives 2:3. No smaller ratio comes before 2:3 in the list.

6.RP-2#1.title: Rates you already know
6.RP-2#1.text: A tap that fills 6 cups in 2 minutes, a job that pays 30 dollars for 3 hours and a heart that beats 70 times in a minute are all rates. Each one joins two different kinds of measure, so both unit names are needed. On its own, 6 in 2 means nothing. Say cups and minutes, and it tells you how fast the sink fills.

6.RP-2#2.title: The first row of the table
6.RP-2#2.text: Write a trip as a table: 2 hours and 100 miles, 3 hours and 150 miles, 4 hours and 200 miles. One row is missing at the top: 1 hour and 50 miles. That row is the unit rate. Every other row is that row multiplied by something, so once you know it you can fill in any row you like.

6.RP-2#3.title: Equal jumps on a number line
6.RP-2#3.text: Draw a line from 0 to 150 miles and mark where the car is after each hour. Three equal jumps must land exactly on 150. Jumps of 50 work, because 50 + 50 + 50 = 150. The length of one jump is the distance for one hour, so the unit rate is 50 miles per hour. Division finds the jump length without the drawing.

6.RP-2#4.title: Deal them out
6.RP-2#4.text: Put the 5 packs in a row and deal the stickers like cards. Round one puts 1 sticker in each pack and uses 5 stickers. Round two puts another sticker in each pack and uses the last 5. The stickers are gone after two rounds, so each pack holds 2 stickers. Dealing in rounds is what dividing by 5 means.

6.RP-2#5.title: Guess and multiply
6.RP-2#5.text: Pick a speed and test it by multiplying by the 3 hours. Try 40 miles per hour: 40 × 3 = 120 miles, which is 30 miles short. The missing 30 miles spread over 3 hours is 10 more for each hour. Try 50 miles per hour: 50 × 3 = 150 miles. That matches the trip, so the car goes 50 miles in one hour.

6.RP-2#6.title: Work in cents
6.RP-2#6.text: Change the money to cents so there is no decimal point: 9 dollars is 900 cents. Share 900 cents among 6 muffins. Since 6 × 100 = 600 and 6 × 50 = 300, and 600 + 300 = 900, each muffin gets 100 + 50 = 150 cents. Written in dollars, 150 cents is 1.50, so one muffin costs 1.50 dollars.

6.RP-2#7.title: Halve the row twice
6.RP-2#7.text: Write the deal as a row: 4 notebooks, 10 dollars. Halve both numbers to get 2 notebooks for 5 dollars. Halve both again to get 1 notebook for 2.50 dollars. Halving twice is the same as dividing by 4, so this is the unit price. Check by doubling back: 2.50, then 5, then 10 dollars for 4 notebooks.

6.RP-2#8.title: Count apples per dollar
6.RP-2#8.text: Turn the question around first. 8 apples for 4 dollars means each dollar buys 8 ÷ 4 = 2 apples. If one dollar is shared by 2 apples, each apple costs half a dollar. Half a dollar is 50 cents, written 0.50 dollars. The answer is less than 1, as it should be when one dollar buys more than one apple.

6.RP-2#9.title: Shrink the pair in steps
6.RP-2#9.text:
Write the run as a pair: 100 meters, 20 seconds. Divide both numbers by 10 to get 10 meters in 2 seconds. Halve both to get 5 meters in 1 second. The pair for 1 second is the unit rate, 5 meters per second.
Check by going forward: 5 meters each second for 20 seconds is 5 × 20 = 100 meters.

6.RP-2#10.title: Check by building back up
6.RP-2#10.text: Test 1.50 dollars per muffin by rebuilding the table from the bottom. One muffin costs 1.50 dollars, so 2 muffins cost 3 dollars. Then 4 muffins cost 6 dollars, and 6 muffins cost 6 + 3 = 9 dollars. That is the price in the question, so 1.50 dollars per muffin is correct.

6.RP-3#1.title: The same fraction every time
6.RP-3#1.text: Write each ratio as a fraction: 1/3, 2/6 and 3/9. All three simplify to 1/3, so they are one number written with different digits. That is what equivalent means. A ratio such as 2:5 does not belong with them, because 2/5 is not 1/3. Simplifying both ratios is a quick test of whether they match.

6.RP-3#2.title: Three patterns in one table
6.RP-3#2.text: Fill a table for 2 cups making 10 cookies: 2 and 10, 4 and 20, 6 and 30, 8 and 40. Read down the cups column and it counts by 2s. Read down the cookies column and it counts by 10s. Read across any row and the cookies are 5 times the cups. A row that breaks any of these patterns has a mistake in it.

6.RP-3#3.title: Why adding does not work
6.RP-3#3.text: Start with 2 cups for 10 cookies, which is 5 cookies from each cup. Suppose you add 2 to both numbers and write 4 cups for 12 cookies. Now each cup makes only 3 cookies, so the row is wrong. Multiply both by 2 instead: 4 cups for 20 cookies, still 5 from each cup. Adding the same number changes a ratio. Multiplying by the same number keeps it.

6.RP-3#4.title: The rule is a straight line
6.RP-3#4.text: Plot the rows 1 and 3, 2 and 6, 3 and 9 as points on a grid. They sit on one straight line that starts at zero. The rule times 3 is how steep the line is: for every 1 across, it goes 3 up. Any new input lands on the same line, so the rule gives its output even when the input is far off the page.

6.RP-3#5.title: Add two rows together
6.RP-3#5.text:
The input 5 is the two known inputs added: 2 + 3 = 5. In a ratio table you can add rows, just as two orders can go in one bag. Add the outputs the same way: 6 + 9 = 15. So 5 turns into 15.
This agrees with the rule, because 5 × 3 is also 15.

6.RP-3#6.title: Skip count down the column
6.RP-3#6.text:
Each time the input goes up by 1, the output goes up by 4: the table shows 4, then 8. Keep counting by 4s, one step for each input: 12 for 3, 16 for 4, 20 for 5 and 24 for 6.
The sixth number in the count is 24, so the output for 6 is 24.

6.RP-3#7.title: Price one pen first
6.RP-3#7.text:
Find what a single pen costs. 3 dollars shared by 4 pens is 300 cents ÷ 4 = 75 cents each. Eight pens cost 8 × 75 cents. Since 4 × 75 is 300, 8 × 75 is 600 cents, which is 6 dollars.
Going through one pen gives the same answer as doubling the order.

6.RP-3#8.title: Read across the row
6.RP-3#8.text: Look across the row instead of down. 10 cookies from 2 cups means the cookie number is 5 times the cup number, since 2 × 5 = 10. That rule holds for every row of the table. Use it on 6 cups: 6 × 5 = 30 cookies. The answer matches tripling the batch.

6.RP-3#9.title: Follow the steps down
6.RP-3#9.text:
Look at how the table moves from one row to the next. The input goes from 3 to 5, up by 2. The output goes from 12 to 20, up by 8. The next input, 7, is 2 more again, so the output goes up by 8 again: 20 + 8 = 28.
Equal steps in one column give equal steps in the other.

6.RP-3#10.title: Go through one
6.RP-3#10.text:
Shrink the known row all the way down. 10 → 40 divided by 10 on both sides gives 1 → 4. Now build up to 5 by multiplying both sides by 5: 5 → 20.
Check by doubling the answer: 5 → 20 doubled is 10 → 40, the row you started from.

6.RP-3#11.title: Stack up batches of two cups
6.RP-3#11.text: Skip the single cup and count whole batches instead. One batch is 2 cups and makes 10 cookies. Two batches are 4 cups and make 20 cookies. Three batches are 6 cups and make 30 cookies. The table reaches 6 cups on the third row, so 6 cups make 30 cookies.

6.RP-4#1.title: Mixing needs only the parts
6.RP-4#1.text: Orange paint made from 3 cups of red and 2 cups of yellow has a part-to-part ratio of 3:2. Neither number is the 5 cups in the can. This kind of ratio is what you follow while mixing: each time you pour 3 cups of red, pour 2 of yellow. You can do that without ever knowing how much paint you will end up with.

6.RP-4#2.title: A test score is part-to-whole
6.RP-4#2.text: A score of 8 out of 10 is a part-to-whole ratio. The 8 right answers are part of the 10 questions. The part-to-part ratio for the same quiz is 8 right to 2 wrong. The second number changed from 2 to 10 because it now counts every question, including the 8 that were already counted as right.

6.RP-4#3.title: One bar shows it all
6.RP-4#3.text: Draw a bar made of 5 equal boxes. Shade 3 boxes for boys and leave 2 white for girls. The whole bar is the class. Three ratios can be read from this one picture: shaded to white is 3:2, shaded to the whole bar is 3:5, and white to the whole bar is 2:5. The bar is as long as the two parts joined end to end.

6.RP-4#4.title: Line up and count
6.RP-4#4.text:
Stand the children in one line: B B B G G. Count everyone in the line: 5. Count only the boys: 3. Boys to the whole group is 3:5.
The boys are counted twice, once as the part and again inside the total. That is correct, because the whole group includes them.

6.RP-4#5.title: Think of a fraction
6.RP-4#5.text: Ask what fraction of the bowl is apples. There are 4 apples among 4 + 6 = 10 pieces, so apples are 4/10 of the fruit. Simplify 4/10 to 2/5. A fraction of 2/5 means 2 out of every 5 pieces are apples, and as a ratio of apples to all fruit that is 2:5.

6.RP-4#6.title: Try real amounts
6.RP-4#6.text: Pick real amounts that fit the ratio. With 2 liters of red and 3 liters of blue there are 5 liters of paint, and red is 2/5 of it. Try a bigger batch: 4 liters of red and 6 of blue make 10 liters, and 4/10 simplifies to 2/5 again. Any batch size gives the same fraction, so 2/5 of the paint is red.

6.RP-4#7.title: Draw ten jerseys
6.RP-4#7.text:
Draw a row of 10 jerseys, one for each player. Mark 7 with an F for forwards and 3 with a D for defenders. Count the D jerseys, 3, and then every jersey, 10. Defenders to the whole team is 3:10.
As a check, forwards to the team is 7:10, and 7 + 3 gives back all 10 players.

6.RP-4#8.title: Pair them up
6.RP-4#8.text: Match each red chip with a blue chip. All 5 red chips get a partner and no chip is left over. So the bag is made of two equal piles, one red and one blue. One pile out of two equal piles is one half, which means 1/2 of the chips are red. There was no need to count to 10.

6.RP-4#9.title: Make three bunches
6.RP-4#9.text: Tie the flowers into 3 equal bunches. Each bunch gets 2 roses and 3 tulips, so it holds 5 flowers. Read both ratios from a single bunch. Roses to tulips is 2:3. Roses to all the flowers in the bunch is 2:5. Every bunch is the same, so these are the ratios for the whole garden, already in simplest form.

6.RP-4#10.title: Check with a small table
6.RP-4#10.text: Make a table with two columns, apples and all fruit. The simplified ratio gives the first row: 2 apples, 5 pieces. Double it for the second row: 4 apples, 10 pieces. That second row is the real bowl, with 4 apples among 4 + 6 = 10 pieces. The bowl sits in the table for 2:5, so 2:5 is right.

6.RP-5#1.title: Shade a hundred grid
6.RP-5#1.text: Picture a square cut into 100 small squares, 10 rows of 10. Shading 25 of them shades 25 percent of the square. That is two and a half rows. It is also one of four equal corner blocks, which is why 25% matches one quarter. Shade all 100 squares and you have 100%, the whole thing.

6.RP-5#2.title: Find one percent first
6.RP-5#2.text: Here is 20% of 45 done slowly. Cut 45 into 100 equal bits. Each bit is 45 ÷ 100 = 0.45, and that is 1% of 45. Twenty of those bits make 20 × 0.45 = 9. Dividing by 100 and then multiplying by 20 is the same as multiplying by 0.20, so the decimal shortcut is these two steps done at once.

6.RP-5#3.title: Benchmarks on a clock
6.RP-5#3.text: Try the benchmarks on an hour, which is 60 minutes. 100% is the full hour. 50% is half an hour, 30 minutes. 25% is a quarter of an hour, 15 minutes. 10% is 6 minutes. A clock face shows the first three as the full circle, half of it and a quarter of it. Other percents grow from these: 75% is 30 + 15 = 45 minutes.

6.RP-5#4.title: Build it from 10%
6.RP-5#4.text:
Skip the fraction and use tenths. 10% of 80 is 8, because the decimal point moves one place left. 50% is five lots of 10%, so multiply: 5 × 8 = 40.
This agrees with halving, since five tenths of a number is the same as half of it.

6.RP-5#5.title: Find 1% first
6.RP-5#5.text:
Start with the smallest slice. 1% of 250 is 250 ÷ 100 = 2.5. Ten percent is ten of those slices, so multiply: 10 × 2.5 = 25.
Dividing by 100 and then multiplying by 10 is the same as dividing by 10 once, so the answer matches the quick trick.

6.RP-5#6.title: Halve it twice
6.RP-5#6.text: Use 50% as a stepping stone. 50% of 40 is half of 40, which is 20. 25% is half of 50%, so halve again: half of 20 is 10. Two halvings cut the number into quarters, so 25% of 40 is 10.

6.RP-5#7.title: Double the 10% amount
6.RP-5#7.text: Find 10% of 45 by moving the decimal point one place left: 4.5. Twenty percent is two lots of 10%, so double it: 4.5 + 4.5 = 9. No decimal multiplying is needed, only one shift and one doubling, and the answer is still 9.

6.RP-5#8.title: Scale the bottom to 100
6.RP-5#8.text: A percent is a fraction with 100 on the bottom, so change 3/4 into that form. Four goes into 100 exactly 25 times. Multiply the bottom by 25 to get 100, and multiply the top by 25 too: 3 × 25 = 75. So 3/4 = 75/100, which is 75%.

6.RP-5#9.title: Half, minus a fifth
6.RP-5#9.text: Thirty percent is 50% take away 20%. Half of 60 is 30. Twenty percent of 60 is one fifth of it, 60 ÷ 5 = 12. Subtract: 30 − 12 = 18. So 30% of 60 is 18, the same as three lots of 10%.

6.RP-5#10.title: Check with the other 80%
6.RP-5#10.text: Check 9 by finding the part that is left. If 20% of 45 is 9, the other 80% should be 45 − 9 = 36. Work out 80% on its own: 10% of 45 is 4.5, and eight of those is 36. The two parts, 9 and 36, add back to 45, so 9 is correct.

6.RP-6#1.title: Write the fact as a table
