6.RP-6#1.text: Put the inch fact in a ratio table. Feet: 1, 2, 3, 4. Inches: 12, 24, 36, 48. It looks just like a table for tickets that cost 12 dollars each. The inches are always 12 times the feet, and that fixed multiplier is the unit rate. Reading the table left to right converts feet to inches, and right to left converts back.

6.RP-6#2.title: Trading dollars for quarters
6.RP-6#2.text: Change 3 dollars into quarters. Each dollar trades for 4 quarters, so you get 3 × 4 = 12 coins. The money is worth the same, but you hold more pieces because each piece is worth less. Feet to inches works the same way. Each foot trades for 12 inches, so 3 feet trade for 3 × 12 = 36 inches.

6.RP-6#3.title: Packing eggs into cartons
6.RP-6#3.text: Think of 48 eggs and cartons that hold 12 each. To find the number of cartons, you ask how many 12s are in 48, and 48 ÷ 12 = 4. There are far fewer cartons than eggs, because each carton swallows 12 of them. Inches and feet behave like eggs and cartons: 48 inches fill 4 feet.

6.RP-6#4.title: Catch a wrong answer
6.RP-6#4.text: Suppose someone converts 3 feet and writes 0.25 inches, because they divided by 12. Picture it. A 3-foot table is about as wide as a doorway, and a quarter of an inch is thinner than a pencil. Those cannot be the same length. Multiplying gives 36 inches, which fits a table. Imagining the real size catches the wrong operation.

6.RP-6#5.title: Count up by twelves
6.RP-6#5.text: Lay three 1-foot rulers along the table and count the inches as you pass each one. The end of the first ruler is 12 inches. The end of the second is 24 inches. The end of the third is 36 inches. Three rulers reach the end of the table, so 3 feet is 36 inches.

6.RP-6#6.title: Take away a foot at a time
6.RP-6#6.text: Cut 1-foot pieces off the shelf and keep count. 48 − 12 = 36 inches left after one piece. Then 24 after two pieces, 12 after three pieces and 0 after four pieces. Nothing is left over, and four pieces were cut, so 48 inches is 4 feet.

6.RP-6#7.title: Double the fact
6.RP-6#7.text:
The fact says 1 quart is 4 cups. The recipe needs twice as much milk as that, 2 quarts. Twice the quarts means twice the cups, so double 4 to get 8.
As a table: 1 quart and 4 cups, then 2 quarts and 8 cups. The recipe needs 8 cups.

6.RP-6#8.title: Half of ten feet
6.RP-6#8.text:
Ten feet is easy to convert: 10 × 12 = 120 inches. The post is 5 feet, which is half of 10 feet. So it is half of 120 inches, and half of 120 is 60.
The post is 60 inches tall, the same answer as splitting 12 into 10 and 2.

6.RP-6#9.title: Count half meters
6.RP-6#9.text: Half a meter is 50 centimeters. A rope of 3.5 meters is 7 half meters, because every meter has two halves and 3.5 × 2 = 7. Seven pieces of 50 centimeters make 7 × 50 = 350 centimeters. Counting in halves avoids multiplying a decimal.

6.RP-6#10.title: Skip count by fours
6.RP-6#10.text: Fill quart jars from the pot, 4 cups at a time, and count the cups used. One jar uses 4 cups. Two jars use 8 cups. Three jars use 12 cups, and the pot is empty. Three jars were filled, so 12 cups is 3 quarts.

6.RP-6#11.title: Double, convert, then halve
6.RP-6#11.text: The decimal goes away if you double the rope first. Twice 3.5 meters is 7 meters, and 7 meters is 700 centimeters. That is two ropes, so halve it for one rope: 700 ÷ 2 = 350 centimeters. Doubling and halving cancel out, so the answer is the true length.

6.RP-7#1.title: Two lines side by side
6.RP-7#1.text: Draw a line from 0 to 80. Under it draw a matching line from 0% to 100%. Halfway along, 40 sits above 50%. Halfway again, 20 sits above 25%. So 25% of 80 is 20, the same as 0.25 × 80. The pair of lines shows that a percent is a position between nothing and the whole amount.

6.RP-7#2.title: Other chunks work too
6.RP-7#2.text: The same idea builds many percents. For 35% of 80, find 10%, which is 8. Then 30% is 24 and 5% is 4, so 35% is 28. For 90% of 80 it is quicker to subtract: the whole is 80, take away 10%, which is 8, and 72 is left. Choose the chunks that make the least work.

6.RP-7#3.title: One price, both stories
6.RP-7#3.text: Take a game priced at 50 dollars, and 10% of it, which is 5 dollars. On sale at 10% off, you pay 50 − 5 = 45 dollars. With 10% tax instead, you pay 50 + 5 = 55 dollars. The 5 dollars was found the same way both times. Only one question is left: will you hand over less than the price tag says, or more?

6.RP-7#4.title: Use 10% blocks
6.RP-7#4.text:
Find 10% of 80 first: 8. Then 25% is two and a half of those blocks. Two blocks are 16. Half a block is 4. Add them: 16 + 4 = 20.
This matches one quarter of 80, because 25 is two and a half tens.

6.RP-7#5.title: Split 250 into pieces
6.RP-7#5.text: Break 250 into 200 and 50. Ten percent of 200 is 20, and ten percent of 50 is 5. Add the two results: 20 + 5 = 25. Taking 10% of each piece and adding gives the same total as taking 10% of the whole number.

6.RP-7#6.title: A quarter minus a tenth
6.RP-7#6.text: Fifteen percent is also 25% take away 10%, and both are benchmark percents. A quarter of 60 is 60 ÷ 4 = 15. A tenth of 60 is 6. Subtract the tenth from the quarter: 15 − 6 = 9. Different chunks give the same answer as 10% plus 5%.

6.RP-7#7.title: Start from half of 100
6.RP-7#7.text:
Half of 100 is 50, and 86 is 14 less than 100. Taking half of something 14 smaller gives an answer 7 smaller, because half of 14 is 7. So half of 86 is 50 − 7 = 43.
Check by doubling: 43 + 43 = 86.

6.RP-7#8.title: Discount on every ten dollars
6.RP-7#8.text: Thirty percent off means 3 dollars come off every 10 dollars of the price. So for each 10 dollars on the tag you pay 7 dollars. The shirt's price is four tens, so you pay 4 × 7 = 28 dollars. The discount is 4 × 3 = 12 dollars, and 28 + 12 gives back the 40 dollar tag.

6.RP-7#9.title: Tip is one fifth
6.RP-7#9.text:
Twenty percent is 20/100, which simplifies to one fifth. One fifth of the 35 dollar meal is 35 ÷ 5 = 7 dollars. That is the tip. Add it to the meal: 35 + 7 = 42 dollars in total.
Another view: you pay six fifths of the price, and 6 × 7 = 42.

6.RP-7#10.title: Cross out boxes on a bar
6.RP-7#10.text: Draw a bar for the 40 dollar price and cut it into 10 equal boxes. Each box is 10% and is worth 4 dollars. A 30% discount crosses out 3 boxes. Seven boxes are left, and 7 × 4 = 28 dollars. The boxes that remain are the 70% you still pay.

6.RP-8#1.title: One number answers every question
6.RP-8#1.text: A sign says 3 pounds of grapes cost 6 dollars. One shopper wants 5 pounds and another wants half a pound. Once you know that 1 pound costs 2 dollars, each question is a single multiplication: 5 pounds cost 10 dollars and half a pound costs 1 dollar. The unit rate is the one number that answers them all.

6.RP-8#2.title: Shrink the row to one
6.RP-8#2.text: Write the trip as a row in a table: 180 miles, 3 hours. To make the hours say 1, divide that side by 3. A ratio table stays true only if both sides get the same treatment, so divide the miles by 3 as well: 60 miles, 1 hour. Finding a unit rate is scaling a row down until the second number is 1.

6.RP-8#3.title: Or buy the same amount
6.RP-8#3.text: Another fair test is to make the amounts equal. Compare 3 bagels for 2 dollars with 5 bagels for 3 dollars. Both deals can reach 15 bagels. Five of the first deal cost 10 dollars. Three of the second deal cost 9 dollars. Same bagels, less money, so the second deal wins. A unit price does this with the shared amount set to 1.

6.RP-8#4.title: Think in minutes
6.RP-8#4.text: Three hours is 3 × 60 = 180 minutes. The bus covers 180 miles in 180 minutes, so it goes 1 mile every minute. An hour has 60 minutes, so in one hour it covers 60 miles. That is 60 miles per hour, with no long division.

6.RP-8#5.title: Halve the trip twice
6.RP-8#5.text: Write the trip as 240 miles in 4 hours. Half the trip is 120 miles in 2 hours. Half of that is 60 miles in 1 hour. Halving both numbers keeps the rate the same, and the row for 1 hour is the speed: 60 miles per hour.

6.RP-8#6.title: Cookies for one dollar
6.RP-8#6.text:
Ask what a single dollar buys. 12 cookies for 6 dollars is 12 ÷ 6 = 2 cookies for each dollar. Two cookies share that dollar equally, so each one costs half of it. Half a dollar is 0.50 dollars per cookie.
Check: 12 cookies at 50 cents is 600 cents, or 6 dollars.

6.RP-8#7.title: Keep halving the bag
6.RP-8#7.text: Start with 8 oranges for 4 dollars. Half the bag is 4 oranges for 2 dollars. Half again is 2 oranges for 1 dollar. Half once more is 1 orange for half a dollar. So one orange costs 0.50 dollars. Three halvings are the same as dividing by 8.

6.RP-8#8.title: Buy twelve pounds each way
6.RP-8#8.text: Make both deals the same size. Twelve pounds works, since 4 × 3 = 12 and 6 × 2 = 12. Three lots of Deal A are 12 pounds for 3 × 10 = 30 dollars. Two lots of Deal B are 12 pounds for 2 × 12 = 24 dollars. Deal B costs less for the same apples. Its price is 24 ÷ 12 = 2.00 dollars per pound.

6.RP-8#9.title: Spend thirty dollars each way
6.RP-8#9.text: Make the money equal instead of the boxes. Thirty dollars works for both deals. With Deal A, 30 dollars is 6 lots of 5 boxes, which is 30 boxes. With Deal B, 30 dollars is 5 lots of 8 boxes, which is 40 boxes. Deal B gives more boxes for the same money, so it is the better buy, at 6 ÷ 8 = 0.75 dollars per box.

6.RP-8#10.title: Buy 24 pens each way
6.RP-8#10.text: Make both deals the same number of pens. Both 6 and 8 go into 24. Four lots of 6 pens cost 4 × 3 = 12 dollars. Three lots of 8 pens cost 3 × 5 = 15 dollars. For the same 24 pens the first deal is cheaper, so 6 pens for 3 dollars is the better buy.

6.RP-9#1.title: Anchors you can picture
6.RP-9#1.text: Tie each fact to something real. A school ruler is 1 foot long and marked with 12 inches. A yardstick is 3 rulers end to end. A meter stick shows 100 centimeters. A kilometer is 1000 meter sticks in a row, about a ten minute walk. A pound of butter is four sticks of 4 ounces, which is 16 ounces. Picture the object and the number comes back.

6.RP-9#2.title: Weeks into days
6.RP-9#2.text: You already do this with time. Two weeks is 2 × 7 = 14 days, because a day is the smaller unit and every week holds 7 of them. Nobody would say 2 weeks is fewer than 2 days. Feet to inches is the same move with a different anchor: 2 feet is 2 × 12 = 24 inches.

6.RP-9#3.title: Minutes into hours
6.RP-9#3.text: A film that runs 180 minutes is 180 ÷ 60 = 3 hours long. The hour is the bigger unit, so it takes fewer of them to cover the same film. Saying the film lasts 10,800 hours, by multiplying, would be silly. Inches to feet follows the same thinking: 36 inches is 36 ÷ 12 = 3 feet.

6.RP-9#4.title: Read it on a meter stick
6.RP-9#4.text: Take a length of 2.35 meters. With meter sticks that is 2 full sticks, then 35 more centimeter marks. Two sticks are 200 centimeters, and 35 more makes 235 centimeters. The digits 2, 3 and 5 never changed. Only the point moved, from 2.35 to 235. Going back, 235 centimeters fills 2 sticks with 35 marks over, which is 2.35 meters.

6.RP-9#5.title: Two rulers end to end
6.RP-9#5.text: A school ruler is 1 foot long and shows 12 inches. The jump rope is as long as two rulers laid end to end. Count the inches along both: 12 on the first ruler and 12 more on the second. 12 + 12 = 24, so 2 feet is 24 inches.

6.RP-9#6.title: Double the fact twice
6.RP-9#6.text: Start with the anchor as a row: 1 yard, 3 feet. Double both numbers: 2 yards, 6 feet. Double both again: 4 yards, 12 feet. Two doublings turn 1 yard into 4 yards and 3 feet into 12 feet, so the pass travels 12 feet.

6.RP-9#7.title: Count up in feet
6.RP-9#7.text: Measure the desk one foot at a time. After 1 foot you have covered 12 inches. After 2 feet you have covered 24 inches. After 3 feet you have covered 36 inches, which is the full width of the desk. Three steps of one foot each means 36 inches is 3 feet.

6.RP-9#8.title: Split off the whole meters
6.RP-9#8.text: Break 250 centimeters into 200 and 50. The 200 centimeters make 2 full meters, since each meter is 100. The 50 left over is half of 100, so it is half a meter, 0.5. Put them together: 2 + 0.5 = 2.5 meters. The door is two and a half meter sticks tall.

6.RP-9#9.title: Count by thousands
6.RP-9#9.text:
Walk the trail one kilometer at a time and add 1000 meters for each. After 1 kilometer: 1000 meters. Then 2000, 3000, 4000 and, after the fifth kilometer, 5000 meters.
Check by going back: 5000 ÷ 1000 = 5 kilometers.

6.RP-9#10.title: Shrink the division
6.RP-9#10.text:
The division 48 ÷ 16 has the same answer when both numbers are halved. Halve them: 24 ÷ 8. Halve them again: 12 ÷ 4. That is an easy fact, 3. So 48 ounces is 3 pounds.
Check: 3 × 16 = 48.

6.RP-9#11.title: Count half pounds
6.RP-9#11.text: Half a pound is 8 ounces, and the 8 times table is easier than counting by 16. 48 ÷ 8 = 6, so the flour is 6 half pounds. Two half pounds make one whole pound, so 6 half pounds are 6 ÷ 2 = 3 pounds.

6.RP-10#1.title: Look inside each ratio
6.RP-10#1.text: Compare the two numbers inside each ratio. In 2:3 the second number is one and a half times the first. In 8:12 the second number, 12, is also one and a half times 8. The same link holds inside both, so they are equivalent. Try 8:10 and it fails: 10 is only one and a quarter times 8.

6.RP-10#2.title: Go down, then up
6.RP-10#2.text: You can avoid the decimal by shrinking before you grow. From 4 servings, halve to get 2 servings, then triple to get 6. Do the same to an ingredient: 6 cups of flour halve to 3, then triple to 9. Halving and then tripling is the same as multiplying by 1.5, the scale factor that division gave.

6.RP-10#3.title: Boxes of equal size
6.RP-10#3.text: Draw 3 boxes for dogs and 5 boxes for cats, all the same size. The 5 cat boxes hold 20 cats, so each box holds 4. The dog boxes are the same size, so 3 boxes hold 12 dogs. The whole drawing has 8 boxes, which is 32 animals. One picture gives every count.

6.RP-10#4.title: New columns from old ones
6.RP-10#4.text: Start with 4 servings and 6 cups. Halve the pair: 2 servings and 3 cups. Add those two pairs: 6 servings and 9 cups. Double the first pair: 8 servings and 12 cups. Each new pair came from old ones by multiplying, dividing or adding two pairs. Every one of them still has 1.5 cups for each serving.

6.RP-10#5.title: Simplify the bigger ratio
6.RP-10#5.text: Go the other way and shrink 8:12. Both numbers divide by 4, giving 8 ÷ 4 = 2 and 12 ÷ 4 = 3. So 8:12 simplifies to 2:3, which is exactly the first ratio. Two ratios with the same simplest form are equivalent, so the answer is yes.

6.RP-10#6.title: Halve it and add it on
6.RP-10#6.text: Six servings is 4 servings plus 2 more. Two servings is half the recipe, so it needs half the flour: 3 cups. Add the full recipe and the half recipe: 6 + 3 = 9 cups of flour for 4 + 2 = 6 servings. No decimal scale factor is needed.

6.RP-10#7.title: Cookies from one egg
6.RP-10#7.text:
Find what a single egg does. 12 cookies from 3 eggs is 12 ÷ 3 = 4 cookies for each egg. To bake 36 cookies, count how many 4s are in 36: 36 ÷ 4 = 9. So 9 eggs are needed.
Check: 9 eggs × 4 cookies = 36 cookies.

6.RP-10#8.title: List the ratio upward
6.RP-10#8.text: Write equivalent ratios of dogs to cats by adding 3 and 5 each time: 3:5, 6:10, 9:15, 12:20. Stop when the cats reach 20, the real count. That happens in the fourth ratio, 12:20. The dogs' number there is 12, so the shelter has 12 dogs.

6.RP-10#9.title: Double, then take some back
6.RP-10#9.text: Double the deal: 10 packs cost 40 dollars. That is 2 packs too many. Two packs are a fifth of the 10 packs, so they cost a fifth of 40 dollars, which is 8 dollars. Take them off: 40 − 8 = 32 dollars for 8 packs.

6.RP-10#10.title: Soda for one cup of juice
6.RP-10#10.text: Find the soda that goes with a single cup of juice. 5 parts soda for 2 parts juice is 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5 cups of soda for each cup of juice. There are 10 cups of juice, so multiply: 10 × 2.5 = 25 cups of soda.

6.RP-10#11.title: Multiply first, then divide
6.RP-10#11.text: Avoid fractions by scaling up before scaling down. Multiply the deal by 8: 24 packs cost 48 dollars. Now 8 packs is one third of 24 packs, so take one third of the cost: 48 ÷ 3 = 16 dollars. Eight packs cost 16 dollars.

6.RP-11#1.title: A table of the trip
6.RP-11#1.text: Follow a car going 60 miles per hour. After 1 hour it has gone 60 miles. After 2 hours, 120 miles. After 3 hours, 180 miles. After half an hour, 30 miles. Speed is the number that fills in this table: the miles are always 60 times the hours. A faster car has a bigger number in every row.

6.RP-11#2.title: One fact family
6.RP-11#2.text: The three formulas are a fact family, like 3 × 4 = 12, 12 ÷ 3 = 4 and 12 ÷ 4 = 3. Walk at 4 miles per hour for 3 hours and you cover 12 miles. Know the 12 miles and the 3 hours, and dividing gives 4 miles per hour. Know the 12 miles and the speed, and dividing gives 3 hours. Learn the multiplication and both divisions come with it.

6.RP-11#3.title: Spot the silly answer
6.RP-11#3.text: At 60 miles per hour for 30 minutes, multiplying 60 × 30 gives 1800 miles. That is like crossing a large country in half an hour. The true answer: a full hour gives 60 miles, so half an hour gives 30 miles. When an answer is wildly too big or too small, check that the time unit matches the unit after the word per.

6.RP-11#4.title: Split the twelve
6.RP-11#4.text: Break the speed into 10 and 2. Riding 10 miles each hour for 3 hours covers 30 miles. The extra 2 miles each hour add 2 × 3 = 6 miles. Together that is 30 + 6 = 36 miles, the same as 12 × 3.

6.RP-11#5.title: Guess and test
6.RP-11#5.text: Pick a speed and test it against the 4 hours. At 50 km each hour the train would cover 50 × 4 = 200 km, which is 40 km short. Forty more over 4 hours is 10 more each hour. Test 60: 60 × 4 = 240 km. That matches, so the speed is 60 km/h.

6.RP-11#6.title: Count the hours
6.RP-11#6.text: Follow the trip hour by hour. After 1 hour the car has gone 50 miles. After 2 hours it has gone 100 miles. After 3 hours it has gone 150 miles, and the trip is done. It took 3 hours. Counting up in 50s is the same question as 150 ÷ 50.

6.RP-11#7.title: Half the time, half the distance
6.RP-11#7.text: A speed of 60 mph means 60 miles in one full hour. Thirty minutes is half of an hour. At a steady speed, half the time covers half the distance, and half of 60 miles is 30 miles. No formula is needed when the time is a simple fraction of an hour.

6.RP-11#8.title: Check by dividing back
6.RP-11#8.text: Test the answer of 40 km by turning it back into a speed. Distance divided by time should give the boat's rate: 40 ÷ 2 = 20 km each hour. That is the speed in the question, so 40 km is right. A smaller answer such as 22 km, from adding 20 and 2, would give only 11 km each hour.

6.RP-11#9.title: Build up in ten-second blocks
6.RP-11#9.text: At 5 meters each second, 10 seconds cover 50 meters. One minute is six blocks of 10 seconds. Six blocks of 50 meters make 6 × 50 = 300 meters. Counting in blocks keeps the time in seconds the whole way, so the units always match.

6.RP-11#10.title: Count ten-minute blocks
6.RP-11#10.text: Sixty miles in 60 minutes means 10 miles in every 10 minutes. Thirty minutes is three blocks of 10 minutes. Three blocks of 10 miles make 30 miles. The blocks do the unit change for you, and the answer agrees with 1 mile per minute for 30 minutes.

6.SP-1#1.title: The balance point on a line
6.SP-1#1.text:
Mark the values 2, 3 and 10 on a number line and look for the spot where they balance. Try 5: the 2 is 3 below and the 3 is 2 below, a total of 5 below. The 10 is 5 above. The two sides match, so 5 is the mean.
Adding and dividing agrees: 15 ÷ 3 = 5.

6.SP-1#2.title: Line up by height
6.SP-1#2.text:
Five friends stand in a row from shortest to tallest. The third friend has two people on each side, so that friend's height is the median.
Now let them stand in any order. The person in the third spot could be the tallest of all, with nobody above. The middle spot only means something after the line-up is sorted.

6.SP-1#3.title: A class vote
6.SP-1#3.text:
A class votes for a pet: hamster, fish, hamster, lizard, hamster, fish. Hamster gets 3 votes, fish gets 2 and lizard gets 1, so the mode is hamster.
If one hamster vote changed to fish, both would have 3 votes and there would be two modes. If six students all picked different pets, nothing would repeat and there would be no mode.

6.SP-1#4.title: Level the stacks
6.SP-1#4.text:
Build three stacks of blocks with heights 4, 6 and 8. Take 2 blocks off the tallest stack and put them on the shortest. The 8 becomes 6 and the 4 becomes 6, so the stacks are now 6, 6, 6.
No blocks were added or lost, and every stack is level at 6. That level height is the mean.

6.SP-1#5.title: Think in tens
6.SP-1#5.text:
Each value is a number of tens: 1 ten, 2 tens and 3 tens. The mean of 1, 2 and 3 is easy to see, because 1 is one below 2 and 3 is one above, so they balance at 2.
The mean is 2 tens, which is 20. Scaling every value by 10 scales the mean by 10 as well.

6.SP-1#6.title: Count smaller and larger
6.SP-1#6.text:
Test each value without sorting. Is 3 the middle? Nothing is smaller than 3 and two values are larger, so no. Is 7 the middle? Two values are smaller and none is larger, so no.
Try 5: one value (3) is smaller and one value (7) is larger. The sides are equal, so the median is 5.

6.SP-1#7.title: Test each value by counting
6.SP-1#7.text:
A median of five values needs two values below it and two above. Test 8: the values 2, 5 and 4 are smaller, which is three, so 8 is too high. Test 4: only 2 is smaller, so 4 is too low.
Test 5: the values 2 and 4 are smaller, and 8 and 9 are larger. Two on each side, so the median is 5.

6.SP-1#8.title: Draw a quick dot plot
6.SP-1#8.text:
Put a dot above each value on a number line. The 2 gets one dot, the 4 gets two dots stacked up, and the 9 gets one dot.
The mode is the tallest stack. Only the stack above 4 is two dots high, so the mode is 4. The picture shows the answer with no arithmetic.

6.SP-1#9.title: Use the symmetry
6.SP-1#9.text:
Look at the list around 5. The 3 is 2 below and the 7 is 2 above, so they cancel and the mean is 5 without adding.
Cross off the two ends, 3 and 7. The pair 5, 5 is left, and halfway between them is 5, so the median is 5.
The only value that repeats is 5, so the mode is 5 too.

6.SP-1#10.title: Add, then divide
6.SP-1#10.text:
Check the balance answer with the usual recipe. The total is 4 + 6 + 8 = 18. There are three values, so share 18 into three equal parts: 18 ÷ 3 = 6.
As a second check, three values of 6 would also total 18. Both routes agree that the mean is 6.

6.SP-2#1.title: One score changes the average
6.SP-2#1.text:
Four quiz scores are 6, 7, 8 and 9. The total is 30, so the mean is 7.5. Now a teacher finds a marking mistake and raises the 6 to 10. The total grows by 4 to 34, and the mean grows to 8.5.
One changed score moved the mean by 4 ÷ 4 = 1 point. Every value has a share in the mean, so no value can change without the mean noticing.

6.SP-2#2.title: The new kid with 50 dollars
6.SP-2#2.text:
Five kids have 1, 2, 2, 2 and 3 dollars. The total is 10, so the mean is 2 dollars, which looks like everyone.
A sixth kid joins with 50 dollars. The total becomes 60 and the mean becomes 60 ÷ 6 = 10 dollars. Five of the six kids have 3 dollars or less, so a mean of 10 no longer describes a typical kid.

6.SP-2#3.title: Swap in something huge
6.SP-2#3.text:
Take 3, 5 and 8. The median is the middle value, 5. Change the 8 to 80 and the list is 3, 5, 80, with median 5. Change it to 8,000 and the median is still 5.
The means tell a different story: about 5.3, then about 29.3, then about 2,669. The big value still fills one seat at the end of the row, so the middle seat keeps the same value.

6.SP-2#4.title: House prices on one street
6.SP-2#4.text:
Five houses sold for 200, 210, 220, 230 and 900 thousand dollars. The total is 1,760, so the mean is 352 thousand. No house on the street sold for anything close to that.
The median is the middle price, 220 thousand, which sits right among four of the five houses. With one mansion in the data, the median gives the more honest picture.

6.SP-2#5.title: Pair off the ends
6.SP-2#5.text:
Match the smallest with the largest: 1 and 5 add to 6, so that pair averages 3. Match the next two: 2 and 4 also add to 6 and average 3. The value left over is 3 itself.
Everything balances at 3, so the mean is 3. It is also the middle of the list, which is why it feels typical.

6.SP-2#6.title: Start from the small values
6.SP-2#6.text:
The values 2, 3 and 4 have a mean of 3. Pretend the fourth value is 3 too, so the mean is still 3.
The real fourth value is 100, which is 97 more than 3. Share that extra among all four values: 97 ÷ 4 = 24.25. The mean climbs to 3 + 24.25 = 27.25, and nearly all of it comes from one number.

6.SP-2#7.title: Cross off the ends
6.SP-2#7.text:
Cross off the smallest value, 2, and the largest value, 100. Removing one from each end keeps the middle where it was.
The values 3 and 4 are left. The median is the point halfway between them, which is 3.5. The 100 was crossed off first, so its size never entered the answer.

6.SP-2#8.title: Count who is close
6.SP-2#8.text:
Estimate the mean: the total is close to 300, and 300 ÷ 4 = 75. Now ask how many salaries are within 10 of 75. None are, since the nearest ones are 35 and 200.
The middle two salaries are 32 and 35, so the median is halfway, 33.5. Three of the four salaries are within 4 of it. Report the median, 33.5.

6.SP-2#9.title: Cross off whatever is largest
6.SP-2#9.text:
Find the median of 4, 4, 10 by crossing off the smallest value and the largest value. One 4 and the 10 go, and 4 is left.
Now do the same with 4, 4, 1,000. One 4 and the 1,000 go, and 4 is left again. The largest value is removed whatever its size, so the median stays 4.

6.SP-2#10.title: Measure the gaps between neighbors
6.SP-2#10.text:
Put 2, 3, 4 and 100 on a number line and look at the spaces between neighbors. From 2 to 3 is 1. From 3 to 4 is 1. From 4 to 100 is 96.
Three values sit one step apart, and then there is an empty stretch of 96 before the last one. A value that far from every neighbor is an outlier, so yes, the 100 is an outlier.

6.SP-3#1.title: A week of temperatures
6.SP-3#1.text:
In one city the coldest day of the week was 12 degrees and the warmest was 30 degrees. The range is 30 − 12 = 18 degrees, so the weather swung a lot.
In another city the week went from 20 to 22 degrees, a range of only 2. If every day had been exactly 21 degrees, the range would be 21 − 21 = 0.

6.SP-3#2.title: Try it with eight numbers
6.SP-3#2.text:
Take 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 50. The bottom half is 1, 2, 3, 4, with middle 2.5. The top half is 5, 6, 7, 50, with middle 6.5. So the IQR is 6.5 − 2.5 = 4.
The range is 50 − 1 = 49 because of the 50. Change the 50 to 8 and the range drops to 7, but the IQR is still 4.

6.SP-3#3.title: Walk to the meeting spot
6.SP-3#3.text:
Four friends live at houses 1, 5, 6 and 8 on a street. They meet at the mean, house 5, because 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
Their walks are 4, 0, 1 and 3 houses long. A walk is never negative, whichever direction it goes. The total is 8, so the average walk is 8 ÷ 4 = 2 houses. That average walk is the MAD.

6.SP-3#4.title: Add the gaps
6.SP-3#4.text:
The list is in order, so measure the gap between each pair of neighbors. From 5 to 9 is 4. From 9 to 12 is 3. From 12 to 20 is 8.
The gaps join end to end and cover the whole stretch of the data: 4 + 3 + 8 = 15. That matches 20 − 5, so the range is 15.

6.SP-3#5.title: Sort, then count up
6.SP-3#5.text:
Write the list in order: 6, 9, 14, 22. Now the ends are the minimum and the maximum, with no scanning needed.
Count up from 6 to 22 in easy jumps. From 6 to 10 is 4, from 10 to 20 is 10, and from 20 to 22 is 2. The jumps total 4 + 10 + 2 = 16, so the range is 16.

6.SP-3#6.title: One stack on a dot plot
6.SP-3#6.text:
Draw the data as a dot plot. All three dots land in one stack above 3. The range is the width of the plot from the leftmost dot to the rightmost dot, and a single stack has no width.
A second check: the mean is 3, and each value is 0 away from it. Every measure of spread gives 0 here.

6.SP-3#7.title: Use the even spacing
6.SP-3#7.text:
The values 2, 4, 6 are evenly spaced, two apart. In an evenly spaced list of three, the middle value is the balance point, so the mean is 4.
On a number line, 6 is the very next value after 4, one step of 2 to the right. So the distance from 6 to the mean is 2.

6.SP-3#8.title: Two thirds of the values
6.SP-3#8.text:
Mark 2, 4 and 6 on a number line. The mean, 4, sits on the middle value. Two of the three values are 2 units away from it, and one is 0 units away.
So the average distance is two thirds of 2. Two thirds of 2 is 4 thirds, which is about 1.33. The MAD is about 1.33.

6.SP-3#9.title: Halfway between the ends
6.SP-3#9.text:
The values go up by 2 each time, so each half is evenly spaced, and the middle of an evenly spaced group is halfway between its ends.
Bottom half 1, 3, 5, 7: halfway between 1 and 7 is 4, so Q1 = 4. Top half 9, 11, 13, 15: halfway between 9 and 15 is 12, so Q3 = 12.
IQR = 12 − 4 = 8.

6.SP-3#10.title: List the values and add gaps
6.SP-3#10.text:
Write out what the dots say: 3, 3, 5, 8, 8. Now walk along the list and add up each move. From 3 to 3 is 0. From 3 to 5 is 2. From 5 to 8 is 3. From 8 to 8 is 0.
The moves total 2 + 3 = 5, the same as 8 − 3. The range is 5.

6.SP-4#1.title: Build one from quiz scores
6.SP-4#1.text:
Five quiz scores come in: 7, 8, 8, 9, 8. Draw a number line and add a dot for each score as you read it. One dot goes above 7, one above 9, and three pile up above 8.
The finished plot has five dots for five scores. The tall stack above 8 shows the most common score at a glance.

6.SP-4#2.title: Sorting ages into decades
6.SP-4#2.text:
At a family party the ages are 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27 and 29. Sort them by decade. The teens box gets 12, 15 and 18, so its bar is 3 tall. The twenties box gets 21, 24, 27 and 29, so its bar is 4 tall.
The two boxes meet at 20 with nothing between, so the bars touch. The bars alone no longer tell you that someone is exactly 24.

6.SP-4#3.title: Find the five numbers yourself
6.SP-4#3.text:
Take 2, 4, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10. The smallest is 2 and the largest is 10, so the whiskers end there. The middle value is 5, so the line inside the box goes at 5.
The bottom half 2, 4, 4 has middle 4, and the top half 7, 8, 10 has middle 8. The box runs from 4 to 8.

6.SP-4#4.title: Write the list behind the stack
6.SP-4#4.text:
Turn the stack back into numbers. Each dot above the 3 is one data value equal to 3, so the stack stands for the list 3, 3, 3, 3.
Count the entries in that list: there are four. So 4 values equal 3. Reading a stack as a list is a good way to check a count.

6.SP-4#5.title: Make a ten
6.SP-4#5.text:
Add the stacks in a friendlier order. The stack of 2 and the stack of 3 together hold 5 dots. The remaining stack also holds 5 dots. Two fives make 10.
You can check by writing the data out: 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3. That list has ten entries, so there are 10 values.

6.SP-4#6.title: Try it with real numbers
6.SP-4#6.text:
Use the data 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70. The middle value is 40. The bottom half 10, 20, 30 has middle 20, and the top half 50, 60, 70 has middle 60.
So the box is drawn from 20 to 60 and the whiskers reach 10 and 70. The only summary number left is 40, and it is drawn inside the box. That line is the median.

6.SP-4#7.title: Compare with a bar graph
6.SP-4#7.text:
A bar graph of favorite pets has bars for cat, dog and fish. Those are separate things, and nothing lies between cat and dog, so the bars stand apart.
A histogram sits on a number line. After the range 0 to 9 the very next number is 10, which starts the next range. The line has no break, so the bars have no gap. Yes, they touch.

6.SP-4#8.title: Count up the grid lines
6.SP-4#8.text:
Go to the bar over 5–9 and climb it one grid line at a time, counting from the bottom: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. The top of the bar is at the seventh line.
Think of the bar as a stack of seven values, each somewhere from 5 to 9, such as 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9, 9. Seven values make a bar 7 tall.

6.SP-4#9.title: Ask each display a question
6.SP-4#9.text:
Ask both displays, "Where is the median?" On a bar graph of favorite foods there is nowhere to point. Pizza, tacos and pasta have no order, so they have no middle.
On a box plot you can point straight at the answer: the line inside the box. The edges of the box are the quartiles. The box plot is the one that shows them.

6.SP-4#10.title: Level the bars
6.SP-4#10.text:
Even out the bar heights without changing the total. Take 2 from the bar of 6 and give it to the bar of 2. The heights 4, 6, 2 become 4, 4, 4.
Three bars of height 4 hold 3 × 4 = 12 values. Moving counts between bars does not add or remove any, so the data set has 12 values.

6.SP-5#1.title: Describe it over the phone
6.SP-5#1.text:
Imagine telling a friend about a data set over the phone so they can sketch it. Say only "it is around 70" and they cannot draw anything yet. Add "the values go from 65 to 75" and they know how wide to make it. Add "most are in the middle, with the same amount on each side" and they can draw the hump.
Center, spread and shape are the three things the sketch needs.

6.SP-5#2.title: Try it with numbers
6.SP-5#2.text:
Look at 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 9. Six values crowd between 1 and 3, and the lone 9 trails far off to the right. This data is skewed right.
Flip it: 1, 7, 8, 8, 9, 9, 9 has its crowd on the right and a lone 1 trailing off to the left, so it is skewed left.
In 4, 5, 5, 6 both sides match, so it is symmetric.

6.SP-5#3.title: Ages at a birthday party
6.SP-5#3.text:
The ages at a birthday party are 9, 9, 10, 10, 10, 11 and 38. Six of the ages sit within two years of each other. That group is a cluster, and it tells you the party is for a ten-year-old.
The 38 is far from all of them. It is an outlier, and it has a story too: a parent is in the room.

6.SP-5#4.title: One number, three meanings
6.SP-5#4.text:
The number 80 means nothing until you know where it came from. A center of 80 points on a test says the class did well. A center of 80 minutes for a bus ride says the trip is far too long. A center of 80 degrees says to pack shorts.
The arithmetic is the same each time. The answer to the real question is different each time.

6.SP-5#5.title: Rule out the other names
6.SP-5#5.text:
Go through the words used for features of data. A cluster is a group of values close together, and the 30 is alone. A gap is an empty space, and the 30 is a value, not a space. The mode is the most common value, and 30 appears once.
The word for a single value far from the rest is outlier, so the 30 is an outlier.

6.SP-5#6.title: The fold test
6.SP-5#6.text:
Imagine folding the plot in half at the middle of the number line. If the two sides landed on top of each other, the data would be symmetric. Here they do not match: the left side is a tall pile and the right side is long and thin.
The side that sticks out long and thin is the tail. It is on the right, so the data is skewed right.

6.SP-5#7.title: Two buses, same typical time
6.SP-5#7.text:
Two bus routes both have a typical trip of 20 minutes. On the first route every trip takes between 19 and 21 minutes. On the second, trips take anywhere from 5 to 35 minutes.
You would plan your morning very differently for each one, yet the center is the same. The missing piece is how much the times vary, which is the spread.

6.SP-5#8.title: Sketch the dot plot
6.SP-5#8.text:
Draw the scores as dots: one dot above 7, three above 8, two above 9 and one above 10.
The tallest stack is at 8, so the center is 8. The dots run from 7 to 10, a width of 3 points. The stacks get shorter on both sides of the peak and no dot sits far away, so the shape is roughly symmetric.

6.SP-5#9.title: Set the 90 aside first
6.SP-5#9.text:
Cover the 90 and look at what is left: 20, 25, 25, 30. These balance at 25 and fit inside 10 minutes, so most students do about 25 minutes.
Now uncover the 90. It is 60 minutes beyond the next value, far outside that group, so it is an outlier. Report both facts: most about 25 minutes, one outlier at 90.

6.SP-5#10.title: Look at the gaps
6.SP-5#10.text:
Place the values on a number line. From 20 to 25 is 5, from 25 to 25 is 0, and from 25 to 30 is 5. Then from 30 to 90 is 60.
Four values crowd together on the left and one sits far away on the right. That long empty stretch ending in a single value is a tail pointing right, so the data is skewed right.

6.SP-6#1.title: A repeat still counts
6.SP-6#1.text:
Take the scores 7, 9, 9, 10. There are four scores, because the 9 was earned twice and both count. The total is 35, so the mean is 35 ÷ 4 = 8.75.
Someone who counts only the different numbers gets n = 3 and a mean of 35 ÷ 3, about 11.7. That is higher than every score, which cannot be right. One wrong count ruined the answer.

6.SP-6#2.title: Three centers, one data set
6.SP-6#2.text:
Try all three on 2, 3, 3, 4, 18. The total is 30, so the mean is 30 ÷ 5 = 6. The middle value of the sorted list is 3, so the median is 3. The value that repeats is 3, so the mode is 3.
Four of the five values are 4 or less. The median and mode match them, and the mean was pulled up by the 18.

6.SP-6#3.title: Same center, different scatter
6.SP-6#3.text:
The lists 9, 10, 11 and 1, 10, 19 both have a center of 10. A report that only says "center 10" makes them sound the same.
Subtract the smallest from the largest in each. The first gives 11 − 9 = 2 and the second gives 19 − 1 = 18. Now the report shows that one list hugs its center and the other is scattered wide.

6.SP-6#4.title: Use the skip-counting pattern
6.SP-6#4.text:
The values are the twos you say when skip counting: 2 × 1, 2 × 2, 2 × 3, 2 × 4, 2 × 5. The list stops at 2 × 5, so it has five values and n = 5.
That tells you the mean will divide by 5. Five is odd, so one value will sit alone in the middle, the third one.

6.SP-6#5.title: Pair them off
6.SP-6#5.text:
Circle the values two at a time: 11 with 13, then 15 with 17. That makes two pairs with nothing left over, so n = 2 × 2 = 4.
Nothing left over means the count is even. An even count has no single middle value, so the median will be found halfway between the two inside values, 13 and 15.

6.SP-6#6.title: Stack the dots
6.SP-6#6.text:
Draw a number line and place a dot for each value. One dot goes above 3. Two dots go above 5, one on top of the other. One dot goes above 7.
The mode is the tallest stack. The stack above 5 is the only one two dots high, so the mode is 5.

6.SP-6#7.title: Sort so repeats sit together
6.SP-6#7.text:
Rewrite the list in order: 2, 6, 6, 6, 9. Sorting pulls equal values next to each other, so repeats show up as a run.
The longest run is the three 6s in a row. The 2 and the 9 each stand alone. The value with the longest run is the mode, so the mode is 6.

6.SP-6#8.title: Balance around 5
6.SP-6#8.text:
Two of the four values are already 5, so guess that the mean is 5. Check the other two. The 3 is 2 below the guess and the 7 is 2 above it.
The 2 below and the 2 above cancel, so nothing pulls the balance point away from 5. The mean is 5, with no adding needed.

6.SP-6#9.title: Read it all off a dot plot
6.SP-6#9.text:
Draw the data: one dot above 3, two above 5, one above 7. Count the dots to get n = 4.
The picture is a mirror image around 5, with the tall stack in the middle, so the center is 5. The dots stretch from 3 to 7, and 7 − 3 = 4, so the range is 4. One sketch gives all three finds.

6.SP-6#10.title: Halfway between the ends
6.SP-6#10.text:
The values go up by 2 each time, so the list is evenly spaced and its middle is halfway between its two ends. Add the ends and halve: 2 + 10 = 12, and 12 ÷ 2 = 6.
Check by counting: 2 and 4 are below 6, and 8 and 10 are above it. Two on each side, so the median is 6.

6.SP-7#1.title: Ask five kids
6.SP-7#1.text:
Ask five sixth graders how tall they are and you might write down 142, 150, 147, 155 and 150 centimeters. No single one of those is "the" answer. To reply you would have to say something like "mostly around 150".
A question whose honest reply needs a list, and then a summary of the list, is a statistical question.

6.SP-7#2.title: One stack on the dot plot
6.SP-7#2.text:
Ask twenty people how many days are in a week. Every reply is 7. Plot the replies and you get one stack of twenty dots above 7, with a range of 7 − 7 = 0.
The twentieth reply told you nothing the first one did not. When the plot can only ever be one stack, the question is a fact question.

6.SP-7#3.title: Rewrite one question two ways
6.SP-7#3.text:
Start with "How long is my bus ride?" It is about one rider, and the reply is one number, such as 15 minutes.
Change the subject to a group: "How long are the bus rides of students at my school?" Now the replies might be 5, 15, 20 and 40 minutes. The topic stayed the same. Only the words naming who is being asked about changed.

6.SP-7#4.title: Picture the data you would get
6.SP-7#4.text:
Imagine collecting the data. You stand against a wall, someone marks your height, and you write down one number. A dot plot of this data has a single dot.
There is nothing to average, no smallest or largest, and no spread. A question that produces one dot is not statistical.

6.SP-7#5.title: Picture the dot plot
6.SP-7#5.text:
Imagine measuring everyone in the class and writing down numbers such as 140, 152, 147 and 160 centimeters. Plot them and the dots spread along the number line, some low, some high, with a few stacks.
To answer the question you would need to describe that spread-out picture. Data that spreads out comes from a statistical question.

6.SP-7#6.title: Check ten calendars
6.SP-7#6.text:
Look up February 2025 on ten different calendars. Each one shows 28 days. A list of the results is 28 written ten times, with no variation.
Compare "How many days are in each month of 2025?" That one gives 31, 28, 31, 30 and so on, which do vary. A number in the reply is not enough. The February question has one fixed reply, so it is not statistical.

6.SP-7#7.title: Time the lunch table
6.SP-7#7.text:
Imagine standing in the lunchroom with a stopwatch. One student is done in 8 minutes, another takes 15, and a slow eater takes 25. Your notebook fills with different times.
To report back you would say something like "most take about 15 minutes". Needing a summary of many different values is the sign of a statistical question.

6.SP-7#8.title: Wrong replies are not variability
6.SP-7#8.text:
Ask a hundred people and a few might say Los Angeles. Does that make the replies vary? No. Those people are mistaken, and a map settles it: the capital is Sacramento.
In a statistical question, different replies are all true at once, like different heights. Here only one reply is true, so the question is not statistical.

6.SP-7#9.title: Test the new question
6.SP-7#9.text:
Check the rewrite by imagining the replies. For "How many pets do I have?" you write one number, such as 2, and you are done.
For "How many pets does each family on my street have?" you knock on doors and write 0, 2, 1, 0, 3. Those replies differ from house to house. Adding the group turned one number into varying data, so the fix works.

6.SP-7#10.title: Look for the group word
6.SP-7#10.text:
Read the subject of the question: "sixth-graders". It is plural, so it points to many people, not one. You cannot look the reply up in one place or measure it once.
You would have to survey many students, and their sleep times would not all match. A group subject plus a quantity that differs between people makes the question statistical.

6.SP-8#1.title: Level three towers
6.SP-8#1.text:
Build towers of 2, 5 and 8 blocks. Take 3 blocks from the tallest tower and add them to the shortest. Now every tower is 5 blocks high.
No block was added or thrown away, so the 15 blocks are simply shared equally. The level height, 5, is the mean, and it matches 15 ÷ 3.

6.SP-8#2.title: The fourth runner home
6.SP-8#2.text:
Seven runners finish a race, and their times are written down in finishing order. The fourth runner has three people ahead and three behind, so that time is the median.
Suppose the last runner stops to tie a shoe and takes an extra hour. The fourth runner is still fourth, with the same time. The order had to be known first, and the slowest time did not matter.

6.SP-8#3.title: Four kids in a row
6.SP-8#3.text:
Four kids line up by height: 130, 134, 138 and 150 centimeters. No kid stands in the middle. But any height between 134 and 138 has two kids shorter and two kids taller.
To agree on one number, everyone uses the point halfway between the two inside kids. Add 134 and 138 to get 272, then halve it to get 136. No kid is 136 tall, and that is fine.

6.SP-8#4.title: Cross off from both ends
6.SP-8#4.text:
Cross off the smallest value and the largest value together: 3 and 11 go. Do it again with the new ends: 5 and 9 go.
Each round removes one value from each side, so the middle never shifts. The only value left is 7, so the median is 7.

6.SP-8#5.title: Find the point between
6.SP-8#5.text:
Put 2, 4, 6 and 8 on a number line. The median must have two values on each side, so it lies between 4 and 6.
The only whole number between them is 5. It is 1 step above 4 and 1 step below 6, so it is exactly halfway. Two values are below it and two are above. The median is 5.

6.SP-8#6.title: Step inward until you meet
6.SP-8#6.text:
The middle two values are 3 and 7. Put a finger on each and move both inward one step at a time. The fingers go to 4 and 6, and then both land on 5.
They moved the same distance, 2 steps each, so 5 is exactly halfway between 3 and 7. The median is 5.

6.SP-8#7.title: Move two blocks across
6.SP-8#7.text:
Picture stacks of 6, 8 and 10 blocks. Lift 2 blocks off the stack of 10 and set them on the stack of 6. All three stacks are now 8 high.
The total did not change, and the stacks are level, so each value's fair share is 8. The mean is 8.

6.SP-8#8.title: Share out the extra 95
6.SP-8#8.text:
Pretend for a moment that all four values are 5. The mean would be 5. The real last value is 100, which is 95 more.
Share that extra among the four values: 95 ÷ 4 = 23.75. The mean is 5 + 23.75 = 28.75.
For the median, cross off one 5 and the 100. The pair 5, 5 is left, so the median is 5. Report 5.

6.SP-8#9.title: Measure how far each center misses
6.SP-8#9.text:
See how close each center is to the actual values. The median, 5, is exactly equal to three of the four values.
The mean, 28.75, is 23.75 away from each 5 and 71.25 away from the 100. It is not close to a single value in the data.
The center that matches most of the data is the median, 5.

6.SP-8#10.title: Use the position formula
6.SP-8#10.text:
Count the values: n = 4. The middle position is (4 + 1) ÷ 2 = 2.5. There is no slot 2.5, so the median sits between slot 2 and slot 3.
Slot 2 holds 3 and slot 3 holds 7. Halfway between them is (3 + 7) ÷ 2 = 5. The median is 5, the same as crossing off gives.

6.SP-9#1.title: Rebuild the list from the plot
6.SP-9#1.text:
Suppose a plot has two dots above 4, one dot above 5, nothing above 6, and three dots above 7. Read it back into a list: 4, 4, 5, 7, 7, 7.
That is six values from six dots. The empty spot at 6 tells you no one got a 6. The plot and the list hold exactly the same information.

6.SP-9#2.title: Seven ages, two bars
6.SP-9#2.text:
Take the ages 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 29. Three of them fall in 10–19 and four fall in 20–29. The histogram is a bar of height 3 next to a bar of height 4.
Someone who sees only the bars knows that four people are in their twenties. They cannot tell whether anyone is exactly 24. The count is kept and the exact ages are dropped.

6.SP-9#3.title: Twelve students in a line
6.SP-9#3.text:
Line up 12 students from shortest to tallest and split the line into four groups of 3. The cut between groups 1 and 2 is Q1, the cut in the center is the median, and the cut between groups 3 and 4 is Q3.
The box covers groups 2 and 3. That is 6 of the 12 students, exactly half, whether their heights are close together or far apart.

6.SP-9#4.title: Make a tiny plot
6.SP-9#4.text:
Plot the data 5, 5, 6 yourself. Read the first 5 and draw a dot above 5. Read the second 5 and draw another dot on top. Read the 6 and draw a dot above 6.
Three values were read and three dots were drawn, one at a time. Each dot stands for one data value.

6.SP-9#5.title: Build the stack dot by dot
6.SP-9#5.text:
Work forwards from the measuring. Each time a measurement comes out as 3, one dot is added above the 3. After the first such measurement the stack is 1 high, then 2, then 3, then 4.
A stack 4 dots high can only come from four measurements equal to 3. So 4 measurements equal 3.

6.SP-9#6.title: Invent data that fits
6.SP-9#6.text:
Make up values that would create this bar, such as 10, 12, 15, 15 and 19. Each one lies in the interval 10–19, and each one raises the bar by 1.
Five values raise it to height 5. A sixth value in the interval would make the height 6, which is not what the bar shows. So 5 values fall there.

6.SP-9#7.title: Two lists, one bar
6.SP-9#7.text:
Here are two different data sets: 20, 20, 20, 20, 20, 20, 20, 20 and 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28. Each has eight values between 20 and 29.
Both give the same bar of height 8 over 20–29. The bar tells you there are 8 values, but it cannot tell these two lists apart, so the exact positions are hidden.

6.SP-9#8.title: Count with eight values
6.SP-9#8.text:
Use the data 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. The bottom half 1, 2, 3, 4 has middle 2.5, so Q1 = 2.5. The top half 5, 6, 7, 8 has middle 6.5, so Q3 = 6.5.
The values inside the box, between 2.5 and 6.5, are 3, 4, 5 and 6. That is 4 of the 8 values, so the box holds the middle 50% of the data.

6.SP-9#9.title: Measure the four sections
6.SP-9#9.text:
Find the length of each piece. Left whisker: 6 − 4 = 2. Left part of the box: 7 − 6 = 1. Right part of the box: 9 − 7 = 2. Right whisker: 10 − 9 = 1.
The box is 1 + 2 = 3 wide and runs from 6 to 9, split at the typical score, 7. All four pieces together are 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 6, the range.

6.SP-9#10.title: Count up along the box
6.SP-9#10.text:
Start at the left edge of the box, 15, and count up to the right edge, 35. From 15 to 20 is 5. From 20 to 35 is 15. Together that is 5 + 15 = 20.
Add back to check: 15 + 20 = 35, which is the right edge. The box is 20 units wide, so the IQR is 20.

6.SP-10#1.title: Can a friend sketch it?
6.SP-10#1.text:
Read this summary: "Quiz scores are symmetric, centered at 8, and run from 6 to 10." A friend who never saw the scores can sketch a hump with its peak at 8 that fades out at 6 and 10.
Remove "centered at 8" and they do not know where the peak goes. Remove "from 6 to 10" and they do not know how wide to draw it.

6.SP-10#2.title: One sort, three answers
6.SP-10#2.text:
Take 9, 3, 6. Sort it once to get 3, 6, 9. Read the left end for the minimum, 3. Read the right end for the maximum, 9. Read the middle for the median, 6.
The range is 9 − 3 = 6. For the mean, add and share: 18 ÷ 3 = 6. A single sorted list gave everything except the sum.

6.SP-10#3.title: Five kids and their allowances
6.SP-10#3.text:
Five kids get weekly allowances of 5, 5, 6, 6 and 78 dollars. The total is 100, so the mean is 20 dollars. Four of the five kids get less than a third of that.
The median is the middle value, 6 dollars, which is what a typical kid here really gets. With the 78 in the data, the median is the center to report.

6.SP-10#4.title: Work in tens
6.SP-10#4.text:
Every value is a number of tens: 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 tens. The small list 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 adds to 15, and 15 ÷ 5 = 3.
So the mean is 3 tens, which is 30. Dividing every value by 10 first keeps the arithmetic small, and multiplying back by 10 at the end gives the same mean.

6.SP-10#5.title: Pair small with large
6.SP-10#5.text:
Match the smallest value with the largest: 2 + 8 = 10, so that pair averages 5. Match the two inside values: 4 + 6 = 10, so they average 5 too.
Both pairs balance at 5, so the mean of all four values is 5. This works because the values are evenly spaced.

6.SP-10#6.title: Count smaller and larger
6.SP-10#6.text:
Skip the sorting and test a value directly. The median of five values needs two values below it and two above.
Test 5: the smaller values are 3 and 1, and the larger values are 7 and 9. Two on each side, so the median is 5. Testing 7 fails, because three values (3, 1, 5) are smaller.

6.SP-10#7.title: Add up the gaps
6.SP-10#7.text:
Sort the list: 5, 7, 12, 18, 20. Measure the gap between each pair of neighbors: 2, then 5, then 6, then 2.
The gaps link the smallest value to the largest with nothing missed, so their sum is the range: 2 + 5 + 6 + 2 = 15. It agrees with 20 − 5.

6.SP-10#8.title: Count up from the minimum
6.SP-10#8.text:
The smallest value is 2 and the largest is 11. Start at 2 and count up to 11 in two jumps. From 2 to 10 is 8, and from 10 to 11 is 1 more.
The distance is 8 + 1 = 9. Check by adding back: 2 + 9 = 11, the maximum. The range is 9.

6.SP-10#9.title: Summarize from a dot plot
6.SP-10#9.text:
Draw one dot above each of 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9. Count five dots, so there are five values.
The dots are evenly spaced and the picture is a mirror image around 5, so the shape is symmetric and the center is 5. The leftmost dot is at 1 and the rightmost is at 9, and 9 − 1 = 8, so the range is 8.

6.SP-10#10.title: Pair the ends
6.SP-10#10.text:
Match the outside values: 10 + 50 = 60, and half of 60 is 30. Match the next two: 20 + 40 = 60, and half of 60 is 30. The value left in the center is 30.
Every pair averages 30 and so does the leftover value, so the mean is 30. Adding everything gives 150 ÷ 5 = 30 as well.

A1-1#1.title: A blank on a form
A1-1#1.text: Think of a form with a blank line: "Tickets bought: ___". The blank is ready before anyone fills it in, and the price rule "8 dollars × blank" already makes sense. A letter such as n is that blank. Write 8n once, and it covers the family that buys 2 tickets (16 dollars) and the family that buys 5 (40 dollars).

A1-1#2.title: Check a translation with numbers
A1-1#2.text: Pick a real number and see whether the words and the symbols agree. Let n = 10. "3 more than n" should be 13, and n + 3 gives 10 + 3 = 13. "Twice n" should be 20, and 2n gives 2 × 10 = 20. If the phrase and the expression give the same result for a test number, the translation is very likely right.

A1-1#3.title: A sale price story
A1-1#3.text: A shop sells a shirt for 5 dollars less than twice its cost. If the cost is 8 dollars, twice the cost is 16, and the price is 16 − 5 = 11 dollars. Nobody would work out 5 − 16 = −11, because a price of −11 makes no sense. The story shows the order: double first, then take the 5 off, so 2n − 5.

A1-1#4.title: A thermometer for the rule
A1-1#4.text: Use a thermometer. The temperature is t degrees and it rises 6 degrees, so the new reading is t + 6. If t = 10, the reading is 16. If t = −4, start four marks below zero and climb six marks to reach 2. The same expression works both times. The letter did not care that its value sat below zero.

A1-1#5.title: Follow a pattern down
A1-1#5.text:
Make a table of 3n + 2 and watch it step down.
n = 1 gives 5, n = 0 gives 2, n = −1 gives −1, n = −2 gives −4.
Each time n drops by 1, the value drops by 3. Keep going: n = −3 gives −7 and n = −4 gives −10. The pattern lands on −10, the same value substitution gave.

A1-1#6.title: Steps on a number line
A1-1#6.text: Treat each x as one step of the same length. −5x means walk 5 steps backward, and +8x means walk 8 steps forward. After both walks you stand 3 steps ahead of the start, which is 3x. Check with x = 2: −5(2) + 8(2) = −10 + 16 = 6, and 3(2) = 6 as well.

A1-1#7.title: Follow the pattern past zero
A1-1#7.text:
List −2x for shrinking values of x and watch the answers.
x = 2 gives −4, x = 1 gives −2, x = 0 gives 0.
Each time x drops by 1, the answer rises by 2. Continue: x = −1 gives 2, x = −2 gives 4, and so on up to x = −6, which gives 12. The pattern confirms the positive answer 12.

A1-1#8.title: A recipe card with a blank
A1-1#8.text: A taxi charges 3 dollars per mile plus a 2 dollar fee, written 3n + 2. The expression is a price list waiting for a trip length. A 4 mile trip costs 3 × 4 + 2 = 14 dollars, and a 10 mile trip costs 32 dollars. Evaluating means choosing the trip, putting its length in place of n, and working out the bill.

A1-1#9.title: Try several bags
A1-1#9.text: Test the story with three different bags. A bag of 2 marbles becomes 5. A bag of 7 becomes 10. A bag of 20 becomes 23. Each time the total is the bag's count with 3 added on, never 3 times the count. Writing that pattern with a letter for the count gives b + 3, the same expression.

A1-1#10.title: Count up level by level
A1-1#10.text: Skip the formula and count. Start with the 20 coin bonus, then add 50 for each level: 70, 120, 170, 220, 270, 320. Six jumps of 50 from 20 land on 320 coins. Six jumps of 50 is 50 × 6, and the starting 20 is the bonus, so the count matches 50L + 20 with L = 6.

A1-1#11.title: Split the coins into piles
A1-1#11.text: Lay the coins out as piles. Four levels make four piles of 50 coins, and the bonus is one small pile of 20. Two piles of 50 are 100, so four piles are 200. Push the bonus pile in and you have 220 coins. The piles show why the 20 is added once and not once per level.

A1-1#12.title: Check with a big number
A1-1#12.text: A second check is to try a level count that is easy to reason about. For 10 levels the story pays 10 × 50 = 500 coins plus the 20 bonus, so 520. The expression 50L + 20 gives 50(10) + 20 = 520 too. A wrong rule such as 70L would give 700, so the test separates the right rule, 50L + 20, from the tempting one.

A1-1#13.title: Count the weeks on a list
A1-1#13.text: Write your money at the end of each week, starting from 15 dollars and adding 10 each time: 25, 35, 45, 55, 65, 75. The sixth number is 75, so you have 75 dollars after 6 weeks. The list climbs by 10 each week and starts from 15, which is exactly what 10w + 15 says.

A1-1#14.title: Test a value for x
A1-1#14.text: Check the simplified form with a number. Let x = 5. The original expression gives 4(5) + 3 + 2(5) = 20 + 3 + 10 = 33. The answer 6x + 3 gives 30 + 3 = 33, which matches. The tempting wrong answer 9x would give 45, so it cannot be right. The test supports 6x + 3.

A1-1#15.title: Use an area picture
A1-1#15.text: Draw strips that are each 1 unit tall and x units long. 4x is four strips and 2x is two more strips, so together they make a block of six strips with area 6x. The 3 is three small unit squares that do not fit the strip shape, so they sit beside the block. Total area: 6x + 3.

A1-2#1.title: Two friends with equal money
A1-2#1.text: Mia and Jo have the same amount of money. If each earns 5 dollars, they still have the same amount. If each spends 3 dollars, still the same. But if only Mia earns 5, they are no longer equal. An equation is that promise of sameness, for example 12 = 12. Add 5 to both and 17 = 17 is true; add 5 to one side only and 17 = 12 is false.

A1-2#2.title: Walk there and walk back
A1-2#2.text: On a number line, x + 9 = 15 says: start at x, walk 9 steps right, and arrive at 15. To find the start, stand on 15 and walk 9 steps left. You stop at 6. Every operation is a trip, and its opposite is the return trip along the same road, which brings you back to the number you began with.

A1-2#3.title: Socks, then shoes
A1-2#3.text: In the morning you put on socks, then shoes. At night you cannot pull the socks off first; the shoes come off first. An equation is dressed the same way. In 8w + 20 = 68, w was multiplied by 8 (socks) and then 20 was added (shoes). Remove the 20: 8w = 48. Then remove the 8: w = 6.

A1-2#4.title: Like trying a key
A1-2#4.text: A locksmith does not argue about whether a key is right. The key goes in the lock and either turns or does not. Your answer is a key and the original equation is the lock. Suppose you solved 3x + 2 = 14 and got x = 5 by mistake. Trying it gives 17, not 14, so the lock stays shut and you know to look again.

A1-2#5.title: Ask the missing-number question
A1-2#5.text: Read the equation as a question: what number plus 9 makes 15? Count up from 9 to 15: 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15. That is 6 counts, so the missing number is 6. You could also test a few values: 5 + 9 = 14 is too small, 7 + 9 = 16 is too big, and 6 + 9 = 15 fits. So x = 6.

A1-2#6.title: Share into four groups
A1-2#6.text: 4x = 28 says four equal groups hold 28 in all. Deal 28 counters into four piles one at a time and each pile ends with 7. You can also skip count by 7: 7, 14, 21, 28 reaches the total in exactly four jumps. Either way one group holds 7, so x = 7.

A1-2#7.title: Read it on a thermometer
A1-2#7.text: Think of a thermometer. Some temperature x rose 9 degrees and now reads 4. To find where it began, go 9 degrees back down from 4. Four degrees down reaches zero, and the remaining 5 degrees go below zero, to −5. A rise of 9 that ends as low as 4 must have started below zero, so x = −5.

A1-2#8.title: Guess, check, and adjust
A1-2#8.text: Try values and watch the sign. If x = 5, then −4 × 5 = −20, which has the right size but the wrong sign. A positive x always gives a negative product here, so x must be negative. Try x = −5: −4 × (−5) = 20. That matches the right side, so x = −5.

A1-2#9.title: Distance on the number line
A1-2#9.text: x − (−3) measures how far x sits to the right of −3 on the number line. The equation says that distance is 10. Start at −3 and walk 10 steps right: three steps reach 0, and seven more reach 7. So x = 7. The walk shows why subtracting −3 behaves like adding 3.

A1-2#10.title: Fill in a savings table
A1-2#10.text:
Track the savings week by week, starting at 20 dollars and adding 8 each time.
Week 1: 28. Week 2: 36. Week 3: 44. Week 4: 52. Week 5: 60. Week 6: 68.
The total first reaches the 68 dollar price in week 6, so w = 6 weeks, the same answer the equation gave.

A1-2#11.title: Find the missing money first
A1-2#11.text: Use the story's numbers directly. The sneakers cost 68 dollars and you already hold 20, so you still need 68 − 20 = 48 dollars. Each week brings in 8 dollars. Count by eights until you reach 48: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48. That is six eights, so w = 6.

A1-2#12.title: Add up the four shares
A1-2#12.text: Each of the four friends put 7 dollars on the table. Add what is on the table: 7 + 7 + 7 + 7 = 28 dollars. That pile is the whole bill, so b = 28. A tape diagram shows the same thing: one long bar for the bill cut into four equal parts, each part labelled 7.

A1-2#13.title: Estimate, then adjust
A1-2#13.text: Start with a guess. If a ticket cost 50 dollars, two tickets and the fee would be 100 + 6 = 106, which is 10 dollars too much. Two tickets share that extra 10, so each ticket should be 5 dollars cheaper. Try 45: two tickets cost 90, and 90 + 6 = 96. That is the right total, so t = 45.

A1-2#14.title: Draw a tape diagram
A1-2#14.text: Draw one long bar labelled 96. Mark off a small piece of 6 at the end for the fee. What is left of the bar is 96 − 6 = 90, and it is made of two equal ticket pieces. Cut it in half: each piece is 45. The picture gives t = 45 without writing an equation.

A1-3#1.title: Three identical gift bags
A1-3#1.text: Pack 3 identical gift bags. Each bag gets x stickers and 2 pencils. Altogether you need 3 lots of stickers and 3 lots of pencils: 3x stickers and 6 pencils. That is 3(x + 2) = 3x + 6. If you multiplied only the stickers, two bags would be missing their pencils. Repeated addition shows it too: (x + 2) + (x + 2) + (x + 2) = 3x + 6.

A1-3#2.title: A bank account in one line
A1-3#2.text: Your account shows these changes: you earn 5x, pay a 5 dollar fee, then spend 2x. Nobody reads the list in that order. You net the earnings against the spending first: 5x − 2x = 3x, and the fee is still 5. The short statement 3x − 5 says the same thing as 5x − 5 − 2x, and it is much easier to work with.

A1-3#3.title: Bags on both pans
A1-3#3.text: Picture a scale with 5 bags of marbles on the left, and 2 bags plus 12 loose marbles on the right. Every bag holds the same count. Take 2 bags off each pan and the scale stays level: 3 bags balance 12 marbles. Now the bags are all on one side, and each bag must hold 4 marbles.

A1-3#4.title: One full run-through
A1-3#4.text: Follow one equation to the end: 2(x − 4) = 6. Distributing gives 2x − 8 = 6. There is nothing more to tidy, and x is already on one side only. Now it is the familiar two-step kind: add 8 to get 2x = 14, then divide by 2 to get x = 7. Check: 2(7 − 4) = 2 × 3 = 6.

A1-3#5.title: Paying back twice
A1-3#5.text: Read −2(x − 5) as "take away two copies of x − 5". Each copy is x with 5 already removed. Taking away two copies removes 2x, but it also removes two of those 5s that were being subtracted, and cancelling a subtraction gives the amount back. So you get −2x and +10. It is like cancelling two 5 dollar charges: your balance goes up by 10.

A1-3#6.title: Divide before you distribute
A1-3#6.text: Treat the bracket as one chunk. −2 times the chunk equals 4, so the chunk is 4 ÷ (−2) = −2. That means x − 5 = −2. Add 5 to both sides and x = 3. No distributing was needed, so there was no second sign to lose. Check: 3 − 5 = −2, and −2 × (−2) = 4.

A1-3#7.title: Work backwards from 2
A1-3#7.text: Rewind the steps. A number was tripled, then 14 was added, and the result was 2. Before the 14 was added the value was 2 − 14 = −12. Before the tripling it was −12 ÷ 3 = −4. So x = −4. A quick sense check agrees: adding 14 gave only 2, so 3x had to be negative.

A1-3#8.title: Test a few values
A1-3#8.text:
Make a small table for 3(x + 2).
x = 3 gives 3 × 5 = 15.
x = 4 gives 3 × 6 = 18.
x = 5 gives 3 × 7 = 21.
Each step up in x adds 3 to the result, and the target 21 appears at x = 5. Larger values overshoot, so x = 5 is the only solution.

A1-3#9.title: Three equal groups
A1-3#9.text: Read 3(x + 2) = 21 as three equal groups that hold 21 altogether. Split 21 into three equal groups and each group holds 7. A group is x + 2, so x and 2 together make 7. The number that joins 2 to make 7 is 5, so x = 5, as before.

A1-3#10.title: Compare both sides in a table
A1-3#10.text:
Work out each side for a few values of x.
x = 3: left 17, right 25.
x = 4: left 24, right 28.
x = 5: left 31, right 31.
The left side starts 8 behind and gains 4 each step, because it grows by 7 while the right grows by 3. Two steps close the gap, and the sides meet at x = 5.

A1-3#11.title: Table of the two bills
A1-3#11.text:
Compare the bills at a few call lengths.
20 minutes: plan A 14 dollars, plan B 6 dollars.
40 minutes: plan A 16, plan B 12.
60 minutes: plan A 18, plan B 18.
Plan B starts cheaper but grows faster, and the two bills meet at 60 minutes. After that, plan B costs more.

A1-3#12.title: Graph the two lines
A1-3#12.text: Graph cost against minutes. Plan A is a line that starts at 12 on the cost axis and rises gently, 1 dollar every 10 minutes. Plan B starts at 0 and rises 3 dollars every 10 minutes. The steeper line catches the other where they cross. At 60 minutes both lines are at 18 dollars, so the plans tie at 60 minutes.

A1-3#13.title: Spend the budget in order
A1-3#13.text: Pay the room first. That takes 40 dollars out of the 100 dollar budget and leaves 60 dollars for guests. Each guest uses 6 dollars. Count guests until the money runs out: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 54, 60. The tenth guest uses the last 6 dollars, so g = 10 guests.

A1-3#14.title: Watch the gap close
A1-3#14.text: Compare the two sides for easy values of x. At x = 0 the left side is 5(−1) − 0 = −5 and the right side is 7, so the left is 12 behind. At x = 1 the left is −2 and the right is 9, so it is 11 behind. The gap shrinks by 1 for each step in x, so it closes after 12 steps: x = 12.

A1-4#1.title: A height sign at a ride
A1-4#1.text: A ride has a sign: you must be taller than 120 cm. That rule does not name one height. A child of 121 cm may ride, and so may an adult of 190 cm. A child of exactly 120 cm may not. On a number line the answer is everything to the right of 120, drawn as an arrow with an open dot at 120.

A1-4#2.title: Four signs, one number
A1-4#2.text:
Use the number 10 for all four phrases and list what is allowed.
At least 10: 10, 11, 12 and up, so x ≥ 10.
At most 10: 10, 9, 8 and down, so x ≤ 10.
More than 10: 11 and up, but not 10, so x > 10.
Fewer than 10: 9 and down, but not 10, so x < 10.

A1-4#3.title: Two friends and their ages
A1-4#3.text: Ana is 12 and Ben is 15, so Ana's age < Ben's age. In 3 years they are 15 and 18: still the same order. Two years ago they were 10 and 13: same order. Double both and you get 24 and 30: same order. But make both negative, −12 and −15, and now −12 is the larger. Only the negative multiplier changed who was ahead.

A1-4#4.title: Debts turn the order around
A1-4#4.text: Think of money. Having 6 dollars is better than having 2 dollars, so 2 < 6. Now turn both into debts by multiplying by −1. Owing 6 dollars is worse than owing 2 dollars, so −6 < −2, which is the same as −2 > −6. The person who was ahead is now behind. A bigger amount becomes a bigger debt, so the sign has to turn around.

A1-4#5.title: Find the boundary, then test
A1-4#5.text: First solve the matching equation: x + 5 = 9 when x = 4. That is the boundary. Now test one number on each side. Try x = 6: 6 + 5 = 11, and 11 > 9 is true. Try x = 0: 0 + 5 = 5, and 5 > 9 is false. The side with 6 is the winning side, so x > 4.

A1-4#6.title: List some bus loads
A1-4#6.text: Write down some possible head counts and say whether the bus allows each one. 25 students: fine. 39: fine. 40: fine, the bus is full. 41: not allowed. 50: not allowed. The allowed numbers are 40 and everything below it. On a number line that is a closed dot at 40 with shading to the left, which is n ≤ 40.

A1-4#7.title: Boundary and test points
A1-4#7.text: Solve the equation −3x = 12 first: x = −4 is the boundary. Now test a number on each side of −4 in the original inequality. x = −6 gives −3(−6) = 18, and 18 > 12 is true. x = 0 gives 0 > 12, which is false. The true side is the one below −4, so x < −4, with no flip rule needed.

A1-4#8.title: Table of values
A1-4#8.text:
Evaluate 5 − 2x at several values and compare with 11.
x = −5 gives 15: too big.
x = −4 gives 13: too big.
x = −3 gives 11: allowed, because equal counts.
x = −2 gives 9 and x = 0 gives 5: both allowed.
The value drops as x grows, so every x from −3 upward works: x ≥ −3.

A1-4#9.title: Boundary first, then test
A1-4#9.text: Solve −2x + 3 = 11 as an equation: −2x = 8, so x = −4. That number is the boundary, and it is included because of the equals bar. Test one side: x = −6 gives 12 + 3 = 15, and 15 ≥ 11 is true. Test the other: x = 0 gives 3, which fails. The true side is below the boundary: x ≤ −4.

A1-4#10.title: Move x to the other side
A1-4#10.text: Add x to both sides so its coefficient becomes positive: 5 < 9 + x. Adding never flips the sign. Now subtract 9 from both sides: −4 < x. Read from the x side, that says x is greater than −4, so x > −4. This route reaches the same answer without ever dividing by a negative number.

A1-4#11.title: Count up the cost
A1-4#11.text: List the cost of each number of credits by counting in fours: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28. The sixth number, 24, is still within the 25 dollars you have. The seventh, 28, is too much. So you can afford 6 credits or fewer, c ≤ 6, and you would have 1 dollar left over.

A1-4#12.title: Use the money still needed
A1-4#12.text: You need 50 dollars and have 18, so you are short by 50 − 18 = 32 dollars. Saving 8 dollars a week, the shortfall shrinks like this: 24, 16, 8, 0. It takes 4 weeks to reach zero. Any week after that also works, since you only have more money. So w ≥ 4.

A1-4#13.title: Use a real-life rule
A1-4#13.text: Turn each inequality into a rule about ages. "Older than 2" is x > 2: a child who is exactly 2 does not qualify, so the dot at 2 stays open, like an empty seat. "2 or older" is x ≥ 2: the child who is exactly 2 does qualify, so the dot is filled in. In both cases older children qualify, so the shading goes right.

A1-5#1.title: A table that never argues
A1-5#1.text: Look at a price list: 1 ticket costs 8 dollars, 2 cost 16, 3 cost 24. Each number of tickets has one price beside it. That list is a function. Now imagine a list where 2 tickets cost 16 on one line and 20 on another. You could not tell what to pay, so that list is not a function.

A1-5#2.title: Compare it with a recipe name
A1-5#2.text: A recipe book has a recipe called Pancakes, and "Pancakes for 4" tells you how many people to cook for. Nobody multiplies the word Pancakes by 4. In the same way, if f(x) = x + 10, then f(3) means run the rule called f with 3 as the input: 3 + 10 = 13. Multiplying would need a number named f, and there is none.

A1-5#3.title: A concrete rule with numbers
A1-5#3.text: A ride charges 2 dollars per ticket and sells 1 to 5 tickets per person. The rule is cost = 2 × tickets. The inputs that are allowed are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5: that list is the domain. Feeding each one in gives 2, 4, 6, 8, 10: that list is the range. The cost 7 is not in the range, because no allowed input produces it.

A1-5#4.title: Check a table of pairs
A1-5#4.text: Test with tables. Table A lists (1, 5), (2, 7), (3, 7). Every input appears once, so A is a function, and it does not matter that two inputs share the output 7. Table B lists (1, 5), (1, 8), (2, 7). The input 1 is paired with both 5 and 8, so B is not a function. Repeated outputs are fine; repeated inputs with different outputs are not.

A1-5#5.title: A temperature converter
A1-5#5.text: A weather app doubles a Celsius reading and adds 30 to estimate Fahrenheit: f(x) = 2x + 30. On a warm day, f(10) = 50. On a freezing day, f(−10) = 2(−10) + 30 = 10. The negative input went in the same way, and it gave a sensible answer. Notice that f(−10) is 10, not −50, so flipping the input does not simply flip the output.

A1-5#6.title: Step down from known outputs
A1-5#6.text:
Start with easy inputs and follow the pattern.
f(0) = 2, f(−1) = −1, f(−2) = −4.
Each step of 1 to the left lowers the output by 3, because the rule multiplies x by 3. Two more steps give f(−3) = −7 and f(−4) = −10. The pattern agrees with the substitution: f(−4) = −10.

A1-5#7.title: Count down from the start
A1-5#7.text: Read the rule as a countdown. At x = 0 the output is 1. Each time x goes up by 1, the output goes down by 2. So the outputs run 1, −1, −3, −5, −7 for x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. The fifth value in the list belongs to x = 4, so f(4) = −7.

A1-5#8.title: Doubling is adding twice
A1-5#8.text: Doubling a number is the same as adding it to itself. Feed in 7 and the machine gives 7 + 7 = 14. A short table shows the same habit: 5 goes to 10, 6 goes to 12, 7 goes to 14. The outputs climb by 2 each time the input climbs by 1, and the row for 7 reads 14.

A1-5#9.title: Skip count by fives
A1-5#9.text: The rule multiplies the input by 5, so the outputs for inputs 1, 2, 3, ... are the multiples of 5. Count them off: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. The sixth multiple is 30, and the sixth one belongs to the input 6. So f(6) = 30, with no multiplying of f by anything.

A1-5#10.title: Read it as a line
A1-5#10.text: Think of f(x) = 3x + 2 as a line. It starts at height 2 when x = 0 and climbs 3 for every step to the right. Four steps to the right climb 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12. Add that climb to the starting height: 2 + 12 = 14. So the point above x = 4 is at height 14, and f(4) = 14.

A1-5#11.title: Break 8 into easy parts
A1-5#11.text: Split the 8 questions into 5 and 3. Five questions earn 5 × 4 = 20 points. Three questions earn 3 × 4 = 12 points. Together that is 20 + 12 = 32 points. You could also double: 2 questions earn 8, 4 questions earn 16, and 8 questions earn 32. Both routes give 32 points.

A1-5#12.title: Add in two friendly jumps
A1-5#12.text: Picture a brightness slider at 40. The filter pushes it 15 marks to the right. Split the push into 10 and 5: the first part takes the slider to 50, and the second part takes it to 55. Check by going back: 55 − 15 = 40, the brightness you began with. The output is 55.

A1-5#13.title: Follow the jumps down the table
A1-5#13.text: Look only at the output column: 5, 10, 15. Each output is 5 more than the one before, while the input goes up by 1. The next input is 4, so make one more jump of 5 from 15 and reach 20. Adding 5 for each new row gives the same result as multiplying the input by 5.

A1-5#14.title: Try inputs until one fits
A1-5#14.text:
Run the machine forward on a few guesses.
f(5) = 13, which is too small.
f(10) = 23, which is too big.
The target 19 lies between them, so the input is between 5 and 10. Each extra 1 of input adds 2 to the output, and 19 is 6 more than 13, so go up 3 from 5: f(8) = 19. The input was 8.

A1-6#1.title: Slope as a unit rate
A1-6#1.text: Think of a hiking trail instead of stairs. One trail climbs 6 metres while you walk 2 metres forward. Another climbs 12 metres while you walk 4 forward. Both gain 3 metres of height for every 1 metre forward, so they are equally steep. Slope is that "per 1 step forward" number: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 and 12 ÷ 4 = 3.

A1-6#2.title: Tables that rise and fall
A1-6#2.text: Look at tables instead of pictures. In the table 0 → 1, 1 → 4, 2 → 7, the outputs grow by 3 each step, so the slope is 3, a positive number. In 0 → 9, 1 → 7, 2 → 5, they shrink by 2 each step, so the slope is −2. In 0 → 4, 1 → 4, 2 → 4, nothing changes, so the slope is 0.

A1-6#3.title: Fill in the missing stairs
A1-6#3.text: Take the points (1, 2) and (3, 8) and list the points in between. From x = 1 to x = 3 is two steps, and y must travel from 2 to 8, a total of 6. Sharing 6 equally over 2 steps gives 3 per step: (1, 2), (2, 5), (3, 8). The formula does this sharing in one line: 6 ÷ 2 = 3.

A1-6#4.title: One job, read as a graph
A1-6#4.text: You earn 9 dollars an hour. After 1 hour you have 9, after 2 hours 18, after 3 hours 27. Plot those as (1, 9), (2, 18), (3, 27). Each step of 1 hour to the right lifts the point 9 dollars higher, so the slope of the line is 9. The pay rate and the steepness of the graph are the same number.

A1-6#5.title: Same two points, both orders
A1-6#5.text: Use the points (1, 2) and (4, 8). Going left to right, the rise is 8 − 2 = 6 and the run is 4 − 1 = 3, so the slope is 2. Now subtract the other way round: 2 − 8 = −6 and 1 − 4 = −3. The slope is −6 ÷ −3, which is still 2. A line has one steepness, whichever point you start from.

A1-6#6.title: Count steps on the grid
A1-6#6.text: Walk from (−4, −1) to (−1, 5) on a grid. Going right, x passes −3, −2 and −1, which is 3 steps. Going up, y passes 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, which is 6 steps. Up 6 for 3 across is up 2 for each 1 across, so the slope is 2. Counting avoids the double minus signs completely.

A1-6#7.title: Find the middle point
A1-6#7.text: The point halfway between (−2, 6) and (2, −2) is (0, 2), since 0 is halfway between −2 and 2, and 2 is halfway between 6 and −2. From (−2, 6) to (0, 2) the line goes 2 across and 4 down. That is 2 down for each 1 across, so the slope is −2.

A1-6#8.title: Split into single steps
