A1-6#8.text: Break the staircase into stairs that are each 1 unit across. A run of 2 makes two such stairs, and they share the rise of 6 equally, so each stair climbs 3. Slope means the climb for one unit across, so the slope is 3. A table shows it too: across 0, 1, 2 goes with heights 0, 3, 6.

A1-6#9.title: Scale the ramp down
A1-6#9.text: Ask how far you must roll forward to gain 1 foot of height. The ramp gains 2 feet over 8 feet of run, so half the ramp gains 1 foot over 4 feet. One foot up for every four feet across is a slope of 1/4, or 0.25. That small number matches a gentle ramp.

A1-6#10.title: Table between the points
A1-6#10.text: Put the two points in a table and fill the gap. x goes 1, 2, 3 and y must go from 2 to 8 in two equal jumps. The total change is 6, so each jump is 3 and the middle value is 5. The table 2, 5, 8 rises by 3 for each step of 1 in x, so the slope is 3.

A1-6#11.title: Step down one at a time
A1-6#11.text: The line drops from height 10 to height 0 while x goes from 0 to 5. That is a fall of 10 shared over 5 steps, so each step loses 2. The points are (0, 10), (1, 8), (2, 6), (3, 4), (4, 2), (5, 0). Losing 2 for every step across is a slope of −2.

A1-6#12.title: Hour by hour
A1-6#12.text: Split the two hours evenly. The battery lost 80 − 56 = 24 percentage points in total, so with a steady drain it lost 12 in each hour: 80, then 68, then 56. Dropping 12 points every hour is a rate of −12 percent per hour. The minus sign records that the level is going down.

A1-6#13.title: Use the slope formula
A1-6#13.text: Treat the pay as points on a graph. Zero walks earn 0 dollars, so one point is (0, 0). Three walks earn 18 dollars, so another is (3, 18). The slope formula gives (18 − 0) ÷ (3 − 0) = 18 ÷ 3 = 6. The slope is 6 dollars per walk, the same as shrinking to one walk.

A1-6#14.title: Subtract the coordinates
A1-6#14.text: Use the slope formula on (2, 1) and (6, 4). The change in y is 4 − 1 = 3. The change in x is 6 − 2 = 4. Slope is the change in y divided by the change in x, which is 3/4. That matches counting 3 squares up and 4 squares across on the grid.

A1-7#1.title: The amount at time zero
A1-7#1.text: Think of a savings jar. You already have 20 dollars in it and add 5 dollars each week, so the total is y = 5x + 20. Before any week has passed, the jar holds 20 dollars. That opening amount is b. In a table it is the row for x = 0, and on the graph it is the point (0, 20) on the y-axis.

A1-7#2.title: A taxi meter ticking
A1-7#2.text: A taxi meter shows 4 dollars when you get in and adds 3 dollars for each mile: y = 3x + 4. Watch the meter: 4, 7, 10, 13. Every mile, the display jumps by the same 3. That steady jump is m. If the meter went backwards by 2 each mile, like a gift card being used up, m would be −2.

A1-7#3.title: Check by testing two inputs
A1-7#3.text: You can confirm what you read off y = 3x − 4 by trying two inputs. At x = 0, y = 3(0) − 4 = −4, so the line crosses the y-axis at −4. At x = 1, y = 3 − 4 = −1. Going from x = 0 to x = 1 lifted y from −4 to −1, a climb of 3. So b = −4 and m = 3, as read.

A1-7#4.title: A flat phone bill
A1-7#4.text: A phone plan costs 30 dollars a month however many minutes you talk. Use 10 minutes, the bill is 30. Use 500 minutes, still 30. Plot the bills against minutes and the dots sit in a level row at height 30. The equation is y = 30, and the cost per extra minute, which is the slope, is 0.

A1-7#5.title: A phone battery draining
A1-7#5.text: A game drains 2 percent of battery each minute from a start of 90 percent: y = −2x + 90. The readings go 90, 88, 86, 84. On a graph each dot is one step to the right and two lower than the last, so the line slants down. The negative sign on m is the word "loses" written in symbols.

A1-7#6.title: Plot from a table
A1-7#6.text: Skip the stepping and substitute. At x = 0, y = −2(0) + 3 = 3. At x = 1, y = −2 + 3 = 1. At x = 2, y = −4 + 3 = −1. The points (0, 3), (1, 1), (2, −1) are the same ones found by stepping. The y-values fall by 2 each time, so m = −2, and the first one shows b = 3.

A1-7#7.title: Check with a table
A1-7#7.text: Substitute a few inputs into y = −x − 4 and watch the outputs. At x = 0, y = −4. At x = 1, y = −1 − 4 = −5. At x = 2, y = −2 − 4 = −6. The outputs −4, −5, −6 drop by 1 for each step to the right, so the slope is −1, and the value at x = 0 gives b = −4.

A1-7#8.title: Test two inputs
A1-7#8.text: Find the two numbers by plugging in. At x = 0, y = 5(0) + 2 = 2, so the line crosses the y-axis at 2 and b = 2. At x = 1, y = 5 + 2 = 7. Moving one step right raised y from 2 to 7, which is a rise of 5, so m = 5.

A1-7#9.title: Use two far-apart points
A1-7#9.text: Choose two easy inputs and substitute. At x = 0, y = 2. At x = 3, y = 3(3) + 2 = 11. Plot (0, 2) and (3, 11) and join them with a ruler. Points that are far apart make the line easier to draw accurately. The line also passes through (1, 5) and (2, 8), so it is the same graph of y = 3x + 2.

A1-7#10.title: Find where it crosses
A1-7#10.text: Put x = 0 into y = 3x − 4 to find the start: y = −4, so the line begins at (0, −4), below the x-axis. Now put in x = 2: y = 6 − 4 = 2. From (0, −4) to (2, 2) the line climbs 6 over 2 steps, which is 3 per step. So the slope is 3 and the start is (0, −4).

A1-7#11.title: Break the ride into chunks
A1-7#11.text: Work in blocks of 10 minutes. At 15 cents a minute, 10 minutes cost 150 cents, which is 1 dollar 50. A 20 minute ride is two such blocks, so the riding costs 3 dollars. Add the 2 dollar unlock fee, which is charged once, and the total is 5 dollars.

A1-7#12.title: Grow it week by week
A1-7#12.text: List the heights instead of substituting. The plant begins at 4 cm and gains 3 cm each week: week 1 is 7, week 2 is 10, week 3 is 13, week 4 is 16, week 5 is 19. After five jumps of 3 from a start of 4, the plant is 19 cm tall.

A1-7#13.title: Start and step instead
A1-7#13.text: Read the graph facts straight from y = 2x + 1. The intercept 1 puts the first dot at (0, 1). The slope 2 says each step right goes up 2, so the next dots are (1, 3) and (2, 5). These are the same three points the table gives, so the two methods check each other.

A1-7#14.title: Substitute into the rule
A1-7#14.text: Use the equation directly. Week 6 means w = 6, so s = 15 + 5(6). Multiply first: 5 × 6 = 30 dollars saved over the six weeks. Then add the 15 dollars you began with: 15 + 30 = 45. The savings at week 6 are 45 dollars, the same as the sixth step of the walk.

A1-8#1.title: A bank balance example
A1-8#1.text: Open an account with 50 dollars and put in 20 dollars every month. The balances are 50, 70, 90, 110. To describe every month at once you need only two facts: 50 to begin and 20 more each month. So the balance after x months is y = 20x + 50. A different account changes the two numbers but never the shape of the equation.

A1-8#2.title: Try it on one table
A1-8#2.text: Take the table x = 1, 2, 3 with y = 7, 9, 11. The y-values rise by 2 each row, so m = 2. There is no row for x = 0, so go back one row from x = 1: 7 − 2 = 5, so b = 5. The equation is y = 2x + 5. Test the last row: 2(3) + 5 = 11, which matches.

A1-8#3.title: Picture the two dots
A1-8#3.text: Mark two dots on grid paper, say (1, 5) and (2, 8). Only one straight ruler line passes through both. From the first dot to the second you go 1 right and 3 up, so the tilt is 3. Slide back 1 to the left along the same tilt and you drop 3, landing on the y-axis at height 2. The line is y = 3x + 2.

A1-8#4.title: Two bills side by side
A1-8#4.text: Compare two bills for a bike hire that costs 5 dollars to unlock and 2 dollars per hour. For 1 hour you pay 7. For 4 hours you pay 13. The 5 appears once in each bill, however long the ride, so it is b. The 2 is paid again every hour, so it multiplies the hours and is m. The rule is cost = 2x + 5.

A1-8#5.title: Step along the line
A1-8#5.text: Start at (0, 5), which is on the y-axis, so b = 5. To reach (4, −3) the line falls from 5 to −3, a drop of 8, over 4 steps. That is a drop of 2 per step: (1, 3), (2, 1), (3, −1), (4, −3). Falling 2 each step means m = −2, so the equation is y = −2x + 5.

A1-8#6.title: Build a table of the points
A1-8#6.text: Put the points in a table and fill the gaps. From x = 0 to x = 3, y goes from −2 to 7, a climb of 9 over 3 steps, so 3 per step. The rows are 0 → −2, 1 → 1, 2 → 4, 3 → 7. The jump of 3 is the slope and the row for x = 0 gives b = −2, so y = 3x − 2.

A1-8#7.title: Table of the tank
A1-8#7.text: Write the level each hour: 40, 34, 28, 22, 16, 10, 4. The level starts at 40 and falls by 6 every hour, so the rule is y = −6x + 40. After 6 hours 4 litres are left, and the next hour would need 6, so the tank empties during the seventh hour, about 6.7 hours after the start.

A1-8#8.title: Build it from a table
A1-8#8.text: Use the two facts to make points. A y-intercept of 1 means the row 0 → 1. A slope of 5 means each row is 5 more: 1 → 6, 2 → 11, 3 → 16. Every output is 5 times the input, plus 1. Writing that pattern with x and y gives y = 5x + 1.

A1-8#9.title: Slope formula on two rows
A1-8#9.text: Treat two rows as points: (0, 3) and (2, 13). The slope formula gives (13 − 3) ÷ (2 − 0) = 10 ÷ 2 = 5. The point (0, 3) is on the y-axis, so b = 3. The equation is y = 5x + 3. The middle row checks it: 5(1) + 3 = 8.

A1-8#10.title: List the bills first
A1-8#10.text: Write what you have paid in total after each month. At month 0 you have paid the 25 dollar fee. Then 35, 45, 55 after months 1, 2 and 3. The totals go up by 10 each month from a start of 25. A start of 25 and a jump of 10 is the line y = 10x + 25. Check month 3: 30 + 25 = 55.

A1-8#11.title: Two points from the story
A1-8#11.text: Turn the story into two points. At hour 0 the candle is 20 cm, giving (0, 20). After 1 hour it is 18 cm, giving (1, 18). The slope is (18 − 20) ÷ (1 − 0) = −2, and the point on the vertical axis gives b = 20. So h = −2t + 20, which is the same as h = 20 − 2t.

A1-8#12.title: Fill in the middle row
A1-8#12.text: Make a table from the two points. At x = 0, y = 6, and at x = 2, y = 12. The value at x = 1 must be halfway, which is 9. So the rows are 6, 9, 12, rising by 3 each step from a start of 6. Jump 3 and start 6 give y = 3x + 6.

A1-8#13.title: Solve for b with algebra
A1-8#13.text: Put what you know into y = mx + b. The slope is 3, so y = 3x + b. The line passes through (1, 5), so replace x with 1 and y with 5: 5 = 3(1) + b, which is 5 = 3 + b. Subtract 3 from both sides and b = 2. The equation is y = 3x + 2.

A1-8#14.title: Read m and b from the words
A1-8#14.text: Pick the two numbers straight from the story. "Starts at 55 degrees" is the value when no hours have passed, so b = 55. "Rises 3 degrees each hour" is the change for each step of x, so m = 3. Put them in y = mx + b to get y = 3x + 55. Check hour 2: 6 + 55 = 61 degrees.

A1-9#1.title: Two tables, one shared row
A1-9#1.text: Make a table for each rule. For y = 2x, the rows x = 0, 1, 2, 3 give y = 0, 2, 4, 6. For y = 6 − x, the same x-values give y = 6, 5, 4, 3. Compare row by row. Only at x = 2 do both tables show the same y, which is 4. That shared row, x = 2 and y = 4, is the solution of the system.

A1-9#2.title: A price tag example
A1-9#2.text: A sandwich and a drink cost 9 dollars together, and the sandwich costs twice as much as the drink. Since the sandwich is worth two drinks, trade it for two drinks on the receipt. Now the receipt says three drinks cost 9 dollars, so a drink is 3 dollars and the sandwich is 6. Trading one thing for its equal value is substitution.

A1-9#3.title: Two shopping baskets
A1-9#3.text: Two numbers have a sum of 10 and a difference of 4. Write x + y = 10 and x − y = 4. Put the two facts together: the sum plus the difference is the bigger number counted twice, because the smaller number is added once and taken away once. So twice the bigger number is 14, and it is 7. The smaller one is 3.

A1-9#4.title: Draw the pets as bars
A1-9#4.text: Draw one bar for dogs and a longer bar for cats. The cat bar is the dog bar with an extra piece of 4. Together the bars make 12. Remove the extra 4 and two equal dog bars are left, totalling 8, so there are 4 dogs and 8 cats. The picture needed both facts: the total and the comparison.

A1-9#5.title: Sum and difference reasoning
A1-9#5.text: Two numbers add to 1 and the first is 7 more than the second. If they were equal, each would be half of 1, which is 0.5. To make them 7 apart, move the first up by 3.5 and the second down by 3.5. That gives x = 4 and y = −3. Check: 4 + (−3) = 1 and 4 − (−3) = 7.

A1-9#6.title: Subtract instead of adding
A1-9#6.text: Take the first equation away from the second. The 3x terms cancel: (3x + 2y) − (3x − 2y) = 4y, and 6 − 12 = −6. So 4y = −6 and y = −1.5. Put that into 3x + 2y = 6: 3x − 3 = 6, so 3x = 9 and x = 3. The solution is (3, −1.5), found by removing x first.

A1-9#7.title: Consecutive number story
A1-9#7.text: The rule y = x + 1 says y is the next number after x. The other rule says the two add to 9. Look for two neighbouring whole numbers with a sum of 9. Half of 9 is 4.5, and the neighbours on either side of it are 4 and 5. So x = 4 and y = 5.

A1-9#8.title: Table of guesses
A1-9#8.text:
Use the first rule to make y, then test the second rule.
x = 1: y = 1, and 3 + 1 = 4.
x = 2: y = 3, and 6 + 3 = 9.
x = 3: y = 5, and 9 + 5 = 14.
The total rises by 5 each row and reaches 14 at x = 3, so the solution is (3, 5).

A1-9#9.title: Halve the sum and the gap
A1-9#9.text: Two numbers add to 10 and differ by 4. If they were equal they would both be 5. Push the larger one up by half the gap and the smaller one down by the same amount: 5 + 2 = 7 and 5 − 2 = 3. So x = 7 and y = 3. Check: 7 + 3 = 10 and 7 − 3 = 4.

A1-9#10.title: Substitute from the easy rule
A1-9#10.text: The rule x + y = 8 says that x is the same as 8 − y. Write that in place of x in the first equation: 2(8 − y) + 3y = 19. Distribute to get 16 − 2y + 3y = 19, so 16 + y = 19 and y = 3. Then x = 8 − 3 = 5. The solution (5, 3) matches the one found by elimination.

A1-9#11.title: Month-by-month table
A1-9#11.text:
List both totals each month.
Month 1: A 25, B 17.
Month 2: A 30, B 24.
Month 3: A 35, B 31.
Month 4: A 40, B 38.
Month 5: A 45, B 45.
Plan B starts 10 dollars lower but gains 2 dollars on plan A every month. They are level at month 5, when both have cost 45 dollars.

A1-9#12.title: Solve it as an equation
A1-9#12.text: Write each plan's total after m months: plan A is 20 + 5m and plan B is 10 + 7m. Set them equal: 20 + 5m = 10 + 7m. Subtract 5m from both sides to get 20 = 10 + 2m, then subtract 10 to get 10 = 2m. So m = 5 months. Both plans then total 45 dollars.

A1-9#13.title: Solve with elimination
A1-9#13.text: Write the receipts as equations: 3a + 2k = 41 and a + 2k = 23. Both contain 2k, so subtract the second from the first. The kid tickets cancel and 2a = 18, so a = 9. Put 9 into the second equation: 9 + 2k = 23, so 2k = 14 and k = 7. Adult tickets cost 9 dollars and kid tickets 7 dollars.

A1-10#1.title: Powers of ten you know
A1-10#1.text: Use powers of ten, where an exponent counts zeros. 10² is 100 and 10³ is 1000. Multiply them: 100 × 1000 = 100,000. That has five zeros, so it is 10⁵, and 2 + 3 = 5. The two zeros and the three zeros simply line up behind the 1. The same joining happens with any base: x² · x³ = x⁵.

A1-10#2.title: Undoing a multiplication
A1-10#2.text: Division asks a multiplication question. x⁵ ÷ x² asks: x² times what gives x⁵? Multiplying adds exponents, so the missing power must add 3 to the 2. The answer is x³. With tens: 100,000 ÷ 100 = 1000. Crossing off two zeros from five leaves three, so 10⁵ ÷ 10² = 10³.

A1-10#3.title: Rows of an egg tray
A1-10#3.text: Picture a tray with 3 rows and 2 eggs in each row. It holds 3 × 2 = 6 eggs. In (x²)³ each row is an x² with 2 copies of x, and there are 3 rows, so there are 6 copies: x⁶. With tens: (10²)³ = 100 × 100 × 100 = 1,000,000, which has six zeros, so it is 10⁶.

A1-10#4.title: Walk down a staircase of powers
A1-10#4.text: List powers of 2 going down: 2³ = 8, 2² = 4, 2¹ = 2. Each step down divides by 2. Keep stepping: 2⁰ = 1, then 2⁻¹ = 1/2, 2⁻² = 1/4, 2⁻³ = 1/8. The pattern never jumps to negative numbers. It passes through 1 at the zero step and then gives smaller and smaller fractions.

A1-10#6.title: Watch the sign alternate
A1-10#6.text: List the powers of −3 one at a time. (−3)¹ = −3. Multiply by −3 again and the sign turns positive: (−3)² = 9. Multiply once more and it turns negative: (−3)³ = −27. Each extra factor of −3 flips the sign, so even exponents give positive results and odd exponents give negative ones: 9 and −27.

A1-10#7.title: Halve your way down
A1-10#7.text: Start from powers you know and step down, dividing by 2 each time. 2² = 4, 2¹ = 2, 2⁰ = 1. Three more steps reach the exponent −3: 2⁻¹ = 1/2, 2⁻² = 1/4, 2⁻³ = 1/8. The pattern of halving lands on 1/8, a small positive fraction, in agreement with 1 over 2³.

A1-10#8.title: Test with tens
A1-10#8.text: Try the base 10, where the answer is easy to see. 10³ is 1000 and 10⁴ is 10,000. Their product is 10,000,000, a 1 followed by seven zeros, so it is 10⁷. Three zeros and four zeros joined to make seven. The exponents were added, not multiplied, so x³ · x⁴ = x⁷.

A1-10#9.title: Ask the multiplication question
A1-10#9.text: Turn the division around: x³ times which power gives x⁸? Multiplying powers adds exponents, so you need 3 + ? = 8, and the missing exponent is 5. Check with x = 10: 100,000,000 ÷ 1000 = 100,000, which is 10⁵. Both the question and the number test give x⁵.

A1-10#10.title: Square, then square again
A1-10#10.text: A fourth power is a square of a square, so do the work in two rounds. First square the group: (x²)² = x² · x² = x⁴. Then square that result: (x⁴)² = x⁴ · x⁴ = x⁸. Check with the number 2 in place of x: 2² = 4, and 4⁴ = 256, while 2⁸ = 256 as well. So (x²)⁴ = x⁸.

A1-10#11.title: Group the factors
A1-10#11.text: Find the fifth power of 2 by grouping the five 2s in pairs instead of listing doubles: (2 × 2) × (2 × 2) × 2 = 4 × 4 × 2 = 16 × 2, which is 32 layers after 5 folds. For ten folds there are five pairs, and each pair is 4: 4 × 4 × 4 × 4 × 4 = 16 × 16 × 4 = 256 × 4, which is 1024 layers.

A1-10#12.title: Pair up the threes
A1-10#12.text: Group the four 3s into two pairs: 3⁴ = (3 × 3) × (3 × 3). Each pair is 9, so the product is 9 × 9 = 81. In the story, this says two rounds turn 1 teller into 9 hearers, and two more rounds turn each of those 9 into 9 again. Round 4 reaches 81 people.

A1-10#13.title: Write out every copy
A1-10#13.text: Skip the numbers and write the factors out. x³ is x · x · x and x⁴ is x · x · x · x. Put them side by side and count: three copies and then four more make seven copies in one chain, so the product is x⁷. Getting x¹² would need twelve copies, and there are only seven on the page.

A1-10#14.title: Divide a number by itself
A1-10#14.text: Use the quotient rule on 4² ÷ 4². Subtracting the exponents gives 4²⁻² = 4⁰. Now work the same division with ordinary numbers: 16 ÷ 16 = 1, because anything divided by itself is 1. Both lines describe the same calculation, so 4⁰ = 1.

A1-11#1.title: Stack paper or fold paper
A1-11#1.text: Take a sheet of paper. If you stack one more sheet on the pile each time, the layers go 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. That is linear: one more every step. If you fold the pile in half each time instead, the layers go 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. That is exponential. After five steps, stacking has reached 6 layers and folding has reached 32.

A1-11#2.title: Read a and b from a table
A1-11#2.text: Look at the table x = 0, 1, 2, 3 with y = 2, 6, 18, 54. The value at x = 0 is 2, so the start a is 2. Each y is 3 times the one before it, so the factor b is 3. The rule is y = 2 · 3ˣ. Test the last row: 2 · 3³ = 2 · 27 = 54, which matches the table.

A1-11#3.title: Ten blocks in a row
A1-11#3.text: Picture the original amount as a bar of 10 equal blocks. Each block is 10 percent. Going up 10 percent adds one block, so you have 11 blocks out of the original 10, which is 1.1 times as much. Going down 20 percent removes two blocks, so 8 of the original 10 remain, which is 0.8 times as much.

A1-11#4.title: Take off a fifth each year
A1-11#4.text: Twenty percent is one fifth. One fifth of 600 is 120, so after the first year the phone is worth 600 − 120 = 480 dollars. One fifth of 480 is 96, so after the second year it is worth 480 − 96 = 384 dollars. The second loss is smaller because it is a fifth of a smaller value. The answer is 384 dollars.

A1-11#5.title: A tripling pattern, rewound
A1-11#5.text: A pattern follows y = 81 · 3ˣ, tripling at each step. Going forward from 81 you get 243, then 729. Rewinding one step must undo a tripling, so the value before 81 was 27, and before that 9. The formula agrees: at x = −2, 3⁻² is 1/9, and 81 × 1/9 = 9. Going back makes the values small, but they stay above zero.

A1-11#6.title: Two pay offers
A1-11#6.text: Job A pays 1000 dollars every day. Job B pays 1 cent on day 1 and doubles the pay each day. On day 11, job B pays only 10.24 dollars, and job A looks far better. On day 17, job B pays 655.36 dollars. On day 18 it pays 1310.72 dollars and passes job A, and on day 21 it pays over 10,000 dollars for one day.

A1-11#7.title: Write a rule for each
A1-11#7.text: Try to describe each list with a rule. The list 3, 6, 12, 24 is 3 × 1, 3 × 2, 3 × 4, 3 × 8: a start of 3 times powers of 2, so it is exponential. The list 3, 6, 9, 12 is 3 × 1, 3 × 2, 3 × 3, 3 × 4: the multiples of 3, which is a straight line pattern, so it is linear.

A1-11#8.title: Follow one bacterium
A1-11#8.text: Watch a single bacterium for 3 hours. It becomes 2, then 4, then 8. So after three doublings each starting bacterium has turned into a family of 8. The dish began with 5 bacteria, so there are 5 families of 8, which is 5 × 8 = 40 bacteria.

A1-11#9.title: Use the fraction four fifths
A1-11#9.text: Keeping 80 percent is keeping 4/5. Two years means 4/5 of 4/5, which is 16/25 of the price. Divide 500 by 25 to get 20, then multiply by 16: 20 × 16 = 320. The phone is worth 320 dollars. As a check, 16/25 is 0.64, and 500 × 0.64 is also 320.

A1-11#10.title: Double the start four times
A1-11#10.text: The rule says: begin at 3 and multiply by 2 once for each step of x. For x = 4 that is four doublings: 3 becomes 6, then 12, then 24, then 48. So y = 48. Doubling one step at a time also shows why the 3 is not multiplied by 2 before the power is taken.

A1-11#11.title: Check by running forward
A1-11#11.text: Suppose the value at x = −2 is 20 and move forward. One step right doubles it to 40 at x = −1. One more step doubles it to 80 at x = 0. That is the starting value in y = 80 · 2ˣ, because 2⁰ = 1. Running forward from 20 lands on the known start, so y = 20 at x = −2 is correct.

A1-11#12.title: Table from week 0
A1-11#12.text:
List both accounts from the beginning.
Week 1: A 20, B 110.
Week 2: A 40, B 210.
Week 3: A 80, B 310.
Week 4: A 160, B 410.
Week 5: A 320, B 510.
Week 6: A 640, B 610.
B leads for five weeks, and A is ahead for the first time in week 6.

A1-11#13.title: Track the gap between them
A1-11#13.text: Record how far B is ahead of A each week. Week 1: 90. Week 2: 170. Week 3: 230. Week 4: 250. Week 5: 190. Week 6: −30. The lead grows more slowly, peaks at week 4, then shrinks quickly. The negative number in week 6 means A is now 30 ahead, so A takes the lead in week 6.

A1-11#14.title: Add or subtract percents first
A1-11#14.text: Work with percents before turning them into decimals. The original amount is 100 percent. A rise of 10 percent makes 100 + 10 = 110 percent, and 110 percent written as a decimal is 1.10. A fall of 20 percent leaves 100 − 20 = 80 percent, which is 0.80. So the factors are 1.10 and 0.80.

A1-12#1.title: Metres and square metres
A1-12#1.text: Units show the idea. 4 metres of rope and 3 metres of rope make 7 metres of rope. But 4 metres of rope and 3 square metres of carpet do not make 7 of anything, because a length and an area are different kinds of quantity. In the same way x measures a length and x² measures an area, so 4x + 3x² has to stay as two terms.

A1-12#2.title: Two shopping lists
A1-12#2.text: One shopping list says 3 apples and 4 bananas. Another says 2 apples and 5 bananas. To shop for both, you add apples to apples and bananas to bananas: 5 apples and 9 bananas. Adding polynomials works the same way. Line the two up in columns, x-terms above x-terms and numbers above numbers, and add each column: 5x + 9.

A1-12#3.title: Paying for two things
A1-12#3.text: You have 20 dollars and buy a sandwich for 5 and a drink for 2. The cost of the order is (5 + 2), so you have 20 − (5 + 2) = 13 dollars left. Paying item by item gives 20 − 5 − 2 = 13 as well. Both items were taken away. If you wrote 20 − 5 + 2 you would be claiming the drink earned you money.

A1-12#4.title: Long multiplication does this
A1-12#4.text: You already use this rule with numbers. To work out 13 × 12, think of it as (10 + 3)(10 + 2). Multiply every part by every part: 10 × 10 = 100, 10 × 2 = 20, 3 × 10 = 30, 3 × 2 = 6. The total is 156, which is 13 × 12. Replace each 10 with x and the same four products give x² + 5x + 6.

A1-12#5.title: Test with a number
A1-12#5.text: Check the result by choosing x = 2. The first bracket is 4(2) − 5 = 3 and the second is 7(2) − 2 = 12, so the difference is 3 − 12 = −9. The answer −3x − 3 gives −6 − 3 = −9 as well. A common slip, −3x − 7, would give −13, so the test confirms −3x − 3.

A1-12#6.title: Try x = 10
A1-12#6.text: Check the expansion with x = 10. The brackets become 10 − 3 = 7 and 10 − 5 = 5, and 7 × 5 = 35. The answer x² − 8x + 15 gives 100 − 80 + 15 = 35, which matches. If the last term were −15, the value would be 5, so the test shows the corner really is +15.

A1-12#7.title: Multiply, then take the opposite
A1-12#7.text: Leave the minus sign until the end. First multiply 3x(2x − 4): 3x times 2x is 6x², and 3x times −4 is −12x, so you have 6x² − 12x. The minus sign in front asks for the opposite of all of that, which flips both signs: −6x² + 12x. Check with x = 1: −3(−2) = 6, and −6 + 12 = 6.

A1-12#8.title: Check with x = 10
A1-12#8.text: Put x = 10 into the original expression: 40 + 30 + 2 = 72. The answer 7x + 2 gives 70 + 2 = 72, so it agrees. The tempting wrong answer 9x would give 90, which does not. The 2 is worth 2 whatever x is, so it cannot be folded into the x-terms. The simplified form is 7x + 2.

A1-12#9.title: Stack them in columns
A1-12#9.text: Write one polynomial under the other, the way you stack numbers to add them. Put 2x under 3x and 5 under 4. Add each column: 3x + 2x = 5x and 4 + 5 = 9, so the sum is 5x + 9. With x = 10 this is the sum 34 + 25 = 59, and 5(10) + 9 is 59 as well.

A1-12#10.title: Check by adding back
A1-12#10.text: Subtraction can be checked with addition. If (5x + 7) − (2x + 3) really is 3x + 4, then adding 2x + 3 back to the answer must return the first polynomial. Add them: 3x + 2x = 5x and 4 + 3 = 7, giving 5x + 7. That is the polynomial you began with, so 3x + 4 is correct.

A1-12#11.title: Subtract in columns
A1-12#11.text: Line up the like terms, with cost under revenue. In the x² column, 3 take away 1 leaves 2, so 2x². In the x column, 5 take away 2 leaves 3, so 3x. The profit is 2x² + 3x. Test x = 1: revenue is 8 dollars, cost is 3 dollars, profit is 5 dollars, and 2 + 3 = 5.

A1-12#12.title: Distribute one bracket at a time
A1-12#12.text: Treat (x + 2) as a single block and hand it to each part of (x + 3). That gives x(x + 2) + 3(x + 2). The first piece is x² + 2x and the second is 3x + 6. Add them and combine the middle terms: x² + 2x + 3x + 6 = x² + 5x + 6 square meters.

A1-12#13.title: Add the bracket twice
A1-12#13.text: 2x times the bracket is the same as x times the bracket, taken twice. One copy is x(3x + 4) = 3x² + 4x. Two copies are 3x² + 4x + 3x² + 4x. Combine like terms: the squares make 6x² and the x-terms make 8x. The product is 6x² + 8x.

A1-12#14.title: Set it out like long multiplication
A1-12#14.text: Multiply the way you would multiply two-digit numbers. First multiply (x + 3) by the 2: that row is 2x + 6. Next multiply (x + 3) by the x: that row is x² + 3x. Add the two rows, lining up like terms: x² + 3x + 2x + 6 = x² + 5x + 6. Each row handles one term of the second bracket, so nothing is skipped.

A1-12#15.title: Try two more numbers
A1-12#15.text: One test can pass by luck, so try others. With x = 0 the brackets give 3 × 2 = 6, and the expanded form gives 0 + 0 + 6 = 6. With x = 10 the brackets give 13 × 12 = 156, and the expanded form gives 100 + 50 + 6 = 156. Both tests agree, just as 56 = 56 did for x = 5, so the expansion checks out.

A1-13#1.title: Factoring numbers first
A1-13#1.text: You already factor numbers. Given the area 15, you look for the sides and find 3 and 5. Algebra does the same with letters. Let x = 10 in x² + 5x + 6 and the area is 156. Its sides are 12 and 13, which are 10 + 2 and 10 + 3. Factoring finds those sides for every x at once: (x + 2)(x + 3).

A1-13#2.title: A rectangle with height 6
A1-13#2.text: Draw a rectangle whose area is 6x + 12, made of a piece with area 6x beside a piece with area 12. Give both pieces the same height, 6. Then the first piece must be x wide and the second must be 2 wide. The whole rectangle is 6 tall and x + 2 wide, so 6x + 12 = 6(x + 2). A shorter height like 3 works too, but leaves 3(2x + 4), which can still be split.

A1-13#3.title: See it in ordinary numbers
A1-13#3.text: Multiply 13 × 14 as (10 + 3)(10 + 4). The parts are 100, then 40 and 30, then 12. The middle parts total 70, which is 7 tens, because 3 + 4 = 7. The last part is 12 because 3 × 4 = 12. So 182 = 100 + 70 + 12. To go backwards from x² + 7x + 12 you need the pair that adds to 7 and multiplies to 12.

A1-13#4.title: Cut and slide a square
A1-13#4.text: Draw a square with side x and cut a small square with side 5 out of one corner. The area left is x² − 25, and it has an L shape. Slice the L into two rectangles and slide one beside the other. They join into a single rectangle that is x + 5 long and x − 5 wide. Same paper, same area, so x² − 25 = (x + 5)(x − 5).

A1-13#5.title: Four cases side by side
A1-13#5.text:
Compare four examples that all use 3 and 4.
x² + 7x + 12 needs 3 and 4: product positive, sum positive.
x² − 7x + 12 needs −3 and −4: product positive, sum negative.
x² + x − 12 needs 4 and −3: product negative, the bigger one is positive.
x² − x − 12 needs −4 and 3: product negative, the bigger one is negative.

A1-13#6.title: Find the zeros by testing
A1-13#6.text: Try small values of x in x² − 7x + 12 and look for a result of zero. At x = 3 you get 9 − 21 + 12 = 0, so (x − 3) is a factor. At x = 4 you get 16 − 28 + 12 = 0, so (x − 4) is a factor. The factored form is (x − 3)(x − 4). Expanding confirms it: x² − 4x − 3x + 12 = x² − 7x + 12.

A1-13#7.title: One zero gives one factor
A1-13#7.text: Test values in x² + 2x − 15. At x = 3 it is 9 + 6 − 15 = 0, so (x − 3) is one factor. The number parts of the two brackets must multiply to −15, and −15 ÷ (−3) = 5, so the other bracket is (x + 5). Check the middle term: 5x − 3x = 2x. The answer is (x + 5)(x − 3).

A1-13#8.title: Try smaller bag counts
A1-13#8.text: Test possible bag counts on 6x + 12. Two bags work: each gets 3x + 6. Three bags work: each gets 2x + 4. Six bags work: each gets x + 2. No larger number divides both 6x and 12 evenly. With 2 or 3 bags the contents could still be split further, but x + 2 cannot, so the complete factoring is 6(x + 2).

A1-13#9.title: Split the middle term
A1-13#9.text: Once you suspect the pair 2 and 3, rewrite 5x as 2x + 3x: x² + 2x + 3x + 6. Factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately: x(x + 2) + 3(x + 2). Both parts contain the block (x + 2), so pull it out: (x + 2)(x + 3).

A1-13#10.title: Measure real banners
A1-13#10.text: Give x a value and factor the number. If x = 2 the area is 4 + 14 + 12 = 30, which is 5 × 6. If x = 5 the area is 25 + 35 + 12 = 72, which is 8 × 9. Each time the sides are 3 more and 4 more than x. That pattern says the banner is (x + 3) ft by (x + 4) ft.

A1-13#11.title: Check with real numbers
A1-13#11.text: Test the pattern with x = 10. Then x² − 25 is 100 − 25 = 75, and (x + 5)(x − 5) is 15 × 5 = 75. Try x = 6 as well: 36 − 25 = 11, and the brackets give 11 × 1 = 11. The two forms agree for both test numbers, which supports the factoring (x + 5)(x − 5).

A1-13#12.title: Hunt for the zeros
A1-13#12.text: Try values of x in x² − x − 6 and look for zero. At x = 3 you get 9 − 3 − 6 = 0, so (x − 3) is a factor. At x = −2 you get 4 + 2 − 6 = 0, so (x + 2) is a factor. That gives (x − 3)(x + 2). Expanding checks the signs: x² + 2x − 3x − 6 = x² − x − 6.

A1-13#13.title: Start from the sum
A1-13#13.text: Search from the other side. List the pairs of whole numbers that add to 5: 1 and 4, 2 and 3. Now multiply each pair: 1 × 4 = 4 and 2 × 3 = 6. Only 2 and 3 give the 6 needed for the last term. So the edges of the box are x + 2 and x + 3, and the factoring is (x + 2)(x + 3).

A1-13#14.title: Arrange the tiles
A1-13#14.text: Picture one big x² tile, 7 long x strips and 12 small unit squares. Build a rectangle: put some strips along the right edge of the big tile and the rest along the bottom. The corner gap must be filled exactly by the 12 units. Splitting the strips 3 and 4 leaves a 3 by 4 gap, which holds 12. The sides are x + 3 and x + 4, so (x + 3)(x + 4).

A1-14#1.title: The area of a growing square
A1-14#1.text: Think of y = x² as the area of a square with side x. A side of 1 gives area 1, a side of 2 gives 4, a side of 3 gives 9, and a side of 10 gives 100. Each extra unit of side adds a longer border than the last one, so the area speeds up. Plotting side against area gives the right half of the U.

A1-14#2.title: Distance from zero
A1-14#2.text: The equation x² = 25 asks which numbers land on 25 when squared. Think of the number line. Squaring cares only about how far a number is from zero, not which side it is on. The numbers 5 steps from zero are 5 on the right and −5 on the left. Both distances square to 25, so both are answers.

A1-14#3.title: Try to make zero
A1-14#3.text: Try to get 0 by multiplying two numbers that are not 0. 2 × 3 = 6. 0.1 × 0.1 = 0.01. −4 × 5 = −20. However small the numbers, the product is never 0. Now use a zero: 0 × 8 = 0. So in (x − 3)(x + 5) = 0, one bracket must be the zero. At x = 3 the product is 0 × 8, and at x = −5 it is −8 × 0.

A1-14#4.title: See it in a table
A1-14#4.text:
Make a table for y = 4x − x².
x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 gives y = 0, 3, 4, 3, 0.
The heights rise, reach 4, and come back down in the same steps. The two zeros are at x = 0 and x = 4, and the largest height sits at x = 2, halfway between them. That middle point (2, 4) is the vertex.

A1-14#5.title: Test values in a table
A1-14#5.text:
Evaluate x² + 3x − 10 for several inputs.
x = 1 gives −6, x = 2 gives 0, x = 3 gives 8.
On the negative side, x = −4 gives −6, x = −5 gives 0, x = −6 gives 8.
The expression is zero at x = 2 and at x = −5. Those are the two roots: −5 and 2.

A1-14#6.title: Reason about signs, then test
A1-14#6.text: If x is positive, all three terms of x² + 7x + 12 are positive, so the total cannot be 0. The roots must be negative. Test them: x = −2 gives 4 − 14 + 12 = 2. x = −3 gives 9 − 21 + 12 = 0. x = −4 gives 16 − 28 + 12 = 0. x = −5 gives 2 again. The roots are −3 and −4.

A1-14#7.title: Two tables, mirror images
A1-14#7.text: Compare y = x² with y = −x² using a table. For x = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, the first gives 4, 1, 0, 1, 4: a bowl with its lowest point at 0. The second gives −4, −1, 0, −1, −4: the same numbers flipped below the axis, an arch with its highest point at 0. The negative sign reflects the whole curve over the x-axis.

A1-14#8.title: Factor as a difference of squares
A1-14#8.text: Move everything to one side: x² − 25 = 0. The left side is a square minus a square, so it factors as (x + 5)(x − 5) = 0. A product is zero only when one factor is zero. So x + 5 = 0, giving x = −5, or x − 5 = 0, giving x = 5. Factoring finds both answers: x = 5 or x = −5.

A1-14#9.title: Expand and test values
A1-14#9.text: Multiply the brackets out to get x² + 2x − 15 = 0, then test numbers. x = 3 gives 9 + 6 − 15 = 0. x = −5 gives 25 − 10 − 15 = 0. Other values fail: x = 0 gives −15 and x = 4 gives 9. Only x = 3 and x = −5 work, the same values that make a bracket zero.

A1-14#10.title: Turn it into a product puzzle
A1-14#10.text: Rearrange x² − 5x + 6 = 0 as 5x − x² = 6, which is x(5 − x) = 6. The two numbers x and 5 − x always add to 5, and here they must multiply to 6. Two numbers with sum 5 and product 6 are 2 and 3. So x is 2, with partner 3, or x is 3, with partner 2. The solutions are 2 and 3.

A1-14#11.title: Table of the fall
A1-14#11.text:
Work out the height second by second.
t = 0: 45 metres.
t = 1: 45 − 5 = 40.
t = 2: 45 − 20 = 25.
t = 3: 45 − 45 = 0.
The height reaches zero at t = 3, so the ball lands after 3 seconds. The drops between rows are 5, 15 and 25, which shows the ball speeding up as it falls.

A1-14#12.title: Table of the jet
A1-14#12.text:
Compute the height of the water at each second.
t = 0: 0.
t = 1: 20 − 5 = 15.
t = 2: 40 − 20 = 20.
t = 3: 60 − 45 = 15.
t = 4: 80 − 80 = 0.
The water leaves the spout at height 0, rises to 20 metres, and is back at height 0 when t = 4 seconds.

A1-14#13.title: Factor and split
A1-14#13.text: Look for two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to −5. They are −2 and −3, so the equation is (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0. A product is zero only when one factor is zero, so x − 2 = 0 or x − 3 = 0. That gives x = 2 or x = 3, the same inputs the table found.

A1-14#14.title: Table around the peak
A1-14#14.text: List the heights each second: at t = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 the height is 0, 15, 20, 15, 0 metres. The list reads the same forwards and backwards, and its largest entry is in the middle. Check half a second either side: t = 1.5 and t = 2.5 both give 18.75, which is lower. The peak is 20 meters, at t = 2.

GEO-1#1.title: Everyday stand-ins
GEO-1#1.text: Use real objects as models. The tip of a sharp pencil pressed on paper marks a point. A string pulled tight between two nails is a segment, and you can measure it. A laser beam leaving a pointer is a ray: it has a start but no finish. A straight road imagined with no beginning and no end is a line, and a calm lake stretching forever in every direction is a plane. The real objects have thickness, but the ideas do not.

GEO-1#2.title: Read it off a ruler
GEO-1#2.text: Lay a ruler along the points so that A is at 0, B is at 12 and C is at 19. Each length is a subtraction of two ruler readings: AB = 12 − 0, BC = 19 − 12, AC = 19 − 0. When you add the first two, the reading at B is added once and taken away once, so it drops out and leaves AC. That only happens when B really sits between the other two readings.

GEO-1#3.title: Fold the number line
GEO-1#3.text: Mark −3 and 11 on a paper strip. Fold the strip so the two marks land on each other. The crease is the midpoint, and it falls at 4. Each mark travelled the same distance to the crease, 7 units, so the full gap is 7 + 7 = 14. That matches the formulas: 11 − (−3) = 14 for the distance and (−3 + 11) ÷ 2 = 4 for the midpoint.

GEO-1#4.title: Use ruler positions
GEO-1#4.text: Put A at the 0 mark of a ruler. B is 12 units along, so B sits at 12. C is 7 units past B, so C sits at 12 + 7 = 19. The length AC is the difference of the end readings, 19 − 0 = 19. Reading positions gives the same total as adding the two pieces, AC = 19.

GEO-1#5.title: Slide both points
GEO-1#5.text: Sliding two points the same amount does not change the gap between them. Move P and Q both 3 units to the right. P goes from −3 to 0 and Q goes from 9 to 12. Now one point sits at zero, so the distance is just the other coordinate. PQ = 12.

GEO-1#6.title: Count up from 18
GEO-1#6.text: Start at the 18 mark where B sits and count up to the end of the segment at 30. From 18 to 20 is 2. From 20 to 30 is 10. Together that is 2 + 10 = 12, so BC = 12. Counting up finds the missing piece without writing an equation.

GEO-1#7.title: Make a table of values
GEO-1#7.text:
Try values of x and watch the two halves.
x = 1: JM = 5, MK = 11. x = 2: JM = 10, MK = 14. x = 3: JM = 15, MK = 17. x = 4: JM = 20, MK = 20.
The gap shrinks by 2 each time, from 6 to 4 to 2 to 0. The halves match only at x = 4, where JM = MK = 20.

GEO-1#8.title: Step in from both ends
GEO-1#8.text: Put one finger on −3 and one on 11. Move both fingers one unit toward each other at the same time: −2 and 10, then −1 and 9, then 0 and 8, 1 and 7, 2 and 6, 3 and 5. On the seventh step both fingers land on 4. They moved equal distances, so 4 is halfway. Averaging agrees: (−3 + 11) ÷ 2 = 8 ÷ 2 = 4.

GEO-1#9.title: Count up in friendly jumps
GEO-1#9.text: Place X at 0 km, so Y is at 2.4 and Z is at 6.1. Count from Y up to Z in easy jumps. From 2.4 to 3 is 0.6. From 3 to 6 is 3. From 6 to 6.1 is 0.1. The jumps total 0.6 + 3 + 0.1 = 3.7, so YZ = 3.7 km.

GEO-2#1.title: Read angles on a clock
GEO-2#1.text: Look at the hands of a clock. They are two rays that meet at the centre, so the centre is the vertex. At 3:00 the hands make a square corner, a right angle of 90°. At 1:00 they are only 30° apart, which is acute. At 4:00 they are 120° apart, which is obtuse. If the hand tips are A and C and the centre is B, the angle is named ABC, with the centre letter in the middle.

GEO-2#2.title: Protractor readings subtract
GEO-2#2.text: Place a protractor at B with ray BA on the 0° mark. Suppose ray BD crosses at 25° and ray BC crosses at 73°. Then angle ABD is 25 − 0 = 25°, angle DBC is 73 − 25 = 48°, and angle ABC is 73 − 0 = 73°. Each angle is a difference of two readings, so adding the two small ones cancels the middle reading and leaves the big one: 25 + 48 = 73.

GEO-2#3.title: Try it with a sheet of paper
GEO-2#3.text: Take a sheet of paper. Draw a line from one corner into the sheet. It splits the square corner into two angles, perhaps 30° and 60°, and they add to 90° however you draw it. Those are complementary. Now pick a point on a straight edge and draw a line from it into the sheet. The two angles along the edge might be 110° and 70°. They always add to 180°, so they are supplementary.

GEO-2#4.title: Count up to 90
GEO-2#4.text: Start at 37 and count up to 90 in easy jumps. From 37 to 40 is 3. From 40 to 90 is 50. The jumps total 3 + 50 = 53, so the complement is 53°. This finds the missing angle by building up to the corner instead of subtracting.

GEO-2#5.title: Split off a right angle
GEO-2#5.text: A straight line is two right angles side by side. The 118° angle uses up one whole right angle and 28° of the second one, because 118 = 90 + 28. The other angle is what remains of the second right angle: 90 − 28 = 62°. Check: 118 + 62 = 180.

GEO-2#6.title: Use the full turn
GEO-2#6.text: The four angles at a crossing fill one full turn, 360°. The 65° angle and the one opposite it are equal, so together they use 65 + 65 = 130°. That leaves 360 − 130 = 230° for the other two angles. Those two are also opposite each other, so they are equal, and each is 230 ÷ 2 = 115°. The four angles are 65°, 115°, 65°, 115°.

GEO-2#7.title: Draw a bar for 90
GEO-2#7.text: Draw a bar that stands for 90°. One angle is two x-blocks. The other is one x-block plus a block of 30. Take the 30 block away from the bar: 90 − 30 = 60 is left, and it is made of three equal x-blocks. Each block is 60 ÷ 3 = 20, so x = 20. The angles are 2 × 20 = 40° and 20 + 30 = 50°.

GEO-2#8.title: Balance around 45
GEO-2#8.text: Two equal complements would be 45° each, because 45 + 45 = 90. The angle 37° is 8 below 45. To keep the total at 90, its partner must be 8 above 45, which is 45 + 8 = 53°. Check by adding: 37 + 53 = 90.

GEO-2#9.title: Use two quarter pizzas
GEO-2#9.text: The straight cut leaves a half pizza, which is two quarter pieces of 90° each. The 40° slice comes out of the first quarter and leaves 90 − 40 = 50° of it. The neighbour is that 50° piece plus the whole second quarter: 50 + 90 = 140°.

GEO-3#1.title: Turning off a straight road
GEO-3#1.text: Picture a straight road that crosses two parallel streets. To turn right onto the first street you swing the wheel through some angle, say 70°. At the second street you need exactly the same 70° turn, because that street points the same way as the first. If the two turns were different, the streets would point in different directions and would meet somewhere, so they would not be parallel.

GEO-3#2.title: Spin the Z half a turn
GEO-3#2.text: Mark the middle of the piece of transversal that lies between the two parallel lines. Spin the whole figure half a turn about that point. The transversal lands on itself, and each parallel line lands on the other one, because a half turn keeps a line pointing the same way. One corner of the Z lands exactly on the other corner. A turn does not change the size of an angle, so the two angles are equal.

GEO-3#3.title: Tilt a perpendicular
GEO-3#3.text: Start with a transversal that crosses both parallel lines at right angles. The two angles inside the C are 90° and 90°, which add to 180°. Now tilt the transversal by 15°. One inside angle closes to 75° and the other opens to 105°. Whatever one angle loses, the other gains, so the total stays at 180°.

GEO-3#4.title: Go through the C angles
GEO-3#4.text: Find the angle between the parallel lines that sits next to the 68° angle on the transversal. It is 180 − 68 = 112°. That angle and the wanted angle at the other crossing lie between the parallels on the same side, so they are co-interior and add to 180°. The wanted angle is 180 − 112 = 68°.

GEO-3#5.title: Share 180 in a ratio
GEO-3#5.text: The angles 3x and 2x are in the ratio 3 to 2, and together they make 180°. So the larger angle is 3 fifths of 180 and the smaller is 2 fifths. One fifth of 180 is 36. The angles are 3 × 36 = 108° and 2 × 36 = 72°, and one share is x = 36.

GEO-3#6.title: Watch the gap close
GEO-3#6.text: Try x = 10. The angles are 5(10) − 10 = 40 and 3(10) + 30 = 60, so the first is 20 behind. Each time x goes up by 1, the first angle gains 5 and the second gains 3, so the gap closes by 2. Closing a gap of 20 takes 10 more steps, which gives x = 20. Both angles are then 90°.

GEO-3#7.title: Use the full turn at one crossing
GEO-3#7.text: Look at one crossing. Its four angles make a full turn, 360°. The 47° angle and its vertical partner use 47 + 47 = 94°. The other two angles are equal to each other and share the remaining 360 − 94 = 266°, so each is 133°. The second crossing is a copy of the first because the lines are parallel, so the only sizes are 47° and 133°.

GEO-3#8.title: Slide the upper rung down
GEO-3#8.text: Imagine sliding the upper rung straight down the ladder until it lies on the lower rung. The rungs are parallel, so the rung does not turn as it slides. The 63° angle between ladder and rung rides down with it and lands exactly on the angle at the lower rung. A slide does not change an angle, so the lower angle is 63°.

GEO-3#9.title: One step with the C angles
GEO-3#9.text: Look between the two avenues on one side of the boulevard. The 55° angle at the first avenue and the obtuse angle at the second avenue are co-interior angles, the pair you trace with a C. Co-interior angles on parallel lines add to 180°, so the obtuse angle is 180 − 55 = 125° in one step.

GEO-4#1.title: A vending machine promise
GEO-4#1.text: Think of a vending machine: if you press button B4, then a juice drops out. Pressing B4 is the hypothesis and the juice is the conclusion. Many statements hide the same pattern. "All squares have four right angles" means "if a shape is a square, then it has four right angles." Rewriting it this way shows that being a square is p and having four right angles is q.

GEO-4#2.title: Dogs and animals
GEO-4#2.text: Start with a true statement: if it is a dog, then it is an animal. Converse: if it is an animal, then it is a dog. A cat shows that is false. Inverse: if it is not a dog, then it is not an animal. The same cat shows that is false. Contrapositive: if it is not an animal, then it is not a dog. That is true, because a rock that is not an animal cannot be a dog.

GEO-4#3.title: A pattern that finally breaks
GEO-4#3.text: Take the claim "n² + n + 41 is prime for every whole number n." Try n = 0, 1, 2, 3 and you get 41, 43, 47, 53, all prime. It keeps working up to n = 39. But n = 40 gives 1681, which is 41 × 41. Forty good cases proved nothing, and one bad case ended the claim. That is why a proof must give a reason for every step.

GEO-4#4.title: List the causes of wet ground
GEO-4#4.text: The converse says "if the ground is wet, then it is raining." List the ways ground gets wet: rain, a sprinkler, a hose, a spilled bucket, morning dew. Rain is only one item on the list. Seeing wet ground does not tell you which cause it was, so the converse is false, even though rain always gives wet ground.

GEO-4#5.title: Circles inside circles
GEO-4#5.text: Draw a circle for "angles that measure 90°" and a circle for "right angles." The statement says the first circle sits inside the second. Now pick anything outside the right-angle circle, such as an 89° angle. It must also be outside the 90° circle. In words: if an angle is not a right angle, then it does not measure 90°. That is the contrapositive, and the picture shows it is true.

GEO-4#6.title: Build one from two triangles
GEO-4#6.text: Take two equilateral triangles with side 1 and glue them together along one side. The outline has four sides and each has length 1, so the hypothesis holds. Its angles are 60° at two corners and 60 + 60 = 120° at the other two. A square needs four 90° angles, so this rhombus is not a square, and the claim is false.

GEO-4#7.title: Think of a mirror
GEO-4#7.text: The name gives it away: reflexive comes from reflect. A quantity looks in the mirror and sees itself, like 7 = 7 or AB = AB. The other properties need more than one thing. Symmetric turns AB = CD around into CD = AB, and Transitive links three quantities in a chain. In a figure, look for a side that belongs to two triangles at once. That shared side equals itself by the Reflexive Property.

GEO-4#8.title: Compare the requirement lists
GEO-4#8.text: Write what each shape needs. A rectangle needs four right angles. A square needs four right angles and four equal sides. The converse says that passing the short list guarantees the long list. It cannot, because the short list never mentions the side lengths. A door is a rectangle that is clearly not a square, so the converse is false.

GEO-4#9.title: Test it with coordinates
GEO-4#9.text: Put the points on a number line: A at 0, B at 3, C at 8 and D at 11. Then AB = 3 and CD = 3, so the Given holds. Now AC = 8 − 0 = 8 and BD = 11 − 3 = 8, so they are equal. The reason is visible: AC is the middle piece BC plus AB, and BD is the same middle piece plus CD. Equal ends on a shared middle give AC = BD.

GEO-5#1.title: Build it with straws
GEO-5#1.text: Join three straws of lengths 5, 6 and 7 cm at their ends. However you try, you get the same triangle. That is SSS. Join four straws and the frame flops about, so four sides do not fix a shape. Next draw a 5 cm side with a 40° angle at one end and a 60° angle at the other. The two rays cross at exactly one point, so the triangle is forced. That is ASA.

GEO-5#2.title: Draw both cases
GEO-5#2.text: Draw sides of 8 cm and 5 cm with a 30° angle between them. Joining the free ends gives one triangle only. Now change the order. Draw an 8 cm side, a 30° angle at its left end, and let the 5 cm side hang from the right end. Swing the 5 cm side like a compass. It crosses the 30° ray in two places, so two different triangles fit the same three facts.

GEO-5#3.title: Read parts off the name
GEO-5#3.text: Suppose triangle ABC ≅ triangle DEF, with AB = 5, BC = 7 and angle B = 40°. The order of the letters is a matching code: A with D, B with E, C with F. So DE = 5, EF = 7 and angle E = 40°, with no measuring. It is like two keys cut from the same pattern: once you know they are copies, every notch on one matches a notch on the other.

GEO-5#4.title: Try to build a different triangle
GEO-5#4.text: Imagine building the second triangle from three sticks cut to the marked lengths. Lay the longest stick down. Swing the other two sticks from its ends like compass arms. Their tips can meet at only one point above the base (and its mirror image below). So no different triangle is possible, and three matching sides are enough. The shortcut is SSS.

GEO-5#5.title: Draw the second triangle
GEO-5#5.text: Try to draw a triangle from the marks. Draw the marked side first. At each end, draw a ray at the marked angle. Two rays that lean toward each other cross at exactly one point, and that point is the third vertex. The side you started with lies between the two angles, so the triangle is fixed by angle, side, angle. The shortcut is ASA.

GEO-5#6.title: Put in numbers
GEO-5#6.text: Suppose each hypotenuse is 13 and the matching legs are 5. In each triangle the other leg is √(13² − 5²) = √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12. So both triangles have sides 5, 12 and 13, and they are congruent by SSS as well. The right angle is what makes this work, and that is why the shortcut is called HL and is saved for right triangles.

GEO-5#7.title: Hunt for two different triangles
GEO-5#7.text: Test each pattern by trying to draw two different triangles that fit it. SAS: two sticks hinged at a fixed angle leave one gap, so one triangle. ASA: two rays from a fixed side meet once, so one triangle. SSA: the last side can swing to two places, so it fails. AAA: triangles with sides 1, 1, 1 and 2, 2, 2 both have three 60° angles but different sizes, so it fails. SAS and ASA work; SSA and AAA do not.

GEO-5#8.title: Try values for x
GEO-5#8.text: AB matches DE, so AB must come out as 13. Test values in 3x + 1. With x = 3 it gives 10, which is too small. With x = 5 it gives 16, which is too big. With x = 4 it gives 3 × 4 + 1 = 13, exactly the length of DE. So x = 4.

GEO-5#9.title: Fold along the diagonal
GEO-5#9.text: Fold the kite along AC. Point A is the same distance from B and from D, and so is point C. Points that are equally far from B and D lie on the mirror line between them, so AC is that mirror line. The fold lands B exactly on D, and triangle ABC covers triangle ADC with nothing left over. The triangles are congruent, which agrees with SSS.

GEO-6#1.title: Tear off the corners
GEO-6#1.text: Cut any triangle out of paper and tear off its three corners. Place the three torn corners together at one point with their edges touching. They always form a straight edge, which is 180°. With numbers: a triangle with angles 50°, 60° and 70° totals 180°. Extend a side at the 70° corner. The outside angle is 180 − 70 = 110°, and that equals 50 + 60, the two far angles.

GEO-6#2.title: Try it with sticks
GEO-6#2.text: Take sticks of length 3, 4 and 10. Lay the 10 flat and hinge the others at its ends. Even pointing straight at each other they cover only 3 + 4 = 7, so their tips never meet and no triangle forms. For isosceles triangles, take sides 5, 5 and 6. A line from the peak to the middle of the base makes two triangles with sides 3, 4 and 5. They are identical, so the two base angles are equal.

GEO-6#3.title: Check on a grid
GEO-6#3.text: Put a triangle on a grid with corners A(0, 0), B(8, 0) and C(2, 6). The midpoint of AC is (1, 3) and the midpoint of BC is (5, 3). The segment joining them stays at height 3, so it is flat, just like side AB. Its length is 5 − 1 = 4, and AB is 8 long. So the midsegment is parallel to the third side and half as long.

GEO-6#4.title: Compare with 60, 60, 60
GEO-6#4.text: If all three angles were equal, each would be 60°. Here 48° is 12 below 60 and 67° is 7 above 60. Together the two known angles are 12 − 7 = 5 below their fair share. The third angle must make up the difference, so it is 5 above 60, which is 65°. Check: 48 + 67 + 65 = 180.

GEO-6#5.title: Go through the neighbour angle
GEO-6#5.text: The exterior angle and the interior angle beside it sit on a straight line. So the interior angle at that corner is 180 − 130 = 50°. Now the triangle has angles 50°, 55° and the unknown one, and they total 180°. The unknown angle is 180 − 50 − 55 = 75°.

GEO-6#6.title: Lay the sticks on a ruler
GEO-6#6.text: Lay the side of 11 along a ruler from 0 to 11. Hinge the side of 4 at the 0 end and the side of 6 at the 11 end. Fold both flat toward each other. The 4 reaches from 0 to 4, and the 6 reaches from 11 back to 5. A gap of 1 remains between 4 and 5. Lifting the sticks only pulls the tips further apart, so there is no triangle.

GEO-6#7.title: Count up with the theorem
GEO-6#7.text: The Exterior Angle Theorem says the two far angles add to the exterior angle, so 55 plus the missing angle makes 130. Count up from 55 to 130. From 55 to 100 is 45, and from 100 to 130 is 30. The missing angle is 45 + 30 = 75°. The straight-line method needed two subtractions, and this needs one.

GEO-6#8.title: Place it on a grid
GEO-6#8.text: Put the third side on a grid from (0, 0) to (18, 0), and choose any top corner, say (4, 10). The midpoints of the two other sides are (2, 5) and (11, 5). They are at the same height, so the midsegment is parallel to the third side, and its length is 11 − 2 = 9. Moving the top corner changes the midpoints but never the length 9.

GEO-6#9.title: Fold the roof in half
GEO-6#9.text: Fold the roof down the middle, from the peak to the centre of the base. The fold cuts the 40° peak into two 20° angles and meets the base at 90°. Each half is a right triangle with angles 90° and 20°, so its third angle is 90 − 20 = 70°. That third angle is a base angle of the roof, so b = 70°.

GEO-7#1.title: One example of each test
GEO-7#1.text: AA: one triangle has angles 50° and 60°, and so does another. Both third angles are 70°, so the shapes match. SSS: sides 3, 4, 5 and 6, 8, 10 give ratios 6 ÷ 3, 8 ÷ 4 and 10 ÷ 5, all equal to 2. SAS: sides 3 and 4 around a 90° angle, and sides 6 and 8 around a 90° angle. Both ratios are 2 and the angle between is the same.

GEO-7#2.title: A table of matching sides
GEO-7#2.text: Small triangle: 3, 4, 5. Big triangle: 7.5, 10, 12.5. Divide each big side by its partner: 7.5 ÷ 3 = 2.5, 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5, 12.5 ÷ 5 = 2.5. The same number appears every time, and that number is the scale factor. A factor above 1 enlarges and a factor below 1 shrinks. To go back from big to small, divide by 2.5.

GEO-7#3.title: Compare sides inside one triangle
GEO-7#3.text: There is a second way to see why x is 15. In the small triangle the sides are 4 and 10, and 10 is 2.5 times 4. Similar triangles have the same shape, so the big triangle keeps that relationship: x must be 2.5 times 6, which is 15. You can compare across the two triangles or within each one, and both give the same answer.

GEO-7#4.title: Ask what multiplies 4
GEO-7#4.text: Think of the scale factor as the number that turns 4 into 6. One times 4 is 4, which leaves 2 more to find. That 2 is half of 4, so the multiplier is 1 and a half. Check: 4 × 1.5 = 6. The scale factor is k = 1.5.

GEO-7#5.title: Scale within the small triangle
GEO-7#5.text: Look only at the small triangle first. Its two sides are 4 and 10, and 10 is 2.5 times as long as 4, because 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5. The big triangle has the same shape, so its matching sides have the same relationship. The side that matches 4 is 6, so x = 2.5 × 6 = 15.

GEO-7#6.title: Draw both from a base
GEO-7#6.text: Draw a base of any length. At one end draw a ray at 40°, and at the other end a ray at 75°. The rays meet and form a triangle whose third angle is 180 − 40 − 75 = 65°. Now repeat with a base twice as long. Every ray points the same way as before, so the new triangle is the old picture enlarged by 2. Same shape, different size: similar by AA.

GEO-7#7.title: Write a proportion for each side
GEO-7#7.text: Use the known pair 4 and 6 in a proportion for each missing side. For the side matching 10: 6/4 = x/10, so 4x = 60 and x = 15. For the side matching 8: 6/4 = y/8, so 4y = 48 and y = 12. The proportions give 10 → 15 and 8 → 12, the same as multiplying by 1.5.

GEO-7#8.title: Compare the two shadows
GEO-7#8.text: Compare shadow with shadow. The tree shadow is 20 ft and the person shadow is 4 ft, so the tree shadow is 20 ÷ 4 = 5 times as long. The sun hits both at the same angle, so the tree is also 5 times as tall as the person. The height is 5 × 6 = 30 ft.

GEO-7#9.title: Double the small triangle
GEO-7#9.text: Enlarge the 3, 4, 5 triangle by 2 and you get 6, 8, 10. A triangle similar to it with sides 6 and 8 would need a third side of 10, but this one has 11. There is a second clue: 3, 4, 5 has a right angle because 9 + 16 = 25, but 36 + 64 = 100 is not 121, so 6, 8, 11 has no right angle. The triangles are not similar.

GEO-8#1.title: Four triangles in a square
GEO-8#1.text: Take four copies of a 3-4-5 right triangle and fit them into the corners of a square with side 3 + 4 = 7. The big square has area 49. Each triangle has area ½ × 3 × 4 = 6, so the four use 24. The tilted square left in the middle has area 49 − 24 = 25, and its side is the hypotenuse. So the hypotenuse squared is 25, which is 9 + 16.

GEO-8#2.title: Three third sides to compare
GEO-8#2.text: Keep two sides at 6 and 8, so a² + b² = 36 + 64 = 100. If the third side is 10, then c² = 100 and the triangle is right. If the third side is 9, then c² = 81, which is less than 100, so the angle has closed and the triangle is acute. If the third side is 12, then c² = 144, more than 100, so the angle has opened and the triangle is obtuse.

GEO-8#3.title: Walking city blocks
GEO-8#3.text: Start at the corner (1, 2) and head for (4, 6). By the streets you walk 4 − 1 = 3 blocks east and then 6 − 2 = 4 blocks north. A bird flies straight across. The two street walks are the legs of a right triangle and the bird path is the hypotenuse, so its length is √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5 blocks.

GEO-8#4.title: Estimate, then test squares
GEO-8#4.text: The hypotenuse is longer than the longer leg, 12, and shorter than the two legs together, 21. The target is 9² + 12² = 225. Test whole numbers above 12: 13² = 169 is too small, 14² = 196 is too small, 15² = 225 is exact. So c = 15.

GEO-8#5.title: Factor the difference of squares
GEO-8#5.text: You need 13² − 5². A difference of squares factors as (13 − 5)(13 + 5), which is 8 × 18 = 144. So b² = 144 and b = 12. Factoring means you never have to square 13, and the result shows the famous 5, 12, 13 right triangle.

GEO-8#6.title: Use a square of side 21
GEO-8#6.text: Fit four copies of the triangle into the corners of a square with side 9 + 12 = 21. The square has area 441. Each triangle has area ½ × 9 × 12 = 54, so the four use 216. The tilted square in the middle has area 441 − 216 = 225, and each of its sides is a hypotenuse. So c = √225 = 15.

GEO-8#7.title: Cut the hypotenuse square
GEO-8#7.text: Build a square on the hypotenuse and draw its two diagonals. They cut it into four right triangles, and each one is a copy of the 45-45-90 triangle with legs 7. Each copy has area ½ × 7 × 7 = 24.5, so the square has area 4 × 24.5 = 98. Its side is √98 = 7√2, about 9.9.

GEO-8#8.title: Subtract the squares
GEO-8#8.text: Check it from the other direction. If there is a right angle, then 25² − 24² must equal 7². Factor the difference: (25 − 24)(25 + 24) = 1 × 49 = 49, and 7² = 49. They match, so 7² + 24² = 25² and the triangle is a right triangle.

GEO-8#9.title: Recognise 5, 12, 13
GEO-8#9.text: The ladder is the hypotenuse, 13 ft, and the foot of the ladder is 5 ft from the wall. The numbers 5 and 13 belong to the whole-number right triangle 5, 12, 13. So the height on the wall is 12 ft. Check: 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169 = 13².

GEO-9#1.title: Two triangles, same ratios
GEO-9#1.text: Take a 3-4-5 right triangle and look at the angle across from the side 3. Opposite ÷ hypotenuse is 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6. Now double the triangle to 6-8-10. The same angle gives 6 ÷ 10 = 0.6. The cosine is 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8 in one and 8 ÷ 10 = 0.8 in the other, and the tangent is 0.75 in both. The size changed but the three ratios did not.

GEO-9#2.title: Same angle, two questions
GEO-9#2.text: Stand at a 30° angle. Question 1: the hypotenuse is 10 and you want the opposite side. Those two sides are in sine, so x = 10 × sin 30° = 10 × 0.5 = 5. Question 2: the adjacent side is 10 and you want the opposite side. Those are in tangent, so x = 10 × tan 30° ≈ 5.77. Always label the sides from the angle you are using before you choose.

GEO-9#3.title: Read the table backwards
GEO-9#3.text: Here is a short tangent table: tan 30° ≈ 0.577, tan 45° = 1, tan 60° ≈ 1.732. Reading left to right, you start with an angle and get a ratio. The inverse reads right to left. If a ramp rises 1.732 m for every 1 m forward, its ratio is 1.732, so its angle is 60°. The calculator key tan⁻¹ does this lookup for any ratio.

GEO-9#4.title: Estimate, then check with Pythagoras
GEO-9#4.text: At 30° the opposite side would be half the hypotenuse, 10. At 45° it would be about 14.1. The angle 35° is a little past 30°, so an answer a little above 10 makes sense, and 11.5 fits. Check with the other leg: 20 × cos 35° ≈ 16.4, and 11.5² + 16.4² ≈ 132 + 269 = 401, close to 20² = 400.

GEO-9#5.title: Find the hypotenuse, then use sine
GEO-9#5.text: The legs 8 and 15 give a hypotenuse of √(64 + 225) = √289 = 17. Now use sine: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse = 8 ÷ 17 ≈ 0.4706. Then θ = sin⁻¹(0.4706) ≈ 28.1°. A different ratio gives the same angle as the tangent did, which is a good check on the answer.

GEO-9#6.title: Use the angle at the treetop
GEO-9#6.text: Work from the top of the tree instead. From that corner the opposite side is the ground, 40 ft, and the adjacent side is the tree, 50 ft. So the tangent there is 40 ÷ 50 = 0.8, and the angle is tan⁻¹(0.8) ≈ 38.7°. The two acute angles of a right triangle add to 90°, so the angle of elevation is 90 − 38.7 = 51.3°.

GEO-9#7.title: Find the other leg first
GEO-9#7.text: Find the leg across from the 55° angle: 20 × sin 55° ≈ 20 × 0.8192 ≈ 16.38. Then use the Pythagorean theorem for x: x² = 20² − 16.38² ≈ 400 − 268.3 = 131.7, so x ≈ 11.5. It agrees with the cosine answer, and it uses only the sine key and the three sides.

GEO-9#8.title: Use the angle at the clifftop
GEO-9#8.text: Inside the triangle, the angle at the top of the cliff is between the cliff face and the line of sight. It is 90 − 25 = 65°. From that corner the distance to the boat is the opposite side and the 60 m cliff is the adjacent side. So tan 65° = d ÷ 60, and d = 60 × tan 65° ≈ 60 × 2.1445 ≈ 129 m. Multiplying replaces the division.

GEO-9#9.title: Find the rise first
GEO-9#9.text: First find how high the ramp climbs: rise = 10 × sin 12° ≈ 10 × 0.2079 ≈ 2.08 m. Then use the Pythagorean theorem for the ground distance: x² = 10² − 2.08² ≈ 100 − 4.32 = 95.68, so x ≈ 9.78 m. The ground distance is only a little shorter than the ramp because the angle is small.

GEO-10#1.title: Cut from a point inside
GEO-10#1.text: Pick a point in the middle of a hexagon and join it to all 6 corners. That makes 6 triangles, worth 6 × 180 = 1080°. But the angles packed around the middle point are not corners of the hexagon. They make a full turn, 360°, so take them away: 1080 − 360 = 720°. For n sides this is n × 180 − 360, which is the same as (n − 2) × 180.

GEO-10#2.title: Check three regular shapes
GEO-10#2.text: Try it with numbers. An equilateral triangle has interior angles of 60°, so each exterior angle is 120°, and 3 × 120 = 360. A square has exterior angles of 90°, and 4 × 90 = 360. A regular hexagon has interior angles of 120°, so each exterior angle is 60°, and 6 × 60 = 360. More sides mean smaller turns, but the total never changes.

GEO-10#3.title: Like dogs and poodles
GEO-10#3.text: Every poodle is a dog, but not every dog is a poodle. In the same way, every square is a rectangle and every square is a rhombus, but most rectangles and rhombuses are not squares. Test a shape with a checklist. A 3 by 5 rectangle has two pairs of parallel sides and four right angles, but its sides are not all equal. So it is a parallelogram and a rectangle, and it is not a rhombus or a square.

GEO-10#4.title: Cut from the centre
GEO-10#4.text: Join the centre of the octagon to all 8 corners. This makes 8 triangles, worth 8 × 180 = 1440°. The 8 angles that meet at the centre are not corners of the octagon, and together they make a full turn of 360°. Remove them: 1440 − 360 = 1080°.

GEO-10#5.title: Six equilateral triangles
GEO-10#5.text: Join the centre of a regular hexagon to its 6 corners. The 6 angles at the centre are 360 ÷ 6 = 60° each, and the two sides from the centre are equal, so every triangle is equilateral with three 60° angles. At each corner of the hexagon two of these triangles meet. The interior angle is 60 + 60 = 120°.

GEO-10#6.title: Count triangles from one corner
GEO-10#6.text: Draw diagonals from one corner of the hexagon to the three corners that are not next to it. The hexagon splits into 4 triangles, so its angles total 4 × 180 = 720°. The hexagon is regular, so the 6 angles are equal, and each is 720 ÷ 6 = 120°. This matches 180 − 60 from the exterior angle.

GEO-10#7.title: Check with the interior angles
GEO-10#7.text: Test the answer 15 from the inside. A 15-sided polygon cuts into 15 − 2 = 13 triangles, so its angles total 13 × 180 = 2340°. Each interior angle of the regular one is 2340 ÷ 15 = 156°. The exterior angle beside it is 180 − 156 = 24°, which matches the given angle. So the polygon has 15 sides.

GEO-10#8.title: Use the total of 360
GEO-10#8.text: The four angles of any quadrilateral total 360°. In a parallelogram opposite angles are equal, so angles A and C are both 65° and use 130°. That leaves 360 − 130 = 230° for angles B and D, which are also equal. Each is 230 ÷ 2 = 115°. The angles are 65°, 115°, 65°, 115°.

GEO-10#9.title: Walk around the sign
GEO-10#9.text: Walk along the edge of the stop sign. At each of the 8 corners you turn by the same amount, and after all 8 you have made one full turn. Each turn is 360 ÷ 8 = 45°. The turn and the inside corner lie along a straight line, so the interior angle is 180 − 45 = 135°.

GEO-11#1.title: A stage seen from two seats
GEO-11#1.text: Picture a round arena with a stage along part of the wall, covering an 80° arc. From the exact centre, the stage fills 80° of your view. Now sit at the wall on the far side. You are further from the stage, and it fills only 40° of your view. Move to any other seat on that far wall and it still fills 40°. Centre seats see the arc itself, and wall seats see half of it.

GEO-11#2.title: A wheel on a flat road
GEO-11#2.text: Think of a wheel resting on a flat road. The road is a tangent, because it touches the wheel at one point. The axle sits directly above that point, so the spoke from the axle to the road points straight down while the road runs level. Straight down and level meet at 90°. If the spoke leaned, the axle would be lower than one radius above the road and the wheel would sink into it.

GEO-11#3.title: One slice of a pizza
GEO-11#3.text: Take a pizza with radius 10 inches. Its crust is 2 × π × 10 = 20π inches long and its area is π × 10² = 100π square inches. Cut a 36° slice. Since 36 ÷ 360 = 1/10, the slice is one tenth of the pizza. It gets one tenth of the crust, 2π inches, and one tenth of the area, 10π square inches. The same fraction works for both.

GEO-11#4.title: Go through the centre
GEO-11#4.text: Draw the inscribed angle so one of its sides passes through the centre. Join the centre to the other end of the arc. The central angle on the 110° arc is 110°. The two radii make an isosceles triangle, and the 110° angle is an exterior angle of it, so it equals the two equal base angles together. Each base angle is 110 ÷ 2 = 55°, and one of them is the inscribed angle.

GEO-11#5.title: Two isosceles triangles
GEO-11#5.text: Join the centre to the vertex of the angle. Now there are three equal radii, to the vertex and to each end of the diameter, and they form two isosceles triangles. Call their base angles a and b. The big triangle has angles a, b and a + b at the vertex, so 2a + 2b = 180°. That makes a + b = 90°, and a + b is the inscribed angle.

GEO-11#6.title: Spot the 5, 12, 13 triangle
GEO-11#6.text: The radius meets the tangent at 90°, so the line to the centre, 13, is the hypotenuse and the radius, 5, is a leg. A hypotenuse of 13 with a leg of 5 is the whole-number right triangle 5, 12, 13. The tangent is the other leg, so t = 12. Quick check without squaring 13: (13 − 5)(13 + 5) = 8 × 18 = 144 = 12².

GEO-11#7.title: Take a fraction of the circumference
GEO-11#7.text: Stay in degrees. The angle 60° is 60 ÷ 360 = 1/6 of a full turn. The whole circumference is 2 × π × 9 = 18π. One sixth of that is 18π ÷ 6 = 3π. The fraction method and the radian method agree: s = 3π.

GEO-11#8.title: Treat the slice like a triangle
GEO-11#8.text: A thin slice is nearly a triangle whose base is the crust and whose height is the radius. The whole crust is 2 × π × 6 = 12π, so one of 8 slices has 12π ÷ 8 = 1.5π inches of crust. Area = ½ × crust × radius = ½ × 1.5π × 6 = 4.5π, about 14.1 square inches.

GEO-11#9.title: Why equal, then test x
GEO-11#9.text: Join the centre O to P, A and B. Triangles OAP and OBP both have a right angle where the radius meets the tangent, they share the side OP, and OA = OB because both are radii. They are congruent by HL, so PA = PB. Now test x = 5 in the expression: 3 × 5 + 2 = 17, which matches the other tangent. So x = 5.

GEO-12#1.title: Count squares on a grid
GEO-12#1.text: Draw the shapes on grid paper. A rectangle 6 wide and 4 tall holds 24 squares. Lean it over into a parallelogram with base 6 and height 4 and it still holds 24. Cut that along a diagonal and each triangle has 12. A trapezoid with bases 4 and 8 and height 4 holds as much as a rectangle 6 wide, 24 again. A circle of radius 2 covers a little over 3 squares of side 2, about 12.6.

GEO-12#2.title: Push a deck of cards
GEO-12#2.text: Stack a deck of cards neatly and look at it from the side. You see a rectangle. Push the top sideways so the deck leans. The side view is now a parallelogram with a longer slanted edge, but no card was added or removed, so the area of the side view is the same. The deck is still the same number of cards tall. That straight-up thickness is the height, and the slanted edge is not.

GEO-12#3.title: A picture frame both ways
GEO-12#3.text: A frame is 10 by 8 on the outside with a 6 by 4 opening, and the border is 2 wide all round. Subtract: 80 − 24 = 56. Or add the pieces: the top and bottom strips are 10 by 2, which is 20 each, and the two side strips are 2 by 4, which is 8 each. That gives 20 + 20 + 8 + 8 = 56. Both plans agree, so choose the shorter one.

GEO-12#4.title: Rectangle plus two triangles
GEO-12#4.text: Drop two heights from the ends of the short base. The middle is a rectangle 8 wide and 5 tall, with area 40. The two triangles at the sides share the extra base length, 14 − 8 = 6, and both have height 5. Pushed together they make one triangle with area ½ × 6 × 5 = 15. The total is 40 + 15 = 55.

GEO-12#5.title: Unroll the ring
GEO-12#5.text: Cut the ring and straighten it into a strip. The strip is 5 − 3 = 2 wide. Its length is the circumference of the circle halfway through the ring, with radius 4, which is 2 × π × 4 = 8π. Area = length × width = 8π × 2 = 16π, about 50.3.

GEO-12#6.title: Count 6 by 4 blocks
GEO-12#6.text: The missing corner is 6 by 4, and the full 12 by 8 rectangle is exactly two of those blocks wide and two blocks tall. So the rectangle holds 4 blocks, and the L-shape is 3 of them. Each block has area 6 × 4 = 24, so the L-shape has area 3 × 24 = 72 square units.

GEO-12#7.title: Sort edges by direction
GEO-12#7.text: Group the edges instead of walking around. The horizontal edges are the 12 at the bottom and the two pieces of 6 above it, and 6 + 6 also makes 12. So the horizontal edges total 24. The vertical edges are the 8 on one side and the two pieces of 4 on the other, so they total 16. P = 24 + 16 = 40 units.

GEO-12#8.title: Box in the half circle
GEO-12#8.text: The half circle fits inside a 4 by 2 box with area 8. A circle fills about 78.5% of the square around it, and half a circle fills the same share of half the square. So the half circle is about 0.785 × 8 ≈ 6.28 square feet. Add the 4 by 3 rectangle: 12 + 6.28 ≈ 18.3 square feet. The answer sits between 12 and 20, as it should.

GEO-12#9.title: Cut and slide a triangle
GEO-12#9.text: Cut a right triangle off one end of the parallelogram with a straight up-and-down cut, and slide it to the other end. The shape becomes a rectangle with the same base, 10, and a side equal to the height, 5. Its area is 10 × 5 = 50. The slanted side 6 does not appear in the rectangle at all, which is why it is not used.

GEO-13#1.title: Check with real numbers
GEO-13#1.text: A box 4 by 3 by 5 has 12 unit cubes on its bottom layer and 5 layers, so 60 cubes. A cylinder with radius 3 and height 4 holds 9π × 4 = 36π, and the cone inside it holds a third, 12π. A sphere of radius 3 just fits in a cylinder of radius 3 and height 6, which holds 54π. The sphere fills two thirds of it: 36π, the same as (4/3) × π × 27.

GEO-13#2.title: Wrap a cereal box
GEO-13#2.text: Think of covering a 4 by 3 by 5 box with paper, one face at a time. Top and bottom are 4 by 3, so 12 each. Front and back are 4 by 5, so 20 each. The two ends are 3 by 5, so 15 each. The paper needed is 12 + 12 + 20 + 20 + 15 + 15 = 94 square units. For a can, the label peels off as a rectangle, and the two lids are circles.

GEO-13#3.title: Double a small box
GEO-13#3.text: A 2 by 3 by 4 box has surface area 2 × (6 + 8 + 12) = 52 and volume 24. Double every edge to get 4 by 6 by 8. The surface area is 2 × (24 + 32 + 48) = 208, which is 4 times 52. The volume is 4 × 6 × 8 = 192, which is 8 times 24. One doubling gives 2² = 4 for area and 2³ = 8 for volume.

GEO-13#4.title: Compare with a square box
GEO-13#4.text: Put the cylinder inside a box 6 by 6 by 10, which holds 360. Looking down, the circle fills π/4 of the 6 by 6 square, because 9π ÷ 36 = π/4. Every layer has that same share, so the cylinder holds 360 × π/4 = 90π, about 282.7. That is a bit over three quarters of the box, which looks right.

GEO-13#5.title: Use the cone formula directly
GEO-13#5.text: Use V = (1/3) × π × r² × h in one line. Here r² = 9 and h = 4. Divide by 3 early to keep numbers small: 9 ÷ 3 = 3, and 3 × 4 = 12. So V = 12π, about 37.7. Dividing the 9 first avoids building the 36π cylinder at all.

GEO-13#6.title: Two thirds of its cylinder
GEO-13#6.text: A sphere of radius 3 just fits inside a cylinder with radius 3 and height 6. That cylinder holds π × 9 × 6 = 54π. A sphere always fills two thirds of the cylinder that wraps it, so V = (2/3) × 54π = 36π, about 113.1. This matches the formula.

GEO-13#7.title: A band plus two lids
GEO-13#7.text: Stand the box on its 4 by 3 base. The four upright faces unfold into one long band. Its length is the distance around the base, 4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 14, and its width is the height, 5, so the band has area 70. The top and bottom are 12 each, which adds 24. SA = 70 + 24 = 94 square units.

GEO-13#8.title: Change to decimetres first
GEO-13#8.text: One litre is a cube 10 cm on each side, which is 1 decimetre each way. Change the tank to decimetres: 50 cm = 5 dm, 30 cm = 3 dm, 40 cm = 4 dm. Then V = 5 × 3 × 4 = 60 cubic decimetres, which is 60 L straight away. Each litre is 1000 cm³, so that is 60,000 cm³.
