GEO-13#9.title: Stack copies of the small box
GEO-13#9.text: Fill the big box with copies of the small one. Three fit along each edge, so it takes 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 small boxes. The volume is 27 × 60 = 1620. Each face of the big box is tiled by 3 × 3 = 9 copies of the matching small face, so the surface area is 9 × 94 = 846. SA grows by 9 and V grows by 27.

GEO-14#1.title: Follow one point
GEO-14#1.text: Plot the point (3, 1) and apply each move to it. Reflect over the x-axis and it drops to (3, −1). Reflect over the y-axis and it jumps to (−3, 1). Rotate it a quarter turn counterclockwise about the origin and it lands on (−1, 3). Dilate it by 2 and it moves out to (6, 2). Watching one point shows which coordinate changes sign, which ones swap, and which ones grow.

GEO-14#2.title: Measure before and after
GEO-14#2.text: Take the triangle (0, 0), (3, 0), (0, 4). Its sides are 3, 4 and 5. Slide it 2 to the right: (2, 0), (5, 0), (2, 4). The sides are still 3, 4 and 5. Reflect it over the x-axis and they are still 3, 4 and 5. Now dilate by 2: (0, 0), (6, 0), (0, 8). The sides are 6, 8 and 10. The right angle is still there, but every length has doubled.

GEO-14#3.title: One segment, three questions
GEO-14#3.text: Join A(0, 0) to B(4, 2). It rises 2 while running 4, so its slope is 1/2. Turn the step "4 right, 2 up" a quarter turn and it becomes "2 left, 4 up", a slope of −2. That is the perpendicular slope, and 1/2 × −2 = −1. The midpoint is halfway in each direction, (2, 1). The length is √(4² + 2²) = √20, about 4.47.

GEO-14#4.title: Fold along the axis
GEO-14#4.text: Plot (3, −2) and fold the paper along the x-axis. The point is 2 units below the fold, so it lands 2 units above the fold, straight up from where it was. Count it: from (3, −2) go up 2 to reach the axis at (3, 0), then up 2 more. The image is (3, 2). The point never moved left or right, so x stayed 3.

GEO-14#5.title: Check with slope and distance
GEO-14#5.text: Test the answer (−5, 2). The line from the origin to (2, 5) has slope 5/2. The line to (−5, 2) has slope 2 ÷ (−5) = −2/5. Their product is −1, so the two lines are perpendicular, a 90° turn. Both points are √(4 + 25) = √29 from the origin. And (−5, 2) is to the left, which is where a counterclockwise turn sends a point from Quadrant I.

GEO-14#6.title: Repeat each walk
GEO-14#6.text: Reach each corner by a walk from the origin, then do the same walk again. To (1, 1): 1 right, 1 up; again gives (2, 2). To (3, 1): 3 right, 1 up; again gives (6, 2). To (1, 2): 1 right, 2 up; again gives (2, 4). Each image is twice as far out in the same direction, so the image is (2, 2), (6, 2), (2, 4).

GEO-14#7.title: Use two reflections
GEO-14#7.text: A quarter turn counterclockwise can be done with two mirror flips. First reflect (2, 5) over the diagonal line y = x, which swaps the coordinates: (5, 2). Then reflect over the y-axis, which changes the sign of x: (−5, 2). Two reflections across mirrors 45° apart make a 90° turn, so the image is (−5, 2).

GEO-14#8.title: Check the diagonals
GEO-14#8.text: A quadrilateral is a parallelogram when its diagonals cut each other in half. One diagonal joins (0, 0) and (5, 4). Its midpoint is (2.5, 2). The other joins (4, 1) and (1, 3). Its midpoint is ((4 + 1) ÷ 2, (1 + 3) ÷ 2) = (2.5, 2). Both diagonals have the same midpoint, so they bisect each other and the quadrilateral is a parallelogram.

GEO-14#9.title: Step straight across the mirror
GEO-14#9.text: The shortest way to the line y = x is at right angles to it, which means stepping 1 right and 1 down each time. From (1, 4), one step gives (2, 3), and half a step more gives (2.5, 2.5), which is on the mirror. That was 1.5 steps. Take 1.5 more steps the same way: (2.5 + 1.5, 2.5 − 1.5) = (4, 1). The image is (4, 1).

PC-1#1.title: Four tables of values
PC-1#1.text:
Put the same inputs 0, 1, 4 and 9 into each rule and compare the outputs.
y = x gives 0, 1, 4, 9. y = x² gives 0, 1, 16, 81. y = |x| gives 0, 1, 4, 9, but it also gives 4 for x = −4. y = √x gives 0, 1, 2, 3.
Steady, speeding up, bouncing back, slowing down: those four behaviors are the four shapes.

PC-1#2.title: Shift a table, keep the gaps
PC-1#2.text:
Take three points on y = x²: (0, 0), (1, 1) and (2, 4). The heights climb by 1 and then by 3.
Now lift every point 5 units: (0, 5), (1, 6), (2, 9). The heights still climb by 1 and then by 3.
The pattern of gaps is the shape, and moving the graph leaves that pattern alone.

PC-1#3.title: An elevator for every point
PC-1#3.text:
Think of f(x) + k as an elevator ride. Each point of the graph steps into its own elevator and rides k floors, without moving left or right.
With y = |x| + 2, the tip (0, 0) rides to (0, 2), and (3, 3) rides to (3, 5). With y = |x| − 2 the elevators go down, so the tip lands at (0, −2).

PC-1#4.title: A head start of h
PC-1#4.text:
Compare tables for y = x² and y = (x − 3)².
The old rule reaches height 0 at x = 0 and height 1 at x = 1. The new rule subtracts 3 before squaring, so it needs x = 3 to reach height 0 and x = 4 to reach height 1.
Every height shows up 3 units later along the x-axis, so the picture sits 3 to the right.

PC-1#5.title: Compare two tables
PC-1#5.text:
Make a table for x = −1, 0, 1, 2.
y = x² gives 1, 0, 1, 4.
y = x² + 3 gives 4, 3, 4, 7.
Each new height is exactly 3 more than the old one at the same x, and the lowest value moved from 0 to 3. The parabola keeps its shape and sits up 3.

PC-1#6.title: Build a small table
PC-1#6.text:
Try x = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 in y = (x − 4)².
The heights are 4, 1, 0, 1, 4.
The smallest height, 0, happens at x = 4, and the heights match on either side of it, so the vertex is (4, 0). The parent has the same pattern 4, 1, 0, 1, 4 centered at x = 0, so the graph slid right 4.

PC-1#7.title: Match heights between the paths
PC-1#7.text:
Ask which x on the new path gives the same height as a point on the old path.
Old path: x = 0 gives 0, x = 1 gives 1, x = 2 gives 4.
New path y = (x − 7)²: x = 7 gives 0, x = 8 gives 1, x = 9 gives 4.
Each height now needs an x that is 7 larger, so the sprite path moved right 7 steps.

PC-1#8.title: Check with two ramp points
PC-1#8.text:
Pick two spots on the old ramp: x = 4 has height √4 = 2, and x = 9 has height √9 = 3.
After a 3 foot lift those spots should be at heights 5 and 6.
The rule y = √x + 3 gives 2 + 3 = 5 and 3 + 3 = 6, and the front edge gives 0 + 3 = 3. All three agree with a straight lift, so the rule is y = √x + 3.

PC-1#9.title: Test it on a simple function
PC-1#9.text:
Use f(x) = x as a test picture. Its points include (5, 5) and (2, 2).
Tripling heights sends (5, 5) to (5, 15) and (2, 2) to (2, 6), and those points lie on y = 3x, which is 3 times f(x).
So the rule is y = 3f(x): each height is multiplied by 3, and a height of 5 becomes 15.

PC-1#10.title: Fold the paper
PC-1#10.text:
Make a table for x = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2.
y = x² gives 4, 1, 0, 1, 4.
y = −x² gives −4, −1, 0, −1, −4.
Each pair of heights is the same distance from the x-axis on opposite sides. If you folded the paper along the x-axis, one graph would land on the other, so the graph is flipped over the x-axis.

PC-1#11.title: Solve for the zero
PC-1#11.text:
Skip the table and reason about the square. A squared number is never negative, so the smallest possible height of (x − 1)² is 0.
That height happens only when x − 1 = 0, which means x = 1.
The parent reaches its lowest point at x = 0, so the lowest point has moved to x = 1, one unit to the right.

PC-1#12.title: Tables on both sides
PC-1#12.text:
Try x = −6, −5, −4, −3, −2 in y = (x + 4)² − 6.
The squares are 4, 1, 0, 1, 4, so the heights are −2, −5, −6, −5, −2.
The heights fall to −6 and rise again, with matching values on each side of x = −4. The lowest point is (−4, −6).

PC-2#1.title: A table is a function too
PC-2#1.text:
A function does not need a machine picture. A table works: for f(x) = x + 4, the row for 1 says 5, the row for 3 says 7, and the row for 10 says 14.
Each input appears once on the left with one answer on the right. A graph is the same list drawn as points: (1, 5), (3, 7), (10, 14).

PC-2#2.title: A relay race of numbers
PC-2#2.text:
Think of a relay. Runner g carries the number first and hands the result to runner f.
Let g(x) = x − 2 and f(x) = x². Start with 5: g hands over 3, and f turns it into 9, so f(g(5)) = 9.
The name written closest to the number is the runner who starts, even though it is read last.

PC-2#3.title: One number, two orders
PC-2#3.text:
Try the single input 5 with a doubling machine and an add 3 machine.
Double first, then add 3: 5 becomes 10, then 13.
Add 3 first, then double: 5 becomes 8, then 16.
The same input and the same two machines give 13 one way and 16 the other, because the doubling also doubles the 3 only when the 3 is added first.

PC-2#4.title: Reverse every arrow
PC-2#4.text:
List some pairs for f(x) = 2x: 1 goes to 2, 3 goes to 6, 5 goes to 10.
The inverse is the same list with every arrow reversed: 2 goes to 1, 6 goes to 3, 10 goes to 5.
Reading the reversed list, each number is halved, so the inverse rule is x ÷ 2. On a graph, reversing the pairs mirrors the picture across the line y = x.

PC-2#5.title: Build one rule first
PC-2#5.text:
Combine the machines into a single rule before using any number.
g turns x into 3x, and f adds 4 to whatever it gets, so f(g(x)) = 3x + 4.
Now put in 2: 3 × 2 + 4 = 6 + 4 = 10.
The combined rule gives 10, the same as running the two machines one after the other.

PC-2#6.title: Combine into one rule
PC-2#6.text:
Write g(f(x)) as a single rule. f turns x into x + 4, and g triples whatever it gets, so g(f(x)) = 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12.
Put in 2: 3 × 2 + 12 = 18.
Compare with the other order, 3x + 4, which gave 10. The two rules differ by 8 for every input, so the order matters.

PC-2#7.title: Find yen per dollar
PC-2#7.text:
Work out what one dollar is worth in yen first. One dollar becomes 0.9 euros, and 0.9 euros becomes 0.9 × 160 = 144 yen.
So the two machines together act as one machine that multiplies by 144.
For 50 dollars: 144 × 50 = 7200 yen, the same answer as doing the two exchanges in turn.

PC-2#8.title: Write one combined rule
PC-2#8.text:
Turn the chain into a formula. Adding 3 turns x into x + 3, and doubling that gives 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6.
Put in 2: 2 × 2 + 6 = 4 + 6 = 10.
The formula agrees with the drawn chain, and it shows why the swapped order differs: doubling first gives 2x + 3, which is 7 for the input 2.

PC-2#9.title: Work in dollar amounts
PC-2#9.text:
Find each change as an amount of money.
The coupon takes a quarter of 80 dollars, which is 20 dollars, leaving 60 dollars.
The tax is one tenth of that 60 dollars, which is 6 dollars.
60 + 6 = 66 dollars.
This route never uses the factors 0.75 and 1.10, yet it lands on the same final price.

PC-2#10.title: Guess and check forward
PC-2#10.text:
Try inputs and run f forward until the output is 9.
f(3) = 2 × 3 + 1 = 7, which is too small.
f(5) = 2 × 5 + 1 = 11, which is too big.
f(4) = 2 × 4 + 1 = 9, exactly right.
The outputs go up by 2 each time, so 4 is the only input that gives 9, and the inverse of f at 9 is 4.

PC-2#11.title: Reverse the steps in words
PC-2#11.text:
Describe f in words: double the input, then add 1.
To undo it, reverse the order and use opposite operations: subtract 1, then halve.
Written as a rule for an input x, that is (x − 1) ÷ 2, the same inverse the swap produced.
Test it on 9: 9 − 1 = 8, and 8 ÷ 2 = 4.

PC-2#12.title: Solve one equation
PC-2#12.text:
Call the original price p and write the whole chain as one equation: 0.8p + 5 = 45.
Subtract 5 from both sides to get 0.8p = 40.
Divide both sides by 0.8 to get p = 50.
The equation packs both machines into one line, and solving it gives the same 50 dollars as peeling the steps off by hand.

PC-3#1.title: Who wins the race?
PC-3#1.text:
Picture each term of 4x³ − 2x + 7 as a runner whose speed depends on x.
At x = 1 they are close together: 4, −2 and 7. At x = 10 they are 4000, −20 and 7.
The highest power pulls far ahead, and its coefficient decides how big and which sign. That is why the degree, 3, and the leading coefficient, 4, describe the polynomial.

PC-3#2.title: Four familiar shapes
PC-3#2.text:
Remember four simple graphs and every case is covered.
y = x² is a cup: both arms up. y = −x² is a cap: both arms down.
y = x³ runs from low on the left to high on the right. y = −x³ runs from high on the left to low on the right.
Any polynomial copies the arms of the simple graph that matches its degree type and sign.

PC-3#3.title: Check with a table
PC-3#3.text:
Make a table for (x − 5)(x + 2).
At x = 4 the brackets are −1 and 6, product −6.
At x = 5 they are 0 and 7, product 0.
At x = 6 they are 1 and 8, product 8.
Only the row where a bracket is 0 gives a product of 0. The same thing happens at x = −2, where the second bracket is 0.

PC-3#4.title: Compare a line and a parabola
PC-3#4.text:
Two simple graphs show both behaviors at the zero x = 0.
The line y = x has the factor x once. Its heights go −1, 0, 1, so it passes straight through the axis.
The parabola y = x² has the factor x twice. Its heights go 1, 0, 1, so it comes down, touches and goes back up.
Odd count crosses, even count bounces.

PC-3#5.title: Test with large inputs
PC-3#5.text:
Check the claim by plugging in x = 10 and x = −10.
At x = 10: 4000 − 20 + 7 = 3987. At x = −10: −4000 + 20 + 7 = −3973.
The 4x³ term supplies nearly all of each value, so the degree is 3 and the leading coefficient is 4. The right side is high and the left side is low, as an odd degree with a positive lead should be.

PC-3#6.title: Expand and use the quadratic formula
PC-3#6.text:
Multiply the factors out: (x − 5)(x + 2) = x² − 3x − 10.
Now solve x² − 3x − 10 = 0 with the quadratic formula, using a = 1, b = −3, c = −10: x = (3 ± √(9 + 40)) ÷ 2 = (3 ± 7) ÷ 2.
That is 10 ÷ 2 = 5 or −4 ÷ 2 = −2.
The long route gives the same two crossings of the x-axis, x = 5 and x = −2.

PC-3#7.title: Plug in big numbers
PC-3#7.text:
Test one large input on each side.
At x = 10: −2 × 10,000 + 30 = −19,970.
At x = −10: −2 × 10,000 − 30 = −20,030.
Both results are far below zero, and larger inputs only make them more negative. So the right arm and the left arm both point down.

PC-3#8.title: Read the leading term
PC-3#8.text:
Use the rule instead of numbers. The leading term of x³ − 4x is x³.
The degree 3 is odd, so the two arms point in opposite directions.
The leading coefficient is +1, which is positive, so the right arm goes up.
The left arm must then go down: left arm down, right arm up.

PC-3#9.title: Use the symmetry of a parabola
PC-3#9.text:
Expand the height: −(x − 2)(x − 8) = −x² + 10x − 16, a parabola that opens downward.
A parabola is symmetric, so its peak is halfway between the two ground points. If the ground points are 2 and 8, the peak is at x = 5.
Check the ends: h(2) = −4 + 20 − 16 = 0 and h(8) = −64 + 80 − 16 = 0. The peak height is h(5) = −25 + 50 − 16 = 9, a hill.

PC-3#10.title: Check signs in a table
PC-3#10.text:
Compute p(x) on each side of the zeros.
Near −1: p(−2) = 25 × (−1) = −25 and p(0) = 9 × 1 = 9. The sign changes, so the graph crosses at −1.
Near 3: p(2) = 1 × 3 = 3 and p(4) = 1 × 5 = 5. The sign stays positive, so the graph touches the axis and bounces at 3.

PC-3#11.title: Think about the parabola
PC-3#11.text:
The factor (x − 3)² is the parabola y = x² slid 3 units to the right.
A parabola opening upward has one lowest point, its vertex, and here that vertex sits on the axis at (3, 0).
Every other point of the parabola is higher than the vertex, so the graph is above the axis on both sides. The sign never flips, so it bounces.

PC-3#12.title: Build the box from its sides
PC-3#12.text:
Forget the formula and picture the box.
Cutting 2 inches from both ends of a 12 inch edge leaves 12 − 2 − 2 = 8 inches. So the base is 8 by 8, an area of 64 square inches.
The folded sides stand 2 inches tall.
Volume is base area times height: 64 × 2 = 128 cubic inches.

PC-4#1.title: Sharing cookies
PC-4#1.text:
Think of top ÷ bottom as cookies shared among people.
If there are 0 cookies and 7 people, everyone gets 0: the top being zero makes the answer zero.
If there are 5 cookies and 0 people, the question has no answer: the bottom being zero breaks it.
A rational function is this sharing with x deciding both numbers.

PC-4#2.title: A wall on both sides
PC-4#2.text:
Look at 1 ÷ (x − 1) from the LEFT of 1 as well. At x = 0.9 it is −10, at x = 0.99 it is −100, and at x = 0.999 it is −1000.
So on one side the graph climbs without end and on the other it dives without end.
The vertical line x = 1 acts like a wall that the two halves of the graph run along but can never cross.

PC-4#3.title: A race between top and bottom
PC-4#3.text:
Treat the top and bottom as two runners.
In 5 ÷ x the bottom runs and the top stands still, so the ratio drops toward 0.
In (4x) ÷ (2x) both run at matched speeds and the ratio stays at 2, which is 4 ÷ 2.
In x² ÷ x the top runs faster, the ratio is x itself, and it never levels off.

PC-4#4.title: The 0 ÷ 0 signal
PC-4#4.text:
Plug the forbidden value into both parts.
For (x² − 1) ÷ (x − 1) at x = 1 you get 0 ÷ 0. Two zeros mean a shared factor, and a shared factor means a hole. Nearby, x = 1.01 gives 2.01, so the hole sits at height 2.
For 3 ÷ (x − 1) at x = 1 you get 3 ÷ 0. Only the bottom is zero, so that one is an asymptote.

PC-4#5.title: Watch values near 6
PC-4#5.text:
Compute 1 ÷ (x − 6) close to the suspect value.
At x = 6.1 it is 10 and at x = 6.01 it is 100.
At x = 5.9 it is −10 and at x = 5.99 it is −100.
The outputs grow huge on one side and hugely negative on the other, which only happens beside a vertical asymptote. So the asymptote is x = 6.

PC-4#6.title: Set the bottom to zero
PC-4#6.text:
Use algebra instead of a table. The only place 1 ÷ (x − 3) can break is where the bottom is zero.
x − 3 = 0 gives x = 3.
The top is 1 there, not 0, so nothing cancels and the break is a true runaway. That means the outputs explode toward infinity near 3, and x = 3 is a vertical asymptote.

PC-4#7.title: Scan a table for zero
PC-4#7.text:
Compute the fraction at a few inputs.
x = 0 gives −2 ÷ 5 = −0.4.
x = 1 gives −1 ÷ 6, about −0.17.
x = 2 gives 0 ÷ 7 = 0.
x = 3 gives 1 ÷ 8 = 0.125.
The outputs move from negative to positive and are exactly 0 at x = 2, so the graph meets the x-axis at x = 2.

PC-4#8.title: Check by multiplying back
PC-4#8.text:
Use multiplication to test each share.
If 8 friends each pay 15 dollars, they collect 8 × 15 = 120 dollars, the whole bill.
If 12 friends each pay 10 dollars, they collect 12 × 10 = 120 dollars as well.
Both shares rebuild the bill exactly, so 15 dollars and 10 dollars are right.

PC-4#9.title: Divide top and bottom by x
PC-4#9.text:
Divide the top and the bottom of 3x ÷ (x² + 1) by x. The value does not change, and the fraction becomes 3 ÷ (x + 1 ÷ x).
For huge x, the piece 1 ÷ x is almost nothing, so the bottom is about x.
The function then behaves like 3 ÷ x, a fixed number over a growing one, which shrinks toward 0. The graph approaches y = 0.

PC-4#10.title: Divide everything by x²
PC-4#10.text:
Divide the top and the bottom by x². The fraction becomes (3 + 1 ÷ x²) ÷ (1 − 4 ÷ x²).
When x is huge, 1 ÷ x² and 4 ÷ x² are both nearly 0.
So the top is close to 3 and the bottom is close to 1, and the whole fraction is close to 3 ÷ 1 = 3. The horizontal asymptote is y = 3.

PC-4#11.title: Shrink every term
PC-4#11.text:
Divide the top and the bottom of (2x + 1) ÷ (x² + 5) by x². The fraction becomes (2 ÷ x + 1 ÷ x²) ÷ (1 + 5 ÷ x²).
For huge x, every piece with x underneath fades to 0.
The top fades to 0 while the bottom settles at 1, so the fraction heads to 0 ÷ 1 = 0. The horizontal asymptote is y = 0.

PC-4#12.title: A table over time
PC-4#12.text:
Tabulate the level hour by hour.
t = 1: 20 ÷ 5 = 4.
t = 2: 40 ÷ 8 = 5.
t = 4: 80 ÷ 20 = 4.
t = 10: 200 ÷ 104, about 1.9.
t = 50: 1000 ÷ 2504, about 0.4.
The row for t = 2 confirms 5 mg per liter, and the later rows keep falling, so the level drifts toward 0.

PC-5#1.title: Two allowance plans
PC-5#1.text:
Plan A pays 5 dollars more each week: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30.
Plan B doubles each week: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32.
Plan A is ahead for five weeks, then Plan B passes it in week 6 and never looks back. In week 10, Plan A pays 50 dollars and Plan B pays 512 dollars.

PC-5#2.title: Read them off a table
PC-5#2.text:
Suppose a table reads 3, 12, 48, 192 for x = 0, 1, 2, 3.
The value at x = 0 is the start, so a = 3.
Divide any entry by the one before it: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 and 48 ÷ 12 = 4, so b = 4.
The rule is y = 3 · 4^x. Two glances at a table are enough to find both numbers.

PC-5#3.title: The shape on a graph
PC-5#3.text:
Picture the two graphs.
With b = 2 the heights 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 make a curve that starts nearly flat and then climbs steeply.
With b = 0.5 the heights 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 make a curve that drops quickly and then levels off just above the x-axis.
With b = 1 the heights never change. One is the dividing line between the two shapes.

PC-5#4.title: Count on a hundred grid
PC-5#4.text:
Shade a 10 by 10 grid to stand for what you have: 100 squares.
Up 8% adds 8 more squares, so you hold 108 squares, which is 1.08 grids.
Down 20% erases 20 squares, so you hold 80 squares, which is 0.80 of a grid.
The factor is just the number of squares you end with, divided by 100.

PC-5#5.title: Double step by step
PC-5#5.text:
Start at x = 0, where y = 4 · 1 = 4.
Each step up in x multiplies by 2.
x = 1 gives 8, x = 2 gives 16, x = 3 gives 32.
Three doublings from 4 land on 32, the same value as working out 2³ = 8 first and then multiplying by 4.

PC-5#6.title: Read them off a table
PC-5#6.text:
Make a table and let the numbers show each job.
x = 0 gives 200, x = 1 gives 300, x = 2 gives 450.
The value at x = 0 is the start, so a = 200.
Divide neighbors: 300 ÷ 200 = 1.5 and 450 ÷ 300 = 1.5, so the factor is b = 1.5.

PC-5#7.title: Double twice, then twice more
PC-5#7.text:
Group the four doublings in pairs. Two doublings in a row multiply by 4.
After the first 2 hours: 50 × 4 = 200 bacteria.
After the next 2 hours: 200 × 4 = 800 bacteria.
Pairing the hours gives the same 800 as computing 50 × 16 in one go.

PC-5#8.title: Find the interest first
PC-5#8.text:
Work with the money instead of the factor.
One percent of 500 dollars is 5 dollars, so 8 percent is 8 × 5 = 40 dollars.
The balance after a year is 500 + 40 = 540 dollars.
Now divide new by old: 540 ÷ 500 = 1.08. The factor is b = 1.08, found from the result instead of from the percent.

PC-5#9.title: One factor for both years
PC-5#9.text:
Combine the two years into one multiplication.
Keeping three quarters twice means keeping 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16 of the value.
One sixteenth of 600 dollars is 37.50 dollars, and nine of those make 9 × 37.50 = 337.50 dollars.
The single fraction 9/16 gives the same worth as taking 75% two times in a row.

PC-5#10.title: Use the formula
PC-5#10.text:
Write the rule y = 200 · 1.1^x, with start 200 and factor 1.1 for a 10% rise.
For two weeks, x = 2, so the growth is 1.1² = 1.21.
Then 200 × 1.21 = 242 followers.
The extra 0.01 in 1.21 is the growth on the first week's growth: 10% of the 20 new followers is the 2 extra followers.

PC-5#11.title: Walk the clock
PC-5#11.text:
List the colony at each doubling time.
Hour 0: 100 cells.
Hour 3: 200 cells.
Hour 6: 400 cells.
Hour 9: 800 cells.
Hour 12: 1600 cells.
The list never uses an exponent, and it reaches the same 1600 cells after four rows of doubling.

PC-5#12.title: Subtract a fifth each hour
PC-5#12.text:
Twenty percent is one fifth, so remove a fifth of the current amount each hour.
Hour 1: a fifth of 100 is 20, leaving 80 mg.
Hour 2: a fifth of 80 is 16, leaving 64 mg.
Hour 3: a fifth of 64 is 12.8, leaving 51.2 mg.
The amounts removed get smaller each hour because each is a fifth of a smaller amount. The factor is 0.8 either way.

PC-6#1.title: Count the multiplications
PC-6#1.text:
Start at 1 and count how many times you multiply by the base to reach the number.
To reach 8 with base 2: 1, 2, 4, 8. That is three multiplications, so the log base 2 of 8 is 3.
To reach 1000 with base 10: 1, 10, 100, 1000. Three again, so the log of 1000 is 3.
A log is a step counter for repeated multiplying.

PC-6#2.title: One table, read two ways
PC-6#2.text:
Write a table of powers of 2: 1 gives 2, 2 gives 4, 3 gives 8, 4 gives 16, 5 gives 32.
Read it left to right and you are raising 2 to a power: the 5 becomes 32.
Read the same table right to left and you are taking a log: the 32 becomes 5.
There is only one table. The direction you read it decides which operation you are doing.

PC-6#3.title: Count the zeros
PC-6#3.text:
Use base 10, where a log just counts zeros.
100 has 2 zeros and 1000 has 3 zeros. Multiply them: 100 × 1000 = 100,000, which has 5 zeros, and 5 = 2 + 3.
Divide instead: 1000 ÷ 100 = 10, which has 1 zero, and 1 = 3 − 2.
Multiplying numbers adds their zero counts, and dividing subtracts them.

PC-6#4.title: Count the zeros again
PC-6#4.text:
Try it in base 10. The log of 100 is 2, because 100 has two zeros.
Now cube it: 100³ = 100 × 100 × 100 = 1,000,000, which has six zeros, so its log is 6.
Six is 3 × 2: three copies of 100 bring three lots of two zeros.
Raising the number to the power n makes n copies, so the log is multiplied by n.

PC-6#5.title: Halve down to 1
PC-6#5.text:
Run the question backwards. Divide 32 by 2 again and again until you reach 1, and count the divisions.
32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
That took five halvings. Each halving removes one factor of 2, so 32 contains five factors of 2 and the log base 2 of 32 is 5.

PC-6#6.title: Use a square you know
PC-6#6.text:
Split 81 into a product you recognize: 81 = 9 × 9.
Each 9 is 3 × 3, which is 3 to the power 2.
So 81 is two factors of 3 times two more factors of 3, four factors in all.
The product rule says the same thing: log base 3 of 9 is 2, and 2 + 2 = 4. The log base 3 of 81 is 4.

PC-6#7.title: Divide by ten until 1
PC-6#7.text:
Go backwards from 1000, dividing by 10 each time and counting the steps.
1000 ÷ 10 = 100.
100 ÷ 10 = 10.
10 ÷ 10 = 1.
Three divisions bring 1000 down to 1, so 1000 holds three factors of 10 and its log is 3. This matches the three zeros you can see in the number.

PC-6#8.title: Turn the logs back into powers
PC-6#8.text:
Read each given value as an exponent on 10. Saying log 2 = 0.301 means 10 to the 0.301 is 2, and log 5 = 0.699 means 10 to the 0.699 is 5.
Multiply the two: 2 × 5 = 10. Multiplying powers of 10 adds their exponents, so 10 equals 10 to the power 0.301 + 0.699, which is 10 to the power 1.
The exponent is 1, so log 10 = 1.

PC-6#9.title: Jump using 32 × 32
PC-6#9.text:
Count only the first five folds: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. Five folds give 32 layers.
Five more folds multiply the layers by 32 again, and 32 × 32 = 1024.
So 5 + 5 = 10 folds reach 1024 layers.
Splitting the job into two equal halves saves writing all ten doublings.

PC-6#10.title: Rewrite 8 as a power of 2
PC-6#10.text:
Change the base of the inside number. Since 8 = 2 × 2 × 2, one 8 holds three factors of 2.
Then 8³ is three 8s multiplied together, which holds 3 + 3 + 3 = 9 factors of 2.
So 8³ is 2 to the power 9, and the log base 2 of it is 9. No large multiplication is needed.

PC-6#11.title: Write both as powers of ten
PC-6#11.text:
Think of the shaking at magnitude 4 as 10 to the power 4 units, and at magnitude 7 as 10 to the power 7 units.
That is 10,000 against 10,000,000.
Divide the larger by the smaller: 10,000,000 ÷ 10,000 = 1000.
The magnitude 7 quake is 1000 times stronger, the same as three steps of times 10.

PC-6#12.title: Add ten per factor of ten
PC-6#12.text:
Build the million one factor of 10 at a time. Each time the intensity is multiplied by 10, the log goes up by 1, so the loudness goes up by 10 decibels.
10 times: 10 dB. 100 times: 20 dB. 1000 times: 30 dB. 10,000 times: 40 dB. 100,000 times: 50 dB. 1,000,000 times: 60 dB.
The concert is 60 decibels louder.

PC-7#1.title: A table with no repeats
PC-7#1.text:
List the powers of 3: 3, 9, 27, 81, 243. Every entry is bigger than the one before, so no value ever appears twice.
If someone tells you 3 to some power is 81, there is only one row it can be: the fourth.
That is all the same-base method does. It finds the one row of the table where the value sits.

PC-7#2.title: A scale with three equal boxes
PC-7#2.text:
Picture a balance scale. One side holds 3 identical boxes and the other side holds 96 marbles.
The scale stays level if you split each side into 3 equal piles and keep one pile from each: 1 box balances 32 marbles.
The box is 2^x. Only now can you ask what is inside it, and since 32 is five doublings from 1, x = 5.

PC-7#3.title: Trap the answer between two powers
PC-7#3.text:
See why a log is needed with 2^x = 10.
2³ = 8 is too small and 2⁴ = 16 is too big, so x is between 3 and 4 and is not a whole number.
No list of doublings will land on 10. The log measures how far between: log 10 ÷ log 2 is about 3.32, a little past 3, which fits because 10 is a little past 8.

PC-7#4.title: Try it in base ten
PC-7#4.text:
Use a base where the answer is easy to see. Suppose the log base 10 of x is 2.
A base 10 log counts zeros after the 1, so x must be 100. Written as a power, that is 10² = 100.
The same move works for any base: the base is raised to the number on the other side. For log base 4 of x = 3, that is 4 × 4 × 4 = 64.

PC-7#5.title: Halve the right side
PC-7#5.text:
Work on 32 instead of on the exponent. Divide by 2 until nothing but 1 is left.
32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
That is five divisions, so 32 is made of five factors of 2.
The left side 2^x is made of x factors of 2, so the two sides match only when x = 5.

PC-7#6.title: Guess and check powers
PC-7#6.text:
Try whole number exponents and watch the outputs.
5² = 25, far too small.
5³ = 125, still too small.
5⁴ = 625, exactly right.
5⁵ = 3125, too big.
The outputs only go up, so the single match is x = 4.

PC-7#7.title: Test candidates in the log
PC-7#7.text:
Try values of x and see which one gives a log of 3.
x = 4 gives log base 4 of 4 = 1.
x = 16 gives 2, because 4 × 4 = 16.
x = 64 gives 3, because 4 × 4 × 4 = 64.
Each time x is multiplied by 4, the log rises by 1, so x = 64 is the value that reaches 3.

PC-7#8.title: Build a table of outputs
PC-7#8.text:
Leave the equation alone and compute 3 · 2^x for several values of x.
x = 3 gives 3 × 8 = 24.
x = 4 gives 3 × 16 = 48.
x = 5 gives 3 × 32 = 96.
x = 6 gives 3 × 64 = 192.
The outputs double with each row and hit the target 96 exactly once, at x = 5.

PC-7#9.title: List the balance by year
PC-7#9.text:
Write the balance at each doubling instead of using a ratio.
Year 0: 2000 dollars.
Year 7: 4000 dollars.
Year 14: 8000 dollars.
Year 21: 16,000 dollars.
The target shows up in the fourth row, after three doublings, so the wait is 21 years.

PC-7#10.title: Solve with exponents
PC-7#10.text:
Write the rival price in month n as 5 · 2^(n − 1) and set it equal to 80.
Divide both sides by 5: 2^(n − 1) = 16.
Since 16 = 2⁴, the exponents match when n − 1 = 4.
Add 1 to get n = 5. The algebra agrees with the list: the plans match in month 5.

PC-7#11.title: Fill in a clock table
PC-7#11.text:
Track the dose every 4 hours.
Hour 0: 400 mg.
Hour 4: 200 mg.
Hour 8: 100 mg.
Hour 12: 50 mg.
Hour 16: 25 mg.
The table reaches 25 mg in the row for hour 16, so no division or powers of 2 are needed to see the answer is 16 hours.

PC-7#12.title: Work backwards by halving
PC-7#12.text:
Start from the target and halve, stepping 10 years back each time.
10,000 people, then 5000 ten years earlier, then 2500 ten years before that, then 1250 another ten years back.
Three halvings return to the starting size of 1250, so the town needs three doublings going forward. Three steps of 10 years make 30 years.

PC-8#1.title: Stand in the corner
PC-8#1.text:
Imagine standing in the corner of your chosen angle inside a triangular room.
The wall you face across the room is the opposite side. The two walls meeting at your corner both touch you: the slanted one facing the square corner is the hypotenuse, and the other is the adjacent side.
Walk to the other sharp corner and the opposite and adjacent walls swap, but the hypotenuse stays put.

PC-8#2.title: Three questions about a ramp
PC-8#2.text:
Think of the angle as the tilt of a ramp.
Sine answers: for each metre along the ramp, how much do I rise?
Cosine answers: for each metre along the ramp, how far forward do I go?
Tangent answers: for each metre forward, how much do I rise? That is the slope.
On a 3-4-5 ramp these are 0.6, 0.8 and 0.75.

PC-8#3.title: Check them with decimals
PC-8#3.text:
Test each special triangle with the Pythagorean theorem.
3-4-5: 9 + 16 = 25.
45-45-90 with legs 1 and 1: the hypotenuse is about 1.414, and 1 + 1 = 2 matches 1.414².
30-60-90 with hypotenuse 2 and short leg 1: the long leg is about 1.732, and 1 + 3 = 4 = 2².
So sin 30° = 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5 and tan 45° = 1 ÷ 1 = 1.

PC-8#4.title: Look it up backwards
PC-8#4.text:
Picture a table with angles on the left and sines on the right: 30° gives 0.5, 45° gives about 0.707, 60° gives about 0.866.
Sine reads the table left to right. Inverse sine reads the same table right to left: 0.5 gives 30°.
For a ratio between entries, such as 0.6, the angle is between 30° and 45°, and a calculator gives about 36.9°.

PC-8#5.title: Test each side with Pythagoras
PC-8#5.text:
Try each side as the hypotenuse and see which one makes the Pythagorean theorem work.
If 3 were the hypotenuse: 4² + 5² = 41, not 9.
If 4 were the hypotenuse: 3² + 5² = 34, not 16.
If 5 is the hypotenuse: 3² + 4² = 25, which equals 5².
Only 5 passes the test, so the hypotenuse is 5.

PC-8#6.title: Scale to a hypotenuse of 1
PC-8#6.text:
Shrink the triangle until the hypotenuse is 1 by dividing every side by 5.
The sides become 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6, 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8 and 5 ÷ 5 = 1.
With a hypotenuse of 1, the opposite side is the sine and the adjacent side is the cosine, with no more dividing to do.
So the sine is 0.6 and the cosine is 0.8.

PC-8#7.title: Sine divided by cosine
PC-8#7.text:
Find the tangent from the other two ratios.
Sine is opposite over hypotenuse: 6 ÷ 10 = 0.6.
Cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse: 8 ÷ 10 = 0.8.
Tangent equals sine divided by cosine, because the hypotenuse cancels: 0.6 ÷ 0.8 = 0.75.
This route uses the hypotenuse twice and still lands on 0.75.

PC-8#8.title: Half of a square
PC-8#8.text:
The wall, the ground and the ladder make half of a square. The ground piece and the wall piece are both 5 m, and they meet at a right angle, like two sides of a 5 by 5 square.
The ladder is the diagonal of that square.
A diagonal splits the 90° corner of a square into two equal angles, so the ladder meets the ground at 90° ÷ 2 = 45°.

PC-8#9.title: Double the triangle
PC-8#9.text:
Flip a copy of the ramp triangle over the ground line and join the two.
The angle at the bottom of the ramp doubles to 60°, and the two slanted sides are both 10 ft, so the joined shape is an equilateral triangle with all sides 10 ft.
Its third side is the height counted twice. So 2h = 10 and h = 5 ft.

PC-8#10.title: Compare with a short stick
PC-8#10.text:
Stand a 1 ft stick upright next to the tree. With the sun at 45°, the stick's shadow is as long as the stick is tall: 1 ft.
The tree and the stick are lit at the same angle, so they make similar triangles.
The tree's shadow is 20 times the stick's shadow, so the tree is 20 times the stick's height: 20 ft.

PC-8#11.title: Check with Pythagoras and cosine
PC-8#11.text:
Find the third side. The ground distance is √(40² − 20²) = √1200, about 34.6 m.
Now use a different ratio: cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, 34.6 ÷ 40, about 0.866.
The angle with cosine 0.866 is 30°.
A second ratio built from a different side points to the same angle, so 30° is confirmed.

PC-8#12.title: The two sharp angles share 90°
PC-8#12.text:
Use the shortcut for right triangles. The right angle already uses 90° of the 180°, so the other two angles must add up to the remaining 90°.
One of them is 55°, so the other is 90° − 55° = 35°.
A single subtraction does the job, and the check 55 + 35 = 90 takes one second.

PC-9#1.title: Points that pass the test
PC-9#1.text:
A point is on the unit circle when its distance from the centre is 1, which means across² + up² = 1.
(1, 0) passes: 1 + 0 = 1.
(0.6, 0.8) passes: 0.36 + 0.64 = 1.
(0.5, 0.5) fails: 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5, so it is inside the circle.
Each point that passes belongs to exactly one direction from the centre, which is its angle.

PC-9#2.title: Read them at the easy angles
PC-9#2.text:
Check the idea at four angles where the tip is easy to find.
0°: the tip is at (1, 0), so cosine is 1 and sine is 0.
90°: the tip is at (0, 1), so cosine is 0 and sine is 1.
180°: the tip is at (−1, 0), so cosine is −1 and sine is 0.
270°: the tip is at (0, −1), so cosine is 0 and sine is −1.

PC-9#3.title: Lay the radius along the rim
PC-9#3.text:
Cut a piece of string as long as the radius and lay it along the rim. The angle it covers is 1 radian, about 57°.
A little over three strings, 3.14 of them, reach halfway round, so a half turn is π radians. About 6.28 strings go all the way round.
Radians count how many radius lengths you have walked along the edge.

PC-9#4.title: A compass for signs
PC-9#4.text:
Think of a map with the centre as home. East is positive across, west is negative across, north is positive up, south is negative up.
Heading northeast, both are positive. Northwest: across negative, up positive. Southwest: both negative. Southeast: across positive, up negative.
For example, 200° points southwest, so cosine and sine are both negative there.

PC-9#5.title: Squash a triangle flat
PC-9#5.text:
Picture a right triangle with hypotenuse 1 and a very small angle, such as 1°. Its opposite side is tiny, about 0.017, and its adjacent side is almost the full 1.
Shrink the angle to 0° and the triangle goes flat: the opposite side becomes 0 and the adjacent side lies on top of the hypotenuse, length 1.
So sin 0° = 0 and cos 0° = 1.

PC-9#6.title: Use the circle equation
PC-9#6.text:
Every point on the unit circle satisfies across² + up² = 1.
At 90° the hand points straight along the y-axis, and every point on the y-axis has across = 0.
So 0² + up² = 1, which makes up equal to 1 or −1. The hand points up, not down, so up = 1.
That gives cosine 0 and sine 1.

PC-9#7.title: A quarter of the face
PC-9#7.text:
Look at the clock face as four equal quarters, marked by the 12, the 3, the 6 and the 9.
Moving from the 12 to the 3 covers exactly one of those quarters.
A whole turn is 360°, so a quarter turn is 360° ÷ 4 = 90°.
You can see it too: a hand at 12 and a hand at 3 make a square corner.

PC-9#8.title: Use a fraction of a full turn
PC-9#8.text:
A full turn is 2π radians, so find what fraction of a full turn π/3 is.
(π/3) ÷ (2π) = 1/6, so the angle is one sixth of a full turn.
In degrees a full turn is 360°, and one sixth of 360° is 60°.
The fraction of a turn is the same in both units, so π/3 radians is 60°.

PC-9#9.title: Add up four quarter turns
PC-9#9.text:
Build the full turn from quarter turns. A quarter turn is 90°, and since 180° is π radians, 90° is π/2 radians.
A full turn is four quarter turns: 4 × π/2 = 2π radians.
As a decimal that is about 6.28, which means the valve travels a little more than 6 radius lengths around the rim in one roll.

PC-9#10.title: Picture the wheel
PC-9#10.text:
Skip the sine and follow the seat. It starts at the far right, level with the centre, so it is 20 m up.
A 90° turn is a quarter of the way round, which carries the seat from the far right to the very top.
The top of a wheel is one radius above the centre: 20 + 15 = 35 m.

PC-9#11.title: Mirror across the x-axis
PC-9#11.text:
Use the unit circle. Mark the tip at 30° above the x-axis and the tip at 30° below it. They are mirror images, so the line joining them is vertical and has length 2 × sin 30°.
The two hands and that line form a triangle with a 60° angle between two sides of length 1, which makes it equilateral.
So the vertical side is 1, and sin 30° = 1 ÷ 2.

PC-9#12.title: Count through the quadrants
PC-9#12.text:
Count forward through the quadrant boundaries: 0° to 90° is Quadrant 1, 90° to 180° is Quadrant 2, 180° to 270° is Quadrant 3, and 270° to 360° is Quadrant 4.
300° is past 270° and short of 360°, so it is in Quadrant 4.
That corner is right of centre and below it, so cosine is positive and sine is negative.

PC-10#1.title: A table that repeats
PC-10#1.text:
Write the sine at every 90°: 0° gives 0, 90° gives 1, 180° gives 0, 270° gives −1, 360° gives 0.
Keep going: 450° gives 1, 540° gives 0, 630° gives −1, 720° gives 0.
The list 0, 1, 0, −1 repeats without end. Plot those values and join them smoothly, and the repeating list becomes the repeating wave.

PC-10#2.title: Swings and volume knobs
PC-10#2.text:
Think of a playground swing. Its resting position is the middle, and the amplitude is how far it travels from rest to its highest point on one side.
A harder push gives a bigger swing, but each back and forth still takes the same time.
Numbers: a wave that peaks at 9 and bottoms out at 1 has amplitude (9 − 1) ÷ 2 = 4.

PC-10#3.title: Daily temperature
PC-10#3.text:
Suppose the temperature over a day rises to 30 degrees in the afternoon and falls to 20 degrees at night, in a smooth wave.
The level it wiggles around is halfway between: (30 + 20) ÷ 2 = 25 degrees.
That 25 is the midline. A model for it would end in + 25, and the wave spends equal time above and below that level.

PC-10#4.title: Count waves, then start late
PC-10#4.text:
Period with numbers: for y = sin(3x), the inside reaches 360° when x is only 120°, so three full waves fit between 0° and 360° and each is 120° wide. Check: 360° ÷ 3 = 120°.
Phase shift as a story: a tide that normally starts rising at noon but runs 2 hours late does everything 2 hours later. In the same way, y = sin(x − 30°) starts rising at 30° instead of 0°.

PC-10#5.title: Compare two tables
PC-10#5.text:
Evaluate both waves at the same angles.
sin(x) at 0°, 90°, 180°, 270° gives 0, 1, 0, −1.
4 sin(x) at those angles gives 0, 4, 0, −4.
Each height is 4 times as far from the middle. The farthest the new wave gets from its middle level of 0 is 4, so the amplitude is 4.

PC-10#6.title: Read it from a table
PC-10#6.text:
Evaluate y = sin(x) + 7 at the quarter turns.
0° gives 7, 90° gives 8, 180° gives 7, 270° gives 6, 360° gives 7.
The values go 7, 8, 7, 6, 7. The wave keeps coming back to 7 and moves 1 above and 1 below it.
The level it returns to is the midline, y = 7.

PC-10#7.title: Plug in the extreme sine values
PC-10#7.text:
The sine part can only run from −1 to 1, so test the two ends directly.
When sin(x) = 1, which happens at 90°: h = 18 × 1 + 22 = 40 m.
When sin(x) = −1, which happens at 270°: h = 18 × (−1) + 22 = 4 m.
No other value of sine is larger or smaller, so the seat stays between 4 m and 40 m.

PC-10#8.title: Count waves in a table
PC-10#8.text:
Evaluate y = sin(2x) every 45°.
0° gives sin 0° = 0.
45° gives sin 90° = 1.
90° gives sin 180° = 0.
135° gives sin 270° = −1.
180° gives sin 360° = 0.
The values 0, 1, 0, −1, 0 are one complete wave, and it finished at x = 180°. So the period is 180°, half of the usual 360°.

PC-10#9.title: Follow the inside to 360
PC-10#9.text:
A sine wave finishes one cycle when its inside reaches 360°. Here the inside is 6x.
Solve 6x = 360 to get x = 60.
Check with values: at x = 15° the inside is 90° and y = 3, the peak. At x = 45° the inside is 270° and y = −3, the trough. At x = 60° the trace is back at 0 and rising, so one beat is 60° wide.

PC-10#10.title: Solve two small equations
PC-10#10.text:
Write what the extremes mean. High tide is midline plus amplitude: k + A = 9. Low tide is midline minus amplitude: k − A = 3.
Add the two equations: 2k = 12, so k = 6.
Subtract them: 2A = 6, so A = 3.
The same numbers come out as from averaging, this time by algebra: amplitude 3 and midline 6.

PC-10#11.title: Track the peak in a table
PC-10#11.text:
Find where the new wave peaks. Plain sine peaks at 90°, where its value is 1.
Try y = sin(x − 30°) at a few inputs: x = 90° gives sin 60°, about 0.87. x = 120° gives sin 90° = 1. x = 150° gives sin 120°, about 0.87.
The peak has moved from 90° to 120°, which is 30° to the right.

PC-11#1.title: Use the distance formula
PC-11#1.text:
The distance from the centre (0, 0) to a point (x, y) is √(x² + y²).
Every point on the unit circle is exactly 1 away from the centre, so x² + y² = 1.
The point for angle θ is called (cos θ, sin θ). Swap those names in and you get cos²θ + sin²θ = 1.
A concrete case: the point (0.6, 0.8) gives 0.36 + 0.64 = 1.

PC-11#2.title: A pie cut in two
PC-11#2.text:
Think of the number 1 as a whole pie cut into two slices, a sin² slice and a cos² slice.
If the sin² slice is 0.3 of the pie, the cos² slice has to be 0.7. If the sin² slice grows to 0.9, the cos² slice shrinks to 0.1.
Knowing one slice always tells you the other: it is whatever is left of the pie.

PC-11#3.title: Go back to the triangle
PC-11#3.text:
Use SOH-CAH-TOA on any right triangle. Sine is opposite ÷ hypotenuse and cosine is adjacent ÷ hypotenuse.
Divide sine by cosine and the hypotenuse cancels, leaving opposite ÷ adjacent, which is tangent.
Numbers: in a 3-4-5 triangle, sine is 0.6 and cosine is 0.8, and 0.6 ÷ 0.8 = 0.75, the same as 3 ÷ 4.

PC-11#4.title: Look at a table of values
PC-11#4.text:
List the sine every 30° through half a turn: 0° gives 0, 30° gives 0.5, 60° gives about 0.87, 90° gives 1, 120° gives about 0.87, 150° gives 0.5, 180° gives 0.
The list reads the same forwards and backwards. Each value except the peak appears twice, at angles that add to 180°, such as 30° and 150°, or 60° and 120°.

PC-11#5.title: Check with a 3-4-5 triangle
PC-11#5.text:
Use an angle from a triangle instead of the unit circle. In a 3-4-5 right triangle, the angle opposite the 3 has sine 3/5 and cosine 4/5.
Square them: 9/25 and 16/25.
Add: 9/25 + 16/25 = 25/25 = 1.
The total is 1 because 9 + 16 = 25, which is just the Pythagorean theorem for this triangle.

PC-11#6.title: Spot the 3-4-5 triangle
PC-11#6.text:
A cosine of 0.6 is 3/5, so picture a right triangle with adjacent side 3 and hypotenuse 5.
The missing side satisfies 3² + opposite² = 5², so opposite² = 25 − 9 = 16 and the opposite side is 4.
Sine is opposite over hypotenuse: 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8.
The triangle gives the same positive value without subtracting decimals.

PC-11#7.title: Find the point on the circle
PC-11#7.text:
The facing direction is a point on the unit circle with across value 0.6. Points on that circle satisfy across² + up² = 1.
Two points have across 0.6: (0.6, 0.8) above the axis and (0.6, −0.8) below it. Check: 0.36 + 0.64 = 1 for both.
Quadrant 1 is the upper right, so the sprite uses the upper point and sin θ = 0.8.

PC-11#8.title: Test it with an angle
PC-11#8.text:
Check the simplified form with a real angle, θ = 60°.
sin 60° is about 0.866, so sin² is 0.75 and the top is 1 − 0.75 = 0.25.
cos 60° is 0.5, so the fraction is 0.25 ÷ 0.5 = 0.5.
The result 0.5 is exactly cos 60°, which agrees with the answer cos θ. One more test, θ = 0°: (1 − 0) ÷ 1 = 1 = cos 0°.

PC-11#9.title: Use a triangle with equal legs
PC-11#9.text:
Draw a right triangle with a 45° angle. Its other sharp angle is 90° − 45° = 45° too, so the two legs are equal. Call each leg 1.
Tangent is opposite over adjacent, which is 1 ÷ 1 = 1.
The legs could be 5 and 5 or 12 and 12 and the ratio would still be 1, so tan 45° = 1 exactly.

PC-11#10.title: Use a 30-60-90 triangle
PC-11#10.text:
A height of 0.5 on a circle of radius 1 makes a right triangle whose opposite side is half its hypotenuse. That is the 30-60-90 triangle, so the angle at the centre is 30°.
The triangle can lean to the right, giving θ = 30°, or lean to the left, where its 30° is measured back from 180°, giving θ = 180° − 30° = 150°.

PC-11#11.title: Test angles in a table
PC-11#11.text:
List the sine every 30°: 0° gives 0, 30° gives 0.5, 60° gives 0.87, 90° gives 1, 120° gives 0.87, 150° gives 0.5, 180° gives 0.
From 210° to 330° every sine is negative, so none of those can equal 0.5.
The value 0.5 appears in the table exactly twice, at 30° and at 150°.

PC-11#12.title: Draw a line across the circle
PC-11#12.text:
Draw the unit circle and a horizontal line at height 0.5. The line cuts the circle at two points, one on the right and one on the left, at the same height.
By the circle equation their across values are √(1 − 0.25), about 0.87 and −0.87.
The right point is at 30°. The left point is its mirror image, 30° short of 180°, which is 150°.

PC-12#1.title: A crooked triangle in the wild
PC-12#1.text:
Picture surveying a triangular field with sides 50 m and 70 m meeting at 80°. There is no square corner, so SOH-CAH-TOA has nothing to hold on to.
You could still measure the third side with a tape. The two laws let you calculate it instead, about 79 m, and they give the same result a tape would for any triangle you can draw.

PC-12#2.title: Test it on a known triangle
PC-12#2.text:
Check the law on a 30-60-90 triangle with sides 1, √3 and 2.
Side 1 faces 30°: 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2.
Side √3, about 1.732, faces 60°: 1.732 ÷ 0.866 = 2.
Side 2 faces 90°: 2 ÷ 1 = 2.
All three partners give the same number, 2. If you know that number from one pair, you can find any other side or angle.

PC-12#3.title: A door swinging open
PC-12#3.text:
Hold two sticks of fixed lengths joined at a hinge, like a door and its frame. The distance between the free ends is side c.
Close the hinge and the ends nearly touch. Open it to 90° and Pythagoras gives the gap. Open it wider and the gap keeps growing.
The term −2ab × cos C is the dial that tracks the hinge: it subtracts when the angle is narrow and adds when it is wide.

PC-12#4.title: Sort four example triangles
PC-12#4.text:
Try sorting.
Angles 40° and 60° with a side of 9 facing the 40°: a side and its facing angle are both known, so use the Law of Sines.
Sides 6 and 9 with 50° between them: no facing pair, so use the Law of Cosines.
Sides 4, 5 and 6: no angles at all, so Law of Cosines.
Sides 7 and 10 with an angle facing the 10: a pair again, so Law of Sines.

PC-12#5.title: Use SOH-CAH-TOA
PC-12#5.text:
Angle B is 90°, so this is a right triangle and the side facing B, length 10, is the hypotenuse.
Side a is opposite the 30° angle, so sine applies: sin 30° = a ÷ 10.
Since sin 30° = 0.5, a = 10 × 0.5 = 5.
The Law of Sines gives the same answer because, for a right triangle, it turns into SOH.

PC-12#6.title: Drop a height
PC-12#6.text:
Split the triangle into two right triangles. From the far end of the side of 3, drop a perpendicular onto the side of 8.
Its foot is 3 × cos 60° = 1.5 from the corner, and its height is 3 × sin 60°, about 2.6, so height² = 6.75.
The rest of the base is 8 − 1.5 = 6.5.
Pythagoras: c² = 6.5² + 6.75 = 42.25 + 6.75 = 49, so c = 7.

PC-12#7.title: It is a right triangle
PC-12#7.text:
The angle at the drone is 90°, so the 100 m line between the friends is the hypotenuse of a right triangle.
The side from B to the drone touches B's 60° angle, so it is adjacent to it: cos 60° = distance ÷ 100.
Since cos 60° = 0.5, the distance is 100 × 0.5 = 50 m. No Law of Sines is needed when a right angle appears.

PC-12#8.title: Plot it on a grid
PC-12#8.text:
Put the turning point at (0, 0) and the start at (5, 0). The second leg leaves the turning point at 120° from the first, so it ends at (16 × cos 120°, 16 × sin 120°) = (−8, about 13.86).
From start to finish the boat is 5 + 8 = 13 across and 13.86 up.
Distance² = 13² + 13.86² = 169 + 192 = 361, so the distance is 19 km.

PC-12#9.title: Shrink it to 3 and 8
PC-12#9.text:
Divide both paths by 10 to get a small triangle with sides 3 and 8 and the same 60° corner.
For the small triangle: c² = 9 + 64 − 2 × 3 × 8 × 0.5 = 73 − 24 = 49, so c = 7.
Scale back up by 10: the far ends are 7 × 10 = 70 m apart.
Same shape, smaller numbers, same answer.

PC-12#10.title: Check by running it forward
PC-12#10.text:
Test the answer by starting from the angle. Take sides 3 and 5 with 120° between them and compute the third side.
c² = 9 + 25 − 2 × 3 × 5 × cos 120° = 34 − 30 × (−0.5) = 34 + 15 = 49.
So c = 7, which is exactly the third side given. Only one angle between 0° and 180° can produce this, so the corner facing 7 is 120°.

PC-12#11.title: Use coordinates
PC-12#11.text:
Put the corner at (0, 0) and the end of the 90 ft edge at (90, 0). The 150 ft edge points at 120°, so its end is at (150 × cos 120°, 150 × sin 120°) = (−75, about 129.9).
The ends are 90 + 75 = 165 apart across and 129.9 apart up.
Distance² = 165² + 129.9² = 27,225 + 16,875 = 44,100, and √44,100 = 210 ft.

PC-12#12.title: Compare with sharp and wide
PC-12#12.text:
See what other long sides would mean for the legs 5 and 12, where 25 + 144 = 169.
If the long side were 12.5, its square is 156.25, less than 169, and the corner would be sharp.
If it were 14, its square is 196, more than 169, and the corner would be wide.
At 13 the square is exactly 169, the balance point, so the corner is exactly 90°.

PC-13#1.title: Positions and values
PC-13#1.text:
Think of a sequence as a table with a position column and a value column: position 1 holds 3, position 2 holds 7, position 3 holds 11, position 4 holds 15.
A rule connects the columns. Here each value is 4 times its position, minus 1, so position 100 holds 4 × 100 − 1 = 399.
Shuffle the list to 7, 15, 3, 11 and that rule no longer fits, so it is a different sequence.

PC-13#2.title: Points on a line
PC-13#2.text:
Plot the terms 3, 7, 11, 15 as points: (1, 3), (2, 7), (3, 11), (4, 15). They lie on a straight line that rises 4 for each step right.
An arithmetic sequence is a line sampled at whole numbers, and d is its slope.
The line here is y = 4x − 1, which is the same as 3 + (x − 1) × 4, so the formula is just the equation of that line.

PC-13#3.title: Folding paper
PC-13#3.text:
Fold a sheet of paper in half again and again. The layers go 1, 2, 4, 8, 16: each fold multiplies by 2, so this is geometric with r = 2.
After 10 folds there are 1 × 2¹⁰ = 1024 layers.
Compare with stacking one extra sheet each time, which gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and only 11 sheets after ten steps.

PC-13#4.title: Average times count
PC-13#4.text:
Another way to see the shortcut: replace every term by the average.
For 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 the average is the middle value, 6, which is also (2 + 10) ÷ 2.
Five terms that average 6 add to 5 × 6 = 30, and adding directly gives 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10 = 30.
So the sum is the number of terms times the average of the first and last.

PC-13#5.title: Find a formula for position
PC-13#5.text:
Compare each term with its position. Positions 1, 2, 3, 4 hold 3, 7, 11, 15.
Four times the position gives 4, 8, 12, 16, and each term is 1 less than that.
So term n is 4n − 1.
For position 5: 4 × 5 − 1 = 19. The formula reaches the next term without looking at the term before it.

PC-13#6.title: Factor each term
PC-13#6.text:
Break each term into prime factors and look at what changes.
2 = 2.
6 = 2 × 3.
18 = 2 × 3 × 3.
54 = 2 × 3 × 3 × 3.
Each term keeps the single 2 and picks up one more 3 than the term before. The next term has four 3s: 2 × 81 = 162.

PC-13#7.title: Count extra seats past row 1
PC-13#7.text:
Think of every row as row 1 plus some extra seats.
Row 2 has 3 extra, row 3 has 6 extra, row 4 has 9 extra. The extras are 3 times the number of rows you have moved back.
Row 20 is 19 rows behind row 1, so it has 19 × 3 = 57 extra seats.
12 + 57 = 69 seats.

PC-13#8.title: Average times count
PC-13#8.text:
Find the average of the numbers and multiply by how many there are.
The numbers 1 to 100 are evenly spaced, so their average is halfway between the ends: (1 + 100) ÷ 2 = 50.5.
One hundred numbers that average 50.5 add up to 100 × 50.5 = 5050.
This is Gauss's pairing seen another way: each pair of 101 averages 50.5.

PC-13#9.title: Add rows in blocks of ten
PC-13#9.text:
Split the pyramid into its bottom ten rows and top ten rows.
The top ten rows are 1 + 2 + … + 10 = 55 cans.
Each of the bottom ten rows, 11 to 20, is 10 more than a matching top row, so they hold 55 + 10 × 10 = 155 cans.
Together: 55 + 155 = 210 cans.

PC-13#10.title: Factor out the 5
PC-13#10.text:
Every weekly amount is a multiple of 5: the list is 5 × 1, 5 × 2, 5 × 3, up to 5 × 12.
So the total is 5 × (1 + 2 + … + 12).
The sum of 1 to 12 is 12 × 13 ÷ 2 = 78.
5 × 78 = 390 dollars. This route never needs the amount saved in week 12.

PC-13#11.title: Work backwards from row 20
PC-13#11.text:
Check the answer by walking from row 20 back to the front.
If row 20 has 69 seats, each row forward has 3 fewer: 66, 63, 60, and so on.
Going from row 20 to row 1 is 19 steps, which removes 19 × 3 = 57 seats.
69 − 57 = 12, which is exactly the size of row 1, so 69 seats is correct.

PC-13#12.title: Pair the rows instead
PC-13#12.text:
Leave the single pyramid alone and pair its own rows.
Bottom row with top row: 20 + 1 = 21. Next pair: 19 + 2 = 21. Then 18 + 3 = 21, and so on.
Twenty rows make 10 pairs, each holding 21 cans.
10 × 21 = 210 cans, the same as half of the 420 can rectangle.

PC-14#1.title: A table of approach
PC-14#1.text:
Take f(x) = x² and let x approach 3.
From below: 2.9 gives 8.41, 2.99 gives 8.9401, 2.999 gives 8.994001.
From above: 3.1 gives 9.61, 3.01 gives 9.0601.
The outputs close in on 9 from both sides, so the limit is 9. You would say the same thing even if someone erased the single point at x = 3 from the graph.

PC-14#2.title: Trace it with a pencil
PC-14#2.text:
Picture drawing the graph without lifting your pencil. If you can trace through x = 2 in one stroke, the pencil is heading for exactly the point it is about to draw.
For y = x² near x = 2, the pencil passes heights 3.61 at 1.9 and 3.9601 at 1.99 and arrives at 4, which is 2².
No lift means no surprise, so plugging in is enough.

PC-14#3.title: Watch the numbers near the hole
PC-14#3.text:
Try (x² − 4) ÷ (x − 2) near x = 2 with a calculator.
x = 1.9 gives −0.39 ÷ −0.1 = 3.9.
x = 1.99 gives 3.99.
x = 2.01 gives 4.01.
x = 2.1 gives 0.41 ÷ 0.1 = 4.1.
At x = 2 itself the calculator shows an error, yet every neighbor points at 4. The 0 ÷ 0 marks a missing dot at height 4, not a missing answer.

PC-14#4.title: Shrink the window with numbers
PC-14#4.text:
A ball's distance is d = 5t² metres. Find its speed at t = 1 by shrinking the time window.
From t = 1 to 2: (20 − 5) ÷ 1 = 15 m/s.
From 1 to 1.1: (6.05 − 5) ÷ 0.1 = 10.5 m/s.
From 1 to 1.01: (5.1005 − 5) ÷ 0.01 = 10.05 m/s.
The averages settle toward 10 m/s, the speed at that instant.

PC-14#5.title: Sneak up with a table
PC-14#5.text:
Ignore the shortcut and watch the outputs.
From below: x = 1.9 gives 6.7, x = 1.99 gives 6.97, x = 1.999 gives 6.997.
From above: x = 2.1 gives 7.3, x = 2.01 gives 7.03, x = 2.001 gives 7.003.
Each output is 3 times as far from 7 as x is from 2, so as x closes in on 2 the outputs close in on 7.

PC-14#6.title: Spot the rule behind the table
PC-14#6.text:
Look for a pattern in the four readings: 1.9 gives 3.9, 1.99 gives 3.99, 2.01 gives 4.01, 2.1 gives 4.1.
Every output is its input plus 2. So away from x = 2 the function behaves like x + 2, a straight line with one point removed.
That line passes through height 2 + 2 = 4 at the gap, so the limit is 4.

PC-14#7.title: Sneak up with a table
PC-14#7.text:
Leave the algebra and compute the fraction at inputs close to 3.
x = 2.9: (8.41 − 9) ÷ (−0.1) = 5.9.
x = 2.99: (8.9401 − 9) ÷ (−0.01) = 5.99.
x = 3.01: (9.0601 − 9) ÷ 0.01 = 6.01.
x = 3.1: (9.61 − 9) ÷ 0.1 = 6.1.
Both sides squeeze toward 6, the same value the cancelling gave, even though x = 3 itself cannot be used.

PC-14#8.title: Read it as a slope
PC-14#8.text:
Plot the car's readings as points: (1, 30) and (3, 150). The line through them rises 120 km over a run of 2 hours, a slope of 60, so the average speed is 60 km/h.
Check by running forward: 30 + 60 × 2 = 150.
For the runner, the points (15, 100) and (75, 400) give slope 300 ÷ 60 = 5 m/s, and 100 + 5 × 60 = 400.

PC-14#9.title: Factor instead of a table
PC-14#9.text:
The average rate from 3 to x is (x² − 9) ÷ (x − 3). Factor the top as (x − 3)(x + 3) and cancel, which leaves x + 3 for any x other than 3.
So the rates are 3.1 + 3 = 6.1, then 3.01 + 3 = 6.01, then 3.001 + 3 = 6.001.
As x slides to 3, x + 3 slides to 6.

PC-14#10.title: Use a table of steps
PC-14#10.text:
Pick actual step sizes and compute the average rate for each.
h = 1: (16 − 9) ÷ 1 = 7.
h = 0.5: (12.25 − 9) ÷ 0.5 = 6.5.
h = 0.1: (9.61 − 9) ÷ 0.1 = 6.1.
h = 0.01: (9.0601 − 9) ÷ 0.01 = 6.01.
Each result is 6 plus the step, so as the step shrinks to nothing the rate settles at 6.

PC-14#11.title: Ask how close it gets
PC-14#11.text:
Measure the gap between the temperature and 18. The gap is exactly 6 ÷ t.
To be within 1 degree of 18 you need t past 6 hours. Within 0.1 degree, past 60 hours. Within 0.01 degree, past 600 hours.
Any closeness you name is reached by waiting long enough, and the gap never turns negative. That is what it means for the limit to be 18 degrees.

SAT-1#1.title: Run the number machine backwards
SAT-1#1.text: Picture x going into a machine that multiplies by 3 and then adds 7, and 22 comes out. To find what went in, send 22 back through the machine in reverse. First take away the 7 to get 15, then divide by 3 to get 5. Every linear equation is a machine like this, and solving it means running each step backwards, last step first.

SAT-1#2.title: Two lines on a graph
SAT-1#2.text: Graph each side as its own line, y = ax + b and y = cx + d. A solution is an x where the lines meet. Lines with different steepness cross at exactly one point, so there is one solution. Lines with the same steepness and different heights are parallel and never meet, so there is none. If steepness and height both match, one line lies on top of the other and every x works.

SAT-1#3.title: A higher or lower guessing game
SAT-1#3.text: Take 5x − 4 = 31 with choices 3, 5, 7 and 9. Try 5 first: 5 × 5 − 4 is 21, which is too small, so the answer must be larger and 3 is ruled out as well. Try 7: 5 × 7 − 4 is 31, a match. Two quick multiplications replaced the algebra, the same way a higher or lower guessing game closes in on a hidden number.

SAT-1#4.title: Cover up the unknown part
SAT-1#4.text: Cover the 3x with your thumb. The equation reads: something plus 7 is 22, so the something is 15. Now uncover it: 3x is 15, which means three equal copies of x make 15, so each copy is 5. No balancing steps are written down, yet the two questions asked are the same two undo steps, and the answer is x = 5.

SAT-1#5.title: Divide by 2 before distributing
SAT-1#5.text: Every part of 4(x − 2) = 2x + 10 is even, so halve both sides first. The left side becomes 2(x − 2) and the right side becomes x + 5. Distribute the smaller number: 2x − 4 = x + 5. Subtract x from both sides to get x − 4 = 5, then add 4. The result is x = 9, reached with smaller numbers.

SAT-1#6.title: Collect the x pieces as fractions
SAT-1#6.text: Leave the fractions in and move x/3 to the right side: 2 = x/2 − x/3. Half of something minus a third of it is one sixth of it, because 3/6 − 2/6 = 1/6. So the equation says 2 = x/6. One sixth of x is 2, and x is six times that, which gives x = 12.

SAT-1#7.title: Watch the gap close
SAT-1#7.text: At x = 7 the left side is 20 and the right side is 24, so the left is behind by 4. Each time x goes up by 1 the left side gains 4 and the right side gains 2, so the gap shrinks by 2 per step. A gap of 4 closes in 4 ÷ 2 = 2 steps. Two steps past 7 is x = 9, with no further testing.

SAT-1#8.title: Try a few values of x
SAT-1#8.text: Plug numbers into both sides of 2(3x + 1) = 6x + 5. At x = 0 the sides are 2 and 5. At x = 1 they are 8 and 11. At x = 10 they are 62 and 65. The left side is always exactly 3 behind the right side, and the gap never shrinks, so the two sides can never be equal. There is no solution.

SAT-1#9.title: Move the x-term to avoid a negative
SAT-1#9.text: Add 3x to both sides of −3x + 4 = 19 so the coefficient of x becomes positive: 4 = 19 + 3x. Subtract 19 from both sides to get −15 = 3x. Now divide by positive 3, which gives −5 = x. The answer x = −5 is the same, and no division by a negative number was needed.

SAT-2#1.title: Slope as a unit price
SAT-2#1.text: Think of 4 pounds of apples costing 12 dollars. The price per pound is 12 ÷ 4 = 3 dollars. Slope is the same idea with y as the cost and x as the pounds: divide the change in y by the change in x to get the change in y for ONE unit of x. Between (2, 5) and (6, 17), 12 units of y are shared over 4 units of x, so each unit of x is worth 3.

SAT-2#2.title: Let the units decide
SAT-2#2.text: Every term in C(h) = 65h + 40 must come out in dollars, because the terms are added to make a cost. The 40 stands alone, so it is simply 40 dollars. The 65 is multiplied by hours, so to end up with dollars it must be dollars per hour: (dollars per hour) × hours = dollars. The units alone say which number is the rate.

SAT-2#3.title: A savings jar and a square
SAT-2#3.text: Start with 40 dollars and add 15 every week: 40, 55, 70, 85. Each jump is 15 because the same thing happens every week, and that steady jump is the slope. Compare the areas of squares with sides 1, 2, 3, 4: 1, 4, 9, 16. The jumps are 3, 5, 7, so they keep growing, and the pattern is not linear.

SAT-2#4.title: Reverse the order, then walk it
SAT-2#4.text: Take the points in the opposite order: (5 − 17) ÷ (2 − 6) = −12 ÷ −4 = 3. The two negatives cancel, so the order does not matter as long as it is the same on top and bottom. Now check by walking: start at y = 5 when x = 2 and add 3 for each step to x = 6. You get 8, 11, 14, 17, which lands on the second point.

SAT-2#5.title: Itemize a three-hour bill
SAT-2#5.text: Write out the bill for a 3-hour job as a list. There is one line for the visit, 40 dollars, and then one line for each hour: 65, 65, 65. The total is 40 + 195 = 235, which matches C(3). The 40 appears once no matter how long the job is, so it is a flat fee. The 65 appears once per hour, so it is the hourly rate.

SAT-2#6.title: Turn each fact into an equation
SAT-2#6.text: Write f(x) = mx + b and plug in each fact. From f(0) = 3 you get m × 0 + b = 3, so b = 3. From f(4) = 11 you get 4m + b = 11, which is now 4m + 3 = 11. Subtract 3 to get 4m = 8, so m = 2. The function is f(x) = 2x + 3, found without the slope formula.

SAT-2#7.title: Halve the interval
SAT-2#7.text: On a line, the value halfway between two inputs is the average of the two outputs. Halfway between x = 0 and x = 4 is x = 2, where f is the average of 3 and 11, which is 7. Halfway between x = 0 and x = 2 is x = 1, where f is the average of 3 and 7, which is 5. So one step from 0 to 1 adds 2, and f(x) = 2x + 3.

SAT-2#8.title: Count down in a table
SAT-2#8.text: List the amount left at easy times. The tank loses 200 liters every 10 minutes, so it holds 500 at the start, 300 after 10 minutes and 100 after 20 minutes. The last 100 liters drain at 20 liters a minute, which takes 5 more minutes. The tank is empty at t = 25 minutes. As one division this is 500 ÷ 20 = 25.

SAT-2#9.title: Walk across the grid
SAT-2#9.text: Start at (−1, 4) and move right to x = 3. That is 4 steps: 0, 1, 2, 3. Over those steps y drops from 4 to −8, a fall of 12. Sharing the fall equally gives 3 down per step. Check by walking: 4, 1, −2, −5, −8. The walk ends at −8 as it should, so the slope is −3.

SAT-3#1.title: One line written three ways
SAT-3#1.text: Take a taxi ride that costs 2 dollars per mile plus a 1 dollar start fee. Slope-intercept form says it directly: y = 2x + 1. If you only know that a 3 mile ride cost 7 dollars at 2 dollars per mile, point-slope writes y − 7 = 2(x − 3). Moving the letters to one side gives standard form, 2x − y = −1. All three describe the same rides.

SAT-3#2.title: Spend it all on one item
SAT-3#2.text: Read 4x + 5y = 20 as a budget: pens cost 4 dollars, notebooks cost 5 dollars and you spend exactly 20 dollars. If you buy only notebooks, x is 0 and 20 dollars buys 4 of them, the point (0, 4). If you buy only pens, y is 0 and 20 dollars buys 5 of them, the point (5, 0). The intercepts are the two all-of-one-thing purchases.

SAT-3#3.title: Check both rules with numbers
SAT-3#3.text: Parallel: at x = 0, 1 and 2 the line y = 2x + 1 gives 1, 3, 5 and y = 2x − 3 gives −3, −1, 1. The gap is always 4, so they never meet. Perpendicular: from (0, 0) go to (3, 2) along slope 2/3 and to (−2, 3) along slope −3/2. Each arm has squared length 13 and the far ends are 26 apart squared. Since 13 + 13 = 26, the corner is a right angle.

SAT-3#4.title: Use the two intercepts
SAT-3#4.text: Find two easy points on 3x + 2y = 12. With x = 0, 2y = 12, so the point is (0, 6). With y = 0, 3x = 12, so the point is (4, 0). Going from (0, 6) to (4, 0) the line falls 6 while it runs 4. The slope is −6/4, which simplifies to −3/2, with no rearranging needed.

SAT-3#5.title: Walk back to the y-axis
SAT-3#5.text: A slope of 4 means each step of 1 to the right raises y by 4, so each step to the left lowers y by 4. From (2, 7) take two steps left: (1, 3), then (0, −1). The line crosses the y-axis at −1, which is b. With slope 4 and intercept −1, the equation is y = 4x − 1.

SAT-3#6.title: Trade x against y
SAT-3#6.text: In 3x + 2y = 12 the total must stay 12. Raise x by 2 and the 3x part grows by 6, so the 2y part must shrink by 6, which means y falls by 3. A run of 2 with a rise of −3 is a slope of −3/2. In general, raising x by B adds AB to the total, and y must drop by A to cancel it, which gives −A/B.

SAT-3#7.title: Swap tickets of equal value
SAT-3#7.text: Two adult tickets cost 24 dollars and so do three child tickets. Start with the all-child sale, 60 child tickets and 0 adult. Swapping 3 child tickets for 2 adult tickets keeps the total at 480: (2, 57), (4, 54), and so on. Ten swaps reach (20, 30) and twenty swaps reach (40, 0). Every one of these mixes fits 12a + 8c = 480, so the equation is right.

SAT-3#8.title: Turn the direction a quarter turn
SAT-3#8.text: The given line moves right 3 and up 2. Turn that movement a quarter turn clockwise and it becomes right 2 and down 3, which is the perpendicular direction. Start at (0, −4) and move that way to reach (2, −7). The new line falls 3 for every 2 across, a slope of −3/2, and it starts on the y-axis at −4. So y = −(3/2)x − 4, and x = 2 gives −7 as expected.

SAT-3#9.title: Step back to the y-axis
SAT-3#9.text: From (1, 3) to (3, −1), x goes up 2 and y goes down 4, so each step of 1 to the right lowers y by 2. Step one unit LEFT from (1, 3) instead and y goes up by 2, landing on (0, 5). That point is the y-intercept. With slope −2 and intercept 5, the line is y = −2x + 5.

SAT-4#1.title: A pen and a notebook
SAT-4#1.text: A pen and a notebook cost 8 dollars together, and the notebook costs 2 dollars more than the pen. Replace the notebook by a pen plus 2 dollars. Now the purchase is two pens plus 2 dollars for 8 dollars, so two pens cost 6 and one pen costs 3. Describing one item in terms of the other left a single unknown price, and that is all substitution does.

SAT-4#2.title: Compare two receipts
SAT-4#2.text: One receipt shows 2 burgers and 1 drink for 11 dollars. Another shows 1 burger and 1 drink for 7 dollars. The only difference between the orders is one burger, and the only difference between the totals is 4 dollars, so a burger costs 4. Subtracting one receipt from the other removed the drink. Elimination does the same thing with equations.

SAT-4#3.title: Two runners on a track
SAT-4#3.text: Let each equation be a runner, with slope as speed and intercept as starting position. Runners at different speeds are level with each other at exactly one moment. Runners at the same speed with different starting positions keep the same gap forever and are never level. Runners with the same speed and the same start are side by side the whole time. Those are the one, none and infinitely many cases.

SAT-4#4.title: Line up and subtract
SAT-4#4.text: Rewrite y = 2x + 1 as −2x + y = 1 so both equations have the letters lined up. Subtract it from 3x + y = 16. The y terms cancel, 3x − (−2x) is 5x, and 16 − 1 is 15. So 5x = 15 and x = 3. Put that into 3x + y = 16 to get 9 + y = 16, so y = 7. The solution is (3, 7).

SAT-4#5.title: Substitute the whole 3y
SAT-4#5.text: The first equation gives 3y = 12 − 2x. The second equation contains 3y as a block, so replace it: 4x − (12 − 2x) = 6. Removing the parentheses gives 6x − 12 = 6, so 6x = 18 and x = 3. Then 3y = 12 − 6 = 6, so y = 2. The solution (3, 2) is the same one that adding the equations gives.

SAT-4#6.title: Sum and difference of two numbers
SAT-4#6.text: Read the system in words: two numbers add to 10 and differ by 4. If they were equal, each would be 5. To make them differ by 4 without changing the sum, move one up 2 and the other down 2. That gives 7 and 3. The larger is x because x − y is positive, so the solution is (7, 3).

SAT-4#7.title: Substitute and watch x disappear
SAT-4#7.text: Put y = 3x + 2 into 6x − 2y = 5. The left side becomes 6x − 2(3x + 2) = 6x − 6x − 4, which is −4 for every x. The equation then claims −4 = 5, which is false. Since the x terms cancelled and left a false statement, no value of x can work, so the system has no solution.

SAT-4#8.title: Start from all notebooks
SAT-4#8.text: Suppose all 9 items were notebooks. That would cost 9 × 5 = 45 dollars, which is 15 dollars too much. Each notebook traded for a pen saves 5 − 2 = 3 dollars. Saving 15 dollars takes 15 ÷ 3 = 5 trades, so there are 5 pens and 9 − 5 = 4 notebooks. Check: 10 dollars of pens plus 20 dollars of notebooks is 30.

SAT-4#9.title: Substitute the shared 2y
SAT-4#9.text: The second equation says 2y = 9 − x. The first equation contains the same 2y, so swap it out: 3x + (9 − x) = 17. Combine the x terms to get 2x + 9 = 17, then subtract 9 for 2x = 8 and divide by 2. The result is x = 4, and y was never needed on its own.

SAT-5#1.title: The flip without dividing by negatives
SAT-5#1.text: Solve −2x ≤ 8 using only safe moves. Add 2x to both sides: 0 ≤ 8 + 2x. Subtract 8: −8 ≤ 2x. Divide by positive 2: −4 ≤ x. Read from the x side, that says x ≥ −4. The sign ended up pointing the other way even though it was never flipped. The flip rule is a shortcut for moving the x term across.

SAT-5#2.title: Signs you see every day
SAT-5#2.text: A ride sign says you must be at least 48 inches tall, so height ≥ 48, and a rider of exactly 48 inches gets on. An elevator holds at most 10 people, so people ≤ 10. A ticket is given for driving more than 65, so speed > 65, and exactly 65 is fine. A child fare is for ages less than 12, so age < 12. Ask each time: is the limit itself allowed?

SAT-5#3.title: Check one column of points
SAT-5#3.text: Stay on the vertical line x = 2, where y = x + 1 gives 3. Now test points in that column against y > x + 1. The point (2, 5) gives 5 > 3, true. The point (2, 4) gives 4 > 3, true. The point (2, 3) gives 3 > 3, false, so the line itself is out. The point (2, 0) gives 0 > 3, false. Every column behaves this way, so the whole region above the line is shaded.

SAT-5#4.title: Make a table of values
SAT-5#4.text: Compute 3x − 5 for a few values of x. At x = 4 it is 7, at x = 5 it is 10, at x = 6 it is 13 and at x = 7 it is 16. The value goes up by 3 each time, reaches exactly 10 at x = 5 and is above 10 for every larger x. So the inequality is true for x > 5, and 5 itself is not included.

SAT-5#5.title: Keep the x-term positive
SAT-5#5.text: Add 2x to both sides of −2x + 4 ≤ 12 so the x-term moves to the right: 4 ≤ 12 + 2x. Subtract 12 from both sides to get −8 ≤ 2x. Divide by positive 2, which changes nothing about the sign: −4 ≤ x. Reading from the x side gives x ≥ −4, the same answer with no flip to remember.

SAT-5#6.title: Ask which way the expression moves
SAT-5#6.text: The expression −2x + 4 gets smaller as x gets larger, because each extra 1 in x takes away 2. It equals 12 exactly when x = −4. Moving right from −4 makes the expression fall below 12, which keeps the inequality true. Moving left makes it rise above 12. So the solutions are −4 and everything to its right: x ≥ −4.

SAT-5#7.title: Work with the leftover capacity
SAT-5#7.text: The driver uses 180 of the 1,200 pounds before any box is loaded, which leaves 1,200 − 180 = 1,020 pounds for boxes. Each box takes 60 pounds, and 1,020 ÷ 60 = 17 exactly. So 17 boxes fill the van to the limit, and any whole number of boxes up to 17 fits. That is b ≤ 17.

SAT-5#8.title: Look at the column x = 2
SAT-5#8.text: Fix x = 2 and ask which heights y are allowed. The first inequality needs y above 2. The second needs y below 2 × 2 − 2, which is also 2. No number is both above 2 and below 2, so no point with x = 2 can be a solution at all. That rules out (2, 3) without even using its y-value twice.

SAT-5#9.title: Set the bus money aside first
SAT-5#9.text: Put the 10 dollars for the bus in a separate pocket. That leaves 100 − 10 = 90 dollars for tickets. Now count up by 15: 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90. The sixth ticket uses the last of the money and a seventh cannot be paid for. You can buy any number of tickets up to 6, so t ≤ 6.

SAT-6#1.title: Test the rules with powers of 2
SAT-6#1.text: Use real numbers to see each rule. Multiplying: 2³ × 2⁴ is 8 × 16 = 128, and 128 is 2⁷, so the exponents 3 and 4 were added. Dividing: 2⁵ ÷ 2² is 32 ÷ 4 = 8, which is 2³, so 2 was subtracted from 5. Power of a power: (2²)³ is 4³ = 64, which is 2⁶, so 2 and 3 were multiplied.

SAT-6#2.title: Place value already uses them
SAT-6#2.text: Look at the columns of a decimal number such as 345.6. The hundreds column is 10², the tens column is 10¹, and each column to the right is worth one tenth of the one before. So the ones column must be 10⁰ = 1, and the tenths column must be 10⁻¹ = 1/10. Zero and negative exponents simply continue the same columns past the ones place.

SAT-6#3.title: Growth over half a year
SAT-6#3.text: A colony grows to 4 times its size every year, so after t years it has been multiplied by 4 to the power t. What happens in half a year? Call that factor f. Two half years make a full year, so f × f = 4 and f is 2. That is why 4 to the power 1/2 is the square root of 4. A third of a year would need a factor that gives 4 when cubed, a cube root.

SAT-6#4.title: Write out every factor
SAT-6#4.text: Expand both pieces into single factors. The first is 2 · x · x · x and the second is 5 · x · x · x · x. Put them in one long product and count. There are two plain numbers, 2 and 5, which multiply to 10. There are 3 + 4 = 7 copies of x. So the product is 10 followed by seven factors of x, which is 10x⁷.

SAT-6#5.title: Cancel before combining
SAT-6#5.text: Write (x⁴)³ as three blocks: x⁴ · x⁴ · x⁴. The divisor x⁵ is one block x⁴ times one extra x. Cancel a whole x⁴ block from the top, which leaves x⁴ · x⁴ divided by x. The two blocks make 8 factors of x, and dividing by one x removes one of them. Seven factors remain, so the answer is x⁷.

SAT-6#6.title: Peel off one factor at a time
SAT-6#6.text: You do not have to spot 3x in one go. First take out the number: 6 and 9 share a 3, so 6x² + 9x = 3(2x² + 3x). Now look inside the parentheses: both terms still share an x, so 2x² + 3x = x(2x + 3). Put the two pieces together to get 3x(2x + 3). Nothing more is shared by 2x and 3, so the factoring is finished.

SAT-6#7.title: Cut and rearrange a square
SAT-6#7.text: Draw a square with side x and cut a 7 by 7 square out of one corner. The area left is x² − 49, in an L shape. Slice the L into two rectangles: one is x by (x − 7) and the other is 7 by (x − 7). Lay them end to end along the shared side of length x − 7.
