They form one rectangle that is (x − 7) wide and (x + 7) long, so x² − 49 = (x − 7)(x + 7).

SAT-6#8.title: Draw the square as four pieces
SAT-6#8.text: A square with side x + 3 has area (x + 3)². Split each side into a piece of length x and a piece of length 3. The square breaks into four parts: an x by x square, two strips that are each x by 3, and a 3 by 3 corner. Their areas are x², 3x, 3x and 9. Adding them gives x² + 6x + 9, and the two strips are the 6x that the choice x² + 9 leaves out.

SAT-6#9.title: Get it from a division
SAT-6#9.text: Work out 2² ÷ 2⁵ in two ways. As plain numbers it is 4 ÷ 32, which simplifies to 1/8. With the rule for dividing powers, you subtract the exponents: 2 − 5 = −3, so the same division is 2⁻³. Both must be the same number, so 2⁻³ = 1/8. The exponent is negative because more twos sit in the bottom than in the top.

SAT-7#1.title: What goes wrong without the zero
SAT-7#1.text: Try x(x − 1) = 6 and split it the wrong way: say x = 6 or x − 1 = 6. Test x = 6: 6 × 5 is 30, not 6. The split fails because the factors of 6 could be anything. Now move the 6 over: x² − x − 6 = 0, which factors as (x − 3)(x + 2) = 0. Here the split is safe and gives x = 3 or x = −2. Check: 3 × 2 = 6 and (−2)(−3) = 6.

SAT-7#2.title: List the factor pairs
SAT-7#2.text: For x² − 5x + 6, write every pair of whole numbers that multiplies to 6 and note each sum. The pair 1 and 6 adds to 7. The pair 2 and 3 adds to 5. The pair −1 and −6 adds to −7. The pair −2 and −3 adds to −5. Only the last pair has the sum you need, so the factors are (x − 2)(x − 3). A short list like this always finds the pair if one exists.

SAT-7#3.title: A center and a distance
SAT-7#3.text: Split the formula into two parts: −b/2a, then plus or minus √(b² − 4ac)/2a. The first part is the middle of the parabola, its line of symmetry. The second part is how far each solution sits from that middle. For x² − 5x + 6 the middle is 5/2 = 2.5 and the distance is √1/2 = 0.5. Step 0.5 left and right of 2.5 to reach 2 and 3.

SAT-7#4.title: Three tiny equations
SAT-7#4.text: Compare x² = 4, x² = 0 and x² = −4. The first has two solutions, 2 and −2. The second has only one, 0. The third has none, because no real number squared is negative. Written as x² − 4 = 0, x² = 0 and x² + 4 = 0, their discriminants are 16, 0 and −16. Positive, zero and negative match the counts two, one and none.

SAT-7#5.title: Test small whole numbers
SAT-7#5.text: If a whole number solves x² − 5x + 6 = 0, it must divide the constant 6, so try 1, 2, 3 and 6. At x = 1 the left side is 1 − 5 + 6 = 2. At x = 2 it is 4 − 10 + 6 = 0, a solution. At x = 3 it is 9 − 15 + 6 = 0, another solution. A quadratic has at most two solutions, so the search is over: x = 2 and x = 3.

SAT-7#6.title: Complete the square
SAT-7#6.text: Move the constant: x² + 2x = 15. Half of 2 is 1 and 1 squared is 1, so add 1 to both sides: x² + 2x + 1 = 16. The left side is (x + 1)². A number whose square is 16 is 4 or −4, so x + 1 = 4 or x + 1 = −4. Subtract 1 from each to get x = 3 or x = −5, the same pair that factoring gives.

SAT-7#7.title: Check with sum and product
SAT-7#7.text: For x² + bx + c = 0 the two solutions must add to −b and multiply to c. Here they should add to 4 and multiply to −1. Add 2 + √5 and 2 − √5: the roots cancel and the sum is 4. Multiply them: this is a difference of squares, 2² − (√5)² = 4 − 5 = −1. Both tests pass, so x = 2 ± √5 is confirmed without redoing the formula.

SAT-7#8.title: Trap each solution between integers
SAT-7#8.text: Evaluate x² − 4x − 1 at whole numbers and watch the sign. At x = 4 it is −1 and at x = 5 it is 4, so one solution lies between 4 and 5. At x = −1 it is 4 and at x = 0 it is −1, so the other lies between −1 and 0. Since √5 is about 2.24, the answers 2 + √5 ≈ 4.24 and 2 − √5 ≈ −0.24 sit exactly in those gaps.

SAT-7#9.title: Find the lowest point instead
SAT-7#9.text: The parabola y = 2x² + 3x + 5 opens upward because 2 is positive, so its lowest point is the vertex. That is at x = −3/4. The height there is 2(9/16) − 9/4 + 5 = 1.125 − 2.25 + 5 = 3.875. The lowest the expression ever gets is 3.875, which is above zero. It can never equal 0, so there are 0 real solutions.

SAT-7#10.title: Match a perfect square
SAT-7#10.text: One solution means the quadratic is a perfect square, (x + k)². Expand that pattern: x² + 2kx + k². Compare with x² + 6x + c. The middle terms must agree, so 2k = 6 and k = 3. The last terms must agree too, so c = k² = 9. The equation is then (x + 3)² = 0, whose only solution is x = −3.

SAT-7#11.title: List the factor pairs of 40
SAT-7#11.text: If the sides are whole numbers, they are a pair that multiplies to 40: 1 and 40, 2 and 20, 4 and 10, or 5 and 8. The length must be exactly 3 more than the width. The differences are 39, 18, 6 and 3, so only 5 and 8 fit. The width is the smaller one, w = 5 cm, and the length is 8 cm.

SAT-8#1.title: One parabola in three outfits
SAT-8#1.text: Take y = x² − 4x + 3. In this standard form, x = 0 gives 3, the y-intercept. Complete the square and it becomes y = (x − 2)² − 1, which shows the lowest point (2, −1). Factor it and it becomes y = (x − 1)(x − 3), which shows the crossings at 1 and 3. Plug x = 5 into all three and each gives 8. The curve is the same, and only the feature on display changes.

SAT-8#2.title: Flip the table of x²
SAT-8#2.text: List y = x² for x from −2 to 2: 4, 1, 0, 1, 4. The values dip to 0 in the middle and rise on both sides, a cup with a lowest point. Now multiply every value by −1 to get y = −x²: −4, −1, 0, −1, −4. The same list is turned upside down, so the middle is now the highest point. A negative a flips the cup into a cap.

SAT-8#3.title: The table is a mirror
SAT-8#3.text: Make a table for y = x² − 2x − 8 from x = −2 to x = 4. The values are 0, −5, −8, −9, −8, −5, 0. Read the list from both ends: 0 and 0, −5 and −5, −8 and −8, with −9 alone in the middle at x = 1. Equal heights pair up around x = 1, so the turning point is there, exactly halfway between the zeros −2 and 4.

SAT-8#4.title: Expand and use −b/2a
SAT-8#4.text: Multiply out (x − 3)² + 5 to get x² − 6x + 9 + 5 = x² − 6x + 14. Now a = 1 and b = −6, so the vertex is at x = −b/2a = 6/2 = 3. Put x = 3 into the expanded form: 9 − 18 + 14 = 5. The vertex is (3, 5), the same point that vertex form shows directly, which confirms the sign reading.

SAT-8#5.title: Expand, then complete the square
SAT-8#5.text: Multiply out: (x + 2)(x − 6) = x² − 4x − 12. Half of −4 is −2, and its square is 4, so write x² − 4x + 4 − 4 − 12 = (x − 2)² − 16. The vertex is (2, −16). For the zeros, set (x − 2)² = 16, so x − 2 is 4 or −4, giving x = 6 or x = −2. Both features match the factored form.

SAT-8#6.title: Find two points at equal height
SAT-8#6.text: The curve y = x² − 8x + 10 has height 10 whenever x² − 8x = 0, which is x(x − 8) = 0. So (0, 10) and (8, 10) are at the same height. A parabola is symmetric, so the vertex is halfway between them at x = 4. Then y = 16 − 32 + 10 = −6. The vertex is (4, −6), found without the formula.

SAT-8#7.title: Expand and use −b/2a
SAT-8#7.text: Multiply out (x − 1)(x − 7): x² − 7x − x + 7 = x² − 8x + 7. With a = 1 and b = −8, the vertex is at x = −b/2a = 8/2 = 4. Substitute into the expanded form: 16 − 32 + 7 = −9. The vertex is (4, −9). This takes longer than averaging the zeros, but it works even when a quadratic is not factored.

SAT-8#8.title: Tabulate each second
SAT-8#8.text: Compute the height at whole seconds. At t = 0 it is 0. At t = 1 it is −16 + 64 = 48. At t = 2 it is −64 + 128 = 64. At t = 3 it is −144 + 192 = 48. At t = 4 it is −256 + 256 = 0. The heights 0, 48, 64, 48, 0 rise and fall evenly around t = 2, so the highest point is 64 feet.

SAT-8#9.title: Locate the vertex from the zeros
SAT-8#9.text: Factor first: x² + 6x + 5 = (x + 1)(x + 5), so the zeros are −1 and −5. The vertex is halfway between, at x = −3. Its height is (−3 + 1)(−3 + 5) = (−2)(2) = −4. The coefficient of x² is 1, so vertex form is 1 times (x − h)² plus k with h = −3 and k = −4. That gives y = (x + 3)² − 4.

SAT-9#1.title: Slide a ruler up the page
SAT-9#1.text: Draw y = x² and lay a ruler flat along y = −1. It sits below the curve and never touches it: no solutions. Slide it up to y = 0 and it just touches the bottom of the curve at one point. Slide it up to y = 4 and it cuts the curve at x = −2 and x = 2. Tilting the ruler changes nothing about the count: a straight edge meets the curve 0, 1 or 2 times.

SAT-9#2.title: Same idea as whole numbers
SAT-9#2.text: With whole numbers, 3 is a factor of 12 because the division leaves nothing over. Polynomials work the same way, and plugging in is the quick test for leftovers. Take p(x) = x³ − x. At x = 1 it gives 1 − 1 = 0, so (x − 1) should be a factor. It is: x³ − x = x(x − 1)(x + 1). Going the other way, any product containing (x − 1) is forced to be 0 at x = 1.

SAT-9#3.title: Like 17 divided by 5
SAT-9#3.text: Dividing 17 by 5 gives 3 with remainder 2, which means 17 = 5 × 3 + 2. Polynomials split the same way. Divide x² + 1 by x − 1: the result is x + 1 with 2 left over, because (x − 1)(x + 1) + 2 = x² − 1 + 2 = x² + 1. Now plug 1 into x² + 1 and you get 2, the same leftover. At x = 1 the divisor is zero, so only the remainder is left.

SAT-9#4.title: Compare the two in a table
SAT-9#4.text: List x² and x + 6 side by side for whole numbers. At x = −3 they are 9 and 3. At x = −2 they are 4 and 4, a match. At x = 0 they are 0 and 6. At x = 2 they are 4 and 8. At x = 3 they are 9 and 9, another match. A line meets a parabola at most twice, so the meeting points are (−2, 4) and (3, 9).

SAT-9#5.title: Divide it out piece by piece
SAT-9#5.text: Build x³ − 4x² + x + 6 from multiples of (x − 2). Use x²(x − 2) = x³ − 2x², which leaves −2x² + x + 6. Use −2x(x − 2) = −2x² + 4x, which leaves −3x + 6. Use −3(x − 2) = −3x + 6, which leaves nothing. The polynomial is (x − 2)(x² − 2x − 3) with no remainder, so the answer is yes, (x − 2) is a factor.

SAT-9#6.title: Do the division directly
SAT-9#6.text: Take multiples of (x − 2) away from x² + 3x − 5. First x(x − 2) = x² − 2x, and subtracting it leaves 5x − 5. Next 5(x − 2) = 5x − 10, and subtracting it leaves 5. Nothing with an x remains, so the division stops. The quotient is x + 5 and the remainder is 5, the same number that plugging in 2 gives.

SAT-9#7.title: Flip both fractions
SAT-9#7.text: If two fractions are equal, their reciprocals are equal too. Turning both sides of 6/x = 3/(x − 2) upside down gives x/6 = (x − 2)/3. Multiply both sides by 6 to clear the denominators: x = 2(x − 2), so x = 2x − 4. Subtract x and add 4 to get x = 4. Neither original denominator is zero there, so the solution stands.

SAT-9#8.title: Compare the numerators
SAT-9#8.text: The top of the left fraction, 6, is twice the top of the right fraction, 3. For the two fractions to be equal, the bottom on the left must also be twice the bottom on the right. So x must be twice x − 2. Ask which number is double the number 2 less than itself: 4 is double 2. So x = 4, and 6/4 and 3/2 are both 1.5.

SAT-9#9.title: Multiply out and test
SAT-9#9.text: Take a = 1 and expand. First (x + 1)(x − 2) = x² − x − 2. Multiply that by (x − 5) to get x³ − 6x² + 3x + 10. Now test the three zeros in this expanded form. At −1: −1 − 6 − 3 + 10 = 0. At 2: 8 − 24 + 6 + 10 = 0. At 5: 125 − 150 + 15 + 10 = 0. All three work, so the product of factors is right.

SAT-10#1.title: Folding a sheet of paper
SAT-10#1.text: Fold one sheet of paper in half and it is 2 layers thick. Fold again for 4, then 8, then 16. Each fold multiplies the layers by 2, so after x folds there are 2 to the power x layers. Start with a stack of 3 sheets instead and the counts are 3, 6, 12, 24, which is 3 times 2 to the power x. The 3 is the start and the 2 is the factor per fold.

SAT-10#2.title: Think of a price tag
SAT-10#2.text: A 50 dollar jacket is 20% off. You could find the discount, 10 dollars, and subtract it. Or notice that you pay the other 80% of the price: 50 × 0.80 = 40 dollars in one step. A 6% tax works the other way. You pay the full price and 6% more, which is 106% of it, so multiply by 1.06. The factor is the percent of the old amount that you end up with.

SAT-10#3.title: Walking halfway to a wall
SAT-10#3.text: Stand 8 meters from a wall and walk half the remaining distance each time. After one walk you are 4 meters away, then 2, then 1, then half a meter. Each walk leaves the other half still in front of you, so there is always some distance left. You get as close as you like, yet no single step finishes the trip. Exponential decay approaches zero in the same way.

SAT-10#4.title: Rule out the straight-line model
SAT-10#4.text: Three percent of 2,000 is 60, so it is tempting to write 2000 + 60t. Test year 2. In year 1 the town grows to 2,060. In year 2 it grows by 3% of 2,060, which is 61.8, reaching 2,121.8. The straight-line guess gives only 2,120. The yearly gain keeps getting bigger because it is 3% of a bigger town, and only repeated multiplying by 1.03 captures that: P(t) = 2000(1.03)^t.

SAT-10#5.title: Subtract the loss each year
SAT-10#5.text: Follow the dollars year by year. In the first year the phone loses 20% of 900, which is 180, so it is worth 900 − 180 = 720. In the second year it loses 20% of 720, not of 900. That is 144, so it is worth 720 − 144 = 576 dollars. The second loss is smaller than the first because it is taken from a smaller value.

SAT-10#6.title: Run the clock backwards
SAT-10#6.text: Check the answer by undoing it. If there are 800 bacteria at hour 12, there were half as many 4 hours earlier: 400 at hour 8. Halve again for 200 at hour 4, and once more for 100 at hour 0. Three halvings cover 3 × 4 = 12 hours and land exactly on the starting amount, so 800 is correct.

SAT-10#7.title: Take a bigger jump
SAT-10#7.text: Two doublings in a row multiply by 4, so the bacteria quadruple every 8 hours. From hour 0 to hour 8 the count goes from 100 to 400. Only 4 hours are left to reach hour 12, which is one more doubling: 400 becomes 800. Grouping the doublings differently gives the same 800, because the total factor over 12 hours is 8 either way.

SAT-10#8.title: Read 0.9 as 90 per 100
SAT-10#8.text: The factor 0.9 is 90/100. So out of every 100 units of value, 90 are kept and 10 are gone at each step. Ten out of a hundred is a 10% decrease. Try a later step to see that the percent holds: from 45 the next value is 40.5, a drop of 4.5, and 4.5 is 10% of 45. The dollar drop changes but the percent does not.

SAT-10#9.title: Each jump equals the term before
SAT-10#9.text: Look at what is added each time: 3 is added to 3, then 6 is added to 6, then 12 is added to 12. Every term grows by its own size, and adding a number to itself is doubling. A linear pattern would add the same 3 each time and give 3, 6, 9, 12. So this one is exponential with factor 2, and the next term would be 24 + 24 = 48.

SAT-11#1.title: Scaling a recipe
SAT-11#1.text: A recipe uses 2 cups of flour for 3 eggs. To use 12 eggs you make 4 batches, so you need 4 × 2 = 8 cups. The proportion 2/3 = x/12 says the same thing: the bottom was multiplied by 4, so the top must be too. Cross-multiplying is a way to find x when the scale factor is not easy to see: 3x = 24, so x = 8.

SAT-11#2.title: Trading dollars for quarters
SAT-11#2.text: Three dollars can be traded for quarters at 4 quarters per dollar, which gives 12 quarters. You hold the same amount of money, but the count went from 3 to 12 because a quarter is a smaller unit. Unit conversion is that trade. Changing 3 feet to inches gives 36 for the same reason: inches are smaller, so more of them are needed. If the number moves the wrong way, the fraction is upside down.

SAT-11#3.title: Turn the ratio into fractions
SAT-11#3.text: In every group of 5 marbles, 2 are red and 3 are blue. So red is 2/5 of any bag mixed this way and blue is 3/5. For 40 marbles, 2/5 of 40 is 16 red and 3/5 of 40 is 24 blue. The ratio compares the parts to each other. The fractions 2/5 and 3/5 compare each part to the whole. Both describe the same bag.

SAT-11#4.title: Set up a proportion
SAT-11#4.text: Write miles over gallons on both sides: 210/6 = m/10. Cross-multiply to clear the fractions: 6 × m = 210 × 10, so 6m = 2,100. Divide by 6 to get m = 350 miles. The unit rate never has to be computed, although it is hidden inside the proportion, since both fractions equal 35 miles per gallon.

SAT-11#5.title: Break 10 gallons into pieces
SAT-11#5.text: Split 10 gallons into 6 + 4. Six gallons take the car 210 miles, which is given. Two gallons are a third of 6, so they take it a third of 210, which is 70 miles. Four gallons are twice that, 140 miles. Add the two pieces: 210 + 140 = 350 miles for 10 gallons.

SAT-11#6.title: Change the fraction to a decimal
SAT-11#6.text: The fraction 3/8 is 0.375, so x is 0.375 of 56. Work it in pieces. One quarter of 56 is 14, which covers 0.25. One eighth of 56 is 7, which covers the other 0.125. Add them: 14 + 7 = 21. So x = 21, and 21 ÷ 56 on a calculator gives 0.375 again.

SAT-11#7.title: Shrink the hour step by step
SAT-11#7.text: In one hour the car covers 90 km, which is 90,000 meters. An hour has 60 minutes, so in one minute it covers 90,000 ÷ 60 = 1,500 meters. A minute has 60 seconds, so in one second it covers 1,500 ÷ 60 = 25 meters. The speed is 25 meters per second, found by asking how far it goes in smaller and smaller pieces of time.

SAT-11#8.title: Count up by groups of nine
SAT-11#8.text: Seat the class in groups of 4 boys and 5 girls, 9 students per group. One group has 5 girls out of 9 students. Two groups have 10 girls out of 18. Three groups have 15 out of 27. Four groups have 20 out of 36, and 36 is the class size. So there are 20 girls, and the 16 boys make up the rest.

SAT-11#9.title: Use 4 inches for 100 miles
SAT-11#9.text: If 1 inch stands for 25 miles, then 4 inches stand for 100 miles, a rounder scale to think with. The towns are 3.2 inches apart, and 3.2 is 0.8 of 4, because 3.2 ÷ 4 = 0.8. So the real distance is 0.8 of 100 miles, which is 80 miles.

SAT-12#1.title: Cut the whole into 100 slices
SAT-12#1.text: Imagine 240 cut into 100 equal slices. Each slice is 240 ÷ 100 = 2.4, and that is what 1% of 240 looks like. Thirty-five percent is 35 of those slices, so it is 35 × 2.4 = 84. Any percent question can be done this way: find the size of one slice, then take as many slices as the percent says.

SAT-12#2.title: A bar of twenty blocks
SAT-12#2.text: Draw the original amount as a bar of 20 equal blocks, so each block is 5%. A 15% increase adds 3 more blocks. The new bar has 23 blocks out of the old 20, and 23/20 = 1.15. A 15% decrease removes 3 blocks and leaves 17 out of 20, which is 0.85. If the bar stands for 200 dollars, each block is 10 dollars, so the results are 230 and 170.

SAT-12#3.title: A kitten and a large dog
SAT-12#3.text: A 1 kg kitten and a 40 kg dog each gain 1 kg. The change is the same, but it means very different things. The kitten doubled, a 100% increase, since 1 ÷ 1 = 1. The dog barely changed, a 2.5% increase, since 1 ÷ 40 = 0.025. Percent change tells you how big the change is compared with what was there before, so the starting amount goes on the bottom.

SAT-12#4.title: The loss follows a pattern
SAT-12#4.text: Start at 100 and go up then down by the same percent. With 10% you get 110, then 99. With 20% you get 120, then 96. With 50% you get 150, then 75. You always finish below 100, because the drop is taken from the larger middle amount. Reversing the order gives the same result: down 20% is 80, then up 20% is 96. Multiplying 0.8 × 1.2 or 1.2 × 0.8 makes no difference.

SAT-12#5.title: Use the fraction 7/20
SAT-12#5.text: Write 35% as a fraction: 35/100 simplifies to 7/20. To take 7/20 of 240, first find one twentieth. 240 ÷ 20 is 12. Then take seven of them: 7 × 12 = 84. Working with a simple fraction avoids decimals, and it is quick whenever the whole divides evenly by the denominator.

SAT-12#6.title: Count the one percents
SAT-12#6.text: One percent of the starting price is 50 ÷ 100 = 0.50 dollars. The price rose by 12 dollars. How many chunks of 0.50 fit into 12? Since two chunks make a dollar, 12 dollars hold 24 chunks. Each chunk is 1% of the original, so the rise is 24%.

SAT-12#7.title: Try 100 and scale up
SAT-12#7.text: Guess an easy original price of 100 dollars. After 25% off it would cost 75 dollars. The real sale price is 90, which is 90 ÷ 75 = 1.2 times the guess result. Discounts scale with the price, so the real original is 1.2 times the guess as well: 1.2 × 100 = 120 dollars. Check: a quarter of 120 is 30, and 120 − 30 = 90.

SAT-12#8.title: Draw the price in quarters
SAT-12#8.text: Draw the original price as a bar cut into 4 equal parts. Taking 25% off removes one part and leaves three, and those three parts together are the 90 dollars paid. So one part is 90 ÷ 3 = 30 dollars. The full bar has four parts, 4 × 30 = 120 dollars. The picture gives the answer directly, so no choice needs testing.

SAT-12#9.title: Use fractions instead of decimals
SAT-12#9.text: Up 20% means multiplying by 6/5, since 120% is 120/100. Down 20% means multiplying by 4/5. Together they multiply the starting value by 6/5 × 4/5 = 24/25. The stock ends with 24 of every 25 dollars it started with, so 1 dollar in every 25 is lost. One twenty-fifth is 4%, so the result is a 4% loss overall.

SAT-12#10.title: Build it from ten percent
SAT-12#10.text: Ten percent of 72 is 7.2. Doubling that, 20% is 14.4, which is not yet 18. The gap is 18 − 14.4 = 3.6, and 3.6 is half of 7.2, so it is another 5%. Altogether 18 is 20% + 5% = 25% of 72. Check: a quarter of 72 is 18.

SAT-13#1.title: A seesaw and a lineup
SAT-13#1.text: Put weights at 1, 2 and 9 on a number line. The mean, 4, is where the line balances: the distances on the left, 3 and 2, add to 5, and the distance on the right is 5. For the median, think of people lined up by height. The person standing in the middle of the line is the median, however tall the people at the ends are. Here that is 2.

SAT-13#2.title: A billionaire walks in
SAT-13#2.text: Five people in a cafe each earn about 50 thousand dollars a year, so the mean and the median are both about 50 thousand. A billionaire walks in. The mean income in the room is now over 100 million dollars, although nobody there earns anything like that. Line the six up by income and the middle is still about 50 thousand. One person changed the mean completely and left the median almost untouched.

SAT-13#3.title: Two small data sets
SAT-13#3.text: Take 2, 3, 3, 4, 18. Most values are small and one sits far to the right. The median is 3, but the mean is 30 ÷ 5 = 6, pulled toward the 18. Now take the mirror image, 2, 16, 17, 17, 18, with one value far to the left. The median is 17 and the mean is 70 ÷ 5 = 14, pulled toward the 2. The mean moves toward the tail each time.

SAT-13#4.title: Two archers, same aim
SAT-13#4.text: Two archers both centre their arrows on the bullseye, so on average each is on target. The first archer's arrows land in a tight cluster. The second archer's arrows are scattered all over the target. The averages match, but the scatter does not. Standard deviation is a number for that scatter: small for the tight cluster, large for the scattered one.

SAT-13#5.title: Check the balance, cross off pairs
SAT-13#5.text: Test the mean of 10 by measuring each value from it: 3 is 7 below, 7 is 3 below, 8 is 2 below, 10 is level and 22 is 12 above. Below totals 7 + 3 + 2 = 12 and above totals 12, so 10 is the balance point. For the median, cross off the smallest and largest together: 3 with 22, then 7 with 10. The value left is 8.

SAT-13#6.title: Share out the change
SAT-13#6.text: Only one value changed, and it fell by 10. That takes 10 off the total, and the total is shared among 5 values, so the mean falls by 10 ÷ 5 = 2. It goes from 10 to 8 without adding the list again. For the median, ask whether the order changed. The new value 12 is still larger than 10, so it is still last and the middle value is still 8.

SAT-13#7.title: Guess, then adjust
SAT-13#7.text: Suppose the fifth score were 88. The total would be 340 + 88 = 428 and the average 428 ÷ 5 = 85.6, which is 2.4 short of 88. Each extra point on the fifth test raises the average by one fifth of a point, because it is shared among 5 tests. Closing a gap of 2.4 takes 2.4 × 5 = 12 extra points. The fifth score must be 88 + 12 = 100.

SAT-13#8.title: Lift everyone by three
SAT-13#8.text: If the fifth score were 85, the average would stay at 85. To raise the average of five tests from 85 to 88, every test needs 3 more points, 5 × 3 = 15 points in all. The first four scores are fixed, so the fifth test has to supply all 15 on its own. That makes the fifth score 85 + 15 = 100.

SAT-13#9.title: Cross off from both ends
SAT-13#9.text: You can find the middle without rewriting the list. Strike out the smallest and the largest together: 1 and 12. From what is left, 4, 9, 7, 6, strike out the smallest and largest again: 4 and 9. Two values remain, 7 and 6, and they are the middle pair. Their average is 13 ÷ 2 = 6.5, which is the median.

SAT-13#10.title: Compare the reach on each side
SAT-13#10.text: Measure how far values can sit from the median of 45. On the high side the plot reaches 150, which is 105 above the median. On the low side an income cannot go below 0, so no value is more than 45 below. The half above the median can be far more extreme than the half below, so the high values outweigh the low ones and the mean lands above 45.

SAT-14#1.title: Study hours and test scores
SAT-14#1.text: Suppose a class's line of best fit is score = 5 × hours + 60. For 3 hours of study it predicts 75. One student who studied 3 hours might score 70 and another 82, and the line is not wrong about either, because it describes the middle of the group. The slope 5 says that students who study one more hour score about 5 points higher on average.

SAT-14#2.title: What happens in the long run
SAT-14#2.text: Roll a fair die 600 times. Each of the six faces comes up about 100 times. The even faces 2, 4 and 6 together come up about 300 times out of 600, which is one half, matching 3 favorable faces out of 6. Now suppose you are told the roll was above 3. Only 4, 5 and 6 are possible, so the total is 3, and the chance of an even number becomes 2 out of 3.

SAT-14#3.title: Sort everyone in the gym
SAT-14#3.text: Picture all 200 students standing in a gym, juniors on the left side and seniors on the right. Within each side, students who play a sport stand at the front. Every student has exactly one spot. A question about all students looks at the whole gym. A question that says given the student is a junior sends you to the left side only, where 60 students stand, and the seniors no longer count.

SAT-14#4.title: Two studies that overreach
SAT-14#4.text: A survey taken at a basketball game finds that most students love school sports. The people asked chose to be at the game, so the result cannot speak for the whole school. Another study finds that students who eat breakfast get better grades. Those students chose breakfast themselves and may also sleep more or have calmer mornings. Only if a coin flip decides who gets breakfast can the grades be credited to breakfast.

SAT-14#5.title: Climb the line in a table
SAT-14#5.text: Build the predictions in steps of 2. At x = 0 the line gives 10. Each step of 2 in x adds 2 × 2.5 = 5 to the prediction. So x = 2 gives 15, x = 4 gives 20, x = 6 gives 25 and x = 8 gives 30. The table reaches the same predicted value of 30, and it shows the steady climb that the slope describes.

SAT-14#6.title: Subtract from the whole
SAT-14#6.text: Among the 60 juniors, 60 − 24 = 36 do not play a sport. The chance that a junior does not play is 36/60, which is 0.6. A junior either plays or does not, so the two chances add to 1. That makes the chance of playing 1 − 0.6 = 0.4, the same answer reached from the other side.

SAT-14#7.title: Think in tenths of the juniors
SAT-14#7.text: Ten percent of the 60 juniors is 6 students. The 24 juniors who play a sport are 4 groups of 6, so they are 4 tenths of the juniors. Four tenths is 0.4, or 40%. Put another way, 24 out of 60 is the same share as 4 out of 10, and no senior ever enters the count.

SAT-14#8.title: Imagine many draws
SAT-14#8.text: Draw a marble, note its colour, put it back and repeat 800 times. Each of the 8 marbles comes out about 100 times. The 5 red marbles together come out about 500 times, so red shows up in about 500 of 800 draws, which is 5/8. The other 300 or so draws are blue, 3/8 of them, and 5/8 + 3/8 = 1 as it should.

SAT-14#9.title: Tasting a pot of soup
SAT-14#9.text: A cook stirs a pot well and tastes one spoonful. The stirring is the random part, and it lets one spoonful stand for the whole pot. It says nothing about a different pot on the next burner. Here the pot is the 9th grade. The sample was stirred fairly, so it speaks for 9th graders, but the 10th, 11th and 12th grade pots were never tasted. The justified conclusion is that most 9th graders like pizza.

SAT-14#10.title: Suppose the truth were 49%
SAT-14#10.text: Imagine that true support is 49%, which is not a majority. A poll with a 4 point margin of error would then be expected to report anything from about 45% to 53%. A result of 52% fits comfortably inside that range. So the poll result is what you might see even when support is below half, and it cannot prove a majority. No, a majority is not certain.

SAT-15#1.title: Open a pair of scissors
SAT-15#1.text: Scissors are two straight lines crossing at the screw. Open the blades by 30° and the handles open by 30° as well, because each blade and its handle are one straight piece. The blade gap and the handle gap are the opposite angles, and they always match. The two side gaps match each other too, and each is what is left of a straight line: 180° − 30° = 150°.

SAT-15#2.title: Fill in all eight angles
SAT-15#2.text: Suppose a line crosses the top parallel line and makes a 70° angle. Its neighbor on the straight line is 110°, and the opposite angles copy these, so that crossing has 70°, 110°, 70°, 110°. The bottom line runs in the same direction, so its crossing looks identical: 70°, 110°, 70°, 110°. Eight angles in total, but only two different numbers, and 70 + 110 = 180.

SAT-15#3.title: Draw a parallel through the corner
SAT-15#3.text: At the corner with the exterior angle, draw a line parallel to the opposite side of the triangle. It cuts the exterior angle into two pieces. One piece is an alternate angle to one far corner, so it has the same size. The other piece is a corresponding angle to the other far corner, so it matches that one. The exterior angle is the two far angles placed side by side, which is why 55° and 75° make 130°.

SAT-15#4.title: Measure both from a right angle
SAT-15#4.text: A straight line is two right angles, 90° + 90°. The 115° angle is 25° more than a right angle, so it leans 25° past the upright. Its partner on the line must then be 25° less than a right angle, which is 90° − 25° = 65°. One angle's extra is exactly the other angle's shortfall.

SAT-15#5.title: Round, subtract, then repair
SAT-15#5.text: Round the known angles to easy numbers: 48° is about 50° and 67° is about 70°. Those use up 120° of the 180°, which would leave 60°. But the rounding added 2° and 3° that are not really there, 5° too much in total. Give those 5° back to the third angle: 60° + 5° = 65°.

SAT-15#6.title: Use all three exterior angles
SAT-15#6.text: The exterior angles of any triangle, one at each corner, add up to 360°. One of them is 130°. The corner with the 55° angle has an exterior angle of 180° − 55° = 125°. That leaves 360° − 130° − 125° = 105° for the exterior angle at the unknown corner. The interior angle there is 180° − 105° = 75°, the same answer as the theorem gives.

SAT-15#7.title: Watch the 180s cancel
SAT-15#7.text: Write both rules in one line before doing any arithmetic. The inside neighbor is 180 − 130, so the unknown is x = 180 − 55 − (180 − 130). Remove the parentheses: x = 180 − 55 − 180 + 130. The two 180s cancel and leave x = 130 − 55 = 75. The long route collapses into the theorem by itself, and the answer is still 75°.

SAT-15#8.title: Add up the full turn
SAT-15#8.text: The four angles around one crossing point make a full turn of 360°. The 72° angle and the angle opposite it are equal, so together they use 144°. The other two angles share the remaining 360° − 144° = 216°, and they are opposite each other, so each is 216° ÷ 2 = 108°. The second crossing has the same four angles, so every partner is 72° or 108°.

SAT-15#9.title: Cut it down the middle
SAT-15#9.text: Draw a line from the 40° vertex straight down to the middle of the base. By symmetry it splits the triangle into two identical right triangles. Each has a right angle at the base and half the vertex angle, 20°, at the top. The third angle of each right triangle is 180° − 90° − 20° = 70°, and that is the base angle of the original triangle.

SAT-15#10.title: Notice the largest part is half
SAT-15#10.text: In the ratio 1 : 2 : 3 the largest part equals the other two added together, because 3 = 1 + 2. So the largest angle is half of the whole 180°, which is 90°. The other two angles share the remaining 90° in the ratio 1 : 2, so one is a third of 90° and the other is two thirds: 30° and 60°. The angles are 30°, 60° and 90°.

SAT-16#1.title: Count the squares
SAT-16#1.text: Draw a 4 by 3 rectangle on grid paper and count: 12 squares, which is 4 × 3. Cut it corner to corner and each right triangle holds half, 6 squares, which is half of 4 × 3. For a circle of radius 1, draw the 2 by 2 square around it, with area 4, and the tilted square inside it, with area 2. The circle's area is in between, and it turns out to be about 3.14, which is π × 1².

SAT-16#2.title: A stack of coins
SAT-16#2.text: A stack of 20 identical coins takes up 20 times the space of one coin, so its volume is the area of a coin face times the height of the stack. Push the stack so it leans and the volume is unchanged. With numbers: a cylinder with base area 12 and height 5 holds 12 × 5 = 60 cubic units. A cone with that same base and height holds one third as much, 20 cubic units.

SAT-16#3.title: Double a rectangle and a box
SAT-16#3.text: A 2 by 3 rectangle has area 6. Double every side to 4 by 6 and the area is 24, which is 4 times as much, not 2 times. A 1 by 2 by 3 box has volume 6. Double every edge to 2 by 4 by 6 and the volume is 48, which is 8 times as much. Doubling gave factors of 2, 4 and 8 for length, area and volume: 2, 2², 2³.

SAT-16#4.title: Compare with the box around it
SAT-16#4.text: The cylinder fits snugly inside a box that is 6 wide, 6 deep and 10 tall, since the diameter is 6. The box has volume 6 × 6 × 10 = 360. A circle fills π/4 of the square drawn around it, which is about 78.5%. So the cylinder holds about 0.785 × 360 ≈ 283. That agrees with 90π ≈ 282.7, so the answer 90π is the right size.

SAT-16#5.title: Add up the rows
SAT-16#5.text: Slice the 10 by 8 rectangle into 8 rows, each 10 units long and 1 unit tall. The hole is 3 units tall, so it cuts into 3 of the rows, and each of those keeps 10 − 4 = 6 square units. The other 5 rows are untouched and keep 10 each. The area left is 3 × 6 + 5 × 10 = 18 + 50 = 68.

SAT-16#6.title: Try an actual triangle
SAT-16#6.text: Pick a triangle with area 5, for example base 5 and height 2, since half of 5 × 2 is 5. Make every length 3 times as long: the base becomes 15 and the height becomes 6. The new area is half of 15 × 6, which is half of 90, or 45. The base and the height each tripled, so the area was multiplied by 3 twice.

SAT-16#7.title: Put 3 into the area formula
SAT-16#7.text: The area of the small triangle is half of base times height, and that equals 5. In the large triangle the base is 3 times as long and the height is 3 times as long. Its area is half of (3 × base) × (3 × height). Pull the two 3s to the front: 9 times half of base times height, which is 9 × 5 = 45.

SAT-16#8.title: Compare sides inside one triangle
SAT-16#8.text: Stay inside the small triangle first. Its side of 10 is 2.5 times its side of 4, because 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5. Similar triangles have the same shape, so the big triangle has the same relationship between its matching sides. The side matching 4 is 6, so the side matching 10 is 2.5 × 6 = 15.

SAT-16#9.title: One formula, easiest order
SAT-16#9.text: Use the cone formula from the reference sheet in a single line: one third × π × radius squared × height. That is one third × π × 9 × 4. Multiply in the easiest order: one third of 9 is 3, and 3 × 4 is 12, so the volume is 12π. As a size check, 12π is about 38, well under the 144 of the 6 by 6 by 4 box around the cone.

SAT-17#1.title: Four triangles in a square
SAT-17#1.text: Take four copies of a right triangle with legs a and b and hypotenuse c. Place them in the corners of a square with side a + b so the hypotenuses form a tilted square in the middle. The uncovered space is c². Now slide the triangles together into two rectangles. The uncovered space becomes two squares, a² and b². The triangles did not change size, so the uncovered areas are equal: a² + b² = c².

SAT-17#2.title: A carpenter's corner check
SAT-17#2.text: Builders use 3-4-5 to test whether a corner is square. Mark 3 feet along one wall and 4 feet along the other. If the corner is a true right angle, the tape between the marks reads exactly 5 feet. For a bigger room they mark 6 and 8 and look for 10, or 30 and 40 and look for 50. Check the last one: 900 + 1,600 = 2,500, which is 50 squared.

SAT-17#3.title: Put numbers on both shapes
SAT-17#3.text: A square tile with side 10 cm has a diagonal of 10 × √2, about 14.1 cm, so the diagonal is roughly 41% longer than a side for any square. An equilateral triangle with side 10 cm, cut in half, gives a right triangle with short leg 5, hypotenuse 10 and height 5 × √3, about 8.7 cm. Check: 5² + 8.7² is about 100. The decimals 1.41 and 1.73 are worth remembering.

SAT-17#4.title: Try it on a 3-4-5 triangle
SAT-17#4.text: Stand at the angle across from the side of length 3. Opposite is 3, adjacent is 4 and the hypotenuse is 5. So sine is 3/5, cosine is 4/5 and tangent is 3/4. Double the triangle to 6-8-10 and the ratios are 6/10, 8/10 and 6/8, the same numbers. Now move to the other acute angle: opposite and adjacent swap, so its sine is 4/5 and its cosine is 3/5.

SAT-17#5.title: Bound it, then test squares
SAT-17#5.text: The hypotenuse is longer than the longer leg, 12, and shorter than the two legs laid end to end, 21. Its square must be 81 + 144 = 225. Try whole numbers just above 12: 13² is 169, 14² is 196 and 15² is 225. The third one fits, so c = 15, and it sits sensibly between 12 and 21.

SAT-17#6.title: Factor the squares
SAT-17#6.text: See why the triple shortcut works by factoring. Since 9 = 3 × 3 and 12 = 3 × 4, the sum 9² + 12² is 3² × 3² + 3² × 4². Take out the shared 3² to get 3² × (3² + 4²) = 9 × 25. The square root of 9 × 25 is 3 × 5 = 15. The common factor 3 passes straight through the theorem, so c = 15.

SAT-17#7.title: Use a difference of squares
SAT-17#7.text: The missing leg squared is 13² − 5². Instead of squaring both, factor it as (13 − 5)(13 + 5) = 8 × 18 = 144. The square root of 144 is 12, so b = 12. This trick turns two squarings and a subtraction into one small multiplication, and it helps most when the numbers are large.

SAT-17#8.title: Rebuild the equilateral triangle
SAT-17#8.text: Place a mirror image of the triangle against its long leg. The two 30° angles join to make 60°, so the doubled shape has three 60° angles and is equilateral, with every side equal to the hypotenuse, 10. The short leg is half of the bottom side, so it is 5. The long leg is the height: its square is 10² − 5² = 75, and √75 = 5√3. The legs are 5 and 5√3.

SAT-17#9.title: Shrink the hypotenuse to 1
SAT-17#9.text: Divide every side of the triangle by 17. The shape and the angle θ stay the same, but the hypotenuse is now 1 and the opposite side is 8/17, about 0.47. So sin θ is simply the height of the triangle when the hypotenuse is 1 unit long. The adjacent side becomes 15/17, and (8/17)² + (15/17)² = 64/289 + 225/289 = 1, as a right triangle with hypotenuse 1 requires.

SAT-17#10.title: Look at values you know
SAT-17#10.text: Recall some familiar values. The sine of 30° and the cosine of 60° are both 1/2. The sine of 60° and the cosine of 30° are both about 0.866. The sine of 45° and the cosine of 45° are both about 0.707. In every matching pair the two angles add to 90°. So the partner of 25° is 90° − 25° = 65°, and a calculator confirms both sin 65° and cos 25° are about 0.906.

SAT-18#1.title: Start at the origin, then slide
SAT-18#1.text: The circle x² + y² = 25 has center (0, 0) and radius 5. Check some points on it: (5, 0) gives 25 + 0, (3, 4) gives 9 + 16 and (0, −5) gives 0 + 25. Now slide the whole circle 2 right and 1 up. The point (3, 4) moves to (5, 5). To test it, undo the slide first: (5 − 2)² + (5 − 1)² = 9 + 16 = 25. That is why the equation becomes (x − 2)² + (y − 1)² = 25.

SAT-18#2.title: Slice a pizza into six
SAT-18#2.text: Cut a pizza of radius 6 into six equal slices from the center. Each slice has a 60° tip, since 360° ÷ 6 = 60°. Each slice gets one sixth of the crust and one sixth of the pizza. The whole crust is 2 × π × 6 = 12π long, so one slice has 2π of crust. The whole pizza is π × 6² = 36π in area, so one slice is 6π.

SAT-18#3.title: Wrap the radius around the edge
SAT-18#3.text: Cut a string as long as the radius of a circle and lay it along the edge. The angle it marks out at the center is 1 radian, about 57°. Keep laying strings end to end. Three of them do not quite reach halfway around, and it takes π of them, about 3.14, to cover exactly half the circle. That is why a half turn of 180° is π radians, and a full turn is 2π.

SAT-18#4.title: Find the left and right edges
SAT-18#4.text: Look along the horizontal line y = −5, where the y bracket is zero. The equation becomes (x − 2)² = 36, so x − 2 is 6 or −6, giving x = 8 or x = −4. Those are the right and left edges of the circle, at (8, −5) and (−4, −5). The center is halfway between them at (2, −5), and the radius is half of the 12 between them, which is 6.

SAT-18#5.title: Test points in the original
SAT-18#5.text: If the center is (−3, 2) and the radius is 5, then the point 5 to the right, (2, 2), must be on the circle. Put it into the original equation: 4 + 12 + 4 − 8 = 12, which is correct. Try the point 5 above the center, (−3, 7): 9 − 18 + 49 − 28 = 12, correct again. Two points at distance 5 both satisfy the equation, which confirms the center and radius.

SAT-18#6.title: Check against the chord
SAT-18#6.text: Join the ends of the 60° arc to the center and to each other. The triangle has two sides of 9 with a 60° angle between them, so it is equilateral and the straight chord is also 9. The arc bulges outward, so it must be a little longer than 9. The answer 3π is about 9.42, which fits. Six of these arcs make the circle: 6 × 3π = 18π, the full circumference.

SAT-18#7.title: Take a third of the semicircle
SAT-18#7.text: Half the circle is a turn of 180°, and its edge is half the circumference: π × 9 = 9π. The 60° angle is one third of 180°, so its arc is one third of the semicircle's edge. One third of 9π is 3π. Thinking in half turns keeps the numbers small, and no conversion formula is needed.

SAT-18#8.title: Use the radian sector formula
SAT-18#8.text: With the angle in radians, the area of a sector is one half × radius squared × angle. A 90° angle is π/2 radians. So the area is one half × 4² × π/2 = one half × 16 × π/2. Half of 16 is 8, and 8 × π/2 is 4π. The formula agrees with the quarter-circle picture.

SAT-18#9.title: Split 135° into familiar pieces
SAT-18#9.text: Break the angle into parts you already know in radians: 135° = 90° + 45°. A right angle is π/2 and half of a right angle is π/4. Add them with a common denominator: π/2 is 2π/4, and 2π/4 + π/4 = 3π/4. You could also start from a half turn and go back: π − π/4 is 3π/4 as well.

STAT-1#1.title: Sort the columns of a spreadsheet
STAT-1#1.text: Picture a class spreadsheet with one row per student. In the "shoe size" column you could sort from smallest to largest and say who is 2 sizes bigger than whom, so it is quantitative. In the "homeroom number" column, room 204 is not twice room 102 and the gap between them means nothing. The room number only says which group a student belongs to, so it is categorical, just like the "eye color" column.

STAT-1#2.title: Scale the class to 100
STAT-1#2.text: Imagine blowing the class of 20 up to exactly 100 students while keeping the same mix. Each real student now stands for 5 students, so the 8 pizza fans become 8 × 5 = 40 out of 100. That is what 40% says: out of every hundred, forty. Doing the same to tacos (6), salad (4) and other (2) gives 30, 20 and 10, and the four numbers fill the hundred exactly.

STAT-1#3.title: Build the plot with students
STAT-1#3.text: Ask the fifteen students to line up behind signs marked 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 pets. Four stand behind 0, six behind 1, three behind 2, and one each behind 3 and 4. Seen from above, the lines are the dot plot. The longest line is at 1, the lines get shorter to the right, and every student can still find their own dot. A histogram does the same after grouping nearby values into bins.

STAT-1#4.title: SOCS on a real data set
STAT-1#4.text: Take commute times for a class. Shape: one peak at short times with a tail toward long ones, so skewed right and unimodal. Outliers: one student at 75 minutes stands far from the rest. Center: a typical commute is about 15 minutes. Spread: most times fall between 5 and 30 minutes. Four short sentences, each with the word "minutes" in it, and a reader who never saw the graph could now sketch it.

STAT-1#5.title: A pay example
STAT-1#5.text: Nine workers at a small shop earn 30 thousand dollars a year and the owner earns 300 thousand. On a number line the nine dots pile up on the left and one dot sits far out to the right, so the tail points right: skewed right. The median pay is 30 thousand, but the mean is 570 ÷ 10 = 57 thousand, more than nine of the ten people earn. The single tail value dragged the mean toward itself.

STAT-1#6.title: Check with a second question
STAT-1#6.text:
Ask of each variable: does "how much more?" have an answer?
Siblings: 4 siblings is 2 more than 2 siblings, a real difference, so quantitative.
Eye color: brown is not "more" than blue by any amount, so categorical.
Zip code: 90210 minus 10001 is 80209, but that number measures nothing about the two places, so categorical.
The result matches the averaging test: quantitative, categorical, categorical.

STAT-1#7.title: Simplify, then scale to 100
STAT-1#7.text: Write the pizza share as a fraction and reduce it: 8 out of 20 is 4 out of 10, which is 2 out of 5. Two fifths is the fraction. To turn it into a percent, scale the bottom to 100: 2 out of 5 is the same as 40 out of 100, so 40%. As a decimal that is 0.40, the same relative frequency as dividing 8 by 20 directly.

STAT-1#8.title: Compare the mean with the median
STAT-1#8.text: Check the shape with numbers. The median of 24 students is between the 12th and 13th values; the first bin holds 9 and the second reaches 16, so the median is in 10–20, about 14 minutes. Using bin midpoints, the mean is about (9×5 + 7×15 + 4×25 + 3×35 + 1×45) ÷ 24 = 400 ÷ 24 ≈ 16.7 minutes. A mean above the median is the sign of a right tail, so the shape is skewed right, with its one peak at 0–10 minutes.

STAT-1#9.title: Cross off from both ends
STAT-1#9.text: Line up the 15 values and cross off the smallest and largest together, pair by pair. Seven pairs go: the four 0s and three of the 1s leave from the low end while 4, 3, the three 2s and two of the 1s leave from the high end. The one value left standing is a 1, so the median is 1 pet. The high side had to reach all the way from 4 down to 1, which shows the long tail is on the right: skewed right.

STAT-1#10.title: Count down from the top instead
STAT-1#10.text: Check by counting from the largest values downward. The middle of 15 values is still position 8, whichever end you start from. Going down: 4 pets is position 1, 3 pets is position 2, the three 2-pet students take positions 3 to 5, and the six 1-pet students take positions 6 to 11. Position 8 falls inside the 1-pet group, so the median is 1 pet, the same answer as counting up.

STAT-1#11.title: Scale each grade to 100 students
STAT-1#11.text: Each grade has 25 students, and 25 × 4 = 100, so multiply every count by 4 to imagine 100 students per grade. In 11th grade, 18 online becomes 72 out of 100, which is 72%. In 10th grade, 12 online becomes 48 out of 100, which is 48%. No division is needed, and the comparison is clear: 72% of 11th graders against 48% of 10th graders, a gap of 24 percentage points.

STAT-1#12.title: Estimate the mean and median
STAT-1#12.text: Confirm the picture with numbers. The median of 24 scores lies between the 12th and 13th. Bins up to 80 hold 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 scores and the 80–90 bin reaches 16, so the median is in 80–90, near 86. With bin midpoints the mean is about (55 + 2×65 + 4×75 + 9×85 + 8×95) ÷ 24 = 2010 ÷ 24 ≈ 83.8. The mean is below the median, which is what a tail on the left produces: skewed left.

STAT-2#1.title: Share out, or line up
STAT-2#1.text: Seven students did 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12 and 16 minutes of homework. Mean: pool all 63 minutes and hand them back equally, 9 minutes each. That is what "fair share" means. Median: line the students up by minutes and tap the one in the middle, who did 8. Now change the 16 to 60. The pool grows, so the fair share jumps to 107 ÷ 7 ≈ 15.3, but the student in the middle of the line still did 8.

STAT-2#2.title: Quartiles with real numbers
STAT-2#2.text: Take 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12, 16. The median is 8. Below it sit 4, 6, 7, whose middle is 6, so Q1 = 6. Above it sit 10, 12, 16, whose middle is 12, so Q3 = 12. The IQR is 12 − 6 = 6. Now replace 16 with 160. The quartiles are still 6 and 12 and the IQR is still 6, while the range leaps from 12 to 156. The IQR only watches the middle of the data.

STAT-2#3.title: Two quiz groups, same mean
STAT-2#3.text: Group A scores 9, 10, 10, 10, 11 and group B scores 2, 6, 10, 14, 18. Both have mean 10. In A the distances from 10 are 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, and the recipe gives s = √(2 ÷ 4) ≈ 0.7. In B the distances are 8, 4, 0, 4, 8, and it gives s = √(160 ÷ 4) ≈ 6.3. The standard deviation is about nine times larger in B, matching what the eye sees: A huddles, B sprawls.

STAT-2#4.title: Fences on real data
STAT-2#4.text: Ages at a club: 12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 18, 20, 45. Here Q1 = 14.5 and Q3 = 19, so the box is 4.5 years wide. One and a half box-widths is 6.75 years, which puts the fences at 14.5 − 6.75 = 7.75 and 19 + 6.75 = 25.75. Everyone from 12 to 20 is inside the fences. The 45 is far outside, so it is drawn as a separate point and the right whisker stops at 20.

STAT-2#5.title: Level the values to find the balance
STAT-2#5.text: Guess a mean of 9 and check that it balances. Distances below 9: 5, 3, 2 and 1, total 11. Distances above 9: 1, 3 and 7, total 11. The two sides match, so the mean is 9. For the median, cross off the smallest and largest in pairs: 4 and 16, 6 and 12, 7 and 10. The value left is 8. The 16 alone supplies 7 of the 11 units on the high side, so it pulls the mean, not the median.

STAT-2#6.title: Count positions on a number line
STAT-2#6.text: Mark the seven values on a number line and count dots. One dot at each end gives min 4 and max 16. The 4th dot from either end is 8, the median. Cover that dot. Of the three dots to its left the middle one is 6, and of the three to its right the middle one is 12. Check: exactly one dot lies below Q1 and one above Q3, the same on both sides. The box runs from 6 to 12, so the IQR is 6.

STAT-2#7.title: Use the shortcut formula
STAT-2#7.text: Another route skips the deviations. Square each value and add: 9 + 25 + 25 + 64 + 81 = 204. Subtract n times the mean squared: 5 × 6² = 180, leaving 204 − 180 = 24, the same sum of squared deviations. Divide by n − 1 = 4 to get 6, then take the square root: s = √6 ≈ 2.45. As a sense check, the distances from the mean are 3, 1, 1, 2, 3, so a typical distance near 2.5 is reasonable.

STAT-2#8.title: Compare the gaps
STAT-2#8.text: Look at the gaps between neighbors in the sorted list: 2, 1, 0, 1, 2, 2, and then 25. The first seven ages span only 8 years in total, but the last jump alone is 25 years, about three times that whole span. The middle half of the data is only 4.5 years wide, and 45 sits 26 years above Q3. That is far more than the 6.75 years the rule allows, so 45 is beyond the fence of 25.75 and is an outlier.

STAT-2#9.title: Find the largest non-outlier
STAT-2#9.text: Turn the question around: how large could an age be without being flagged? The limit is Q3 plus 1.5 box-widths, which is 19 + 6.75 = 25.75, so anyone 25 or younger passes. A 45-year-old is nearly 20 years past that limit. Even if the rule used 3 box-widths, a stricter standard some books call an extreme outlier, the limit would be 19 + 13.5 = 32.5, and 45 would still be flagged. Outlier.

STAT-2#10.title: Reason without recomputing
STAT-2#10.text: Removing the 45 takes away a value 25.6 above the mean of 19.4. Those 25.6 extra years were being shared among the remaining ages, so the mean falls by about 25.6 ÷ 7 ≈ 3.7 years. The median only shifts half a position: from between the 4th and 5th ages (15.5) to the 4th age (15), a move of 0.5. It would move the same if the 45 had been 21 or 99. The median is the resistant one.

STAT-2#11.title: Put numbers on each box
STAT-2#11.text: Suppose each box is centered on its median. Class A's middle half then runs from about 73 to 83, and Class B's from about 75 to 95. B's box reaches 12 points higher at the top, yet its bottom edge is only 2 points above A's. So a typical B student scores higher (85 against 78), but B's middle students differ from each other by up to 20 points while A's differ by at most 10. B has the higher center, A the smaller spread.

STAT-3#1.title: One bell, different rulers
STAT-3#1.text: Draw one bell curve on a sheet of paper and leave the axis blank. Label the center 500 and mark every 100 points: the sheet now shows test scores, N(500, 100). Erase the labels, write 64.5 in the center and mark every 2.5 inches: the same drawing now shows women's heights, N(64.5, 2.5). Nothing about the curve was redrawn. Only the ruler under it changed, and a ruler needs just two facts: where its center is and how long one step is.

STAT-3#2.title: Count 1,000 test takers
STAT-3#2.text: Picture 1,000 students with scores that are N(500, 100). About 680 of them score between 400 and 600. About 950 score between 300 and 700, which leaves 50 outside: roughly 25 below 300 and 25 above 700. About 997 score between 200 and 800, so only 3 students in the thousand land farther out than that. Change the test to one with mean 20 and standard deviation 4 and the same head counts fall within 16 to 24, 12 to 28 and 8 to 32.

STAT-3#3.title: Which score is better?
STAT-3#3.text: Maya scores 82 on a history test where the class mean is 70 and the standard deviation is 8. She scores 75 on a chemistry test where the mean is 60 and the standard deviation is 5. History looks better, but count steps: 82 is 12 points above the mean, which is 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 standard deviations. In chemistry, 75 is 15 points above, which is 15 ÷ 5 = 3 standard deviations. Compared with her classmates, chemistry was the stronger result.

STAT-3#4.title: Read it as a percentile
STAT-3#4.text: A left-area is a percentile. For scores that are N(500, 100), a 600 has z = 1 and the table says 0.8413, so 600 beats about 84 of every 100 scores. The other 16 scored higher: 1 − 0.8413 = 0.1587. A 400 has z = −1 with left-area 0.1587. The share of scores from 400 to 600 is everyone below 600 minus everyone below 400: 84 − 16 = 68 out of 100.

STAT-3#5.title: Walk out from the mean
STAT-3#5.text: Scores are N(500, 100) and a prize goes to the top 10%. Start at the mean, 500, where half the scores are below you. Walk right until 90% are below you. The table says that takes 1.28 steps, and each step is 100 points long, so you travel 128 points and stop at 628. For the bottom 10% you would walk the same distance left and stop at 500 − 128 = 372. The percent tells how many steps; σ tells how long each step is.

STAT-3#6.title: Count the steps on a number line
STAT-3#6.text: Mark the mean, 500, on a number line and put a tick every 100 points, one standard deviation each: 600, 700, and so on. The score 650 lies past the first tick at 600 and exactly halfway to the second at 700. That is one full step plus half a step above the mean, so z = 1.5. Check by reversing: 500 + 1.5 × 100 = 650.

STAT-3#7.title: Count out of 1,000 scores
STAT-3#7.text: Imagine 1,000 scores. The middle 680 lie within one standard deviation, between 400 and 600, so that is 68%. For the second part, 950 lie between 300 and 700, leaving 50 outside. Symmetry splits those evenly, 25 below 300 and 25 above 700. Twenty-five out of 1,000 is 2.5%. Another check: half the scores, 500, are above 500, and half of the 950, which is 475, lie between 500 and 700, so 500 − 475 = 25 are above 700.

STAT-3#8.title: Bracket it with the empirical rule
STAT-3#8.text: Estimate before using the table. Below 600 (one σ up) is 50% + 34% = 84%. Below 700 (two σ up) is 50% + 47.5% = 97.5%. Since 650 lies between 600 and 700, the answer must be between 0.84 and 0.975. The curve is taller near 600 than near 700, so more than half of that 13.5% band lies below 650, putting the answer above 0.91. The table value 0.9332 fits.

STAT-3#9.title: Middle equals one minus two tails
STAT-3#9.text: Use symmetry instead of two left-areas. The values 62 and 67 are each 2.5 inches, one standard deviation, from the mean of 64.5, so the two tails outside them are equal. The lower tail, below z = −1, has area 0.1587, and the upper tail matches it. Both tails together hold 2 × 0.1587 = 0.3174. The middle is what is left: 1 − 0.3174 = 0.6826.

STAT-3#10.title: Count steps of 2.5 inches
STAT-3#10.text: Skip the z-score formula and step along the height axis. One standard deviation is 2.5 inches, so from the mean of 64.5, one step down lands on 62 and one step up lands on 67. Those are exactly the two endpoints, so the question is asking for the share within one step of the mean. That share is always about 68% for a normal curve, which agrees with the table value 0.6826.

STAT-3#11.title: Test nearby scores
STAT-3#11.text: Work forward and check candidate cutoffs. Try 600: z = 1 and the area below is 0.8413, so 16% score higher. Too many, so move up. Try 650: z = 1.5 and the area below is 0.9332, leaving 6.7% above. Too few, so the cutoff is between 600 and 650. Try 628: z = 1.28 and the area below is 0.8997, leaving almost exactly 10% above. The cutoff is about 628.

STAT-3#12.title: Flip to the right tail
STAT-3#12.text: By symmetry, the share of bags more than 0.3 oz under the mean equals the share more than 0.3 oz over it. So count bags above 10.3 oz instead. That value has z = (10.3 − 10) ÷ 0.2 = 1.5, and the area to its left is 0.9332. The area to the right is 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668. The lower tail matches, so 0.0668 of the bags, about 6.7%, are rejected.

STAT-4#1.title: Describing one plot aloud
STAT-4#1.text: Plot the age of ten used cars (x) against their price (y). The dots fall from upper left to lower right: older cars cost less, a negative direction. They follow a gentle curve that flattens, because cars lose value fastest when new, so the form is curved. The dots stay close to that curve, so it is fairly strong. One 30-year-old car priced far above the rest is a collector's model, an unusual point worth a comment.

STAT-4#2.title: What different r values look like
STAT-4#2.text: Think of four plots. Height in inches against height in centimeters: every point on one rising line, r = 1. Hours studied against test score: a tight rising band, r near 0.9. Shoe size against quiz score: a round cloud, r near 0. Car age against price: a falling band, r near −0.8. Measure the heights in feet instead, or put price on the x-axis, and each r stays the same, because r only reports how well the dots line up.

STAT-4#3.title: Try a rival line
STAT-4#3.text: For the study data (1, 60), (2, 65), (3, 75), (4, 80), (5, 90), compare two lines. The least-squares line 51.5 + 7.5x misses by 1, −1.5, 1, −1.5 and 1, so its squared misses total 7.5. A rival joining the first and last points, 52.5 + 7.5x, misses by 0, −2.5, 0, −2.5 and 0, for a total of 12.5. Every other line you try also scores worse than 7.5. The winner also passes through (3, 74), the point of means.

STAT-4#4.title: Residuals for five students
STAT-4#4.text: The line 51.5 + 7.5x predicts 59, 66.5, 74, 81.5 and 89 for 1 to 5 hours. The actual scores were 60, 65, 75, 80 and 90, so the residuals are 1, −1.5, 1, −1.5 and 1. Three students beat the prediction and two fell short, and the five residuals add to exactly 0. Their squares total only 7.5, while the scores vary around their mean by 570 in squared units, so the line leaves just 7.5 ÷ 570 ≈ 1.3% unexplained.

STAT-4#5.title: Check the steps between points
STAT-4#5.text: Use numbers instead of the eye. Each extra hour changes the score by 5, 10, 5 and 10 points. All four changes are increases, so the direction is positive. The changes do not grow steadily or shrink steadily, so nothing suggests a curve: the form is linear. They stay close to their average of 7.5 points per hour, so the points sit near one line and the relationship is strong.

STAT-4#6.title: Slope from pairs of points
STAT-4#6.text: Estimate the line a different way and compare. The first and last points give a slope of (90 − 60) ÷ (5 − 1) = 7.5, and the second and fourth give (80 − 65) ÷ (4 − 2) = 7.5 as well. A line with slope 7.5 through the point of means (3, 74) has intercept 74 − 22.5 = 51.5. That is ŷ = 51.5 + 7.5x, in agreement with the formula. With data this symmetric the shortcut matches exactly; in general only the formula is guaranteed.

STAT-4#7.title: Build a small table
STAT-4#7.text: Put the line into a table. At 0 hours it gives 51.5, at 1 hour 59, at 2 hours 66.5, at 3 hours 74. Each row is 7.5 higher than the one before, so the slope means +7.5 predicted points for each extra hour. The first row is the intercept: a predicted 51.5 for a student who does not study. Since no one in the data studied fewer than 1 hour, that first row is a starting value for the line, not a trusted prediction.

STAT-4#8.title: Step from the point of means
STAT-4#8.text: The line passes through (3, 74), so start there. For 3.5 hours, move half an hour right: half of 7.5 is 3.75, and 74 + 3.75 = 77.75. For the 2-hour student, move one hour left: 74 − 7.5 = 66.5 predicted. That student scored 65, which is 1.5 below the prediction, so the residual is −1.5. Both results match the substitution method.

STAT-4#9.title: Check with z-scores
STAT-4#9.text: Regression says a student one standard deviation above average in hours is predicted r standard deviations above average in score. Test it: 3 + 1.58 = 4.58 hours should predict 74 + 0.993 × 11.94 ≈ 85.9 points. The line gives 51.5 + 7.5 × 4.58 ≈ 85.9. They agree, so the slope 7.5 and intercept 51.5 are right: ŷ = 51.5 + 7.5x.

STAT-4#10.title: Compare the misses directly
STAT-4#10.text: Compute r² from prediction errors. Guessing the mean, 74, for every student misses by −14, −9, 1, 6 and 16, and those squares total 570. Using the line instead misses by 1, −1.5, 1, −1.5 and 1, and those squares total 7.5. The line removed 570 − 7.5 = 562.5 of the 570, and 562.5 ÷ 570 ≈ 0.987. So 98.7% of the variation in score is explained by hours studied.

STAT-4#11.title: A reasonableness check
STAT-4#11.text: Test the answer against what a score can be. If the test is out of 100, the line already predicts 51.5 + 7.5x = 100 at about 6.5 hours. Past that point every prediction is above the maximum, so the line must stop describing reality somewhere just beyond the data. At 20 hours it gives 201.5, more than double a perfect score. The arithmetic is right and the answer is impossible, which is the mark of extrapolation.

STAT-5#1.title: Tasting the soup
STAT-5#1.text: A cook wants to know how salty a whole pot of soup is. The pot is the population and its true saltiness is the parameter, a fixed fact nobody can measure without drinking it all. So the cook stirs and tastes one spoonful. The spoonful is the sample and its saltiness is the statistic. A second spoonful might taste slightly different, but the pot did not change. In the school survey, the 100 students are the spoonful and 62% is what it tasted like.

STAT-5#2.title: Names in a hat
STAT-5#2.text: Write each of the 40 students' names on identical slips, mix them in a hat and draw 5 without looking. Any five slips are as likely to come out together as any other five, which is exactly what an SRS requires. A random digit table is the same hat on paper: label students 01 to 40 and read two digits at a time. A pair like 73 is a slip with no name on it, and a repeated pair is a slip already drawn, so both are passed over.

STAT-5#3.title: One school, three plans
STAT-5#3.text: A school has 4 grades and 40 homerooms, and you want 80 students. Stratified: draw 20 at random from each grade, so freshmen and seniors are both sure to be heard. Cluster: draw 4 homerooms at random and survey all 20 students in each, with only four rooms to visit. Systematic: stand at the entrance, pick a random start from 1 to 15, then stop every 15th student who walks in. Same school, same sample size, three different ways of choosing.

STAT-5#4.title: Four ways a gym poll goes wrong
STAT-5#4.text: A town asks, "Should we build a new gym?" Voluntary response: a web poll draws mostly people with strong feelings. Convenience: asking people leaving the current gym finds mostly gym users. Undercoverage: calling only landlines misses most young adults, who never had a chance to be picked. Nonresponse: mailing 1,000 surveys and hearing back from 150 leaves 850 chosen voices missing. In every case you can guess which way the result leans before seeing a single answer.

STAT-5#5.title: A scale that reads heavy
STAT-5#5.text: A bathroom scale that jitters by a pound each time has variability: weigh yourself ten times, average, and the jitter mostly cancels. A scale that always reads 5 pounds heavy has bias: weigh yourself a thousand times and the average is a very steady number that is still 5 pounds too high. A leading question such as "Do you agree that our hardworking teachers deserve a raise?" is the second kind of scale. More respondents steady the answer without correcting it.

STAT-5#6.title: Ask what would change
STAT-5#6.text: Imagine the school repeats the survey with a different 100 students. The group of 1,200 stays the same, so that is the population. The 100 people asked would be new, so that is the sample. The 62% would probably come out a little different, perhaps 58% or 65%. A number that changes when the sample changes is a statistic. The true percent among all 1,200 would not move at all, and that fixed, unknown number is the parameter.

STAT-5#7.title: Check the selection rules
STAT-5#7.text: Verify the answer against the rules. The line read in pairs is 41, 05, 09, 20, 31, 06, 44, 90, 50, 59. Rule one: labels must be 01 to 40, which removes 41 at the start. Rule two: no repeats, and 05, 09, 20, 31, 06 are all different. Rule three: stop at five. Five valid labels are in hand after the sixth pair, so the sample is 05, 09, 20, 31, 06, and the last four pairs are never used.

STAT-5#8.title: Ask who could be left out
STAT-5#8.text: Look at which students can end up in each sample. Under Plan A, exactly 10 students come from every grade, so no grade can be missed, though most homerooms contribute only a student or two. Sampling some individuals from every group is stratified. Under Plan B, only 3 homerooms appear, and a whole grade could be absent if no chosen room belongs to it. Taking every individual from a few randomly chosen groups is cluster sampling.

STAT-5#9.title: Invent numbers to see the push
STAT-5#9.text: Suppose 1,000 readers see the poll and opinion is truly split: 500 think taxes are too high and 500 do not. If 30% of the upset readers bother to click, that is 150 yes votes. If only 4% of the content readers click, that is 20 no votes. The poll reports 150 out of 170, which is 88% yes, while the truth was 50%. Self-selection is voluntary response bias, and it overstates the yes share.

STAT-5#10.title: Cross off as you go
STAT-5#10.text: Write the numbers 1 to 40 on a sheet and circle each one the calculator gives. Circle 17. Circle 3. The next output is 3 again, already circled, so nothing new happens. Circle 28, then 40, which is on the sheet because the range includes both ends. Four circles so far, so one more is needed: circle 9. Five circled numbers means the sample is complete: students 17, 3, 28, 40 and 9.

STAT-5#11.title: Flip the loaded word
STAT-5#11.text: Test the question by loading it the other way: "Do you agree that hardworking athletes should keep more of what they earn?" Many people who said yes to the first version would say yes to this one too, even though the two answers contradict each other. When the answer follows the adjective instead of the issue, the wording is leading. Remove the adjective and ask plainly whether professional athletes should pay a higher tax rate.

STAT-5#12.title: Cut the line into blocks
STAT-5#12.text: Split the line of 500 into blocks of ten: shoppers 1–10, 11–20, and so on. That makes 500 ÷ 10 = 50 blocks, one for each person needed. Roll a ten-sided die once, say it shows 7, and take the 7th person in every block: 7, 17, 27, up to 497. Check the count: (497 − 7) ÷ 10 + 1 = 50 shoppers. Each shopper had a 1 in 10 chance, decided by that single roll.

STAT-6#1.title: Does music help plants grow?
STAT-6#1.text: Two ways to ask whether music helps plants. Observe: survey 200 gardeners, and those who play music report taller plants. But gardeners who play music may also water more carefully or own sunnier windows. Experiment: take 40 identical seedlings, flip a coin for each, and play music only to the heads group, with the same soil, light and water for all. If the music group grows taller now, the coin left nothing else to explain it.

STAT-6#2.title: Draw the grid
STAT-6#2.text: Make a grid with one factor down the side and the other across the top. Rows: fertilizer A, fertilizer B. Columns: daily water, weekly water. The grid has four boxes, and each box is one treatment: A-daily, A-weekly, B-daily, B-weekly. Every plant goes into exactly one box, and its growth is the response written inside. Add a third watering level and the grid becomes 2 rows by 3 columns, so there would be 6 treatments.

STAT-6#3.title: Ice cream and sunburn
STAT-6#3.text: On days when a beach kiosk sells more ice cream, the first-aid tent treats more sunburn. Does ice cream burn skin? Hot sunny weather raises both numbers at once. Ice cream sales and sunshine rise and fall on the same days, so from the daily records alone you cannot tell which one goes with the sunburn. That is confounding. To untangle them you would need sunny days with no ice cream, which only a planned design can supply.

STAT-6#4.title: Break each principle in turn
STAT-6#4.text: A coach tests a new stretching routine. No comparison: all 30 runners stretch and get faster, but the season was starting and they would have improved anyway. No random assignment: the coach lets keen runners choose the routine, so the stretching group was more motivated from the start. No replication: one runner stretches and one does not, and the faster one may simply have slept better. Fix all three with a coin flip for each of 30 runners and a comparison of the group averages.

STAT-6#5.title: A headache study with numbers
STAT-6#5.text: Give 100 people a sugar pill and about 35 report less pain: that is the placebo effect. Give another 100 the real pill and 60 improve. The drug deserves credit for the difference, 25, not for all 60. If doctors knew who had the real pill, they might nudge borderline ratings upward, so nobody learns the groups until the end. And if headaches differ by age, split into under-40 and over-40 blocks before flipping coins, so age cannot tip the result.

STAT-6#6.title: Imagine the missing experiment
STAT-6#6.text: Ask what it would take to prove coffee prevents heart disease. Researchers would have to take a few thousand volunteers, flip a coin for each, and make the heads group drink 3 cups a day for years while the tails group drinks none. Nothing like that happened here. Records were read after people chose their own habits, so this is an observational study. It can show that coffee and healthy hearts go together, an association, but not that one causes the other.

STAT-6#7.title: Shuffle a deck of cards
STAT-6#7.text: Randomize without a number generator. Take 40 index cards, write A on 20 and B on 20, and shuffle well. Walk along the plants and deal one card to each pot: the card says which fertilizer that plant gets. The groups are sure to be 20 and 20, and chance alone decided the split. Then give every pot the same light, water and soil, and after 8 weeks compare the mean height of the A plants with the mean height of the B plants.

STAT-6#8.title: Fill in a two-by-two grid
STAT-6#8.text: Draw a grid. The two things the researchers set go on the edges: fertilizer (A, B) down the side and watering (daily, weekly) across the top. Those are the 2 factors. What gets written inside the boxes is the measured growth, the response. Count the boxes: 2 rows by 2 columns gives 4, and each box is one treatment: A-daily, A-weekly, B-daily, B-weekly. So there are 2 factors and 4 treatments.

STAT-6#9.title: Hold sleep fixed and look again
STAT-6#9.text: Test whether sleep could be the real cause with a thought experiment. Look only at students who all sleep about 8 hours and compare breakfast eaters with skippers inside that group. If the grade gap shrinks or vanishes, sleep was doing the work. That can happen only because sleep differs between the breakfast groups and also affects grades by itself. A variable with both of those links is a confounder, and sleep fits.

STAT-6#10.title: See what blocking prevents
STAT-6#10.text: Suppose sun adds 10 cm of growth and fertilizer A adds 2 cm over B. With plain randomization, chance might put 13 sunny plants in group A and 7 in group B. Then A looks about 3 cm better from sunlight alone, and the real 2 cm effect is buried. Splitting each bench 10 and 10 makes that impossible: both fertilizers get exactly 10 sunny and 10 shady plants, so the sun cancels out of the comparison. That is a randomized block design.

STAT-6#11.title: Put numbers on the placebo effect
STAT-6#11.text: Suppose 60 of 100 people on the new pill say their headache eased. That sounds good, but if 40 of 100 on a sugar pill say the same, only the 20-person difference belongs to the drug. Without the sugar pill group there is no way to see this. If subjects knew their group, hope would raise the first number, and if doctors knew, their ratings could drift too. So the study needs a placebo control and must be double-blind.

STAT-6#12.title: Compare the two designs with numbers
STAT-6#12.text: Suppose soles wear between 1 mm and 5 mm depending on how much a person walks, and material X truly wears 0.3 mm less than Y. With 10 people per material, a group that happens to include more heavy walkers could differ by a full millimeter, hiding the 0.3. With both materials on one walker, a heavy walker shows 5.0 against 4.7 and a light one 1.3 against 1.0. Each pair shows the 0.3 directly. That is the strength of matched pairs.

STAT-7#1.title: Three coin flips, counted out
STAT-7#1.text: Flip a coin three times. The sample space has 8 equally likely outcomes: HHH, HHT, HTH, THH, HTT, THT, TTH, TTT, each with probability 1/8, and 8 × 1/8 = 1. What is the chance of at least one head? Counting directly, seven of the eight outcomes qualify. Counting the complement, only TTT has no heads, so the answer is 1 − 1/8 = 7/8. Both give the same number, but the second needed one outcome instead of seven.

STAT-7#2.title: Hearts or kings in a deck
STAT-7#2.text: Draw one card from 52. How likely is a heart or a king? There are 13 hearts and 4 kings, but 13 + 4 = 17 counts the king of hearts twice, once as a heart and once as a king. Only 16 different cards qualify, so the answer is (13 + 4 − 1)/52 = 16/52. Now ask for a heart or a spade: no card is both, so nothing is double counted and the answer is simply 13/52 + 13/52 = 26/52.

STAT-7#3.title: A face-down card and a hint
STAT-7#3.text: A card lies face down. The chance it is a king is 4/52, about 0.08. A friend peeks and says, "It is a face card." Now only 12 cards are possible: 4 jacks, 4 queens, 4 kings. The chance of a king has become 4/12, about 0.33. The formula says the same: P(king and face card) is 4/52, P(face card) is 12/52, and dividing gives 4/12. New information threw away 40 cards and the 12 that remain became the whole deck.

STAT-7#4.title: Count the late bus riders
STAT-7#4.text: At a school of 200 students, 40% ride the bus, which is 80 students. Of those bus riders, 25% were late today, which is 20 students. So 20 out of 200, or 0.10, both ride the bus and were late. The multiplication rule gets there without head counts: 0.40 × 0.25 = 0.10. Notice that the 25% is a rate among bus riders only. That is the "given A" part of the rule.

STAT-7#5.title: Test it with a deck of cards
STAT-7#5.text: Draw one card. P(king) = 4/52 = 1/13. If you learn the card is a heart, the chance of a king is 1 of 13 hearts, still 1/13. Knowing the suit told you nothing, so king and heart are independent, and indeed (1/13)(1/4) = 1/52, the king of hearts. If you learn instead that the card is a queen, the chance of a king drops to 0. King and queen are mutually exclusive, and that makes them strongly dependent.

STAT-7#6.title: Count the 36 outcomes in a grid
STAT-7#6.text: Draw a 6 by 6 grid: rows for the first die, columns for the second. All 36 squares are equally likely. Shade the row where the first die is 6, six squares, and the column where the second die is 6, six more. The corner square (6, 6) was shaded twice, so the shaded region has 6 + 6 − 1 = 11 squares. The probability of at least one six is 11/36, about 0.306.

STAT-7#7.title: Fill in the Venn diagram
STAT-7#7.text: Sort the 100 students into regions. The overlap holds the 30 who do both. Sport only: 55 − 30 = 25. Music only: 50 − 30 = 20. Students in at least one circle: 25 + 30 + 20 = 75. So P(sport or music) = 75/100 = 0.75. As a check, the remaining 100 − 75 = 25 students do neither, and the four regions 25, 30, 20 and 25 add back to 100.

STAT-7#8.title: Gather the athletes in the gym
STAT-7#8.text: Send everyone who plays a sport to the gym. There are 55 students in the room, and the music players among them are exactly the 30 who do both. Pick one person in the gym at random: the chance of a musician is 30 out of 55. Reduce by dividing top and bottom by 5 to get 6/11, which is about 0.545. No probability formula was needed, only a count inside the smaller group.

STAT-7#9.title: Compare with the count independence predicts
