STAT-7#9.text: If sport and music were independent, musicians would be just as common among athletes as in the whole school. Half of all students play music, so half of the 55 athletes, 27.5, would be expected to play music. The actual number is 30. Since 30 is not 27.5, the events are not independent. This is the same comparison as 30/55 ≈ 0.545 against 0.50: athletes are a little more likely than average to play music.

STAT-7#10.title: Count ordered draws
STAT-7#10.text: Name the marbles R1, R2, R3, B1, B2. There are 5 choices for the first draw and 4 for the second, so 20 equally likely ordered draws. Both red: 3 choices then 2, which is 6 draws, so 6/20 = 3/10. One of each: red then blue is 3 × 2 = 6 draws and blue then red is 2 × 3 = 6 draws, 12 in all, so 12/20 = 3/5. The last 2 draws are both blue, and 6 + 12 + 2 = 20.

STAT-7#11.title: Count what stays in the bag
STAT-7#11.text: Look at the three marbles left behind instead. Choosing 3 of 5 to stay can be done in 10 ways, matching the 10 pairs. Both drawn are red when the bag keeps 1 red and both blues: 3 ways, so 3/10. One of each is drawn when the bag keeps 2 reds and 1 blue: 3 × 2 = 6 ways, so 6/10 = 3/5. Both drawn are blue when all 3 reds stay: 1 way, so 1/10. The same three answers.

STAT-7#12.title: Count 100 people
STAT-7#12.text: Imagine 100 people. Ten have the condition, and 90% of them, 9 people, test positive. Ninety do not have it, and 20% of them, 18 people, test positive anyway. That makes 9 + 18 = 27 positive tests. Of those 27 people, only 9 really have the condition, and 9/27 = 1/3, about 0.333. Two out of every three positives are false alarms, because the healthy group is so much larger.

STAT-8#1.title: Two coins, one table
STAT-8#1.text: Flip two coins and let X be the number of heads. The outcomes HH, HT, TH, TT are words, but X turns them into the numbers 2, 1, 1, 0. Each outcome has probability 1/4, so the table reads: X = 0 with probability 1/4, X = 1 with probability 2/4, X = 2 with probability 1/4. The three probabilities add to 1 because the four outcomes were all used exactly once. If they added to less, some outcome would be missing.

STAT-8#2.title: The balance point of the bars
STAT-8#2.text: Draw the cars distribution as bars standing on a ruler: height 0.10 at 0, 0.40 at 1, 0.35 at 2 and 0.15 at 3. Slide a finger under the ruler until it balances. It balances at 1.55. On the left, 0.10 × 1.55 + 0.40 × 0.55 = 0.375. On the right, 0.35 × 0.45 + 0.15 × 1.45 = 0.375. The pulls match. No bar stands at 1.55, just as a seesaw balances at a spot where nobody sits.

STAT-8#3.title: Two games with the same mean
STAT-8#3.text: Game A: flip a coin, win 1 dollar or lose 1 dollar. Game B: flip a coin, win 10 dollars or lose 10 dollars. Both have mean 0, so the mean cannot tell them apart. In game A every result is 1 away from the mean, so the variance is 1² = 1 and σ = 1 dollar. In game B every result is 10 away, so the variance is 100 and σ = 10 dollars. The standard deviation reports the typical swing, in dollars.

STAT-8#4.title: Three values, before and after
STAT-8#4.text: Let X be 2, 4 or 6, equally likely: mean 4, with the outer values 2 away. Add 3 to get 5, 7, 9: the mean is 7, and the outer values are still 2 away. Now use Y = 3 + 2.5X to get 8, 13, 18: the mean is 13, which is 3 + 2.5 × 4, and the outer values are 5 away, which is 2.5 × 2. The shift moved the center only. The multiplier moved the center and stretched the distances.

STAT-8#5.title: Two dice
STAT-8#5.text: One die has mean 3.5 and variance about 2.92. For the sum of two dice the mean is 3.5 + 3.5 = 7 and the variance is 2.92 + 2.92 = 5.83, so the SD is about 2.42, not 1.71 + 1.71 = 3.42. For the difference, first die minus second, the mean is 3.5 − 3.5 = 0. But the difference runs from −5 to 5, just as wide as the sum runs from 2 to 12. Subtracting does not cancel spread, so its variance is 5.83 as well.

STAT-8#6.title: Pair the faces
STAT-8#6.text: Use symmetry instead of the weighted sum. Pair the smallest face with the largest, 1 and 4: their average is 2.5. Pair the two middle faces, 2 and 3: their average is also 2.5. All faces are equally likely, so the long-run average is 2.5 too. Check with 400 imagined rolls, 100 of each face: the total is 100 + 200 + 300 + 400 = 1,000, and 1,000 ÷ 400 = 2.5. No face shows 2.5, but the average of many rolls does.

STAT-8#7.title: Use the shortcut formula
STAT-8#7.text: Find the variance as the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean. The faces squared are 1, 4, 9 and 16, and their average is 30 ÷ 4 = 7.5. The mean squared is 2.5² = 6.25. So the variance is 7.5 − 6.25 = 1.25, with no deviations needed. The standard deviation is √1.25 ≈ 1.12. That is sensible: two faces are 0.5 from the mean and two are 1.5 away, so a typical distance is near 1.

STAT-8#8.title: Buy every ticket
STAT-8#8.text: Imagine buying all 100 tickets. You pay 100 × 2 = 200 dollars and you are certain to hold the winning ticket, so you collect 100 dollars. Overall you are down 100 dollars. Spread over the 100 tickets, that is a loss of 1 dollar per ticket. A single ticket is just one equal share of that whole deal, so its expected net gain is −1.00 dollars.

STAT-8#9.title: Count 100 households
STAT-8#9.text: Picture 100 households that match the table: 10 with no car, 40 with one, 35 with two, 15 with three. Cars in total: 0 + 40 + 70 + 45 = 155, so the mean is 1.55. Squared distances from 1.55 are 2.4025, 0.3025, 0.2025 and 2.1025. Multiplied by the head counts they give 24.025 + 12.1 + 7.0875 + 31.5375 = 74.75. Dividing by 100 gives a variance of 0.7475, and its square root is about 0.865 cars.

STAT-8#10.title: Shift the values first
STAT-8#10.text: Sliding every value by the same amount does not change the spread, so subtract 1 from each car count. The new values −1, 0, 1, 2 keep the probabilities 0.10, 0.40, 0.35, 0.15. Their mean is −0.10 + 0 + 0.35 + 0.30 = 0.55. The mean of their squares is 0.10 + 0 + 0.35 + 0.60 = 1.05. So the variance is 1.05 − 0.55² = 1.05 − 0.3025 = 0.7475, the same value with smaller numbers.

STAT-8#11.title: Price three typical rides
STAT-8#11.text: Work out the fare for an average ride and for rides one SD either side. A 6-mile ride costs 3 + 2.5 × 6 = 18 dollars. A 4-mile ride costs 3 + 10 = 13 dollars and an 8-mile ride costs 3 + 20 = 23 dollars. The fares 13, 18 and 23 are centered at 18 and step by 5. So the mean fare is 18 dollars and one standard deviation of fare is 5 dollars.

STAT-8#12.title: Try a simple up-or-down model
STAT-8#12.text: Simplify: say the morning is either 6 above or 6 below its mean, and the afternoon either 8 above or 8 below, each by a coin flip. The day total is then off by +14, −2, +2 or −14, all equally likely. Those average to 0, so the mean total is 40 + 50 = 90. Their squares, 196, 4, 4 and 196, average to 100, so the SD is √100 = 10. Half the time the two swings partly cancel, which is why it is not 14.

STAT-9#1.title: Four settings that fail
STAT-9#1.text: See each condition by breaking it. Roll a die 10 times and record the face: six outcomes, not two, so not Binary. Deal 5 cards and count aces: each card dealt changes what is left, so not Independent. Flip a coin until heads appears: the Number of flips is not fixed. Count the makes in 20 free throws as a shooter tires: the Success chance drifts. Count heads in 10 coin flips and all four hold, so that count is binomial.

STAT-9#2.title: Two makes in three free throws
STAT-9#2.text: A player makes 80% of free throws and takes 3. For exactly 2 makes, write out the ways: make-make-miss, make-miss-make, miss-make-make. The first has probability 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.2 = 0.128, and the other two contain the same three numbers in another order, so each is 0.128 too. Total: 3 × 0.128 = 0.384. The formula packs this up: C(3, 2) = 3 ways, 0.8² for the makes, 0.2 for the miss.

STAT-9#3.title: Many batches of 50 parts
STAT-9#3.text: Imagine 1,000 batches of 50 parts, each part defective 10% of the time. That is 50,000 parts with about 5,000 defects, or 5 per batch: np. Single batches vary, with most between about 3 and 7 defects, matching an SD of √(50 × 0.1 × 0.9) ≈ 2.1. Compare 50 coin flips: mean 25 and SD √(50 × 0.5 × 0.5) ≈ 3.5, the widest possible for n = 50. If p were 0, every batch would have 0 defects and no spread.

STAT-9#4.title: Six hundred players rolling
STAT-9#4.text: Have 600 people each roll a die until they get a six. On roll 1 about 100 succeed and sit down, so 500 remain. On roll 2 about one sixth of those, 83, succeed. On roll 3 about one sixth of the remaining 417, which is 69, succeed. As fractions of 600 these are 1/6, then (5/6)(1/6), then (5/6)²(1/6). Each round keeps 5/6 of the previous one. Averaged over everyone, the number of rolls taken comes to about 6.

STAT-9#5.title: Big shipment, small shipment
STAT-9#5.text: A shipment of 10,000 bulbs has 500 defective. The first bulb is defective with chance 500/10,000 = 0.0500. If it was, the next has chance 499/9,999 = 0.0499. The change is too small to matter. A box of 20 with 1 defective is different: 1/20 = 0.05 at first, then 0/19 = 0. For at least one defect in 3 bulbs at p = 0.05, skip the cases 1, 2 and 3: none has probability 0.95³ ≈ 0.857, so the answer is 0.143.

STAT-9#6.title: Read it from Pascal's triangle
STAT-9#6.text: Four flips of a fair coin give 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 equally likely sequences. The row of Pascal's triangle for 4 flips is 1, 4, 6, 4, 1. It says how many sequences have 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 heads, and the entries add to 16. The middle entry is 6, so 6 of the 16 sequences have exactly 2 heads. The probability is 6/16 = 0.375.

STAT-9#7.title: Count equally likely tickets
STAT-9#7.text: Model each shot as drawing one of 5 tickets, 4 marked make and 1 marked miss. Five shots give 5 × 5 × 5 × 5 × 5 = 3,125 equally likely ticket sequences. For exactly 4 makes, choose which shot is the miss (5 ways), then the four makes can each be any of 4 tickets: 5 × 4 × 4 × 4 × 4 = 1,280 sequences. The probability is 1,280 ÷ 3,125 = 0.4096.

STAT-9#8.title: Split on the first four shots
STAT-9#8.text: Watch the first four shots, then the fifth. If all four go in, she already has at least 4: probability 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.4096. If exactly three of the four go in, she needs the fifth. Three of four has probability 4 × 0.512 × 0.2 = 0.4096, and making the fifth multiplies by 0.8, giving 0.32768. With two or fewer she cannot reach 4. Total: 0.4096 + 0.32768 = 0.73728, about 0.737.

STAT-9#9.title: Count the good parts instead
STAT-9#9.text: Check by counting good parts. Each part is good with probability 0.9, so a batch of 50 averages 50 × 0.9 = 45 good parts, leaving 50 − 45 = 5 defects. The good count has SD √(50 × 0.9 × 0.1) = √4.5 ≈ 2.12. Defects are just 50 minus the good count, and subtracting from a constant does not change spread, so defects also have SD 2.12. Expect 5 defects, give or take about 2.

STAT-9#10.title: Go through the emails in order
STAT-9#10.text: Follow the emails one at a time and stop at the first that gets through. Email 1 gets through with probability 0.2. If it is caught (0.8), email 2 gets through with probability 0.2: that is 0.8 × 0.2 = 0.16. If both are caught (0.64), email 3 gets through: 0.64 × 0.2 = 0.128. These three cases do not overlap, so add them: 0.2 + 0.16 + 0.128 = 0.488.

STAT-9#11.title: Follow 216 players
STAT-9#11.text: Let 216 people each roll until a six. On roll 1, one sixth succeed: 36 people, leaving 180. On roll 2, one sixth of 180 succeed: 30 people, leaving 150. On roll 3, one sixth of 150 succeed: 25 people. So 25 of the 216 get their first six on the third roll, and 25/216 ≈ 0.116. For the wait: over 600 rolls about 100 sixes appear, which is one six per 6 rolls on average.

STAT-9#12.title: Build 0.95 to the 20th by squaring
STAT-9#12.text: Get the probability without a power key. Two good bulbs: 0.95² = 0.9025. Four: 0.9025² ≈ 0.8145. Five: 0.8145 × 0.95 ≈ 0.7738. Ten: 0.7738² ≈ 0.5987. Twenty: 0.5987² ≈ 0.358. For the expected number, 5% is 1 bulb in 20, and the inspector tests 20, so about 1 defect is expected. Both fit together: one defect on average, yet no defects about 36% of the time.

STAT-10#1.title: A jar of beads
STAT-10#1.text: A jar holds 10,000 beads and exactly 40% are red. That 40% is the parameter: one fixed fact about the jar, unknown to anyone who has not counted every bead. Scoop out 50 beads and 18 are red, so the statistic is 0.36. Pour them back, scoop again, and get 23 red, 0.46. A third scoop gives 20 red, 0.40. The jar never changed, but the scoops did. In practice you get one scoop and must judge the jar from it.

STAT-10#2.title: A thousand pollsters
STAT-10#2.text: Suppose 60% of a city owns a bike and 1,000 pollsters each ask 100 random adults. Their results pile up around 0.60 in a bell shape, with about 950 of them landing between 0.50 and 0.70. If each had asked 400 adults instead, the pile would be half as wide, roughly 0.55 to 0.65. But if only 2% owned a bike and each asked 50 people, results could only be 0, 0.02, 0.04 and so on, bunched against zero. Expecting just 1 success fails Large Counts, and the bell is gone.

STAT-10#3.title: Averaging dice
STAT-10#3.text: One die has mean 3.5 and SD about 1.71, and a 6 comes up one time in six. Average 4 dice and the mean is still 3.5, but the SD drops to 1.71 ÷ 2 ≈ 0.85. An average of 6 now needs four sixes at once, a 1 in 1,296 event. Average 100 dice and the SD is 1.71 ÷ 10 ≈ 0.17, so nearly every average falls between 3 and 4. The center never moves, and four times the dice gives half the spread.

STAT-10#4.title: From flat to bell with dice
STAT-10#4.text: One die is as far from bell-shaped as it gets: six bars of equal height. Add two dice and the totals form a triangle peaked at 7, because there are six ways to make 7 and only one way to make 2 or 12. Add three and the corners round off. By 30 dice the histogram of averages is a smooth bell centered at 3.5. Nothing about a single die changed. Middle totals simply have far more combinations behind them than extreme totals.

STAT-10#5.title: Go through the variance
STAT-10#5.text: Work with variances, which follow a simple rule. One score has variance 12² = 144. The variance of a mean of 36 scores is the single-score variance divided by the sample size: 144 ÷ 36 = 4. Take the square root to return to points: √4 = 2. So the sample mean has standard deviation 2, the same answer as 12 ÷ 6, and the reason the divisor is 6 and not 36 is that the root comes last.

STAT-10#6.title: Start from the count of owners
STAT-10#6.text: Describe the number of bike owners first. In a sample of 100 the count is binomial with mean 100 × 0.6 = 60 and SD √(100 × 0.6 × 0.4) = √24 ≈ 4.9 owners. A proportion is the count divided by 100, so divide both: mean 0.60 and SD 0.049. With 60 expected owners and 40 expected non-owners, the binomial is close to bell-shaped, so the proportion is approximately normal with mean 0.6 and SD 0.049.

STAT-10#7.title: Ask about the total instead
STAT-10#7.text: A mean above 73 for 36 students is the same event as a total above 36 × 73 = 2,628 points. The total of 36 scores has mean 36 × 70 = 2,520 and SD 12 × √36 = 72. So 2,628 is 108 points above the expected total, and 108 ÷ 72 = 1.5 standard deviations. The area above z = 1.5 is 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668, the same probability found using the mean.

STAT-10#8.title: Work with the count of owners
STAT-10#8.text: A sample proportion of 0.65 or more means 65 or more owners among 100. The count has mean 60 and SD √(100 × 0.6 × 0.4) ≈ 4.90. Sixty-five is 5 owners above the mean, and 5 ÷ 4.90 ≈ 1.02 standard deviations. With 60 and 40 expected, the normal curve fits, and the area above z = 1.02 is 1 − 0.8461 = 0.1539. About a 15% chance, or 0.154.

STAT-10#9.title: Scale up from what you know
STAT-10#9.text: Use the pattern instead of solving an equation. The SD of the mean must go from 2 to 1, which is half. Spread shrinks with the square root of the sample size, so halving it needs a sample 2² = 4 times as large: 4 × 36 = 144 students. Check: √144 = 12 and 12 ÷ 12 = 1. Had the goal been one third of the spread, the sample would need to be 9 times larger.

STAT-10#10.title: Total minutes for 50 patients
STAT-10#10.text: A mean wait above 5 minutes for 50 patients means their waits total more than 250 minutes. The total has mean 50 × 4 = 200 minutes and SD 3 × √50 ≈ 21.2 minutes, and with 50 waits added together its shape is close to normal. A total of 250 is 50 minutes above 200, and 50 ÷ 21.2 ≈ 2.36 standard deviations. The area above z = 2.36 is 1 − 0.9909 ≈ 0.009.

STAT-11#1.title: A bike survey, piece by piece
STAT-11#1.text: A survey finds 60 bike owners among 100 adults. Estimate: 0.60. Standard error: about 0.049, the usual miss for a sample this size. For 95% confidence the critical value is 1.96, so the margin is 1.96 × 0.049 ≈ 0.096 and the interval is 0.60 ± 0.096. Want 99% instead? Keep the 0.60 and the 0.049 and swap in 2.576: the margin grows to about 0.126. Want 90%? Use 1.645 and the margin shrinks to 0.081.

STAT-11#2.title: Distance works both ways
STAT-11#2.text: If you stand within 10 steps of a lamp post, the lamp post is within 10 steps of you. Sample proportions behave the same way. Say the true p is 0.60 and the SE is 0.05. About 95% of samples give a p̂ between 0.50 and 0.70, within 0.10 of the truth. A sample with p̂ = 0.66 draws the interval 0.56 to 0.76, which contains 0.60. A rare sample with p̂ = 0.72 draws 0.62 to 0.82, which misses. The interval catches p whenever p̂ landed close.

STAT-11#3.title: Watch t* shrink as n grows
STAT-11#3.text: Compare 95% critical values. With 5 measurements, df = 4 and t* = 2.776. With 16, df = 15 and t* = 2.131. With 30, df = 29 and t* = 2.045. With 1,000, t* is 1.962, nearly the normal value 1.960. Five measurements give a shaky estimate of the spread: s could easily be half or double the true σ, so the interval is stretched by 2.776 to stay honest. With a thousand measurements, s is almost exactly σ and no extra stretch is needed.

STAT-11#4.title: One hundred classes, one hundred intervals
STAT-11#4.text: Suppose 40% of all students at a huge school walk to school, and 100 statistics classes each survey their own random sample of 50 and build a 95% interval. About 95 classes get an interval that contains 0.40, like 0.29 to 0.56. About 5 classes are unlucky and get something like 0.44 to 0.72. No class can tell which kind it has, because nobody knows the 0.40. Each can only say: the recipe we followed works for about 95 classes in 100.

STAT-11#5.title: Work in counts of people
STAT-11#5.text: Build the interval for the number of owners in a sample of 100, then convert. The count is 60, with standard error √(100 × 0.6 × 0.4) = √24 ≈ 4.9 people. The margin is 1.96 × 4.9 ≈ 9.6 people, so the count interval is 50.4 to 69.6. Dividing by 100 gives 0.504 to 0.696. Quick check: near one half, the 95% margin is roughly 1 ÷ √n = 0.10, close to 0.096.

STAT-11#6.title: Sort good sentences from bad
STAT-11#6.text:
Test each sentence against a checklist: confidence level, the parameter in context, the interval.
Good: "We are 95% confident that between 50.4% and 69.6% of all adults own a bike."
Bad: "95% of adults own between 0.504 and 0.696 bikes." Wrong meaning.
Bad: "95% of samples have p̂ in this interval." It is about p, not other samples.
Bad: "60% of the sample owns a bike, give or take." The sample value is known exactly.
Only the first one says the interval (0.504, 0.696) captures the true proportion.

STAT-11#7.title: Count supporters, then divide
STAT-11#7.text: Work in voters. The sample has 100 supporters, and the standard error of that count is √(400 × 0.25 × 0.75) = √75 ≈ 8.66 voters. For 90% confidence the margin is 1.645 × 8.66 ≈ 14.2 voters, so the count interval is about 85.8 to 114.2 supporters per 400. Divide both ends by 400: 0.214 to 0.286. This matches 0.25 ± 0.036.

STAT-11#8.title: Test candidate means
STAT-11#8.text: The interval holds every mean that sits within t* = 2.131 standard errors of 50. The SE is 8 ÷ √16 = 2 oz. Try 46 oz: it is 4 oz away, which is 2.0 SEs, so it is inside. Try 45 oz: 5 oz away is 2.5 SEs, so it is outside. The edge is exactly 2.131 SEs away, 4.26 oz, on each side. That gives 50 − 4.26 = 45.74 and 50 + 4.26 = 54.26 oz.

STAT-11#9.title: Solve two small equations
STAT-11#9.text: Write what the endpoints mean. Lower end: p̂ − ME = 0.42. Upper end: p̂ + ME = 0.50. Add the two equations and the margins cancel: 2 × p̂ = 0.92, so p̂ = 0.46. Subtract the first from the second and the estimates cancel: 2 × ME = 0.08, so ME = 0.04. On a number line, 0.46 sits halfway between the ends and each end is 0.04 away.

STAT-11#10.title: Estimate, then refine
STAT-11#10.text: Rough version first. The standard error is 1.5 ÷ 5 = 0.3 hours, and for 95% the multiplier is a little over 2, so the margin is a little over 0.6. Expect an interval near 6.6 to 7.8 hours. Now refine: with 24 degrees of freedom the multiplier is 2.064, so the margin is 2.064 × 0.3 ≈ 0.62. The interval is 7.2 − 0.62 = 6.58 to 7.2 + 0.62 = 7.82 hours, slightly wider than the rough guess, as expected.

STAT-11#11.title: Try sample sizes and watch the margin
STAT-11#11.text: With p̂ = 0.5 the margin is 1.96 × 0.5 ÷ √n = 0.98 ÷ √n. Try n = 400: 0.98 ÷ 20 = 0.049, too wide. Try n = 1,000: 0.98 ÷ 31.62 ≈ 0.0310, still just over. Try n = 1,067: 0.98 ÷ 32.665 ≈ 0.030001, over by a hair. Try n = 1,068: 0.98 ÷ 32.680 ≈ 0.02999, finally at most 0.03. So 1,068 people are needed, and the near miss at 1,067 shows why rounding up matters.

STAT-12#1.title: A friend's free-throw claim
STAT-12#1.text: A friend says she makes 80% of her free throws. You have watched her and suspect it is lower. Before she shoots, write H0: p = 0.80 (her claim, the boring version) and Ha: p < 0.80 (your suspicion). Here p is her true long-run rate. Then she makes 13 of 20, so p̂ = 0.65. Writing "H0: p̂ = 0.80" would be silly, since everyone can see p̂ is 0.65. The open question is about the rate nobody can see.

STAT-12#2.title: The same gap, two sample sizes
STAT-12#2.text: Two coins each show 60% heads, a gap of 0.10 from fair. Coin A was flipped 20 times. Its standard error under H0 is √(0.5 × 0.5 ÷ 20) ≈ 0.112, so z = 0.10 ÷ 0.112 ≈ 0.9: twelve heads in twenty is ordinary. Coin B was flipped 1,000 times. Its standard error is about 0.0158, so z ≈ 6.3: six hundred heads in a thousand almost never happens with a fair coin. The gaps are equal, but the test statistics tell very different stories.

STAT-12#3.title: A thousand fair coins
STAT-12#3.text: You flip a coin 100 times and get 60 heads. Is that strange for a fair coin? Imagine 1,000 people who each flip a coin known to be fair 100 times. Most get between 45 and 55 heads. About 23 of them get 60 or more, and about 23 get 40 or fewer. So roughly 46 in 1,000 see a result at least as lopsided as yours, in either direction. That fraction, 0.046, is the two-sided p-value.

STAT-12#4.title: Two studies, two verdicts
STAT-12#4.text: Set α = 0.05 first. Study one: a new fertilizer, p-value 0.03. Since 0.03 ≤ 0.05, reject H0: there is convincing evidence that the fertilizer raises mean yield. Study two: a new study app, p-value 0.20. Since 0.20 > 0.05, fail to reject H0: the data do not give convincing evidence that the app raises mean scores. That is not proof the app does nothing. A jury says "not guilty", never "innocent", for the same reason.

STAT-12#5.title: A spam filter's two mistakes
STAT-12#5.text: A spam filter treats each email as legitimate (H0) unless the evidence says spam. Type I error: a real message from your teacher lands in the spam folder. Type II error: a scam reaches your inbox. Power is the share of real spam it catches. Make the filter stricter about calling anything spam and fewer good emails are lost, but more scams slip through. The only way to cut both errors at once is better evidence, which in statistics means more data.

STAT-12#6.title: Count heads instead of proportions
STAT-12#6.text: Run the test on the number of heads. If the coin is fair, 100 flips give a count with mean 50 and standard deviation √(100 × 0.5 × 0.5) = 5 heads. Sixty heads is 10 above the mean, which is 10 ÷ 5 = 2 standard deviations, the same z = 2.0. A result that far out in either direction has probability 2 × 0.0228 = 0.0456. Since 0.0456 < 0.05, reject H0: the coin does not appear fair.

STAT-12#7.title: Count satisfied customers
STAT-12#7.text: If the 80% claim is true, a sample of 200 should contain about 200 × 0.8 = 160 satisfied customers, with standard deviation √(200 × 0.8 × 0.2) = √32 ≈ 5.66 customers. The sample had 150, which is 10 fewer, and 10 ÷ 5.66 ≈ 1.77 standard deviations below. The chance of landing that low or lower is 0.0384. Since 0.0384 < 0.05, reject H0: there is evidence that satisfaction is below 80%.

STAT-12#8.title: Find the cutoff in grams
STAT-12#8.text: Decide before looking how low the sample mean must be. With 15 degrees of freedom and α = 0.05, the one-sided critical value is 1.753. The standard error is 8 ÷ 4 = 2 g, so the cutoff is 500 − 1.753 × 2 = 496.5 g: any sample mean below that is too low to blame on chance. The observed mean is 495 g, below the cutoff. This agrees with the p-value 0.012 < 0.05, so reject H0. The bags appear underfilled.

STAT-12#9.title: Let a confidence interval decide
STAT-12#9.text: Build a 95% interval for the true mean and see whether 10 g is inside. The standard error is 1.5 ÷ 5 = 0.3 g and t* for 24 degrees of freedom is 2.064, so the margin is 2.064 × 0.3 ≈ 0.62 g. The interval is 10.4 ± 0.62, or 9.78 to 11.02 g. The claimed 10 g lies inside, so it is a plausible value for the mean. Verdict at the 5% level: fail to reject H0.

STAT-12#10.title: Mark the unusual head counts
STAT-12#10.text: Work from the null side in counts. A fair coin flipped 100 times gives a mean of 50 heads with standard deviation 5. The middle 95% of fair-coin results runs from 50 − 1.96 × 5 = 40.2 to 50 + 1.96 × 5 = 59.8 heads, so counts of 41 to 59 are ordinary and anything at or beyond 40 or 60 is in the rejection region. Sixty heads falls just outside the ordinary range. Verdict: reject p = 0.5.

STAT-12#11.title: Lay out the four cases
STAT-12#11.text: Make a two-by-two table: truth (no fire, fire) against detector (silent, alarm). No fire and silent: correct. Fire and alarm: correct, and the chance of this is the power. No fire but alarm: Type I, burnt toast sets it off and you open a window. Fire but silent: Type II, the house burns while you sleep. The costs are not close, so Type II is worse. Designers accept more toast alarms, a larger α, to make silent fires rarer.

STAT-13#1.title: Two shooters, one null rate
STAT-13#1.text: Player 1 makes 40 of 50 free throws and player 2 makes 30 of 50. The gap is 0.80 − 0.60 = 0.20. If they are really equally good, the best guess at their shared rate uses all 100 shots: 70 ÷ 100 = 0.70. A gap between two 50-shot samples from 0.70 shooters has standard error √(0.7 × 0.3 × (1/50 + 1/50)) ≈ 0.092. So z = 0.20 ÷ 0.092 ≈ 2.2: the gap is about 2.2 times what chance alone usually produces.

STAT-13#2.title: A right triangle of standard errors
STAT-13#2.text: Picture a right triangle. One leg is the standard error of the first sample mean and the other leg is the standard error of the second. The standard error of the difference is the hypotenuse. If the legs are 3 and 4, the difference has standard error √(9 + 16) = 5, not 3 + 4 = 7. The hypotenuse is longer than either leg, so a difference is always less certain than either mean alone, but it is shorter than the two legs laid end to end.

STAT-13#3.title: Four students, before and after
STAT-13#3.text: Four students score 50, 70, 85, 95 before tutoring and 53, 74, 88, 97 after. As two separate groups, the means are 75 and 78, a 3-point gap buried in scores that range over 45 points. Nothing looks different. As pairs, the gains are 3, 4, 3 and 2: every student improved, the mean gain is 3, and the gains vary by less than 1 point. The same data, treated correctly, give clear evidence.

STAT-13#4.title: The same gap, different surprise
STAT-13#4.text: A die is rolled 60 times, so each face expects 10. If sixes come up 20 times, the gap is 10 and the contribution is 10² ÷ 10 = 10, a large surprise: twice as many sixes as expected. Now a huge survey expects 1,000 people in a category and sees 1,010. The gap is also 10, but the contribution is 100 ÷ 1,000 = 0.1, no surprise at all. Chi-square adds these contributions over all the cells into one total.

STAT-13#5.title: Fill the table cell by cell
STAT-13#5.text: Survey 200 people: 120 women, 80 men, and 100 of the 200 prefer tea. If tea preference has nothing to do with gender, half of each group should prefer tea: 60 women, which is 120 × 100 ÷ 200. Write 60 in that cell and the rest are forced: 60 women for coffee, then 40 and 40 for the men. One free cell means df = 1. For a bag of 200 candies claimed to be 40%, 30%, 20%, 10% by color, expect 80, 60, 40, 20, with df = 3.

STAT-13#6.title: Chi-square on the two-by-two table
STAT-13#6.text: Put the counts in a table: 60 and 40 for the drug, 45 and 55 for the placebo. If the drug does nothing, each group expects 52.5 improved and 47.5 not. Every cell is off by 7.5, so chi-square = 2 × 56.25 ÷ 52.5 + 2 × 56.25 ÷ 47.5 ≈ 4.51, and its square root is z ≈ 2.12. The chi-square p-value, 0.034, covers both directions. The data point the way Ha predicted, so halve it: 0.017 < 0.05, reject H0.

STAT-13#7.title: Build an interval for the difference
STAT-13#7.text: Estimate the difference in means with a 95% interval. The difference is 78 − 72 = 6 points and the standard error is √(4 + 4) ≈ 2.83. With 24 degrees of freedom t* = 2.064, so the margin is 2.064 × 2.83 ≈ 5.84. The interval is 6 ± 5.84, from 0.16 to 11.84 points. Zero is not inside, so "no difference" is not plausible at the 5% level, matching p ≈ 0.044 < 0.05: reject H0.

STAT-13#8.title: How big a gain is needed?
STAT-13#8.text: Set the bar before comparing. With 7 degrees of freedom, a one-sided test at α = 0.05 has critical value 1.895. The standard error of the mean gain is 4 ÷ √8 ≈ 1.41 points, so the mean gain must exceed 1.895 × 1.41 ≈ 2.68 points to count as convincing. The observed mean gain is 3.0, above the bar. That agrees with the p-value 0.036 < 0.05: reject H0, tutoring appears to help.

STAT-13#9.title: Check each face against chance wobble
STAT-13#9.text: A fair die rolled 60 times shows each face 10 times on average, with a standard deviation of √(60 × 1/6 × 5/6) ≈ 2.9. The observed counts differ from 10 by −2, 2, −1, 4, −3 and 0. The largest gap, 4, is only about 1.4 standard deviations, and the rest are smaller. Nothing here is beyond ordinary chance variation. That fits the small statistic 3.4 and the p-value near 0.64: fail to reject H0.

STAT-13#10.title: The two-by-two shortcut
STAT-13#10.text: A two-by-two table has a one-line formula: chi-square = n(ad − bc)² ÷ (product of the four row and column totals), where a, b, c, d are the cells. Here ad − bc = 30 × 30 − 20 × 20 = 500. So chi-square = 100 × 500² ÷ (50 × 50 × 50 × 50) = 25,000,000 ÷ 6,250,000 = 4.0. With df = 1 the cutoff is 3.841, and 4.0 is beyond it. Reject H0: there is evidence of an association between group and preference.

STAT-13#11.title: Compare the two dog counts
STAT-13#11.text: Work with counts of dog lovers. If both groups share a rate of 0.5, each group of 50 has a count with variance 50 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 12.5. The difference of two independent counts has variance 12.5 + 12.5 = 25, so a standard deviation of 5. The observed difference is 30 − 20 = 10 people, and 10 ÷ 5 gives z = 2.0. Squaring gives 4.0, the chi-square statistic, so the two tests agree.

STAT-13#12.title: Match five situations
STAT-13#12.text:
Practice on cases.
Clicks out of 100 for ad 1 and out of 100 for ad 2: success rates in two groups, a two-proportion z-test.
Hours of sleep for 30 juniors and 30 seniors: measurements in two groups, a two-sample t-test.
Reaction time for the same 12 people before and after coffee: pairs, a t-test on the differences.
Color counts in one bag against the company's claim: chi-square goodness of fit.
Grade level by lunch choice in a table: chi-square for independence.
Then check the conditions for the test you picked.

STAT-14#1.title: Run the study again
STAT-14#1.text: Suppose the truth for a whole school is that each extra hour of study raises the mean score by 2.5 points. You sample 20 students and fit a line: slope 2.40. A friend samples a different 20 and gets 2.95. A third sample gives 1.90. None of the three hit 2.5, but they scatter around it. If such slopes typically miss by about 0.6, that typical miss is the standard error of b. You see only your own 2.40 and must reason about the 2.5 behind it.

STAT-14#2.title: Four questions, four places to look
STAT-14#2.text: Treat the output like a lookup sheet. What score is predicted for 5 hours? Use the two Coef values: 12.5 + 2.40 × 5 = 24.5. Is the slope clearly different from zero? Look at T in the Hours row: 4.00, with a small P beside it. How far off is a typical prediction? Read S, in exam points. How much of the variation in scores does the line account for? Read R-Sq. Everything else on the printout can usually be ignored.

STAT-14#3.title: Five ways data can break the rules
STAT-14#3.text: Linear fails for the height of a thrown ball against time: the plot is an arch. Independent fails if the 20 points are one student measured on 20 days. Normal fails if most residuals are small and a few are huge on one side. Equal spread fails for income against age: the points fan out as age rises. Random fails if only volunteers from an honors class were used. A straight band of even width from a random sample passes all five.

STAT-14#4.title: A small worked case
STAT-14#4.text: Ten plants give a slope of b = 1.5 cm of growth per hour of light, with a standard error of 0.5. Test: t = 1.5 ÷ 0.5 = 3.0. Degrees of freedom: 10 − 2 = 8. The 95% critical value for 8 df is 2.306, and 3.0 is beyond it, so there is evidence that light and growth are linearly related. Interval: 1.5 ± 2.306 × 0.5, or 0.35 to 2.65 cm per hour. Zero is outside, telling the same story as the test.

STAT-14#5.title: Like a court case
STAT-14#5.text: A trial follows a fixed order, and so does an inference answer. State: the charge is read, here the parameter and hypotheses. Plan: the judge rules on which evidence is admissible, here naming the procedure and checking conditions. Do: the evidence is presented, here the statistic, df and p-value. Conclude: the verdict is given in plain words about the actual defendant, here a sentence about hours and scores at the chosen α. Skip a stage in court and the verdict does not stand.

STAT-14#6.title: Make a table of predictions
STAT-14#6.text: Use the line to fill a table. At 2 hours: 12.5 + 4.8 = 17.3. At 3 hours: 19.7. At 4 hours: 22.1. Each extra hour adds 2.40 points, which is the slope. Extend the pattern down to 0 hours and the table starts at 12.5, the intercept, though no student in the data studied that little. So the line is ŷ = 12.5 + 2.40x. Students with equal hours still differ in score, and r² says hours account for about 47% of the variation.

STAT-14#7.title: How large must the slope be?
STAT-14#7.text: Find the bar the slope has to clear. With 18 degrees of freedom, a two-sided test at α = 0.05 has critical value 2.101. The standard error is 0.60, so a sample slope farther than 2.101 × 0.60 ≈ 1.26 from zero is too large to blame on chance. The observed slope is 2.40, almost twice that distance. This agrees with p ≈ 0.001 < 0.05: reject H0, there is convincing evidence of a linear relationship.

STAT-14#8.title: Test candidate slopes
STAT-14#8.text: The interval is the set of slopes within 2.101 standard errors of 2.40. Try 1.0: it is 1.40 away, which is 1.40 ÷ 0.60 ≈ 2.33 SEs, so it is outside. Try 1.2: 1.20 away is 2.0 SEs, so it is inside. Try 3.5: 1.10 away is 1.83 SEs, inside. The edges sit exactly 2.101 × 0.60 ≈ 1.26 away: 2.40 − 1.26 = 1.14 and 2.40 + 1.26 = 3.66 points per hour.

STAT-14#9.title: Measure the distance to zero
STAT-14#9.text: Count standard errors on a number line. The estimate 2.40 is 2.40 ÷ 0.60 = 4 standard errors above 0. A 95% interval with 18 degrees of freedom only reaches 2.101 standard errors to either side of the estimate. Zero is nearly twice as far away as the interval stretches, so it cannot be inside. A slope of 0 is not plausible, and the verdict is to reject H0: β = 0.

STAT-14#10.title: Ask which hours would predict 40
STAT-14#10.text: Turn the line around. A score of 40 is predicted when 12.5 + 2.40x = 40, so x = 27.5 ÷ 2.40 ≈ 11.46 hours. This student reached 40 after only 10 hours, as if 1.46 extra hours had been studied. Each hour is worth 2.40 points, so the student is 1.46 × 2.40 ≈ 3.5 points ahead of the line. The prediction at 10 hours is therefore 40 − 3.5 = 36.5, and the residual is +3.5.

STAT-14#11.title: Check with the t statistic
STAT-14#11.text: Test the slope directly and compare. The statistic is t = −0.85 ÷ 0.30 ≈ −2.83, so the slope is 2.83 standard errors below zero. A 90% interval with 10 degrees of freedom reaches only 1.812 standard errors each way, so zero must lie outside it. The ends are −0.85 − 1.812 × 0.30 ≈ −1.39 and −0.85 + 1.812 × 0.30 ≈ −0.31. The interval (−1.39, −0.31) is entirely negative, and 0 is not a plausible slope.
